parole.significato: Able to be done; fit to be done.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -able, borrowed from Old French -able, from Latin -ābilis, from -a- or -i- + -bilis (“capable or worthy of being acted upon”), from Proto-Indo-European i-stem form *-dʰli- of *-dʰlom (“instrumental suffix”). Not closely related etymologically, though currently related s

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns and verb stems.
parole.testo: From (1) -aci(ty) + -ous and (2) from Old French -acieux, both ultimately from Latin -ācitās.

parole.significato: Forming nouns with the sense of appurtenance or collection.
parole.testo: From Middle English -age, from Old French -age, from Latin -āticum. Cognates include French -age, Italian -aggio, Portuguese -agem, Spanish -aje, Occitan -atge, Romanian -aj. Doublet of -atic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to; an adjectival suffix appended to various words, often nouns, to make an adjective form. (Often add…
parole.testo: From Middle English -an, regularly -ain, -ein, -en, from Old French -ain, -ein, or before i, -en (modern French -ain, -en, feminine -aine, -enne), from Latin -ānus (feminine -āna), which forms adjectives of belonging or origin from a noun, being -nus [cognate with Ancient Greek -νος (-nos)] preceded

parole.significato: Added to an adjective or verb to form a noun indicating a state or condition, such as result or capacity, associated wi…
parole.testo: From Middle English -aunce, -ance, from Anglo-Norman -aunce and continental Old French -ance, from Latin -ant-, -ent- + -ia, from stem of Latin -āns, -ēns.

parole.significato: An action or process.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -acioun, borrowed from Old French -ation, a learned borrowing from Latin -ātiō, from -tiō, from Proto-Italic *-tiō, from Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō, from *-tis + *-Hō. By surface analysis, -ate + -ion.

parole.significato: Suffix, originally diminutive, in words of mostly Romance origin.
parole.testo: From Middle English -el, a merger of two suffixes: * Old English -el (diminutive suffix) * Old French -el (diminutive suffix), from Latin -ellus

parole.significato: Same as -ance; having the state or condition of.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ence, from Old French -ence, from Latin -entia. Compare Old English -ende, -endu (“-ing, -ence”).

parole.significato: Causing, doing, or promoting a certain action.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ent, also -ant, -aunt, etc., from Old French -ent and its source Latin -ēns (accusative singular -entem), suffix of present participles of verbs in the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th conjugations.

parole.significato: Used to form female equivalents.
parole.testo: From Middle English -esse, borrowed from Old French -esse, from Late Latin -issa, from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa). Displaced Old English -en (feminine suffix of nouns).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns from adjectives.
parole.testo: From Old French -esse, from Latin -itia.

parole.significato: Used to form diminutives, loosely construed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -et, from Old French -et, from Late Latin -ittus, -ettus.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns meaning a smaller form of something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -ette, borrowed from Old French -ette, from Latin -ittus.

parole.significato: Forms a noun from a verb ending in -y.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -ial, derived from Old French -ial, derived from Latin -ālis after radical in -ius, -ia, -ium. Equivalent to -i- + -al.

parole.significato: An adjective suffix, now usually in a passive sense; forms adjectives meaning "able to be", "relevant or suitable to, i…
parole.testo: From Middle English -ible, from Old French -ible, from Latin -ibilis.

parole.significato: An instrumental suffix; forms nouns representing:
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin -i- + -bulum (instrumental suffix) or -bula (instrumental suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom. Related to Latin suffixes -brum (candelabrum) and -bra (vertebra).

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns with the meaning “of or pertaining to”.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ik, from Old French -ique, from Latin -icus, from Proto-Indo-European *-kos, *-ḱos, formed with the i-stem suffix *-i- and the adjectival suffix *-kos, *-ḱos. Compare Ancient Greek -ικός (-ikós), Sanskrit -इक (-ika) and Old Church Slavonic -ъкъ (-ŭkŭ). Doublet of -y; compare als

parole.significato: Forms nouns denoting the act or process whereby a subject becomes something else.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ificacioun (ending on words generally borrowed whole from Old French), from Old French -ification, in turn from Latin -ficātiō, a noun ending which appears on action nouns formed using the suffix -tiō (English -tion) from verbs ending in -ficō (English -ify). Compare -faction.

parole.significato: Forms transitive verbs meaning "to make" from adjectives and nouns.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ifien, from Old French -ifier, from Latin -ificāre, from -ficus, from faciō (“to make, do”). For example, purify from purificare, from purificus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to.
parole.testo: From Middle English -in, -ine, from Old French -in, -ine, from Latin -īnus, from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos. More at -en § Etymology 4.

parole.significato: Suffix used in loanwords from French to form abstract nouns of quality or function.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ise, from Old French -ise, borrowed from Latin -itia.

parole.significato: An ending found on some verbs; see usage notes.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ishen, -ischen, -issen, from Old French -iss-, -is- (a termination of the stem of some forms [present participle, etc.] of certain verbs), from Latin -ēscere, -īscere (an inchoative suffix), the formative -esc-, -isc- (-sc-, Greek -σκ- (-sk-)) being ultimately cognate with Engli

parole.significato: Added to words to form nouns denoting:
parole.testo: From Middle English -ist, -iste, from Old French -iste and Latin -ista, from Ancient Greek -ιστής (-istḗs), from -ίζω (-ízō, “-ize, -ise”, verbal suffix) + -τής (-tḗs, agent-noun suffix). Equivalent to -ism + -t. Doublet of -ista. The speaker of a language sense is influenced by Esperanto -isto.

parole.significato: Used to form an uncountable noun from an adjective; especially, to form the noun referring to the state, property, or q…
parole.testo: From Middle English -ite, -itee, from Old French -ite, -ete, -eteit (“-ity”), from Latin -itātem, from -itās, from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts (suffix). Cognate with Gothic -𐌹𐌸𐌰 (-iþa, “-th”), Old High German -ida (“-th”), Old English -þo, -þu, -þ (“-th”). More at -th. By surface analysis, -i- (“co

parole.significato: An adjective suffix signifying relating or belonging to, of the nature of, tending to, or serving to; as: affirmative,…
parole.testo: From Middle English -yf, from Anglo-Norman -if from Latin -īvus. Until the fourteenth century, all Middle English loanwords from Anglo-Norman ended in -if (compare actif, natif, sensitif, pensif etc.). Under the influence of literary Neo-Latin, both languages introduced the form -ive. Those forms th

parole.significato: Attached to a verb to form a noun meaning the action denoted by the verb or its result.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ment, from Old French -ment, from Latin -mentum.

parole.significato: Forming nouns relating to measures and measurement.
parole.testo: From Old French -métrie, from Latin -metria, from Ancient Greek -μετρία (-metría), from μέτρον (métron, “measurement”) + -ίᾱ (-íā, “-y: forming abstract nouns”). Equivalent to -meter + -y.

parole.significato: Forming nouns, usually abstract, and usually from adjectives in -ous or -ose.
parole.testo: From Middle English -ouste, from Old French -ouseté, from Latin -ōsitās; later modified to the current form. It is equivalent to -ose or -ous + -ity.

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns, to denote:
parole.testo: From Middle English -ous, from Old French -ous, -os, -us, from Latin -ōsus (“full of”). Doublet of -ose and -wise in unstressed position. Many English adjectives ending in -ous were taken from preexisting French or Latin adjectives that end in one of the above suffixes (e.g. envious corresponds dire

parole.significato: Used to form nouns meaning "the action of (a verb)" or "the result of (a verb)". Words ending in this suffix are almost…
parole.testo: From rebracketed Middle English -cioun, rebracketed borrowing of Old French -tion, -cion, borrowed from the stem of Latin -tiō. The Middle English -cioun became -tion in Modern English under the influence of the Middle French -tion and original Latin spellings. Always -ate or t-final/te-final base +

parole.significato: To make something change its shape.
parole.testo: From Old French tort, from Latin tortum, substantive use of the past participle of torqueō (“twist, turn”). Compare with torsion, torture.

parole.significato: A process; a condition; a result of an action.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English -ure, borrowed from Old French -ure, from Latin -(ā)tūram.

parole.significato: Forming abstract nouns denoting a condition, quality, or state.
parole.testo: From Middle English -y, -ie, -ee, -e, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French -ie and -é, from Latin -ia, -ium, -tās, Ancient Greek -ίᾱ (-íā), -ειᾰ (-eiă), -ιον (-ion). Cognate (as far as Latin -ia is involved) with German -ei and Dutch -ij.

parole.significato: The first letter of the English alphabet, written in the Latin script.
parole.testo: The letter name is from Middle English ā, from Old French, ultimately from Latin ā. Use of the Latin letter in (Old) English displaced the futhorc letter ᚪ (a) beginning in the 7th century, and partially also ᚫ (æ).

parole.significato: A female superior or governess of a nunnery, or convent of nuns, having the same authority over the nuns which the abbo…
parole.testo: From Middle English abbesse, from Old French abeesse (French abbesse), from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbatissa, feminine of Latin abbas, abbatis (“abbot”).

parole.significato: The office or dominion of an abbot or abbess.
parole.testo: From A.D. 1250 in Middle English abbey, abbeye (“convent headed by an abbot”) (compare archaic English abbaye), itself borrowed from Old French abaïe, abbaïe, abeïe, abbeïe (Modern French abbaye) from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbātia, from Classical Latin abbās (“abbot”). Doublet of abbacy

parole.significato: The white poplar (Populus alba).
parole.testo: From Middle English abelle, albell, aubel, from Old French aubel, aubiel, from Medieval Latin albellus (“white poplar”), diminutive of Latin albus (“white”). Some forms after Middle Dutch abeel, from Old French.

parole.significato: Suitableness.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1300s. From Middle English abilite (“suitability, aptitude, ability”), from Old French ableté, from Latin habilitās (“aptness, ability”), from habilis (“apt, fit, skillful, able”); equivalent to able + -ity.

parole.significato: Applied to one of the cases of the noun in some languages, the fundamental meaning of the case being removal, separatio…
parole.testo: From Middle English ablative, ablatife, ablatyf, ablatif, from Old French ablatif (“the ablative case”), from Latin ablātīvus (“expressing removal”), from ablātus (“taken away”), from auferō (“to take away”). The engineering/nautical sense originates from ablate + -ive.

parole.significato: Having the necessary powers or the needed resources to accomplish a task.
parole.testo: From Middle English able, from Old Northern French able, variant of Old French abile, habile, from Latin habilis (“easily managed, held, or handled; apt; skillful”). Doublet of habile.

parole.significato: The act of washing something.
parole.testo: From Middle English ablucioun (“cleansing of impurities”), from Old French ablution, and its source, Late Latin ablūtiō (“a washing away”), from abluō (“wash away”), from ab- (“away”) + lavō (“wash”).

parole.significato: Worthy of, or causing, abhorrence, as a thing of evil omen; odious in the utmost degree; very hateful; detestable; loat…
parole.testo: From Middle English abhomynable, from Old French abominable, from Late Latin abōminābilis (“deserving abhorrence”), from abōminor (“abhor, deprecate as an ill omen”), from ab (“from, away from”) + ōminor (“forebode, predict, presage”), from ōmen (“sign, token, omen”). Formerly erroneously folk-etymo

parole.significato: Produced by abortion; born prematurely and therefore unnatural.
parole.testo: First attested in 1382, with the meaning "causing stillbirth or miscarriage". From Middle English abortif, from Old French abortif, from Latin abortīvus (“causing abortion”), from aborior (“miscarry, disappear”), from ab (“amiss”) + orior (“appear, be born, arise”).

parole.significato: To be full to overflowing; to bristle.
parole.testo: * First attested around 1325. * From Middle English abounden, abounde, from Old French abonder, abunder, from Latin abundāre (“overflow”), which comes from ab (“from, down from”) + undō (“surge, swell, rise in waves, move in waves”), from unda (“wave”).

parole.significato: To deprive; to cut off.
parole.testo: From Middle English abreggen, abregge, abrigge (“curtail, lessen”), from Old French abregier, abreger, from Late Latin abbreviō, abbreviāre (“make brief”). Doublet of abbreviate.

parole.significato: A state of being away or withdrawn from a place or from companionship
parole.testo: From Middle English absence, from Old French absence, ausence, from Latin absentia, from absēns (“absent”), present active participle of absum (“to be away or absent”), from ab (“from, away from”) + sum (“to be”).

parole.significato: To keep (oneself) away.
parole.testo: From Middle English absenten, from Old French absenter, from Late Latin absentāre (“keep away, be away”).

parole.significato: An absolving of sins from ecclesiastical penalties by an authority.
parole.testo: From Middle English absolucion, absolucioun, from Old French absolution, from Latin absolūtiōnem, accusative singular of absolūtiō (“acquittal”), from absolvō (“absolve”). See also absolve.

parole.significato: Keep or withhold oneself.
parole.testo: First attested around 1380. From Middle English absteynen, absteinen, abstenen, from Old French astenir, abstenir, from Latin abstineō (“to hold oneself back”) from abs- (“from”) + teneō (“to hold”). See also tenable.

parole.significato: The act or practice of abstaining, refraining from indulging a desire or appetite.
parole.testo: From Middle English abstinence, from Old French abstinence, from Latin abstinentia, from abstinēns, present participle of abstineō (“to withhold”). Equivalent to abstain + -ence.

parole.significato: Refraining from indulgence, especially from the indulgence of appetite.
parole.testo: First attested in the late 14th century as Middle English abstinent, abstynent, from Old French abstinent, from Latin abstinēns, present participle of abstineō. See abstain.

parole.significato: A large quantity; many.
parole.testo: From Middle English abundaunce, habaundance, from Old French habundance, abondance, from Latin abundantia (“fullness, plenty”), from abundō (“to overflow”). Equivalent to abound + -ance. Displaced Old English geniht (“abundance, plenty”).

parole.significato: Misuse, abuse; in particular, illegal behaviour; verbal, physical or sexual abuse.
parole.testo: From Middle English abusioun, from Old French abusion, from Latin abūsiō (“abuse, misuse”), from abūtor (“misuse”). Doublet of abusio.

parole.significato: Hell; the infernal pit; the great deep; the primal chaos.
parole.testo: From Middle English abime, from Old French abisme from Late Latin *abyssimus, a superlative of abyssus (“bottomless pit”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos). Cognate to French abîme. See also abyss.

parole.significato: To or with.
parole.testo: Assimilated form of ad- before c, k, q. Around 1500 the c was added to some versions of the a- prefix. From Middle English a-, from Old French a-, from Latin ad- (“to, toward”).

parole.significato: To receive, especially with a consent, with favour, or with approval.
parole.testo: First attested about 1380. From Middle English accepten, borrowed from Old French accepter, or directly from Latin acceptō, acceptāre (“receive”), frequentative of accipiō, formed from ad- + capiō (“to take”). Displaced native Old English onfōn.

parole.significato: An unexpected event with negative consequences occurring without the intention of the one suffering the consequences, a…
parole.testo: First attested in the late 14th century. From Middle English accident, from Old French accident, from Latin accidēns, present active participle of accidō (“happen”); from ad (“to”) + cadō (“fall”). See cadence, case. In the sense “unintended pregnancy”, first attested in 1932.

parole.significato: To drive a nail into a horseshoe; to lame.
parole.testo: From Middle English acloyen, from Old French encloyer, encloer (“to drive in a nail”), from Medieval Latin inclavare, from Latin in- + clavus (“nail”).

parole.significato: To embrace; cling to.
parole.testo: From Middle English acolen, from Old French acoler (whence modern French accoler), from Latin ad- + collum (“neck”).

parole.significato: An associate in the commission of a crime; a participator in an offense, whether a principal or an accessory.
parole.testo: First attested in 1550. From a complice, from Middle English complice, from Old French complice (“confederate”), from Latin complicāre (“fold together”). The article a became part of the word, through the influence of the word accomplish.

parole.significato: To finish successfully.
parole.testo: From Middle English accomplisshen, acomplissen, from Old French acompliss-, extended stem of acomplir (Modern French accomplir), from Vulgar Latin *(ac)complīre, from Latin complēre (“fill up/out, complete”, whence English complete). First attested in the late 14th century.

parole.significato: To make to agree or correspond; to suit one thing to another; to adjust.
parole.testo: From Middle English accorden, acorden, borrowed from Old French acorder (compare modern French accord and accorder), from Vulgar Latin *accordāre, from Latin concordāre via prefix substitution (with Latin ad-), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr ~ *ḱr̥d-, and thus distantly related to English

parole.significato: To increase, to rise
parole.testo: First attested in mid 15th century. From Middle English acrewen, borrowed from Old French acreüe, past participle of accreistre (“to increase”), from Latin accrēsco (“increase”), from ad (“in addition”) + crēscō (“to grow”). Compare accrete.

parole.significato: The act of accusing.
parole.testo: First attested in the late 14th century. Inherited from Middle English accusacion, borrowed from Old French acusacion (French: accusation), from Latin accūsātiō (“accusation, indictment”), from accūsō (“blame, accuse”). Doublet of accusatio. More at accuse. Equivalent to accuse + -ation.

parole.significato: To find fault with, blame, censure.
parole.testo: First attested around 1300. From Middle English acusen, from Old French acuser, from Latin accūsō (“to call to account, accuse”), from ad (“to”) + causa (“cause, lawsuit, reason”). Akin to cause. Displaced native English bewray and Old English sċyldan.

parole.significato: One who accuses; one who brings a charge of crime or fault.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English acuser, accusour, borrowed from Old French accusour, from Latin accūsātor, from accūsāre. Equivalent to accuse + -er. Doublet of accusator.

parole.significato: A playing card showing a single pip, typically the highest or lowest ranking card in a game.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English as, from Old French as, from Latin as, assis (“unity, copper coin, the unit of coinage”), probably borrowed from Etruscan. Doublet of as.

parole.significato: Any of several species of plants, such as smallage, wild celery, parsley.
parole.testo: From Middle English ache, from Old French ache, from Latin apium (“parsley”).

parole.significato: Parsley.
parole.testo: From Middle English ache, from Old French ache, from Latin apium (“celery”). Reinforced by modern French ache.

parole.significato: One who has received the highest of the four minor orders in the Catholic Church, being ordained to carry the wine, wat…
parole.testo: From Middle English acolite, acolit, from Old French acolyt and Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”).

parole.significato: To furnish or give experimental knowledge of; to make (one) know; to make familiar.
parole.testo: From Middle English aqueynten, acointen, from Old French acointier, from Early Medieval Latin accognitāre, from Late Latin accognitus, past participle of accognoscō, from Latin cognoscō, from nōscō. See also quaint, know.

parole.significato: Acquisition; the thing gained.
parole.testo: From Middle English aqueste (later conflating with enqueste), from Old French aquest, (French acquêt), from Vulgar Latin *acquaesitum, ultimately from Latin quaerere (“seek”). Doublet of acquis.

parole.significato: To get.
parole.testo: From Middle English acqueren, from Old French aquerre, from Latin acquirō; ad- + quaerō (“to seek for”). See quest.

parole.significato: The act or process of acquiring.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French acquisicion, from Latin acquisītiō, from acquīrō, acquīrere; equivalent to acquire + -ition.

parole.significato: To do something.
parole.testo: From Middle English acte, from Old French acte, from Latin ācta (“register of events”), plural of āctum (“decree, law”), from agere (“to do, to act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti. Compare German Akte (“file”). Partially displaced deed, from Old English dǣd (“act, deed”).

parole.significato: The effort of performing or doing something.
parole.testo: From Middle English accioun, accion, from Old French aucion, acciun, from Latin āctiō(n) (“act of doing or making”), from āct(us) + action suffix -iō(n), perfect passive participle of agere (“do, act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti. See also act, active. By surface analysis, act + -i

parole.significato: The act of adding anything.
parole.testo: Sense of “what is added” dates from 14th century, from Middle English addicioun, addition, from Old French adition, from Latin additiōnem, accusative singular of additiō, from addō (“add, put”).

parole.significato: Adhesive, sticking to something.
parole.testo: From Middle English adherent, from Old French adherent, from Latin adhaerēns, present participle of adhaereō (“to stick to, cling”).

parole.significato: Said to wish a final farewell; goodbye.
parole.testo: From Middle English adieu also adew, adewe, adue, from Old French adieu (“to God”), a shortening of a Dieu vous comant (“I commend you to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Doublet of adios.

parole.significato: A word that modifies a noun or noun phrase or describes a noun’s referent.
parole.testo: From Middle English adjectif, adjective, from Old French adjectif, from Latin adiectivus, from adiciō + -īvus, from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + iaciō (“throw”). The Latin word adiectivus in turn was a calque of Ancient Greek ἐπιθετικόν (epithetikón, “added”), a derivative of the compound verb ἐπιτίθημ

parole.significato: Being in contact at some point or line; joining to.
parole.testo: From Middle English ajoinen, from Old French ajoindre, (compare French adjoindre), from Latin adiungō (“join to”), formed from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + iungō (“join”).

parole.significato: To declare to be.
parole.testo: From Middle English ajugen, adjugen, from Old French ajugier, from Latin adiudicare. Doublet of adjudicate.

parole.significato: To apportion out, distribute.
parole.testo: From Middle English administren, from Old French aminister, from Latin administrare (“to manage, execute”), from ad (“to”) + ministrare (“to attend, serve”), from minister (“servant”); see minister.

parole.significato: The act of administering; government of public affairs; the service rendered, or duties assumed, in conducting affairs;…
parole.testo: From Middle English administracioun, from Old French administration, from Latin administratio, from administrare; see administer; compare French administration. Equivalent to administrate + -ion.

parole.significato: The commander of a naval squadron or fleet, regardless of formal rank.
parole.testo: From Middle English admiral etc., from Anglo-Norman and Old French admiral etc., from Medieval Latin admiralis, admirallus, and admiralius, from irregular modification of amiralis etc. under the influence of the prefix ad- and particularly admiror (“to admire, respect”), from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “

parole.significato: To allow to enter; to grant entrance (to), whether into a place, into the mind, or into consideration.
parole.testo: From Middle English admitten, amitten, borrowed from Old French admettre, amettre (“to admit”), from Latin admittō (“to allow entrance, inlet”, literally “to send to”), from ad- + mittere (“to send”).

parole.significato: To inform or notify of a fault; to rebuke in a serious tone; to tell off.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English a(d)monisshen (adapted through -ishen (“-ish”) from earlier amonesten), from Old French amonester (modern French admonester), from an unattested Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *admonestāre, from Latin admoneō (“to remind, warn”), from ad- + moneō (“to warn, advise”).

parole.significato: A rebuke by an authority that one has erred and should not persist in one's actions.
parole.testo: From Middle English amonicioun, from Old French amonicion, from Latin admonitio, stem of admonere. The -d- was restored in English in the 17th century.

parole.significato: The transitional period of physical and psychological development between childhood and maturity, beginning at the onse…
parole.testo: From Middle English adolescence, from Old French adolescence, from Latin adolēscentia, from adolēscēns (“young”); see adolescent.

parole.significato: To worship.
parole.testo: From Middle English *adoren, aouren, from Old French adorer, aorer, from Latin adōrō (“to pray to”), from ad (“to”) + ōrō (“to speak”).

parole.significato: Sexual intercourse by a married person with someone other than their spouse. See more synonyms at Thesaurus:cuckoldry
parole.testo: With change of suffix, from the Old French adultere (“violation of conjugal faith”) (in Bernard of Clairvaux, Sermons, 12c.), a learnèd borrowing from Latin adulterium, from adulterō. Replaced the older form avoutrie, from the inherited Old French forms avouterie or aoulterie, while keeping its suff

parole.significato: To promote or advantage.
parole.testo: From Middle English avauncen, avancen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman avauncier, from Vulgar Latin *abanteāre, from Late Latin ab ante, from Latin ab + ante (“before”). ⟨d⟩ added in analogy to Latin ad- (cf. Middle French advancer). Compare avaunt.

parole.significato: A feeling of desire for new and exciting things.
parole.testo: From Middle English aventure, aunter, anter, from Old French aventure, from Vulgar Latin *adventūra, from Latin adventūrus (“about to arrive, (Vulgar Latin) about to happen”), future active participle of adveniō (“to arrive”), which in the Romance languages took the sense of "to happen, befall" (see

parole.significato: Unfavorable; antagonistic in purpose or effect; hostile; actively opposing one's interests or wishes; contrary to one's…
parole.testo: First attested around 1374, from Old French avers (French adverse), from Latin adversus (“turned against”), past participle of advertere, from ad- (“to”) + vertere (“to turn”). See also versus.

parole.significato: The state of adverse conditions; state of misfortune or calamity.
parole.testo: From Old French adversité, from Latin adversitātem, the accusative singular of adversitās, from adversus, the perfect passive participle of advertō (“to turn toward”).

parole.significato: To take notice, to pay attention (to).
parole.testo: From Middle English adverten, from Old French advertir (“to notice”), from Latin advertere (“to turn toward”). See also adverse.

parole.significato: Someone whose job is to speak for someone's case in a court of law; a counsel.
parole.testo: From Middle English advocat, advoket, from Old French advocat, from Latin advocātus (“an advocate”), from the substantivization of the perfect passive participle of advocāre (“to call for”) (see -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from a calque of Ancient Greek παράκλητος (paráklētos) (whence English parac

parole.significato: An adulterer.
parole.testo: From Middle English advouterer, advoutrer, advowtrer, from Old French avoutrier, from Latin adulterō or adulter, noun use of an adjective.

parole.significato: adultery
parole.testo: From Middle English avoutrie, from Old French avouterie, variant (perhaps influenced by vout, vut (“vow”)) of aouterie, aolterie, from Late Latin adulterium. Doublet of adultery, which replaced it in modern English.

parole.significato: The act of affecting or acting upon.
parole.testo: From Middle English affection, affeccion, affeccioun, from Old French affection, from Latin affectiōnem, from affectiō; equivalent to affect + -ion.

parole.significato: To assess or reduce an arbitrary penalty or amercement to a precise sum; to fix the market value of.
parole.testo: From Middle English afferen, aferen, from Old French aferer, afuerer, afeurer, aforer, from Medieval Latin afforāre.

parole.significato: To agree, verify or concur; to answer positively.
parole.testo: From Middle English affermen, from Old French afermer, affermer, from Latin affirmare, adfirmare (“to present as fixed, aver, affirm”), from ad (“to”) + firmare (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”). By surface analysis, af- + firm.

parole.significato: That which is affirmed; a declaration that something is true.
parole.testo: From Old French afermacion, from Latin affirmare (“to assert”). Doublet of affirmatio.

parole.significato: pertaining to truth; asserting that something is; affirming
parole.testo: From Middle English affirmative, affirmatyve, from Old French affirmatif, from Latin affirmativus, from affirmare (“to assert”).

parole.significato: A state of pain, suffering, distress or agony.
parole.testo: From Middle English affliction, affliccioun, from Old French afliction, borrowed from Latin afflīctiōnem (“pain, suffering, torment”), from Latin afflīctō (“to damage, harass, torment”), from ad- + flīctus, past participle of afflīgō (“strike, beat”), from ad- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence af-). By sur

parole.significato: An abundant flow or supply.
parole.testo: From Old French affluence, from Latin affluentia. Only relation to antonym indigence is common Latinate suffix; affluence only acquired sense of wealth in 16th century English and French, while indigentia meant “poverty” or “lack” in Latin.

parole.significato: To reinforce (a team etc.) with extra people
parole.testo: From Old French afforcer, aforcer, from Latin exfortiāre, from fortis (“strong”). By surface analysis af- + force.

parole.significato: To insult intentionally, especially openly.
parole.testo: From Middle English afrounten, from Old French afronter (“to hit in the face; to defy”), from Vulgar Latin *affrontare (“to hit in the face”), from Latin ad (“to”) + frōns (“forehead”) (English front). By surface analysis, af- + front.

parole.significato: The amount of time that some being has been alive, or that some thing has been in existence, as measured from its birth…
parole.testo: From Middle English age, Old French aage, eage, edage, from an assumed Vulgar Latin *aetāticum, derived from Latin aetātem, itself derived from aevum (“lifetime”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital force”). Compare French âge. Displaced native Old English ieldu. The verb is from Mi

parole.significato: To make heavy; to aggravate, make graver.
parole.testo: From Old French agreger, from Vulgar Latin *aggraviō, variant of Classical Latin aggravō. Doublet of aggravate and aggrieve.

parole.significato: To cause someone to feel pain or sorrow to; to afflict
parole.testo: From Middle English agreven, from Old French agrever; a (Latin ad) + grever (“to burden, injure”), from Latin gravare (“to weigh down”), from gravis (“heavy”). See grieve, and compare with aggravate.

parole.significato: Extreme pain or anguish.
parole.testo: 14th century, via Old French and Latin from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía, “emulation, competition, struggle”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”). Specifically of the struggle that precedes death (mortal agony) from the 1540s. By surface analysis, agon + -y. The sense of "extreme pain" from c. 1600.

parole.significato: To be in harmony about an opinion, statement, or action; to have a consistent idea between two or more people.
parole.testo: From Middle English agreen, from Old French agreer (“to accept or receive kindly”), from a gré (“favorably”), from Latin ad (“to”) + gratum (“pleasing”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to welcome, greet, praise”).

parole.significato: To provide support to; to further the progress of; to help; to assist.
parole.testo: From Middle English aiden, from Old French eider, aider, aidier, from Latin adiuto, frequentative of adiuvō (“assist”, verb).

parole.significato: The pointing of a weapon, as a gun, a dart, or an arrow, or object, in the line of direction with the object intended t…
parole.testo: The verb is from Middle English amen, aimen, eimen (“to guess at, to estimate, to aim”), borrowed from Old French esmer, aesmer, asmer, from Latin ad- plus aestimare (“to estimate”), the compound perhaps being originally formed in Medieval Latin (adaestimare), perhaps in Old French. The noun is from

parole.significato: The substance constituting Earth's atmosphere: a gaseous mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, and various trace gases.
parole.testo: From Middle English aire, from Old French air, from Latin āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr). Displaced native Old English lyft. More at lift, loft.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter H/h.
parole.testo: From Middle English ache, borrowed from Old French ache, from Vulgar Latin *acca. The source is unclear, but may descend from the vowelless alphabetic sequence ha ka 'H, K' (becoming [aka] when the [h] ceased to be pronounced), as K had low frequency in Late Latin. Doublet of ecchi.

parole.significato: A fine-grained white or lightly-tinted variety of gypsum, used ornamentally.
parole.testo: From Middle English alabastre, from Old French alabastre, from Latin alabaster (“box for perfumes or unguents”), from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρος (alábastros), from earlier ἀλάβαστος (alábastos, “vase without handles for storing perfumes”). This may further derive from Egyptian ꜥj-r-bꜣstjt (“vessel of

parole.significato: Used to express sorrow, regret, compassion, grief, resignation, or disappointment.
parole.testo: From Middle English alas, from Old French a las (French hélas), from a (“ah”) + las, from Latin lassus (“weary”). Compare Dutch helaas, North Frisian ielas, West Frisian eilaas.

parole.significato: A long, white robe worn by priests and other ministers, underneath most of the other vestments.
parole.testo: From Middle English aube, awbe, albe, abbe, from Late Old English albe (but later reinforced by Old French aube, Medieval Latin alba), borrowed from Latin alba (as in tunica alba (“white tunic”), vestis alba (“white garment”)), feminine of albus (“white”). Doublet of alba.

parole.significato: whitethorn; hawthorn
parole.testo: From Old French albespine, aubespine (modern French aubépine), from Latin alba spina (“white thorn”).

parole.significato: One who practices alchemy.
parole.testo: From Old French alquemiste (French alchimiste), from Medieval Latin alchemista. Equivalent to alchemy + -ist.

parole.significato: The premodern and early modern study of physical changes, particularly in Europe, Arabia, and China; and chiefly in pur…
parole.testo: From Old French alkimie, arquemie (French alchimie), from Medieval Latin alchēmia, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “ingot, bar”). Compare Spanish alquimia and Italian alchimia.

parole.significato: A person, animal, plant, or other thing which is from outside the family, group, organization, or territory under consi…
parole.testo: From Middle English alien, a borrowing from Old French alien, aliene, from Latin aliēnus (“belonging to someone else”, later “exotic, foreign”), from Latin alius (“other”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos. Related to English else.

parole.significato: The act of alienating.
parole.testo: From Middle English alienacioun, from Old French alienacion, from Latin aliēnātiōn(em).

parole.significato: To lighten, diminish.
parole.testo: From Middle English alleggen, from Old French alegier, from Latin alleviāre (“lighten”), from ad + levis (“light”). Doublet of alleviate.

parole.significato: Allegation.
parole.testo: From Middle English allegement, alleggement, from Old French alegement, alegemant, from the verb alegier, from Latin allego (“send for, to bring forth, name, produce in evidence”), from ad (“to”) + lego (“to depute, send”).

parole.significato: An illuminator of manuscripts and books; a limner.
parole.testo: From Old French alumineor, from Latin ad + liminare. See luminate.

parole.significato: A book or table listing nautical, astronomical, astrological or other events for the year; sometimes, but not essential…
parole.testo: From Middle English almenak, from Old French almanach, from Medieval Latin almanachus, from Andalusian Arabic الْمَنَاخ (al-manāḵ, “almanac, calendar”), from Arabic الْمُنَاخ (al-munāḵ, “climate”).

parole.significato: The seed within the drupe of a small deciduous tree in family Rosaceae, Prunus amygdalus, considered a culinary nut.
parole.testo: From Middle English almond, almaund, from Old French almande, amande, from Vulgar Latin *amendla, *amandula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē), of uncertain origin. Influenced by amandus and by many European words of Arabic origin beginning with the Arabic definite article

parole.significato: A person who distributes alms, especially the doles and alms of religious houses, almshouses.
parole.testo: From Middle English aumener, aulmener, from Old French almosnier, from almosne (“alms”), from Latin eleemosyna. See alms, Almosen.

parole.significato: A table or similar flat-topped structure used for religious rites.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English auter, inherited from Old English altar and borrowed from Old French auter, both derived from Latin altāre, probably related to adolere (“burn”); thus "burning place", influenced by altus (“high”). Displaced native Middle English wēved.

parole.significato: To change the form or structure of.
parole.testo: From Old French alterer (French altérer), from Medieval Latin alterāre (“to make other”), from Latin alter (“the other”), from al- (seen in alius (“other”), alienus (“of another”), etc.; see alias, alien, etc.) + compar. suffix -ter.

parole.significato: The act of altering or making different.
parole.testo: From Old French alteracion (French altération), from Medieval Latin alterātiō. Morphologically alter + -ation.

parole.significato: Bitterness, sorrow.
parole.testo: From Middle English amarytude, from Old French amaritude, from Latin amāritūdō, from Latin amārus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: Indirect or roundabout ways of talking; circumlocution.
parole.testo: From Middle English ambages, from Old French ambages (modern French ambages), from Latin ambāges, from ambi- + agere (“to drive”).

parole.significato: The state of being ambiguous; the state of leaving room for more than one interpretation.
parole.testo: From Middle English ambiguite, from Old French ambiguite (French ambiguïté), from Latin ambiguitas, equivalent to ambiguous + -ity.

parole.significato: Eager or inordinate desire for some object that confers distinction, as preferment, honor, superiority, political power…
parole.testo: From Middle English ambicioun, from Old French ambition, from Latin ambitiō (“ambition, a striving for favor, literally 'a going around', especially of candidates for office in Rome soliciting votes”), from ambiō (“to go around, solicit votes”). See ambient, issue. By surface analysis, ambit + -ion.

parole.significato: Two ones; the lowest throw at dice; a pair of aces.
parole.testo: From Old French ambes as (“both aces”), from Latin ambo + as.

parole.significato: The act of concealing oneself and lying in wait to attack or kill by surprise.
parole.testo: From Middle English enbuschen, from Old French enbuscier, anbuchier (verb) (whence Middle French embusche (noun)), from Old French en- + Vulgar Latin boscus (“wood”) (whence also bouquet), from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, heavy stick”). Compare ambuscade. The change

parole.significato: To make better; improve.
parole.testo: From Middle English amenden, from Old French amender, from Latin ēmendō (“free from faults”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mendum (“fault”). Compare aphetic mend. Doublet of emend.

parole.significato: Friendly; kind; sweet; gracious.
parole.testo: From Middle English amyable, from Old French amiable, from Late Latin amīcābilis (“friendly”), from Latin amīcus (“friend”), from amō (“love”, verb). The meaning has been influenced by French amiable and Latin amābilis (“loveable”) (whence English aimable and amable). Doublet of amicable. Compare wi

parole.significato: A hood, or cape with a hood, made of or lined with grey fur, formerly worn by the clergy.
parole.testo: From Middle English amit, from Old French emit, from Latin amictus, from amiciō (see there for more). Compare French amict, Italian amitto, Portuguese amicto.

parole.significato: Friendship; friendliness.
parole.testo: From Middle English amite, from Old French amisté, amitie, amistiet, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”), from amō (“love”).

parole.significato: Inclined or having a propensity to love, or to sexual enjoyment.
parole.testo: From Middle English amorous, amerous (14th century), from Old French amoros, amoreus, from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, from Latin amor (“love”), related to amāre (“to love”). Compare French amoureux (“in love”). Doublet of amoroso and amoureux.

parole.significato: To alienate (property) in mortmain.
parole.testo: From Middle English amortisen, from Old French amortir (via the stem amortiss-), from Vulgar Latin *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”).

parole.significato: An ambiguous grammatical construction.
parole.testo: From Old French amphibolie, from Latin amphibolia, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιβολία (amphibolía, “ambiguity”).

parole.significato: To render larger, more extended, or more intense.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English amplifiyen, borrowed from Old French amplifier, borrowed from Latin amplificāre, from amplus (“abundant, ample”) + -ficō. By surface analysis, ample + -ify.

parole.significato: The science that deals with the form and structure of organic bodies; anatomical structure or organization.
parole.testo: From Middle English anatomie, from Old French anatomie, from Latin anatomia, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “dissection”, literally “cutting up”), from ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, incise”). By surface analysis, ana- + -tomy. Doublet of ottomy.

parole.significato: Having lasted from a remote period; having been of long duration; of great age, very old.
parole.testo: From Middle English auncyen, from Old French ancien, from Vulgar Latin *anteānus, composed of Latin ante (“before”) + -ānus (adjective-forming suffix). The non-etymological excrescent /t/ is by analogy with the common ending -ent.

parole.significato: Belonging to, or proceeding from, angels; resembling, characteristic of, or partaking of the nature of, an angel.
parole.testo: From Middle English angelik, aungillik, aungellike, (also angellich, aungellich > English angelly), from Old English anġelīċ, engellīċ, englelīċ, coalescing with Old French angélique, from Latin angelicus, from Ancient Greek ἀγγελικός (angelikós, “of or for a messenger”), from ἄγγελος (ángelos, “ang

parole.significato: A multicellular organism of the kingdom Animalia that is usually mobile, with cells that are not encased in a rigid cel…
parole.testo: From Middle English animal, from Old French animal, from Latin animal, a nominal use of the adjective form animāle, neuter of animālis, from anima (“breath, spirit”). Displaced native English deer (outside puristic usage) in the general animal sense, from Middle English der, deor (“animal”), from Ol

parole.significato: An umbelliferous plant (Pimpinella anisum) growing naturally in Egypt, and cultivated in Spain, Malta, etc., for its ca…
parole.testo: From Middle English anys, borrowed from Old French anis, from Latin anīsum, from Ancient Greek ἄνισον (ánison), from Egyptian jnst.

parole.significato: A type of green-skinned pear.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Anjow, from Old English Anġeow, from Old French Anjou, from Latin Andecāvum, Andegāvum; compare Angers and obsolete Anjoy; the modern pronunciation is a refashioning after modern French Anjou.

parole.significato: To add something to another thing, especially territory; to incorporate.
parole.testo: From Middle English annexen, anexen, from Old French annexer (“to join”), from Medieval Latin annexāre, infinitive of annexō, frequentative of Latin annectō (“bind to”), from ad (“to”) + nectō (“tie, bind”). Compare the rare annect. Doublet of adnex.

parole.significato: To give public notice of, especially for the first time; to make known.
parole.testo: From Old French anoncier, from Latin annūntiāre, from ad + nūntiō (“report, relate”), from nūntius (“messenger, bearer of news”). See nuncio. Doublet of annunciate. See also an-.

parole.significato: To disturb or irritate, especially by continued or repeated acts; to bother with unpleasant deeds.
parole.testo: From Middle English anoyen, from Old French anoier (“to bother, disturb”), from Late Latin inodiāre (“to make loathsome”), derived from Latin odium (“loathing, hatred”). Displaced native Old English dreċċan, gremman.

parole.significato: To formally revoke the validity of.
parole.testo: From Middle English annullen, from Old French anuller, from Latin annullō (“annihilate, annul”), from ad (“to”) + nūllus (“none, not any”).

parole.significato: To adorn.
parole.testo: From variant forms of Old French aorner, aourner (whence also enurny), from Latin adornare (“to adorn”).

parole.significato: Earlier, either in time or in order.
parole.testo: From Middle English antecedent, borrowed from Old French antecedent, from Latin antecēdēns (“going before”), from antecēdō (“to precede; excel; surpass”).

parole.significato: Any of several African mammals of the family Bovidae distinguished by hollow horns, which, unlike deer, they do not she…
parole.testo: From Middle English antelope, from Old French antelop, from Medieval Latin antilops, from Byzantine Greek ἀνθόλοψ (anthólops), which is of obscure origin.

parole.significato: Antiphon.
parole.testo: From Middle English anteme, from Old English antefn, antefen and Old French antiene, anteine, anteivne, from Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna), from ἀντί (antí, “over against”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice, sound”). Doublet of antiphon.

parole.significato: Ancient times; faraway history; former ages.
parole.testo: From Middle English antiquyte, antiquite, antiquytee, a borrowing from Old French antiquité, antiquitet, from Latin antiquitas, from antiquus. Equivalent to antique + -ity. See antique, antic. Compare with French antiquité.

parole.significato: A deciduous branching and bony structure on the head of deer (Cervidae), normally in pairs, grown and shed each year.
parole.testo: From Middle English auntelere, hauntelere, from Old French antoillier (“antler, horn”), from ante- (“in front of”) + oillier (oil (“eye”) + -ier (a suffix indicating location)), possibly from an unattested Latin *anteocularis (“before the eye”).

parole.significato: To satisfy, please.
parole.testo: From Middle English apaien, from Old French apaiier (“to appease”). See Latin pax (“peace”).

parole.significato: open; uncovered; revealed
parole.testo: From Middle English apert, from Old French apert, from Latin apertus, past participle of aperire. Doublet of ouvert and overt.

parole.significato: Unconsciousness or incapacity resulting from a cerebral hemorrhage or stroke.
parole.testo: Late Middle English from Old French apoplexie, from Late Latin apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξία (apoplēxía, “madness; apoplexy, paralysis”), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō, “to cripple by a stroke”) + -ία (-ía, nominal suffix). See plague.

parole.significato: An abscess; a pustulent swelling.
parole.testo: From Middle English aposteme (“a swelling, inflamation”), from Old French aposteme and Late Latin apostēma, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστημα (apóstēma, “abcesse”) (source of Modern Greek απόστημα (apóstima, “abscess”)), related to ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “to remove”).

parole.significato: A missionary, or leader of a religious mission, especially one in the early Christian Church (but see Apostle).
parole.testo: From Middle English apostle, from Old French apostle, from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “one sent forth, apostle”). Merged with Old English apostol, borrowing from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: Synonym of pharmacist: a person who sells medicine, especially (historical) one who made and sold their own medicines i…
parole.testo: From Old French apotecaire (whence French apothicaire), from Medieval Latin apothēcārius (“storekeeper”), from Latin apothēca (“(originally) repository, storehouse, warehouse; (later) shop, store”) + -ārius (occupational suffix), from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “a repository, storehouse”), fro

parole.significato: Capable of being seen, or easily seen; open to view; visible to the eye; within sight or view.
parole.testo: From Middle English apparaunt, aparaunt, from Old French aparent, aparant, in turn from Latin appārēns, appārentis, present participle of appāreō.

parole.significato: To come or be in sight; to be in view; to become visible.
parole.testo: From Middle English apperen, aperen, borrowed from Old French aparoir (French apparoir), from Latin appāreō (“to appear”), from ad (“to”) + pāreō (“to come forth, to become visible”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).

parole.significato: A name or title by which someone is addressed or identified; a designation.
parole.testo: From late Middle English appellacion, from Old French apellatiun, from Latin appellātiō (“a naming”).

parole.significato: To hang or attach to, as by a string, so that the thing is suspended.
parole.testo: From Latin appendere (“to hang up, suspend on, pay out”), via Old French apendre, appendre, via Middle English appenden; from ad (“on, upon, against”) + pendere (“to suspend, hang”), equivalent to ad- + pend. Compare with Old English appenden, apenden (“to belong”). See also pendant.

parole.significato: To perceive.
parole.testo: From Middle English aperceiven, from Old French aperceveir, apercevoir, from Late Latin *appercipiō, from ad- + percipiō.

parole.significato: To belong to or be a part of, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom; to relate to.
parole.testo: From Middle English apperteinen, apertenen, borrowed from Old French apartenir (French appartenir), from Late Latin appertinēre, from ad (“to”) + Latin pertinēre (“to reach to, belong”). More at pertain.

parole.significato: A desire to eat food or consume drinks.
parole.testo: From Middle English appetit, from Old French apetit (French appétit), from Latin appetitus, from appetere (“to strive after, long for”); ad + petere (“to seek”). See petition, and compare with appetence.

parole.significato: Suitable for application; relevant.
parole.testo: From Old French applicable, from Medieval Latin applicabilis.

parole.significato: The act of physically applying or laying on.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English applicacioun, borrowed from Old French aplicacion (French application), from Latin applicātiōnem, accusative singular of applicātiō (“attachment; application, inclination”), from applicō (“join to, attach; apply”). Equivalent to apply + -ication.

parole.significato: To lay or place; to put (one thing to another)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English aplien, borrowed from Old French applier, from Latin applicō, from ad- + plicō (“fold; arrive”). See applicant, ply.

parole.significato: To set, fix or determine (a time or place for something such as a meeting, or the meeting itself) by authority or agree…
parole.testo: From Middle English apointen, borrowed from Old French apointier (“to prepare, arrange, lean, place”) (French appointer (“to give a salary, refer a cause”)), from Late Latin appunctō (“to bring back to the point, restore, to fix the point in a controversy, or the points in an agreement”); Latin ad +

parole.significato: To determine the value or worth of (something), particularly as a person appointed for this purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English apreisen, from Old French aprisier (“apraise, set a price on”) (compare modern French apprécier), from Late Latin appretiare, from ad- + Latin pretium (“price, value”) (English precious), from which also appreciate, a doublet.

parole.significato: To be or become aware of (something); to perceive.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English apprehenden (“to grasp, take hold of; to comprehend; to learn”), from Old French apprehender (modern French appréhender (“to apprehend; to catch; to dread”)), from Latin apprehendere, adprehendere, the present active infinitive of apprehendō, adprehendō (“to grab, grasp, sei

parole.significato: A trainee, especially in a skilled trade.
parole.testo: From Middle English apprentice, apprentesse, apprentyse, apprentis, from Old French aprentis, plural of aprentif, from Old French aprendre (verb), Late Latin apprendō, from Classical Latin apprehendō. Compare typologically Latin discipulus (akin to capiō); Russian ухвати́ть (uxvatítʹ), нахвата́ться

parole.significato: To come or go near, in place or time; to move toward; to advance nearer; to draw nigh.
parole.testo: From Middle English aprochen, borrowed from Old French aprochier (modern French approcher), from Late Latin appropiāre, a verb based on Latin prope (“near”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pro- (a variant of *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + *-kʷe (“suffix forming distributives from interro

parole.significato: The act of approving; an assenting to the propriety of a thing with some degree of pleasure or satisfaction; approval,…
parole.testo: From late Middle English approbacioun, from Old French approbacion (French approbation), from Latin approbatio, from approbare (“to assent to as good, approve, also show to be good, confirm”), from ad (“to”) + probare (“approve, commend”), from probus (“good”). By surface analysis, approbate + -ion.

parole.significato: To officially sanction; to ratify; to confirm; to set as satisfactory.
parole.testo: From Middle English aproven, appreoven, appreven, apreven, borrowed from Old French aprover, approver, approuvir, appreuver (“to approve”), from Latin approbō, from ad + probō (“to esteem as good, approve, prove”). Doublet of approbate. By surface analysis, ad- + prove.

parole.significato: To make profit of; to convert to one's own profit — said especially of waste or common land appropriated by the lord of…
parole.testo: From Middle English approuen, approven, from Old French aprouer; a- + a form apparently derived from the pro, prod, in Latin prōsum (“be useful or profitable”). Compare with improve.

parole.significato: An article of clothing worn over the front of the torso and/or legs for protection from spills; also historically worn…
parole.testo: Rebracketing of napron (a napron → an apron), from Middle English naperoun, napron, apron, from Old French napperon, diminutive of nappe (“tablecloth”), from Latin mappa (“napkin”). For other similar cases of rebracketing, see adder, daffodil, newt, nickname, orange, trickle, umpire.

parole.significato: To tear up by the roots; to draw away.
parole.testo: From Middle English aracen, arasen, from Old French arachier, esracier (modern French arracher), from Latin exradicare, eradicare. The prefix a- is perhaps due to Latin ab. See eradicate.

parole.significato: A steel crossbow.
parole.testo: From Middle English arblast, from Old French arbaleste (modern arbalète), from Late Latin arcuballista, from Latin arcus + ballista.

parole.significato: A person appointed, or chosen, by parties to determine a controversy between them; an arbitrator.
parole.testo: From Middle English arbiter, arbytour, arbitre, from Old French arbitre, from Latin arbiter (“a witness, judge, literally one who goes to see”).

parole.significato: The act or process of arbitrating.
parole.testo: From Middle English arbitracion, borrowed from Old French arbitration, from Latin arbitratio, from arbitrari (“to arbitrate, judge”); see arbitrate.

parole.significato: A wooden crossbow with a special drawing mechanism, used to fire bolts, stones, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English arblast, from late Old English arblast, from Old French arbaleste (modern French arbalète), from Late Latin arcuballista, from Latin arcus (“bow”).

parole.significato: A shady sitting place or pergola usually in a park or garden, surrounded by climbing shrubs, vines or other vegetation.
parole.testo: From Middle English arbour, erbour, from Old French erbier (“field, meadow, kitchen garden”), from erbe (“grass, herb”), from Latin herba (“grass, herb”) (English herb). (Compare Late Latin herbārium, although erbier is possibly an independent formation.) The spelling was influenced by Latin arbor (

parole.significato: To move following a curved path.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ark, from Old French arc, from Latin arcus (“a bow, arc, arch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷos (“bow, arrow”). Doublet of arch, arco, and arrow.

parole.significato: An inverted U shape.
parole.testo: From Middle English arch, arche, from Old French arche (“an arch”), a feminine form of arc, from Latin arcus (“a bow, arc, arch”). Doublet of arc and arco. Displaced native Old English bīeġels and Old English hwealf.

parole.significato: A powerful angel that leads many other angels, but is still loyal to a deity, and often seen as belonging to a particul…
parole.testo: From Middle English archangel, from Old French archangele, from Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos) from Ancient Greek prefix ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”). By surface analysis, arch- + angel.

parole.significato: One who shoots an arrow from a bow or a bolt from a crossbow.
parole.testo: from Middle English archer, archere, from Old French archier, from Vulgar Latin *arcārius, alteration of arcuārius, from Latin arcus (“bow”). Displaced native Old English sċytta.

parole.significato: The practice or sport of shooting arrows with a bow.
parole.testo: From Middle English archerie, from Old French archerie, from archier (“archer”). Equivalent to archer + -ery.

parole.significato: An original model of which all other similar concepts, objects, or persons are merely copied, derivative, emulated, or…
parole.testo: From Old French architipe (modern French archétype), from Latin archetypum (“original”), from Ancient Greek ἀρχέτυπον (arkhétupon, “model, pattern”), the neuter form of ἀρχέτυπος (arkhétupos, “first-moulded”), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning, origin”) (from ἄρχω (árkhō, “to begin; to lead, rule”), from

parole.significato: To impute (something) as a fault to or upon someone.
parole.testo: From Old French àreter, from à + reter, from Latin reputāre (“to count”).

parole.significato: The metal silver.
parole.testo: From Middle English argent, from Old French argent m (“silver”), from Latin argentum n (“white money, silver”).

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Argentina or its people.
parole.testo: From Old French argentin (“silvery”), from Latin argentum (“silver”).

parole.significato: Containing or resembling silver.
parole.testo: From Middle English argentyne, borrowed from Old French argentin (“silvery”), from Latin argentum (“silver”), equivalent to argent + -ine.

parole.significato: To show grounds for concluding (that); to indicate, imply.
parole.testo: From Middle English arguen, from Old French arguer, from Latin arguere (“to declare, show, prove, make clear, reprove, accuse”), q.v. for more. Displaced native Old English flītan and reċċan.

parole.significato: To put forward as an argument; to argue.
parole.testo: The obsolete senses are derived from Middle English argumenten (“to argue, discuss; to consider, reflect”), from Old French argumenter (“to argue”), from Latin argūmentārī (“to adduce arguments or proof, prove, reason; to adduce (something) as argument or proof; to conclude”), from argūmentum (“argu

parole.significato: spider
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English arayne, arane, from Old French araigne, aragne, from Latin arānea, related to or derived from Ancient Greek ἀράχνη (arákhnē). Doublet of Arachne.

parole.significato: Towards the rear, backwards.
parole.testo: From Middle English arere, from Old French arere, from Vulgar Latin *ad retro (literally “to the rear”).

parole.significato: A check; a stop; an act or instance of arresting something.
parole.testo: From Middle English arest (noun) and aresten (verb), from Old French areste (noun) and arester (“to stay, stop”, verb), from Vulgar Latin *arrestō, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“to stop, remain behind, stay back”), from re- (“back”) + stō (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”)

parole.significato: A sharp edge or ridge formed by the intersection of two surfaces
parole.testo: From Old French areste, from Latin arista (“beard (of grain), fishbone”). Doublet of arista.

parole.significato: To reach; to get to a certain place.
parole.testo: From Middle English arriven, ariven, from Old French ariver, from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre (“to land, come ashore”), derived from Latin rīpa (“shore, river-bank”). parole.significato: Having excessive pride in oneself, often with contempt or disrespect for others.
parole.testo: From Middle English arrogaunt, from Old French arrogant, from Latin arrogāns, present active participle of arrogō.

parole.significato: A saddlebow.
parole.testo: From Middle English arsoun, from Old French arçon, from Vulgar Latin *arciō (“saddlebow”), from Latin arcus (“bow”); compare Italian arcione, Portuguese arção, and Spanish arzón.

parole.significato: The conscious production or arrangement of sounds, colours, forms, movements, or other elements in a manner that affect…
parole.testo: From Middle English art, from Old French art, from Latin artem, accusative of ars (“art”). Partly displaced native Old English cræft, whence Modern English craft. See also archaic English list (“art, craft, cunning, skill”).

parole.significato: sinew, ligament, tendon, artery
parole.testo: Late Middle English arterie, borrowing from Old French artaire and Latin artēria (“a windpipe; an artery”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā, “windpipe; artery”).

parole.significato: Any of the muscular- and elastic-walled blood vessels forming part of the circulation system by which blood is conveyed…
parole.testo: Late Middle English arterie, borrowing from Old French artaire and Latin artēria (“a windpipe; an artery”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā, “windpipe; artery”).

parole.significato: To bind by articles of apprenticeship.
parole.testo: From Middle English article, from Old French article, from Latin articulus (“a joint, limb, member, part, division, the article in grammar, a point of time”), from Latin artus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂értus (“that which is fit together; juncture, ordering”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join, fit (

parole.significato: A joint or the collection of joints at which something is articulated, or hinged, for bending.
parole.testo: From Middle English articulacioun, from Old French articulacion, from Medieval Latin articulatio. Equivalent to articulate + -ion.

parole.significato: Man-made; made by humans; of artifice.
parole.testo: From Middle English artificial (“man-made”) via Old French (modern French artificiel), from Latin artificiālis from artificium (“skill”), from artifex, from ars (“skill”), and -fex, from facere (“to make”). Displaced native Old English cræftlīċ.

parole.significato: Large projectile weapons, in modern usage usually large guns, but also rocket artillery.
parole.testo: From Middle English artillerie, from Old French artillerie (“collection of military engines, crossbows, lances etc.”), from artillier (“to equip, provide with contraptions”), alteration of atiller (“to arrange, adjust, put on clothes or, especially, pieces of armour”) (influenced by art), itself fro

parole.significato: To move upward, to fly, to soar.
parole.testo: From Middle English ascenden, borrowed from Old French ascendre, from Latin ascendō (“to go up, climb up to”), from ad (“to”) + scandō (“to climb”); see scan. Unrelated to accede other than common ad prefix.

parole.significato: Moving upward; ascending, rising.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₂éd The adjective is derived from Late Middle English ascendent (“ascending, rising; increasing in quantity; (astronomy) rising above the horizon”) [and other forms], borrowed from Old French ascendant, from Latin ascendentem, the accusative singular of ascendēns (“ascending, rising”), t

parole.significato: The act of ascending; an ascent.
parole.testo: From Middle English ascencioun, from Old French ascension, from Latin ascēnsiō, ascēnsiōnem (“ascent”). Displaced native Old English upfæreld.

parole.significato: To find out definitely; to discover or establish.
parole.testo: From Middle English acerteynen, from Old French acertener, from a- (“to, towards”) + certener (“make sure of”), from the adjective certain, from Latin certus (“certain, fixed”). Compare to Spanish acertar.

parole.significato: To regard as arising from a specified cause or source.
parole.testo: From Middle English ascriben, from Old French ascrivre (“inscribe, attribute, impute”), from Latin āscrībere (“to state in writing”), equivalent to a- + scribe.

parole.significato: Masonry employing flat and well-squared stone or brick, creating an appearance similar to wooden flooring.
parole.testo: From Middle English assheler, acheler, etc., from forms of Old French esselier (“wooden support, traverse beam”), from Medieval Latin ascelāris and assellāris (equivalent to a diminutive of early forms of ais (“plank”)), variant of *axillāris (attested only after the Renaissance), from Latin axilla

parole.significato: A water snake.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspe, from Old French aspe, from Latin aspis, aspidis (“asp, viper”), from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís, “shield; Egyptian cobra Naja haje”); compare Middle English aspide.

parole.significato: Rough or harsh; severe, stern, serious.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspre, from Old French aspre (modern French âpre), from Latin asper (“rough”).

parole.significato: The quality of having a rough or uneven surface; roughness, unevenness; (countable, chiefly in the plural) a protruding…
parole.testo: From Middle English asprete, asperite, from Old French aspreté (modern French âpreté), from Latin asperitātem, the accusative singular of asperitās (“roughness, unevenness; fierceness, severity; harshness, sharpness; acidity, tartness”), from asper (“coarse, rough, uneven; bitter, fierce harsh; rude

parole.significato: To have a strong desire or ambition to achieve something.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspiren, from Old French aspirer, from Latin aspīrō (“breathe on; approach; desire”).

parole.significato: To attack with harsh words or violent force.
parole.testo: From Middle English assailen, from Old French assaillir, assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assault.

parole.significato: Someone who attacks or assails another violently, or criminally.
parole.testo: From Old French assaillant, from the verb assaillir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“to, towards”) + salīre (“to jump”). Equivalent to assail + -ant.

parole.significato: A violent onset or attack with physical means, for example blows, weapons, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English assaut, from Old French noun assaut, derived from the past participle of the verb assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assail. Spelling Latinized around 1530 to add an l.

parole.significato: To put together.
parole.testo: From Middle English assemblen, from Old French assembler (“to assemble”), from Medieval Latin assimulāre (“to bring together”), from ad- + simulō (“copy, imitate”), from similis (“like, similar”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”). Doublet of assimilate.

parole.significato: To agree to a proposal.
parole.testo: From Middle English assent (noun) and assenten (verb), from Old French assent (noun) and assentir (verb), from Latin assentiō (whence as-).

parole.significato: To determine, estimate or judge the value of; to evaluate; to estimate.
parole.testo: From Middle English assessen, from Old French assesser, from Medieval Latin assessare, originally the frequentative of Latin assessus, past participle of assidēre, from ad (“to, towards, at”) + sedeō (“sit; settle down”). Cognate with Spanish asentar (“to settle”).

parole.significato: One who assesses a property for tax or insurance evaluation.
parole.testo: From Middle English assessour, from Old French assessour, from Latin assessor (“assistant judge; assessor of taxes”). Cognate with French assesseur.

parole.significato: To designate or set apart (something) for some purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English assignen, from Old French assigner, asigner, from Latin assignō, from ad- + signō (“mark, sign”).

parole.significato: An appointment for a meeting, generally of a romantic or sexual nature.
parole.testo: From Middle English assignacioun, from Old French assignacion, from Latin assīgnātiō.

parole.significato: To help.
parole.testo: From Middle English assisten, from Old French assister (“to assist, to attend”), from Latin assistō (“stand at, bestand”, verb).

parole.significato: A session or inquiry made before a court or jury.
parole.testo: From Middle English assise, from Old French assises, feminine plural participle of Old French asseoir (“to sit”), from Latin assidere.

parole.significato: To lessen the intensity of, to mitigate or relieve (hunger, emotion, pain, etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English aswagen, from Old French asuagier (“to appease, to calm”), from Vulgar Latin *assuāviō (“to sweeten, to butter up, to calm”), derived from Latin ad- + suāvis (“sweet”) + -iō.

parole.significato: To make sure and secure; ensure.
parole.testo: From Old French asseurer (Modern French assurer), from Latin ad- + securus (“secure”). Cognate with Spanish asegurar. Doublet of assecure.

parole.significato: In shock or confusion; bewildered, astonished.
parole.testo: Apparently from astony, astonie, from Old French estonner, from Vulgar Latin *extonare. Compare English astonish, of which this was claimed in olden sources to be the more "correct" (or at least Biblical) version of the word.

parole.significato: To store; to furnish with stores.
parole.testo: From Middle English astoren, from Old French estorer, from Latin instaurare.

parole.significato: Away from the proper path; in a wrong or unknown direction.
parole.testo: From Middle English astraien or by apheresis straien, from Old French estraier (“to stray”), from late Medieval Latin extravagari (“to wander beyond”), from Latin extra (“beyond”) + vagārī (“to wander, stray”).

parole.significato: To temper by adjusting relative quantities, or blending qualities.
parole.testo: From Middle English attempren, from Old French atemprer (French attremper), from Latin attemperare. Doublet of attemperate.

parole.significato: To try.
parole.testo: Late 14th century, as Middle English attempten, from Old French atempter, from Latin attemptō (“to try, solicit”), from ad- (“to”) + temptō; see tempt.
