parole.significato: Senses relating to caring for or waiting on someone, or accompanying or being present.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₂éd From Middle English attenden, atenden (“to devote oneself (to a task, etc.); to pay attention to (something), to look after; to consider (something); to expect or look forward to (something); to intend to do (something); to help or serve (someone), attend upon; to take care of (somet

parole.significato: The tendency to attract.
parole.testo: From Middle English attraccioun, from Old French attraction, from Latin attractio from past participle of attrahō (= ad + trahō), equivalent to attract + -ion.

parole.significato: A dark reddish-brown colour, often used to describe hair colour.
parole.testo: Early Modern English auburn (“brown, reddish brown”) from Middle English aubourne, abron, abroune, abrune (“light brown, yellowish brown, blond”), alteration (due to conflation with Middle English brun (“brown”)) of earlier auborne (“yellowish-white, flaxen”) from Old French auborne, alborne (“blond

parole.significato: The act or process of augmenting.
parole.testo: From Middle English augmentation, augmentacion, augmentacioun, from Old French augmentacion, from Latin augmentātiō, verbal noun from augmentō (“increase”, verb).

parole.significato: To surround with, or as if with, a halo.
parole.testo: From Middle English aureole, from Old French aureole, from Medieval Latin aureola (corona) (“golden (crown)”). Doublet of oriole.

parole.significato: Of the same origin as claimed; genuine.
parole.testo: From Middle English authentik, from Old French autentique, from Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós, “authentic, genuine”), from Ancient Greek αὐθέντης (authéntēs, “perpetrator, murderer, absolute ruler”). Doublet of effendi.

parole.significato: Power or right to make or enforce rules, give orders, or impose obligation; or a position having such power or right.
parole.testo: From Middle English auctorite, autorite (“authority, book or quotation that settles an argument”), from Old French auctorité, from Latin stem of auctōritās (“invention, advice, opinion, influence, command”), from auctor (“master, leader, author”). For the presence of the h, compare the etymology of

parole.significato: To grant (someone) the permission or power necessary to do (something); to permit; to sanction or consent to.
parole.testo: From Middle English auctorisen, from Old French auctorisier, from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre, from Latin auctor. See author about the orthography with ⟨h⟩. Doublet of octroy.

parole.significato: Excessive or inordinate desire of gain; greed for wealth
parole.testo: From Middle English avarice, from Old French, from Latin avāritia, from avārus (“greedy”).

parole.significato: Actuated by avarice; extremely greedy for wealth or material gain; immoderately desirous of accumulating property.
parole.testo: From Middle English avaricious, from Old French avaricieux, from avarice, from Latin avaritia (“greed”), from avarus (“greedy”), of avere (“crave, long for”).

parole.significato: Begone; depart; used in contempt or abhorrence.
parole.testo: First used 1275–1325; Middle English, from Old French avant (“to the front”).

parole.significato: A quantity of oats paid by a tenant to a landlord in lieu of rent.
parole.testo: From Old French avenage, from avene, from Latin avena (“oats”).

parole.significato: A curtain or flap of mail, fastened to a helmet, or to a coif (hood) of mail, covering the lower face, neck, and should…
parole.testo: From Middle English aventayle, from Old French esventail (“air-hole”), from esventer (Modern French éventer), from Latin ex (“out”) + ventus (“wind”). Related to ventail.

parole.significato: To assert the truth of (something); to affirm (something) with confidence; to declare (something) in a positive manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English averren, from Old French averer, from Early Medieval Latin advērō, a verb derived from Latin vērus (“true”). Compare Modern French avérer.

parole.significato: To turn aside or away.
parole.testo: From Middle English averten, adverten, from Old French avertir (“turn, direct, avert; turn the attention, make aware”), from Latin āvertere, from ab + vertō (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Greediness; strong appetite.
parole.testo: From Middle English avidite, from Old French avidite (modern French avidité), from Latin aviditās (“avidity, covetousness”), equivalent to avid + -ity.

parole.significato: An advocate; a lawyer.
parole.testo: From Middle English avocat, from Old French avocat, from Latin advocātus. Doublet of advocate.

parole.significato: To declare freely and openly; to assert.
parole.testo: From Old French avouchier, from Latin advocāre. Doublet of advocate, advoke, and avow.

parole.significato: An adulterer.
parole.testo: From Middle English avounterer, avouterer, avoutrer(e), avowterer, avowtreer, avowtrer(e), awowterer, from Old French avoutrier, from Latin adulterō or adulter, noun use of an adjective.

parole.significato: To declare openly and boldly, as something believed to be right; to own, acknowledge or confess frankly.
parole.testo: From Middle English avowen, from Old French avouer, from Latin advocare (“to call to, call upon, hence to call as a witness, defender, patron, or advocate”), from ad (“to”) + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of advoke, avouch, and advocate. Not related to vow.

parole.significato: adultery
parole.testo: From Middle English avoutrie, from Old French avouterie, variant (perhaps influenced by vout, vut (“vow”)) of aouterie, aolterie, from Late Latin adulterium. Doublet of adultery, which replaced it in modern English.

parole.significato: A grandfather.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ayel, aiel, from Old French aiol, aiuel, from Vulgar Latin *aviolus, ultimately from Latin avus. Compare modern French aïeul.

parole.significato: An Old World monkey of the genus Papio, having dog-like muzzles and large canine teeth, cheek pouches, a short tail, an…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English babewin, baboin, from Old French babouin, from baboue (“grimace; muzzle”) (whence French babouin), from an imitative origin. According to Oxford English Dictionary, it was an imitative base *bab-, which is in turn from the (reduplicated) syllable ba, characteristic of e

parole.significato: Security, usually a sum of money, exchanged for the release of an arrested person as a guarantee of that person's appea…
parole.testo: From Middle English baille, from the Old French verb bailler (“to deliver or hand over”) and noun bail (“lease”), from Latin bāiulāre (“carry or bear”), from baiulus (“porter; steward”) (English: bailiff).

parole.significato: The outer wall of a feudal castle.
parole.testo: From Old French baile (“palisade, enclosure”), from Latin bacula, plural of baculum (“stick, rod”).

parole.significato: A bath.
parole.testo: From Middle English bayne~baine, from Old French bain, from Latin baneum, variant of balneum. Doublet of bagnio, balaneion, and banya.

parole.significato: A state in which opposing forces harmonise; equilibrium.
parole.testo: From Middle English balaunce, from Old French balance, from Late Latin *bilancia, from (accusative form of) Latin bilanx (“two-scaled”), from bi- + lanx (“plate, scale”). Displaced the word — Old English wǣġ akin to Modern English: wey from Proto-West Germanic *wāgu (“scales; weight”).

parole.significato: A rounded bundle or package of goods in a cloth cover, and corded for storage or transportation.
parole.testo: From Middle English bale (“bale”), from Old French bale and Medieval Latin bala, of Germanic origin. Doublet of ball.

parole.significato: keratinous material that makes up the plates in the mouth of the baleen whale (Mysticeti), which it uses to trap its fo…
parole.testo: From Middle English baleyne, from Old French baleine (“whale, whalebone”), from Latin balaena (“whale”), from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina, “whale”).

parole.significato: arrowslit (a narrow opening through which arrows can be fired).
parole.testo: From balister (“crossbow”), from Old French balestre, ultimately from Latin balaustium, Ancient Greek βαλαύστιον (balaústion). See also arbalister (“crossbowman”).

parole.significato: A Christian sacrament, by which one is received into a church and sometimes given a name, generally involving the candi…
parole.testo: From Middle English bapteme, baptesme, from Old French batesme or bapteme, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptisma, from Ancient Greek βάπτισμα (báptisma, “dipping, baptism”), from βαπτίζω (baptízō, “I dip in liquid”). Displaced native Old English fulwiht.

parole.significato: A person who baptizes.
parole.testo: From Middle English baptist, baptiste, borrowed from Old French baptiste, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptista, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs).

parole.significato: To perform the sacrament of baptism by sprinkling or pouring water over someone or immersing them in water.
parole.testo: From Middle English baptisen, baptizen, from Old French baptiser, batisier, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptizāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to immerse, plunge, baptize”).

parole.significato: A solid, more or less rigid object of metal or wood with a uniform cross-section smaller than its length.
parole.testo: From Middle English barre, from Old French barre (“beam, bar, gate, barrier”), from Vulgar Latin *barra, of uncertain origin. Doublet of barre.

parole.significato: To obstruct the passage of (someone or something).
parole.testo: From Middle English barren, from Old French barrer, from Medieval Latin barrare (“to bar”), from the noun. Cognate to Occitan barrar, Spanish barrar, Portuguese barrar. Preposition properly imperative of the verb. Compare barring.

parole.significato: of or relating to a barbarian; uncivilized, uncultured or uncouth
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English barbarik, from Old French barbarique (“barbarous”), from Latin barbaricus, from Ancient Greek βαρβαρικός (barbarikós, “barbaric, savage, fierce”), from βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “barbarian”) + -ικός (-ikós, adjective suffix). See βάρβαρος (bárbaros) for more.

parole.significato: barbarian; non-Christian
parole.testo: From Middle English barbarye (“barbarian, non-Christian”), from Old French [Term?] and Medieval Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A freshwater fish of the genus Barbus or other closely related taxa in the cyprinid family.
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰardʰéh₂ From Middle English barbel, from Old French barbel, from Vulgar Latin *barbellus, from Late Latin barbulus, diminutive of Latin barbus (“barbel”); barbus itself is from barba (“beard”). By surface analysis, Latin barb(us) (“beard, barbel”) + -el (diminutive suffix), and also, by

parole.significato: A large flat-bottomed towed or self-propelled boat used mainly for river and canal transport of heavy goods or bulk car…
parole.testo: From Middle English barge, borrowed from Old French barge (“boat”), from Vulgar Latin *barga, a variant of Late Latin barca, a regular syncope of Vulgar Latin *barica, from Classical Latin bāris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris, “Egyptian boat”), from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare, “small boat”), from Demotic

parole.significato: The male ruler of a barony.
parole.testo: From Middle English baroun, from Old French baron, from Latin barōnem, from Proto-West Germanic *barō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear”). parole.significato: To give as its foundation or starting point; to lay the foundation of.
parole.testo: From Middle English base, bas, baas, from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis). Doublet of basis and bass.

parole.significato: A mythical snake-like dragon, so venomous that even its gaze is deadly.
parole.testo: From Middle English basilicke, borrowed from Old French basilique, from Latin basiliscus, from Ancient Greek βασιλίσκος (basilískos, literally “minor king or chieftain”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king”), possibly based on descriptions or rare encounters with different types of cobra which have crow

parole.significato: A wide bowl for washing, sometimes affixed to a wall.
parole.testo: From Middle English basyn, from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinum (“wide bowl”).

parole.significato: A person who was born out of wedlock, and hence often considered an illegitimate descendant.
parole.testo: From Middle English bastard, bastarde, from Old English bastard (used as an epithet), from Anglo-Norman bastard, Old French bastart (“illegitimate child”), perhaps via Medieval Latin bastardus, of obscure origin. Likely from Frankish *bāst (“marriage, relationship”) + Old French -ard, -art (pejorati

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: To hit with a bat or (figuratively) as if with a bat.
parole.testo: From Middle English batten, baten (“to beat”), from Old French batre (“to beat”), from Late Latin battere, from Latin battuere, of uncertain origin; perhaps of Germanic or Celtic origin. In modern English reinterpreted as a verbal derivative of Etymology 2. Compare batter, battery.

parole.significato: Strife; contention.
parole.testo: * Noun: From the verb, or directly from the noun debate. * Verb: From Middle English bate (“contention”), from Old French batre (French battre), from Latin battere.

parole.significato: A plank or strip of wood, or several of such strips arranged side by side, used in construction to hold members of a st…
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English bataunt, batent (“finished bar or board (as for panelling)”), from Old French batent (“a beating”), a noun use of the present participle form of batre (“to beat, hit, strike”), from Late Latin battere, the present active infinitive of battō (“to beat”), from Latin bat

parole.significato: A cheap showy ornament or piece of jewellery; a gewgaw.
parole.testo: From Middle English bable, babel, babull, babulle, from Old French babel, baubel (“trinket, child's toy”), most likely a reduplication of bel, ultimately from Latin bellus (“pretty”).

parole.significato: A tree or shrub of species Laurus nobilis (family Lauraceae), having dark green leaves and berries.
parole.testo: From Middle English baye, baie, from Old English beġ (“berry”), as in beġbēam (“berry-tree”), conflated with Old French baie, from Latin bāca (“berry”).

parole.significato: An opening in a wall, especially between two columns.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French baee, beee, from the verb beer (“gape open”), from Early Medieval Latin batāre. Compare Modern French baie. More at bevel, badinage.

parole.significato: Of a reddish-brown colour with a black mane and tail.
parole.testo: From Middle English bay, bai, from Old French bai, from Latin badius (“reddish brown, chestnut”).

parole.significato: Any four-footed land mammal.
parole.testo: From Middle English beeste, beste, from Old French beste (French bête), from Latin bēstia (“animal, beast”); many cognates – see bēstia.

parole.significato: A man with a reputation for fine dress and etiquette; a dandy or fop.
parole.testo: From Middle English beau, beu, bew, bewe, from Old French beau, from Latin bellus (“beautiful”). Doublet of bello and boo.

parole.significato: To make beautiful; to increase the beauty of.
parole.testo: From Middle English beutifien, from Old French beaute (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fine”), + -ify, from Latin facio (“make”).

parole.significato: To smear upon; to soil.
parole.testo: From be- (“thoroughly, extensively”) + daub, from Old French dauber (“to plaster, whitewash”), from Latin dealbō (“whiten over, plaster”).

parole.significato: A grandmother.
parole.testo: Inherited from late (1400–1450) Middle English beldame, beldam, from Middle English bel (“attractive, fine, good”) (from Old French bel (“beautiful”), from Latin bellus) + dame, dam (“a mother, lady”), itself ultimately from Latin domina (“a mistress, lady”).

parole.significato: A tower or steeple typically containing bells, especially as part of a church.
parole.testo: From Middle English belfry, bellfray, belfray, berfrey, barfray, from Old French belfroi, berfroi, berfrey, from Late Latin berfrēdus, from Frankish *bergafriþu, from Proto-Germanic *bergafriþuz, equivalent to barrow + frith. English forms containing bel- as opposed to ber- were preferred due to fal

parole.significato: A tree, Moringa oleifera or horseradish tree of Arabia and India, which produces oil of ben.
parole.testo: From Middle English been, from Old French and Medieval Latin, probably from a North African pronunciation of Arabic بَان (bān, “ben tree”).

parole.significato: Land granted to a priest in a church that has a source of income attached to it.
parole.testo: From Old French benefice, from Latin beneficium.

parole.significato: Disposition to do good.
parole.testo: Circa 1400, original sense “good will, disposition to do good”, Old French benivolence from Latin benevolentia (also directly from Latin), literally “good will”, from bene (“well, good”) + volentia, form of volēns, form of volō (“to wish”), components cognate to English benefit and voluntary, more d

parole.significato: Having a disposition to do good.
parole.testo: From Old French benevolent, borrowed from Latin benevolēns ("benevolent"). Displaced native Old English welwillende (literally well-wishing).

parole.significato: Kind; gentle; mild.
parole.testo: From Middle English benigne, benygne, from Old French benigne, from Latin benignus (“kind, good”), from bene (“well”) + genus (“origin, kind”). Compare malign.

parole.significato: A blessing; benediction.
parole.testo: From Middle English benysoun, beneson, borrowed from Old French beneïson, from Latin benedictiō, benedictiōnem. First known use: 14th century. Doublet of benediction.

parole.significato: Wood avens or herb bennet, a common yellow-flowered plant of Europe (Geum urbanum).
parole.testo: From Middle English *benet (found in Middle English herbe-benet (“hemlock”, literally “blessed plant”)), from Old French benëit, benoit and Latin (herba) benedicta. Doublet of benedict.

parole.significato: A mineral of pegmatite deposits, often used as a gemstone (molecular formula Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English beryl, from Old French beril, from Latin bērillus, bēryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”), in turn borrowed from Middle Indic forms like Pali veḷuriya or Prakrit 𑀯𑁂𑀭𑀼𑀮𑀺𑀅 (verulia), from Dravidian, probably named after Velur (modern day Belur) in south

parole.significato: Beast-like.
parole.testo: From Middle English bestial, from Old French bestial, from Late Latin bēstiālis, from Latin bēstia (“beast”) (whence English beast).

parole.significato: A liquid to consume; a drink, such as tea, coffee, liquor, beer, milk, juice, or a soft drink, often excluding water.
parole.testo: From Middle English beverage, from Old French beverage, variant of bevrage, from beivre (“to drink”), variant of boivre (“to drink”), from Latin bibō. Related to imbibe.

parole.significato: A small strip of leather by which bells are fastened to a hawk's legs.
parole.testo: From Middle English bewette, diminutive of Old French beue, bue, buie, boie (“bond, chain”), from Latin boia (“neck collar, fetter”). Compare buoy.

parole.significato: A coin made of gold or silver, minted at Byzantium and used in currency throughout mediaeval Europe.
parole.testo: From Middle English besaunt, from Old French bezant, nominative bezanz, from Latin byzantius (“of Byzantium”).

parole.significato: A semi-finished length of metal.
parole.testo: From Middle English billet, bylet, belet, billette, from Old French billette, from bille (“log, tree trunk”), from Vulgar Latin *bilia, probably of Gaulish origin (compare Old Irish bile (“tree”)).

parole.significato: A small, flat, baked good which is either hard and crisp or else soft but firm; a cookie.

parole.significato: Several bird species in the Botaurinae subfamily of the heron family Ardeidae.
parole.testo: From Middle English bitour, botor, from Old French butor, from Gallo-Roman *butitaurus, a blend of Latin būtiō (“bittern”) and taurus (“bull, ox”).

parole.significato: Censure.
parole.testo: From Middle English blame, borrowed from Old French blame, blasme, produced from the verb blasmer, which in turn is derived from Late Latin blastēmāre, variant of blasphēmāre, from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω (blasphēméō). Doublet of blaspheme. Displaced native Old English tǣling (“blame”) and tǣlan (“t

parole.significato: To assert or consider that someone is the cause of something negative; to place blame; to attribute responsibility (for…
parole.testo: From Middle English blamen, borrowed from Old French blasmer, from Late Latin blasphēmāre (“to reproach, to revile”), from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω (blasphēméō). Compare blaspheme, a doublet. Overtook common use from the native wite (“to blame, accuse, reproach, suspect”) (from Middle English wīten,

parole.significato: To grow or become white.
parole.testo: From Middle English blaunchen, from Old French blanchir, from Old French blanc (“white”), from Early Medieval Latin blancus, from Frankish *blank, from Proto-Germanic *blankaz (“bright, shining, blinding, white”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”). Cognates Cognate with blench (“to dece

parole.significato: To commit blasphemy; to speak against God or religious doctrine.
parole.testo: From Middle English blasfemen, blasphemen, from Old French blasfemer, from Late Latin blasphēmāre, from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω (blasphēméō). Doublet of blame.

parole.significato: An act of irreverence or contempt toward a god or toward something considered sacred; an impious act, utterance, view,…
parole.testo: From Middle English blasfemie, from Old French blasfemie, from Ecclesiastical Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “profanity”), from βλασφημέω (blasphēméō, “to slander”). Displaced native Old English tāl.

parole.significato: Gray; grayish or light blue.
parole.testo: From Middle English plunket (noun), from plunket (“of a blue or greyish colour”, adjective), perhaps the past participle of *plunken (“to cover with lead or lead-colouring”), from Old French plonquier, plonchier (“to cover with lead”), in imitation of Old French plunkié, plonquié (“lead-coloured", a

parole.significato: The point at which fluid begins to change to a vapour; the boiling point.
parole.testo: From Middle English boillen, from Old French boillir (see French bouillir) from Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”). Displaced native Old English weallan (intransitive) and wiellan (transitive). More at wall, well.

parole.significato: Cotton wool made from raw cotton, typically used as padding in clothing or as a stopper.
parole.testo: From Old French bombace (“cotton, cotton wadding”), from Late Latin bombax (“cotton”), a variant of bombyx (“silkworm”), from Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux, “silkworm”), possibly related to Middle Persian pmbk' (“cotton”), from a Proto-Indo-European.

parole.significato: Cotton, or cotton wool.
parole.testo: From Old French bombace (“cotton, cotton wadding”), from Late Latin bombax (“cotton”), a variant of bombyx (“silkworm”), from Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux, “silkworm”), possibly related to Middle Persian pmbk' (“cotton”), from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to twist, wind”.

parole.significato: Merry; happy.
parole.testo: From Middle English *bonie (attested only rarely as bon, boun), probably from Old French bon, feminine bonne (“good”), from Latin bonus (“good”). See bounty, and compare bonus, boon.

parole.significato: A place set with trees or mass of shrubbery, a grove or thicket.
parole.testo: From the Middle English boskage, from the Old French boscage, from Vulgar Latin *boscāticum, from Late Latin boscus, from Frankish *busk (compare Middle Dutch busch), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“forest, woods”).

parole.significato: A lump, protuberance, or swelling in an animal, person or object.
parole.testo: From Middle English bos, bose, boce, from Old French boce (“lump, bulge, protuberance, knot”), from Frankish *bottja, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to hit, strike, beat”). Doublet of beat; see there for more.

parole.significato: A container, typically made of glass or plastic and having a tapered neck, used primarily for holding liquids.
parole.testo: From Middle English botel (“bottle, flask, wineskin”), from Old French boteille, from Late Latin butticula, diminutive of buttis (“cask”). Doublet of botija. Displaced native pinne and non-native Old English ampella. Partially displaced Old English flasce.

parole.significato: A boundary, the border which one must cross in order to enter or leave a territory.
parole.testo: From Middle English bounde, from Old French bunne, from Medieval Latin bodina, earlier butina (“a bound, limit”).

parole.significato: The burden or bass of a melody.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English burdoun (“accompaniment”), from Old French bordon, from Medieval Latin burdō, burdōnem (“drone”), probably from Frankish *buʀdō (“grub, beetle, cricket, bumblebee”), related to Old English budda (“beetle”), Saterland Frisian Budde (“worm or grub used as fishbait”), Icel

parole.significato: a pilgrim's staff.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English burdoun (“pilgrim's staff”), from Old French bordon, from Medieval Latin burdō, burdōnem (“pilgrim's staff”). The modern pronunciation and form is also influenced by modern French bourdon.

parole.significato: The ball rolled by players in the game of lawn bowls.
parole.testo: From Middle English bowle, boule, from Old French boule (“ball”), from Latin bulla (“bubble, stud, round object”). Doublet of poll.

parole.significato: A curved instrument or handle of iron or wood, for holding and turning bits, etc.; a bitstock.
parole.testo: From Middle English brace, from Old French brace (“arm”), from Latin bracchia, the nominative and accusative plural of bracchium (“arm”).

parole.significato: A small rope used to truss up sails.
parole.testo: From Middle English brayle, from Old French braiel, from Medieval Latin bracale (“girdle”) (from bracae (“breeches”)).

parole.significato: The woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing.
parole.testo: From Middle English branche, braunche, bronche, from Old French branche, branke, from Late Latin branca (“footprint”, later also “paw, claw”) (whence Middle High German pranke, German Pranke (“paw”)), of unknown origin. Perhaps of Celtic origin, from a hypothetical Gaulish *vranca, from Proto-Indo-E

parole.significato: A partition in a coal mine, made from wood or from canvas sheeting coated in tar.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bretage, bretace, from Old French bretesce, bretesche, breteske, from Late Latin brittisca.

parole.significato: A semicircular diacritical mark (˘) placed above a vowel, commonly used to mark its quantity as short.
parole.testo: From Middle English breve, variant of bref, from Old French brieve, breve (feminine form of brief, bref), from Latin brevis (“short”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant of Great Britain, particularly (historical) a Celt from the area of Roman Britain or (obsolete) a Welshma…
parole.testo: From Old French Breton, from Latin Brittō. Doublet of Breton and Brython.

parole.significato: To make a hole in, especially a cask of liquor, and put in a tap in order to draw the liquid.
parole.testo: From Middle English broche, from Old French broche, from Vulgar Latin *brocca, originally a feminine form of Latin broccus, perhaps ultimately of Gaulish origin (see Scottish Gaelic bròg). Doublet of brochure.

parole.significato: Oatmeal mixed with boiling water or milk.
parole.testo: From the Doric dialect of North East Scotland, from earlier browes, from Old French broez, nominative of broet (“stew, soup made from meat broth”) (French brouet) diminutive of breu, from Medieval Latin brodium, from Proto-Germanic *bruþą (“broth”). See broth.

parole.significato: An implement consisting of multiple more or less flexible bristles or other filaments attached to a handle, used for an…
parole.testo: From Middle English brusshe, from Old French broisse (Modern French brosse), from Vulgar Latin *brustia, from Frankish *bursti, from Proto-Germanic *burstiz (“bristle”), or also Vulgar Latin *bruscia, from Proto-Germanic *bruskaz (“tuft, thicket, underbrush”), which could be from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: A metal clasp with a hinged tongue or a spike through which a belt or strap is passed and penetrated by the tongue or s…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English bokel (“spiked metal ring for fastening; ornamental clasp; boss of a shield; a shield, buckler; (figurative) means of defence”) [and other forms], from Old French boucle, bocle (“spiked metal ring for fastening; boss of a shield; a shield”) [and other forms],

parole.significato: One who buckles something.
parole.testo: From Middle English bukler, bokler, bokeler, bokeleer, from Old French bocler, boucler, bucler, (French bouclier) from Vulgar Latin *bucculārius (“bossed”), from Latin buccula (“boss”). Merged with buckle + -er.

parole.significato: A heretic.
parole.testo: From Middle English bougre (“heretic”), from Old French bougre, from Medieval Latin Bulgarus (“Bulgar”), from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ, “Bulgarian”), used in designation of heretics (especially the Bogomils, who arose around the 10th century AD in the First Bulgarian Empire), to whom

parole.significato: A medieval wind instrument with a very long, straight and slender body, usually made of metal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old French buisine, busine (an earlier, Middle English-era borrowing bosyne did not survive into modern English), from Latin būcina. Doublet of buccina and posaune.

parole.significato: A papal bull, an official document or edict from the Pope.
parole.testo: From Middle English bulle, from Old French bulle, from Latin bulla, from Gaulish. Doublet of bull (“bubble”) and bulla.

parole.significato: A bubble.
parole.testo: From Middle English bowle, boule, from Old French bulle, boule (“ball”), from Latin bulla (“round swelling”), of Gaulish origin. Doublet of bull (“papal bull”) and bulla.

parole.significato: A purse.
parole.testo: From bouget (“wallet, purse or bag”), from Middle English bogett, bouget, bowgette (“leather pouch”), from Old French bougette, diminutive of bouge (“leather bag, wallet”), from Late Latin bulga (“wallet, purse”), from Gaulish bolgā, from Proto-Celtic *bolgos (“sack, bag, stomach”), from Proto-Indo-

parole.significato: A phrase or theme that recurs at the end of each verse in a folk song or ballad.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English burdoun (“accompaniment”), from Old French bordon (“drone”), from Medieval Latin burdō. Doublet of bourdon.

parole.significato: A coarse woolen cloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English burel, burrel, borel, from Old French burel, diminutive of *bure (compare Middle French bure (“coarse woolen cloth”), French bourre (“hair, fluff”)), from Late Latin burra (“wool, fluff, shaggy cloth, coarse fabric”). Doublet of bureau, which was taken from later (early modern) F

parole.significato: A medieval tenure in socage under which property in England and Scotland was held under the king or a lord of a town an…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English burgage, from Old French bourgage and Medieval Latin burgāgium; equivalent to burg + -age.

parole.significato: Citizenship.
parole.testo: From Middle English burgeisie, borgeysye, from Old French bourgesie, borgoisie (“citizenship”), from borgeis, burgeis (“a citizen”), from Medieval Latin burgensis, derivative of burgus (“a borough, town”), from Frankish *burg (“town”), from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“burg, castle, stronghold, town”). D

parole.significato: A tree growth in which the grain has grown in a deformed manner; a burr knot.
parole.testo: From Middle English burle (“a knot or flaw in cloth”), from Old French bourle (“flocks or ends of threads which disfigure cloth”), diminutive of Old French bourre, from Medieval Latin burra (“flock of wool, coarse hair”).

parole.significato: A person who prepares and sells meat (and sometimes also slaughters the animals).
parole.testo: From Middle English bocher, boucher, from Old French bouchier (“goat slaughterer”), from Old French bouc (“goat”), from Medieval Latin buccus (“he-goat”), from Frankish *bukk, from Proto-Germanic *bukkaz (“male goat, male deer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuǵ- (“buck, ram”). See also English buck.

parole.significato: A manservant having charge of wines and liquors.
parole.testo: From Middle English butler, butlere, boteler, botelere, from Old French buttiler, butiller, boteillier (“officer in charge of wine”), from Medieval Latin botellārius, equivalent to bottle + -er. Piecewise doublet of bottler.

parole.significato: A butler's pantry; a serving pantry.
parole.testo: From Middle English buttillary, buttlarye, botelerye, botelerie, from Old French boteillerie, butelerie and Medieval Latin butellaria.

parole.significato: A room for keeping food or beverages; a storeroom.
parole.testo: From Middle English boterie, from Old French boterie and Medieval Latin buteria, from Late Latin botāria, from a variant form of butta (“cask, bottle”). The form was probably influenced by butter.

parole.significato: A small dwelling characteristic of the frontier, especially when built from logs with simple tools and not constructed…
parole.testo: From Middle English caban, cabane, from Old French cabane, from Medieval Latin capanna (“a cabin”); see further etymology there. Doublet of cabana and cabane.

parole.significato: To confine in a cage; to put into and keep in a cage.
parole.testo: From Middle English cage, from Old French cage, from Latin cavea. Doublet of cadge and cavea and related to jail.

parole.significato: To heat (a substance) to remove its impurities and refine it.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English calcinen (“(alchemy, medicine) to heat (something) until it turns to powder; to change the nature of (something) by heating”) [and other forms], from Old French calciner (modern French calciner (“to calcinate; to calcine”)) and from its etymon Medieval La

parole.significato: To calculate, reckon.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English calcule /calculen /calclen, derived from Old French calculer (compare French calculer, Spanish calcular, Portuguese calcular, Italian calculàre), derived from Latin calculāre (“reckon, calculate”). Doublet of calculate.

parole.significato: Any system by which time is divided into days, weeks, months, and years.
parole.testo: From Middle English kalender, from Old French calendier, from Latin calendarium (“account book”), from kalendae (“the first day of the month”), from kalō (“to announce solemnly, to call out (the sighting of the new moon)”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-. Doublet of calendarium. Displaced native O

parole.significato: The holder of a monarchical title based on a claim to be a successor of Muhammad.
parole.testo: From Middle English calife, caliphe, from Old French caliphe, from Medieval Latin calipha, from Arabic خَلِيفَة (ḵalīfa, “caliph”) and خَلِيف (ḵalīf, “successor”).

parole.significato: A clay tobacco pipe used by Native Americans, especially as a symbol of truce or peace.
parole.testo: From a Norman variant of Old French chalumeau (imported to Canada with Norman colonists), from Latin calamellus, diminutive of calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos).

parole.significato: A false accusation or charge brought to tarnish another's reputation or standing.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English calumnīe (“false accusation, slander; (law) objection raised in bad faith”), borrowed from Old French calomnie (“slander, calumny”) (modern French calomnie), or directly from its etymon Latin calumnia (“false statement, misrepresentation; false accusation, malicious charge”)

parole.significato: A slight convexity, arching or curvature of a surface of a road, beam, roof, ship's deck etc., so that liquids will flo…
parole.testo: From Old French cambre (“bent”), from Latin camurum, from camur (“arched”).

parole.significato: A white transparent waxy crystalline isoprenoid ketone, 1,7,7-trimethylbicyclo[2.2.1]heptan-2-one, with a strong pungen…
parole.testo: From Old French camphore or Medieval Latin camphora, from Arabic كَافُور (kāfūr), in turn from an Austronesian word such as Malay kapur.

parole.significato: A plant with simple stems, like bamboo or sugar cane, or the stem thereof:
parole.testo: From Middle English cane, canne, from Old French cane (“sugar cane”), from Latin canna (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”). Doublet of canna and kaneh. Related to channel and canal.

parole.significato: To declare (a deceased person) as a saint, and enter them into the canon of saints.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English canonizen (“to declare as a saint; to appoint to an ecclesiastical office”), from Old French canonisier (modern French canoniser (“to canonize”)), or from its etymon Medieval Latin, Late Latin canōnizāre, the present active infinitive of Latin canōnizō (“to recognize as a sa

parole.significato: A high cover providing shelter, such as a cloth supported above an object, particularly over a bed.
parole.testo: From Middle English canapy, canepie, canapee, canape, canope, from Old French conopé, Medieval Latin canapeum, canopeum, from Latin cōnōpēum (“mosquito net, canopy”), from Ancient Greek κωνωπεῖον (kōnōpeîon, “mosquito net”), from Ancient Greek κώνωψ (kṓnōps, “mosquito”), of uncertain origin. More at

parole.significato: The ability to hold, receive, or absorb.
parole.testo: From Middle English capacite, from Old French capacite, from Latin capācitās (whence -acity), from capāx (“able to hold much”), from capiō (“to hold, to contain, to take, to understand”).

parole.significato: A piece or point of land, extending beyond the adjacent coast into a sea or lake; a promontory; a headland.
parole.testo: From Middle English cape, gappe, cap, from Old French cap (“cape, headland”), from Latin caput (“head”). Compare Old Norse kobbi (“islet, small cape”). Doublet of capo, caput, chef, and chief, and distantly with head and Howth. For sense development, compare English ness (“a promontory point, cape”)

parole.significato: Money and wealth: the means to acquire or produce goods and services, especially in a non-barter system.
parole.testo: From Middle English capital, borrowed partly from Old French capital and partly from Latin capitālis (“of the head”) (in sense “head of cattle”), from caput (“head”) (English cap) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives). Use in trade and finance originated in Medieval economies when a common but expensi

parole.significato: The uppermost part of a column.
parole.testo: From Middle English capitale, partly from Old French capital and partly from Late Latin capitellum (“capital or chapiter of a column”), a form of Latin capitulum (“head-like object or structure; chapter”) (whence English capitulum, chapter, and the synonym chapiter (“uppermost part of a column”)), f

parole.significato: A chief or leader.
parole.testo: From Middle English capitain, capteyn, from Old French capitaine, from Late Latin capitāneus, from Latin caput (“head”) (English cap). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of chieftain, also from Old French.

parole.significato: A deep-red or fiery colored garnet or other dark red precious stone, especially when cut cabochon.
parole.testo: From Middle English carbuncle, charbocle, from Old French carbuncle, charbuncle, from Latin carbunculus (“a small coal; a reddish kind of precious stone; a kind of tumor”), diminutive of carbō (“a coal, charcoal”). Doublet of Garfinkel and Garfunkel.

parole.significato: To check IDs, especially against a minimum age requirement.
parole.testo: From Middle English carde (“playing card”), from Old French carte, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “paper, papyrus”). Doublet of carte and chart.

parole.significato: An herb, native to India (Elettaria cardamomum).
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Old French cardamome or Latin cardamōmum, from Ancient Greek καρδάμωμον (kardámōmon).

parole.significato: Any member of the species Cynara cardunculus of prickly perennial plants which has leaf stalks eaten as a vegetable, re…
parole.testo: From Middle English cardoun, from Old French cardon, from Late Latin cardōnem, from Latin cardus, alternative form of carduus (“thistle”). Respelled on analogy of -oon nouns. Doublet of cardon and chard.

parole.significato: Relating to the physical and especially sexual appetites or activities.
parole.testo: From Middle English carnal, from Old French charnel, from Late Latin carnālis (“fleshy”), from oblique stem of Latin carō, carnis (“meat, flesh”) + -ālis (whence -al).

parole.significato: Any of various freshwater fish of the family Cyprinidae.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English carpe (“the common carp (Cyprinus carpio)”), from Old French carpe, from Late Latin carpa, possibly from Proto-West Germanic *karpo (possibly due to the introduction from the fish from the Danube into England in the 14th century; whence Middle Low German karpe and Old High G

parole.significato: A fabric used as a complete floor covering.
parole.testo: From late Middle English carpette, from Old French carpite, from Medieval Latin carpita or Italian carpita, introduced in the 13th century by the Florentines from the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, from Middle Armenian կարպետ (karpet, “carpet, rug”), earlier կապերտ (kapert).

parole.significato: An actual event, situation, or fact.
parole.testo: From Middle English cas, from Old French cas (“an event”), from Latin cāsus (“a falling, a fall; accident, event, occurrence; occasion, opportunity; noun case”), perfect passive participle of cadō (“to fall, to drop”).

parole.significato: To render moot or void; to annul; to reject
parole.testo: From Middle English cassen, from Old French casser, from Late Latin cassō, from Latin cassus (“empty, hollow”), and perhaps influenced by quassō (“to shake, shatter”).

parole.significato: A feudal lord with a fortified manor.
parole.testo: From Middle English castelain, from Old French castelain (compare modern châtelain), from Latin castellanus (“pertaining to a castle, an occupant of a castle, or a governor of a castle”), from castellum castle, citadel, diminutive of castrum fortified place. See castle. By surface analysis, Old Fren

parole.significato: A systematic list of books, names, pictures, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English cathaloge, from Old French catalogue, from Late Latin catalogus, itself from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “enrollment, register”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, make a list”), from κατα- (kata-, “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (légō, “to say, to speak, to tell”). Equi

parole.significato: Relating to the office of a bishop or an archbishop.
parole.testo: From Middle English cathedral, chathedral, cathiderall, from Old French [Term?], from Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra + -ālis, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra, “chair of a teacher, throne”).

parole.significato: A member of a Catholic (western Christian) church.
parole.testo: From Old French catholique, from Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós, “universal”), from κατά (katá, “according to”) + ὅλος (hólos, “whole”).

parole.significato: The source of, or reason for, an event or action; that which produces or effects a result.
parole.testo: * From Middle English cause (also with the sense of “a thing”), borrowed from Old French cause (“a cause, a thing”), borrowed from Latin causa (“reason, sake, cause”), from Proto-Italic *kaussā, which is of unknown origin. Doublet of chose (“(law) a thing; personal property”). See accuse, excuse, re

parole.significato: Prudence when faced with, or when expecting to face, danger; care taken in order to avoid risk or harm.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1297 as Middle English caucioun (“bail, guarantee, pledge”), from Old French caution (“security, surety”), itself from Latin cautiō, from cautus, past participle of caveō, cavēre (“be on one's guard”).

parole.significato: A large, naturally-occurring cavity formed underground or in the face of a cliff or a hillside.
parole.testo: From Middle English cave, borrowed from Old French cave, from Latin cava (“cavity”), from cavus (“hollow”). Cognate with Tocharian B kor (“throat”), Albanian cup (“odd, uneven”), Ancient Greek κύαρ (kúar, “eye of needle, earhole”), Old Armenian սոր (sor, “hole”), Sanskrit शून्य (śūnya, “empty, barre

parole.significato: A large cave.
parole.testo: From Middle English caverne, borrowing from Old French caverne, from Latin caverna (“hollow, cavity, cave”), from cavus (“hollow, excavated, concave”).

parole.significato: Resembling a cavern in size, shape, or atmosphere.
parole.testo: Late Middle English cavernous, cavernose, borrowing from Old French caverneux or Latin cavernōsus (“full of hollows or cavities”), from caverna (“a hollow, cavity, cave”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to cavern + -ous.

parole.significato: To criticise for petty or frivolous reasons.
parole.testo: From Old French caviller (“mock, jest, rail”), from Latin cavillor (“jeer, mock, satirise, reason captiously”), from cavilla (“jeering, raillery, scoffing”); cognate with Italian cavillare, Portuguese cavillar, and Spanish cavilar; nominal usage developed within English from the original verbal usag

parole.significato: A coniferous tree of the genus Cedrus in the family Pinaceae.
parole.testo: From Middle English cedre, probably from Old French cedre, from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros). Some suggest that the Middle English word was partially from Old English ċeder, but the gap in attestation between the two words makes this proposal unlikely. Possible doublet of citrus.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Chelidonium.
parole.testo: From Middle English celidoine, Old French celidoine, French chélidoine, from Latin chelīdonia, from chelīdonius (“relating to the swallow”), from Ancient Greek χελιδόνιος (khelidónios), χελιδών (khelidṓn). parole.significato: The formal performance of a solemn rite, such as Christian sacrament.
parole.testo: From Old French celebration, from Latin celebratio. Equivalent to celebrate + -ion.

parole.significato: A rite or ceremony.
parole.testo: From Middle English celebritē, from Old French celebrite (compare French célébrité), from Latin celēbritās.

parole.significato: Speed, swiftness.
parole.testo: From Old French celeritee (compare French célérité), from Latin celeritas, from celer (“fast, swift”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or located in the sky or outer space, where the Sun, Moon, planets, and stars are visible.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English celestial (“relating to the heavens or sky; (Christianity) relating to heaven, divine, heavenly”), borrowed from Old French celestial (modern French céleste), from Medieval Latin caelestiālis (“celestial”), or directly from its etymon Latin caelestis

parole.significato: Synonym of celestial: of or resembling the heavens.
parole.testo: From Old French celestin, Latin caelestīnus, from caelestis (“heavenly”) + -inus (“-ine”), from caelum (“sky, heavens, Heaven”). Equivalent to celest + -ine.

parole.significato: A powdered substance produced by firing (calcining) calcium carbonate (limestone) and clay that develops strong cohesiv…
parole.testo: From Middle English syment, cyment, from Old French ciment, from Latin caementum (“quarry stone; stone chips for making mortar”), from caedō (“to cut, hew”). Doublet of cementum.

parole.significato: A place where the dead are buried; a graveyard or memorial park.
parole.testo: From Middle English cimiterie, from Old French cimitiere, from Medieval Latin cimitērium, from Late Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion), from κοιμάω (koimáō, “I put to sleep”); compare cœmeterium. Displaced Middle English charnel (“mass grave, cemetery”) and Old English l

parole.significato: A dining room, especially one on an upper floor (traditionally the room in which the Last Supper took place).
parole.testo: From Middle English cenacle, from Old French cenacle (modern French cénacle), from Latin cēnāculum (“dining room”).

parole.significato: A new or recent member of a Greek monastic religious order; a caloyer.
parole.testo: From Old French cenobite or Ecclesiastical Latin coenobīta, from coenobium, from Ancient Greek κοινόβιον (koinóbion, “community life, convent”), from κοινός (koinós, “common”) + βίος (bíos, “life”).

parole.significato: A census.
parole.testo: Old French cense, French cens, Latin census.

parole.significato: The act of blaming, criticizing, or condemning as wrong; reprehension.
parole.testo: From 1350–1400 Middle English censure, from Old French, from Latin censūra (“censor's office or assessment”), from censēre (“to consider, to assess, to value, to judge, to tax, etc.”).

parole.significato: A period of one hundred consecutive years; often specifically a numbered period with conventional start and end dates,…
parole.testo: From Middle English centurie (“a count of one hundred (of anything); a division of the Roman army; century; a division of land”), from Old French centurie, from Latin centuria, from centum (“one hundred”). The most common modern use is an ellipsis of century of years.

parole.significato: A fleshy, waxy area at the base of the upper beak in certain birds.
parole.testo: From Middle English sere, from Old French cire, from Latin cēra (“wax, cere”), or via Latin cērō (“to smear or coat with wax”).

parole.significato: Sure in one's mind, positive; absolutely confident in the truth of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English certeyn, certein, certain, borrowed from Old French certain, from a Vulgar Latin unattested form *certānus, extended form of Latin certus (“fixed, resolved, certain”), of the same origin as cretus, past participle of cernere (“to separate, perceive, decide”). Displaced native Mid

parole.significato: Certainly, indeed.
parole.testo: From Middle English certes, from Old French [Term?], from Latin certus (“certain”).

parole.significato: Heat excited by friction.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English chaufen (“to warm”), borrowed from Old French chaufer (modern French chauffer), from Latin calefacere, calfacere (“to make warm”), from calere (“to be warm”) + facere (“to make”). See caldron.

parole.significato: A series of interconnected rings or links usually made of metal.
parole.testo: From Middle English cheyne, chaine, from Old French chaeine, chaene (“chain”), from Latin catēna (“chain”), from Proto-Indo-European *kat- (“to braid, twist; hut, shed”). Doublet of catena. Displaced native Middle English rakil and rakent (from Old English racente (“chain”)); see rackan.

parole.significato: To act as chairperson at; to preside over.
parole.testo: From Middle English chayere, chayer, chayre, from Old French chaiere, chaere, from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). Partially displaced native stool and settle, which now have more specialised senses. Doublet of cathedra

parole.significato: A confrontation; a dare.
parole.testo: From Middle English chalenge, variant with palatalization of Middle English kalange (“an accusation, claim”), from Old French chalenge, chalonge, palatalized Central French variants of Old Northern French calenge, calonge (see Continental Norman calengier), from Latin calumnia (“a false accusation,

parole.significato: To enclose in a room.
parole.testo: From Middle English chambre, borrowed from Old French chambre, from Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “vaulted chamber”). Doublet of camera.

parole.significato: A high-ranking female servant who attends in a royal's or noble's chamber.
parole.testo: From Middle English chamberere, chamberer, from Old French chamberiere, feminine of chamberier; ultimately from Latin cambra (“room”). By surface analysis, chamber + -er.

parole.testo: From Middle English camelion, from Old French cameleon, from Latin chamaeleon, from Ancient Greek χαμαιλέων (khamailéōn), from χαμαί (khamaí, “on the earth, on the ground”) + λέων (léōn, “lion”); ultimately a calque from Akkadian 𒌨𒈤𒊭𒆠 (nēšu ša qaqqari, “chameleon, reptile”, literally “lion of the gr

parole.significato: Open countryside, or an area of open countryside.
parole.testo: From Old French champaigne, from Late Latin campānia.

parole.significato: An ongoing winner in a game or contest.
parole.testo: From Middle English champioun, from Old French champion, from Medieval Latin campio (“combatant in a duel, champion”), from Frankish *kampijō (“fighter”), from Proto-West Germanic *kampijō (“combat soldier”), a derivative of *kampijan (“to battle, to campaign”), itself a derivative of *kamp (“battle

parole.significato: The rank or post of a chancellor.
parole.testo: From Middle English chancelrie, from Old French chancelerie (Modern French chancellerie), from Late Latin cancellaria. Doublet of chancery.

parole.significato: A person who makes or sells candles.
parole.testo: From Middle English chaundeler, from Old French chandelier, from Latin candelarius (“a candle-maker; a candlestick”), from the Latin candela (“a candle”); compare the English term candle.

parole.significato: The hollow bed of running waters; (also) the bed of the sea or other body of water.
parole.testo: From Middle English chanel (also as canel, cannel, kanel), a borrowing from Old French chanel, canel, from Latin canālis (“groove; canal; channel”). Doublet of canal.

parole.significato: To sing, especially without instruments, and as applied to monophonic and pre-modern music.
parole.testo: From Middle English chaunten, from Old French chanter, from Latin cantāre (“sing”). Doublet of cant.

parole.significato: One who chants or sings.
parole.testo: From Middle English chauntour, from Old French chanteor, from Latin cantor; equivalent to chant + -er. Compare French chanteur. Doublet of cantor.

parole.significato: A place of worship, smaller than or subordinate to a church.
parole.testo: From Middle English chapele, chapel, from Old French chapele, from Late Latin cappella (“little cloak; chapel”), diminutive of cappa (“cloak, cape”). Doublet of capelle. parole.significato: A member of a religious body (who is often, although not always, of the clergy) officially assigned to provide pastoral…
parole.testo: From Middle English chapeleyn, from Old French chapelain, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin cappellānus, from cappella. Doublet of capelin. Displaced Old English handprēost.

parole.significato: One of the main sections into which a published work is divided, especially a book.
parole.testo: From Middle English chapitre, from Old French chapitre, from Latin capitulum (“a chapter of a book, in Medieval Latin also a synod or council”), diminutive of caput (“a head”); see capital, capitulum, and chapiter, which are doublets of chapter.

parole.significato: A letter or character.
parole.testo: From Old French characte, from Latin *characta, from Ancient Greek χαρακτός (kharaktós).

parole.significato: A being involved in the action of a story; a persona.
parole.testo: From Middle English caracter, from Old French caractere, from Latin character, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “type, nature, character”), from χαράσσω (kharássō, “to engrave”). Displaced native English thew from Old English þēaw (in the plural) and Old English hād (“person, character”). Dou

parole.significato: The amount of money levied for a service.
parole.testo: From Middle English chargen, from Old French chargier, from Late Latin carricō (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“a car, wagon”); see car. Doublet of cargo.

parole.significato: A two-wheeled horse-drawn cart, used in Bronze Age and Early Iron Age warfare.
parole.testo: From Middle English chariot, from Old French chariot, from char (“cart”), from Latin carrus (“wagon”), itself borrowed from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós. Displaced native Old English hrædwæġn (literally “fast wagon”).

parole.significato: An organization, the objective of which is to carry out a charitable purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English charite, from Old French charité, cherte, chariteit, cariteit, from Latin cāritās. * The Tyndale Bible uses native English love instead.

parole.significato: An object, act or words believed to have magic power (usually carries a positive connotation).
parole.testo: From Middle English charme, from Old French charme (“chant, magic spell”), from Latin carmen (“song, incantation”). Displaced native Old English lybb (“drug, poison, charm”).

parole.significato: Part of a helm, now usually identified as the hinge (near the neck) by which the helm was secured to the breastplate.
parole.testo: From Old French charnel, from Latin cardinālis (“relating to a hinge”); related to French charnière.

parole.significato: Straight threads obtained by unraveling old linen cloth, used for surgical dressings.
parole.testo: From the feminine past participle of Old French charpir (“to pluck”), carpir (“to pluck”), from Latin carpō (“to pluck”). Compare carpet.

parole.significato: A document issued by some authority, creating a public or private institution, and defining its purposes and privileges.
parole.testo: From Middle English charter, chartre, borrowed from Old French chartre, from Latin chartula (diminutive of charta). See chart. Doublet of chartula.

parole.significato: Synonym of pure and virtuous, particularly
parole.testo: From Middle English chaste, from Old French chaste (“morally pure”), from Latin castus (“pure”).

parole.significato: To make chaste.
parole.testo: From Middle English chastien, from Old French chastier (“punish”), from Latin castīgō. Doublet of chastise and castigate and related to chaste.

parole.significato: To punish, especially by corporal punishment.
parole.testo: From Middle English chastisen, from Old French chastier, from Latin castīgō. See also the doublets chasten and castigate and cf. also chaste.

parole.significato: The act of chastising; rebuke; punishment.
parole.testo: Old French chastiement, from the verb chastier, from Latin castīgō

parole.significato: The quality of being chaste: the state of abstaining from any sexual activity considered immoral; avoidance of sexual s…
parole.testo: From Middle English chastite, from Old French chasteté, a semi-learned adaptation of Latin castitas, equivalent to chaste + -ity.

parole.testo: From Middle English chesible, from Old French chesible, from Late Latin casubla, an alteration of Latin casula (“little cottage, hooded cloak”), a diminutive of casa (“house”).

parole.significato: Tangible, movable property.
parole.testo: From Middle English chatel, from Old French chatel, from Medieval Latin capitāle (English capital), from Latin capitālis (“of the head”), from caput (“head”) + -alis (“-al”). parole.significato: The entrails of an animal, especially when used as a food ingredient; offal.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English chaudon, chaudoun, chaudron (“sauce made from chopped entrails”), from Old French chaudun (“animal entrails; sauce made from such entrails”) (modern French chaudin (“wrapping of sausages made from pigs’ intestines; Louisiana meat dish cooked in a pig’s stomach”)), from Late

parole.significato: To violate rules in order to gain, or attempt to gain, advantage from a situation.
parole.testo: Verb from Middle English achetan, variant of escheten, from Old French escheat, past participle of escheoir, escheoiter, from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall away, fall out”), from (Latin) ex- + cadere (“fall”). parole.significato: An inspection or examination.

parole.significato: A pattern made up of a grid of squares of alternating colors; a checkered pattern.
parole.testo: By shortening from chequer, from Old French eschequier (“chessboard”), from Medieval Latin scaccarium, ultimately from the same Persian root as above.

parole.significato: A fetid water snake.
parole.testo: From Middle English chelidre, chelyder, chelydre, from Old French chelidre, chelydre, from Latin chelȳdrus (“fetid water serpent”), from Ancient Greek χέλυδρος (khéludros, “amphibious serpent”), from χέλυς (khélus, “tortoise”) + ὕδρος (húdros, “water serpent”). parole.significato: To treat with affection, care, and tenderness; to nurture or protect with care.
parole.testo: From Middle English charish, cherishen (“to have affection for, hold dear, treat kindly; to esteem, respect; to cherish; to take care of; to greet; to entertain, treat hospitably; to cheer; to encourage, incite”), from Old French cheriss-, chieriss-, extended stem of cherir, chierir (“to cherish”) (

parole.significato: Of a deep reddish-brown colour, like that of a chestnut fruit (noun sense 1).
parole.testo: The noun is a contraction of chest(en) (“(obsolete) chestnut tree; fruit of this tree, chestnut”) + nut. parole.significato: A military raid by cavalry through enemy territory, designed to disrupt rural communities and weaken an opponent.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English chyvachie, from Old French chevauchie, chevauchée, from Medieval Latin caballicāta; the modern form is after modern French chevauchée. Doublet of cavalcade.

parole.significato: A V-shaped pattern; used in architecture, and as an insignia of military or police rank, on the sleeve.

parole.significato: The leader or head of a tribe, organisation, business unit, or other group.

parole.significato: surgery

parole.significato: A perennial plant, Allium schoenoprasum, related to the onion.

parole.significato: A group of people who sing together; a company of people who are trained to sing together.

parole.significato: Originally, any of various green-coloured gems; later specifically peridot.

parole.significato: To heal a wound through scarring (by causing a scar or cicatrix to form).

parole.significato: An alcoholic, often sparkling (carbonated) beverage made from fermented apples.

parole.significato: A kind of belt or other girdle.
parole.testo: From Middle English sengle, from Old French sengle, cengle (Modern French sangle), from Late Latin cingula, from Latin cingulum (“girdle”), from cingere (“to gird”). Doublet of cinch. Compare also Middle English kyngle, kyngll (“girdle, brooch”) from Old Norse kinga (“brooch”).

parole.significato: A deep red mineral, mercuric sulfide, HgS; the principal ore of mercury; such ore used as the pigment vermilion.

parole.significato: To move in a circle; to go round; to circulate.
parole.testo: From Middle English circuit, from Old French circuit, from Latin circuitus (“a going round”), from circuire (“go round”), from circum (“around”) + ire.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a circle.
parole.testo: From Middle English circuler, circuleer, circulere, from Old French circulier (French circulaire), from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus, diminutive of circus (“ring”). By surface analysis, circle + -ar.

parole.significato: To surgically remove the foreskin (prepuce) from the penis of.

parole.significato: The surgical excision of the foreskin and usually all or most of the penile frenulum.
parole.testo: From Middle English circumcisioun, from Old French circumcisiun (modern French circoncision) and its etymon Latin circumcīsiō, from circumcīdō (“cut around”), from circum (“about, around; through”) + caedō (“cut, hew”). By surface analysis, circumcis(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: Something which is related to, or in some way affects, a fact or event.
parole.testo: From Middle English circumstaunce, from Old French circonstance, from Latin circumstantia.

parole.significato: A reservoir or tank for holding water, especially for catching and holding rainwater for later use.
parole.testo: From Middle English cisterne, from Old French cisterne (Modern French citerne) from Latin cisterna, from cista (“box”), from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē, “box”). Doublet of cisterna.

parole.significato: An official summons or notice given to a person to appear.
parole.testo: From Middle English citacioun, from Old French citation, from Latin citātiō. By surface analysis, cite + -ation.

parole.significato: To quote; to repeat, as a passage from a book, or the words of another.

parole.significato: A great outcry or vociferation; loud and continued shouting or exclamation.

parole.significato: To make or become clear or bright by freeing from impurities or turbidity.
parole.testo: From Middle English clarifien, from Old French clarifiier, from Latin clārificō, clārificāre; clārus (“clear”) + faciō, facere (“make”). Semantically clear + -ify.

parole.significato: The state or measure of being clear, either in appearance, thought or style; lucidity.

parole.significato: Synonym of clemency.
parole.testo: From Middle English clemence, from Old French clemence, from Latin clēmentia. Doublet of clemency.

parole.significato: Lenient or merciful; charitable.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin clēmēns (“merciful”). Equivalent to clīnō + participial suffix -menos. https://www.etymonline.com/word/clemency

parole.significato: A body of persons, such as priests, who are trained and ordained for religious service.

parole.significato: An event or occurrence that signifies an ending.

parole.testo: From Middle English coler, borrowed from Old French coler (Modern French collier), from Late Latin collāre, from Latin collāris, from collum (“neck”). parole.testo: Recorded since c.1378, from Old French, from Medieval Latin collaterālis, from Latin col- (“together with”) (a form of con-) + the stem of latus (“side”). By surface analysis, col- + lateral.

parole.significato: Bringing together.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a dove or pigeon.
parole.testo: From Middle English columbyne, from Old French columbin (French colombin), from Latin columbinus, from columba (“dove, pigeon”).

parole.testo: From Middle English columne, columpne, columpe, borrowed from Old French columne, from Latin columna (“a column, pillar, post”), originally a collateral form of columen, contraction culmen (“a pillar, top, crown, summit”). parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle English combinacioun, combynacyoun, from Old French combination, from Late Latin combīnātiō. Morphologically combine + -ation.

parole.significato: The act or process of burning.
parole.testo: From Old French combustion, from Latin combustio, from comburere (“to burn”), itself from the intensifying prefix com- + the root burere (a faulty sep. of amburere "to burn around", itself from ambi- + urere "to burn, singe"); equivalent to combust + -ion.

parole.significato: A confection consisting of a nut, seed or fruit coated with sugar.
parole.testo: From Old French confit (“preserved fruit”), from Latin cōnfectum. Doublet of confect, confetto, confit, and konfyt. Compare confit.

parole.significato: Contentment, ease.
parole.testo: From Middle English comfort, from Old French cunfort, confort, from the stem of Late Latin confortō. It replaced Old English frofor, Middle English frovre.

parole.significato: To relieve the distress or suffering of; to provide comfort to.
parole.testo: From Middle English comforten, from Old French conforter, from Late Latin confortō (“to strengthen greatly”), itself from Latin con- (“together”) + fortis (“strong”).

parole.significato: The act of commemorating; an observance or celebration to honor the memory of some person or event.
parole.testo: First attested in 1384, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English commemoracioun, from Old French commemoration (French commémoration), from Latin commemorātiō. By surface analysis, commemorate + -ion

parole.significato: To congratulate or reward.
parole.testo: From Middle English commenden, from Old French comender, from Latin commendō (“commend, entrust to, commit, recommend”), from com- + mandō (“to commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand”) + dō (“to put”). Doublet of command.

parole.significato: The act of commending; praise; favorable representation in words; recommendation.
parole.testo: From Middle English commendacioun, from Old French commendacion (“approval, praise”), from Latin commendatio (“recommendation, commendation”), from commendare.

parole.significato: Of a form of symbiosis in which one organism derives a benefit while the other is unaffected.
parole.testo: From Middle English commensal, from Old French commensal, from Medieval Latin commensālis, from com- + mensa (“table”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: A spoken or written remark.
parole.testo: From Middle English coment, comment, from Old French coment (“commentary”), from Late Latin commentum (“comment, interpretation”), from Classical Latin commentum (“invention, fabrication”).

parole.significato: A sending or mission (to do or accomplish something).
parole.testo: From Middle English commissioun, from Old French commission, from Latin commissiō (“sending together; commission”), from committō + -tiō (suffix forming nouns of action), from com- (“with”) + mittō (“to send”).

parole.significato: The common people; the commonality.
