parole.significato: doubt; uncertainty
parole.testo: From Middle English doutaunce, from Old French doutance, from Medieval Latin dubitantia. Equivalent to doubt + -ance. Compare dubitancy.

parole.significato: Sweet; nice; pleasant.
parole.testo: From Middle English douce, from Old French dolz, dous, Middle French doux, douce, from Latin dulcis (“sweet”). Doublet of dolce, doux, and dulce.

parole.significato: To furnish with a dower; to endow.
parole.testo: From Middle English dowen, from Old French douer, from Latin dōtō.

parole.significato: dower; dowry.
parole.testo: From Old French douage, from douer + -age, from Latin dōtō (“to endow”), from dōs (“dowry”). By surface analysis, dow + -age.

parole.significato: The part of or interest in a deceased husband's property provided to his widow, usually in the form of a life estate.
parole.testo: From Middle English dower, dowere, from Old French doeire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs. Doublet of dowry.

parole.significato: A set of twelve.
parole.testo: From Middle English dozen, dozein, doseyne, from Old French dozaine (“a group of twelve”) (Modern French douzaine), from doze (“twelve”) + -aine (“-ish”), from Latin duodecim (“twelve”) (from duo (“two”) + decem (“ten”)) + -ana (“-ish”).

parole.significato: An interpreter, especially for the Arabic and Turkish languages.
parole.testo: From Middle English dragman, from Old French drugeman, from Medieval Latin dragumannus, from Byzantine Greek δραγομάνος (dragomános), from Arabic تُرْجُمَان (turjumān), from Classical Syriac ܬܰܪܓܡܳܢܳܐ (targmānā), from Akkadian 𒅴𒁄 (targumannum, “interpreter”). With the plural form -men, through reint

parole.significato: A mythical reptilian or serpentine creature.
parole.testo: From Middle English dragoun, borrowed from Old French dragon, from Latin dracō(n), from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, “a serpent of huge size, a python, a dragon”), probably from δέρκομαι (dérkomai, “to see clearly”). Displaced Old English wyrm, whence modern worm. Mostly displaced Old English draca

parole.significato: To drink drams.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dragme /dramme, from Old French dragme, from Late Latin dragma, from Latin drachma, from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ, “unit of weight; a handful”). Doublet of drachma, diram, dirham, dirhem, and adarme.

parole.significato: A curtain; a drapery.
parole.testo: From Middle English drape (“a drape”, noun), from Old French draper (“to drape; to full cloth”), from drap (“cloth, drabcloth”), from Late Latin drappus, drapus (“drabcloth, kerchief”), a word first recorded in the Capitularies of Charlemagne, probably from Frankish *drapi, *drāpi (“that which is fu

parole.significato: A large shaker for sprinkling spices or seasonings during food preparation.
parole.testo: From Middle English dragge, from Old French dragee, dragie, from Latin tragēmata, from Ancient Greek τραγήματα (tragḗmata, “spices”), plural of τράγημα (trágēma, “dried fruit”).

parole.significato: The single-humped camel (Camelus dromedarius).
parole.testo: From Middle English dromedari, dromedarie (“dromedary; any camel”) [and other forms], from Old French dromedaire, from Late Latin dromedārius (“kind of camel”), from Latin *dromadārius, from dromas, dromadis (“dromedary”) + -ārius (suffix forming nouns denoting agents of use). Dromas and dromadis ar

parole.significato: Edema, swelling.
parole.testo: From Middle English dropesie, idropesie, from Old French idropsie, ydropisie, from Latin hydrōps, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”). Doublet of hydropsy and hydrops.

parole.significato: A female tree spirit; a woodnymph or tree nymph.
parole.testo: From Old French driade (“wood nymph”), from Latin Dryas, Dryadis, from Ancient Greek Δρυάς (Druás, “dryad”), from δρῦς (drûs, “oak”), from Proto-Indo-European *derew(o)- (“tree, wood”); cf. Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”).

parole.significato: Capable of being pulled or stretched into thin wire by mechanical force without breaking.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin ductilis (“easily led”).

parole.significato: Owed or owing.
parole.testo: From Middle English dewe, dew, due, from Old French deü (“due”), past participle of devoir (“to owe”), from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”), from dē- (“from”) + habeō (“to have”).

parole.significato: The male ruler of a duchy (female equivalent: duchess).
parole.testo: From Old French duc, through Middle English duk, duke, from Latin dux, ducis. Displaced native Old English heretoga. Was present as duc in late Old English, from the same Latin source. Doublet of doge, duc, duce, and dux. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-, which is also the source of the se

parole.significato: Sweet, especially when describing voice or tones; melodious.
parole.testo: From Middle English doucet, from Old French doucet, from dulz, dulce (“sweet, pleasant”) + diminutive -et, from Latin dulcis (“sweet, pleasant”). Cognate with Spanish dulce, French doux, Italian dolce, Portuguese doce, and Romanian dulce. Doublet of dolcetto and doucet.

parole.significato: A stringed instrument, with strings stretched across a sounding board, usually trapezoidal, played by plucking on the s…
parole.testo: From Old French doulcemelle, probably from Latin dulce melos (“sweet song”), from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “melody, song”).

parole.significato: The ability to last a long time by virtue of the power to resist stress or force.
parole.testo: From Middle English durabilite, from Old French durabilité, from Latin dūrābilitās (“durability”). Corresponding to durable + -ity.

parole.significato: Able to resist wear or decay; lasting; enduring.
parole.testo: From Middle English durable, from Old French durable, from Latin dūrābilis (“lasting, permanent”), from dūrō (“harden, make hard”).

parole.significato: An amount of time or a particular time interval.
parole.testo: From Middle English duracioun, from late Old French duracion, from Medieval Latin dūrātiō.

parole.significato: To last, continue, endure.
parole.testo: From Middle English duren (“to last”), from Old French durer, from Latin dūrō, dūrāre. Related to Dutch duren (“to last, dure”), German dauern (“to last, dure”). Doublet of endure.

parole.significato: Harsh treatment.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English duresse, from Old French duresse, from Latin dūritia (“hardness”), from dūrus (“hard”).

parole.significato: A bodily disorder; an imbalance of the humours
parole.testo: From Middle English discrasie, from Old French discrasie, from Medieval Latin dyscrāsia, from Ancient Greek δυσκρασία (duskrasía, “bad temperament”), from δυσ- (dus-, “dys-”) + κρᾶσις (krâsis, “mixing, tempering”). By surface analysis, dys- + -crasy.

parole.significato: A disease characterised by inflammation of the intestines, especially the colon (large intestine), accompanied by pus (…
parole.testo: From Middle English dissenterie, from Old French dissenterie, from Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”).

parole.significato: Desirous; keen to do or obtain something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English egre, eger, from Old French aigre, egre (modern French aigre), from Latin ācrus, variant of ācer (“sharp, keen”); see acid, acerb, etc. Compare vinegar, alegar.

parole.significato: Ebony; an ebony tree.
parole.testo: From Old French eban (modern ébène), from Latin ebenus, from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos, “ebony tree”).

parole.significato: The act of boiling.
parole.testo: From Old French ebullition, from Latin ēbullītiō, from ēbulliō (“to boil”).

parole.significato: An alignment of astronomical objects whereby one object comes between the observer (or notional observer) and another o…
parole.testo: From Middle English eclipse, from Old French eclipse, from Latin eclīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “eclipse”), from ἐκλείπω (ekleípō, “to abandon, go missing, vanish”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and λείπω (leípō, “to leave behind”). Doublet of eclipsis. See also ellipse, ellipsis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an economy.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English economike, iconomique (“household management”), and then: * from Middle French iconomique, oeconomique, and Old French iconomike (“(noun) household management; person in charge of household management; (adjective) relating to household management; relating to

parole.significato: Effective management of a community or system, or especially its resources.
parole.testo: From Middle English yconomye, yconomy, borrowed via Old French yconomie or Medieval Latin from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νέμω (némō, “distribute, allocate”). By surface analysis, eco- + -nomy.

parole.significato: Intense pleasure.
parole.testo: From Old French estaise (“ecstasy, rapture”), from Latin ecstasis, from Ancient Greek ἔκστασις (ékstasis), from ἐξίστημι (exístēmi, “to displace”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: The act of edifying, or the state of being edified or improved; a building process, especially morally, emotionally, or…
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin aedificationem (“building, construction”), an accusative form of aedificatio, from aedificare.

parole.significato: A building; a structure; an architectural fabric, especially a large and spectacular one.
parole.testo: From Middle English edifice, from Old French edifice, a classical borrowing of Latin aedificium (“building”), derived from aedificāre (“to build, establish”) (whence also English edify).

parole.significato: To build, construct.
parole.testo: From Old French edifier (“to build, to edify”), from Latin aedificare (“build”).

parole.significato: Producing the intended result; entirely adequate.
parole.testo: From Middle English effectual, effectuel, from Old French effectuel, from Late Latin effectualis.

parole.significato: Effective; possessing efficacy.
parole.testo: From Old French efficacieux (whence -acious), from Latin efficāx (“efficacious”) + -ous, from efficere (“to effect, to accomplish”); see effect.

parole.significato: The ability to produce a desired effect under ideal testing conditions.
parole.testo: From Old French efficace, from Late Latin efficācia (“efficacy”) (whence -acy), from efficāx (“efficacious”); see efficacious.

parole.significato: Making good, thorough, or careful use of resources; not consuming extra. Especially, making good use of time or energy.
parole.testo: 1398, “making,” from Old French, from Latin efficientem, nominative efficiēns, participle of efficere (“work out, accomplish”) (see effect). Meaning “productive, skilled” is from 1787. Efficiency apartment is first recorded 1930, American English.

parole.significato: Equal; impartial.
parole.testo: From Middle English egal, from Old French egal, igal, from Latin aequālis. Doublet of equal and aequalis.

parole.significato: The act or result of egesting
parole.testo: From Old French egestion, from Latin ēgestiōnem, accusative of ēgestiō (“emptying, voiding”), action noun from the perfect passive participle of ēgerō (“to carry out”), from ex- + gerō.

parole.significato: vinegar, verjuice
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English aisel, eisel, from Old French aisil, eisil (“vinegar”), from Vulgar Latin *acētillum, a diminutive of Latin acētum (“vinegar”). Compare Cornish aysel and Welsh aesel.

parole.significato: An exhilarating psychological state of pride and optimism.
parole.testo: From Middle English elacioun, from Old French elacion, from Latin ēlātiōnem, accusative singular of ēlātiō (“exaltation, elevation; pride, elation”), from ēlātus, perfect passive participle of efferō (“bring forth or out; raise; exalt”), from ē (“out of”), short form of ex, + ferō (“carry, bear”).

parole.significato: One of the simplest or essential parts or principles of which anything consists, or upon which the constitution or fund…
parole.testo: From Middle English element, from Old French element, from Latin elementum (“a first principle, element, rudiment”) (see further etymology there). The verb is from Middle English elementen, from the noun.

parole.significato: A large mammal of the family Elephantidae in the order Proboscidea, having a trunk, and native to Africa and Asia.
parole.testo: From Middle English elefant, elefaunt, from Old French elefant, elefan, olifant, re-latinized in Middle French as elephant, from Latin elephantus, from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās) (gen. ἐλέφαντος (eléphantos)). Believed to be derived from an Afroasiatic form such as Proto-Berber *eḷu (“elephant”)

parole.significato: The act of raising from a lower place, condition, or quality to a higher; said of material things, persons, the mind, t…
parole.testo: From Old French elevation, from Latin elevatio, equal to elevate + -ion.

parole.significato: Of high birth or social position; aristocratic or patrician.
parole.testo: From Middle English elit, from Old French elit, eslit (“chosen, elected”) past participle of elire, eslire (“to choose, elect”), from Latin eligere (“to choose, elect”), with past participle electus; see elect.

parole.significato: The quality of artistry and persuasiveness in speech or writing.
parole.testo: From Middle English eloquence, from Old French eloquence, from Latin ēloquentia. Doublet of eloquency, directly from Latin.

parole.significato: Fluently persuasive and articulate.
parole.testo: From Old French eloquent, from Latin eloquens (“speaking, having the faculty of speech, eloquent”), present participle of eloquor (“to speak out”), from e (“out”) + loquor (“to speak”).

parole.significato: Oblique.
parole.testo: From Middle English embelif (“oblique (adj.); obliquely (adv.)”) (compare Middle English embelink), from Old French en belif / beslif, related to Latin ob-līquus.

parole.significato: A representative symbol, such as a trademark, a badge or logo.
parole.testo: From Old French embleme, from Latin emblēma (“raised ornaments on vessels, tessellated work, mosaic”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma, “an insertion”), from ἐμβάλλειν (embállein, “to put in, to lay on”). Doublet of emblema.

parole.significato: An annual crop produced by cultivation, treated as personal property.
parole.testo: 1485, from Old French emblayement, emblaiment (“harvest, crop”), from emblaer, emblaier, emblader (French emblaver, “to sow with grain”), from Medieval Latin imblādāre (“to sow with grain”), from im- + blādum (French blé, “grain”), from Frankish *blād (“produce”), from Proto-Germanic *blēdaz, *blēdō

parole.significato: An obstruction or occlusion of a blood vessel by an embolus, that is by a blood clot, air bubble or other matter that h…
parole.testo: The term was coined in 1848 by Rudolf Virchow. From Old French embolisme (“intercalation of days in a calendar to correct errors”), from Late Latin embolismus, from Ancient Greek ἐμβολισμός (embolismós, “intercalary”), from ἐμβάλλω (embállō, “to insert, throw in”).

parole.significato: To cause (something) to stick out or swell; to extrude; also, to cause (someone or something) to be covered in swelling…
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁én The verb is derived from Late Middle English embossen, embosen, embocen (“to be bloated; to bulge; to cause to bulge; to ornament in relief, emboss”) [and other forms], from Old French embocer (modern French embosser), from em- (a variant of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + boce (“

parole.significato: Of a hunted animal: to take shelter in a forest or wood.
parole.testo: From Middle English embosen, embose, enbose (“of game: to become exhausted from hunting”), possibly from em- (a variant of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + Old French bos, bois (“woodland, woods”) (modern French bois) (from Late Latin boscus, Medieval Latin boscus (“woodlands, woods”), ultimately

parole.significato: To clasp (someone or each other) in the arms with affection; to take in the arms; to hug.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English embracen (“to clasp in one's arms, embrace; to reach out eagerly for, welcome; to enfold, entwine; to ensnare, entangle; to twist, wrap around; to gird, put on; to lace; to be in or put into bonds; to put a shield on the arm; to grasp (a shield or spear); to a

parole.significato: Any of various green gemstones, especially a green transparent form of beryl, highly valued as a precious stone.
parole.testo: From Middle English emeraude, borrowed from Old French esmeraude, from Vulgar Latin *smaralda, *smaraldus, *smaraudus, variant of Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language. Compare Hebrew בָּרֶקֶת (bāréqeṯ, “emerald, flashing gem”), Akkad

parole.significato: Someone of high rank, reputation or social status.
parole.testo: From Old French eminence, from Latin ēminentia (“prominence”, “protuberance”; “eminence”, “excellence”).

parole.significato: Payment for employment or an office; compensation for a job, which is usually monetary.
parole.testo: From Middle English emolument, from Old French emolument, from Latin ēmolumentum.

parole.significato: An empire; the status or dominion of an emperor.
parole.testo: From Middle English emperie, from Old French emperie, from Latin imperium, inperium (“command, control, dominion, sovereignty, a dominion, empire”), from imperare, inperare (“to command, order”), from in (“in, on”) + parare (“to make ready, order”). Doublet of imperium and empire.

parole.significato: A political state, often a monarchy, that has achieved a much greater current size than its initial size by conquering…
parole.testo: From Middle English empire, from Old French empire, empere, from Latin imperium, inperium (“command, control, dominion, sovereignty, a dominion, empire”), from imperare, inperare (“to command, order”), from in (“in, on”) + parare (“to make ready, order”). Doublet of empery and imperium.

parole.significato: A plaster.
parole.testo: From Old French emplastre, from Latin emplastrum, from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron).

parole.significato: An enterprise or endeavor, especially a quest or adventure.
parole.testo: Noun is from Middle English emprise, from Old French emprise, emprinse, from Late Latin *imprensa, from Latin in- + prehendere (“to take”). The verb is from emprisen, from the same source.

parole.significato: Forms a transitive verb whose meaning is to make the attached adjective
parole.testo: From Middle English en- (“en-, in-”). Originally from Old French en- (also an-), from Latin in- (“in, into”) and Frankish *in-, *int-, *anda-; but also from an alteration of in-, from Middle English in-, from Old English in- (“in, into”), from Proto-Germanic *in (“in”). Both the Latin and the German

parole.significato: To make (a bill) into law.
parole.testo: From Middle English enacten, from en-, from Old French en- (“to cause to be”), from Latin in- (“in”) and Old French acte (“perform, do”), from Latin actum, past participle of ago (“set in motion”).

parole.significato: To attract and delight, to charm.
parole.testo: From Middle English enchaunten, from Old French enchanter, from Latin incantāre. Doublet of incant.

parole.significato: One who enchants or delights.
parole.testo: From Middle English enchantour, from Old French enchanteor (Modern French enchanteur), from Latin incantātor (“enchanter; spellcaster; conjurer”), from incantāre (“to sing, to consecrate with spells”). Doublet of incantator. Equivalent to enchant + -er.

parole.significato: To surround with a wall, fence, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English enclosen, inclosen, from Middle English enclos, from Old French enclose, feminine plural past participle of enclore, from Vulgar Latin *inclaudō, *inclaudere, from Latin inclūdō (doublet of include), from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂

parole.significato: Something that is enclosed, i.e. inserted into a letter or similar package.
parole.testo: From Middle English enclosure, from Old French enclosure, from enclore, from Latin inclūdere, inclūdō, from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“key, hook, nail”). Alike to inclusion.

parole.significato: To continue or carry on, despite obstacles or hardships; to persist.
parole.testo: From Middle English enduren, from Old French endurer, from Latin indūrō (“to make hard”). Displaced Old English drēogan, which survives dialectally as dree. Doublet of dure.

parole.significato: Someone who is hostile to, feels hatred towards, opposes the interests of, or intends injury to someone else.
parole.testo: From Middle English enemy, enemye, enmy, borrowed from Old French enemi, anemi (Modern French ennemi), from Latin inimīcus, from in- (“not”) + amīcus (“friend”). Displaced Middle English fend (“enemy”), from Old English fēond (“enemy”), which survived into Modern English as fiend, but with a differe

parole.significato: To keep up, impose or bring into effect something, not necessarily by force.
parole.testo: From Middle English enforcen, from Old French enforcier, from Late Latin infortiāre, from in- + fortis (“strong”).

parole.significato: Mixed with lightning or fire.
parole.testo: From en- + Old French fouldre (“lightning”), from Latin fulgur (“lightning”), fulgere (“to flash”), + -ed.

parole.significato: To beget (of a man); to bear or conceive (of a woman).
parole.testo: From Middle English engendren, from Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerāre.

parole.significato: To encourage, to insist upon.
parole.testo: Early uses are a survival of Middle English enhorten, from Old French enorter, from Latin inhortor. The verb fell out of use during the 19th century and was formed anew in the last few decades of the 20th century as a blend of enjoin + exhort or a similar formation.

parole.significato: To lay upon, as an order or command; to give an injunction to; to direct with authority; to order; to charge.
parole.testo: From Middle English enjoinen, from Old French enjoindre (“to join with”), from Latin iniungo (“to attach”), a compound of in- (“into” “upon”) and iungo.

parole.significato: The quality of being an enemy; a hostile or unfriendly disposition.
parole.testo: From Middle English enemyte, from Old French enemisté, ennemistié, from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin *inimīcitās, *inimīcitātem, from Latin inimīcus (“enemy”). Cognate with French inimitié, Portuguese inimizade, Spanish enemistad. By surface analysis, en(e)m(y) + -ity.

parole.significato: Deviation from what is normal or standard; irregularity, abnormality.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ēnorme (“monstrous or unnatural act; enormity”), from Old French énormité (“enormity”), from Latin ēnormitās (“irregularity; enormity”), from ēnōrmis (“irregular, unusual; enormous, immense”) + -itās (suffix forming nouns indicating states of being). Ēnōrmis is derived from

parole.significato: A badge of office, rank, or power.
parole.testo: From Middle English ensigne, from Old French enseigne, from Latin īnsignia, nominative plural of īnsigne, meaning marked, distinguished. Doublet of insignia.

parole.significato: To bewitch or enchant.
parole.testo: From Old French ensorceler (“to cast a spell, enchant; to captivate”), a variant of ensorcerer, from en- (prefix meaning ‘caused’) + sorcier (“sorcerer”) (ultimately from Latin sors (“fate, lot; oracular response”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”)).

parole.significato: To follow (a leader, inclination etc.).
parole.testo: From Old French ensu-, stem of some conjugated forms of ensuivre (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French ensuivre), from Latin īnsequere, from īnsequi (“to pursue, follow, follow after; come next”), from in- (“upon”) (see in-) + sequi (“follow”) (see sequel).

parole.significato: To imply, require, or invoke.
parole.testo: From Middle English entaillen, from Old French entaillier, entailler (“to notch”, literally “to cut in”); from prefix en- + tailler (“to cut”), from Late Latin taliare, from Latin talea. Compare late Latin feudum talliatum (“a fee entailed, i.e., curtailed or limited”).

parole.significato: To go or come into an enclosed or partially enclosed space.
parole.testo: From Middle English entren, from Old French entrer, from Latin intrō (“enter”, verb), from intrā (“inside”). Has been spelled as "enter" for several centuries even in the United Kingdom, although British English and the English of many Commonwealth Countries (e.g. Australia, Canada) retain the "re"

parole.significato: To lure; to attract by arousing desire or hope.
parole.testo: From Middle English enticen, from Old French enticier (“to stir up or excite”), from a Vulgar Latin *intitiāre (“I set on fire”), from in- + titiō (“firebrand (tool)”), from Proto-Italic *tītjō (“heating”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *teih₁- (“to become hot, melt or to end”).

parole.significato: The whole; the complete or amount.
parole.testo: From Middle English enterete, from Old French entiereté, from Latin integritās, from integer (“complete, whole”). Doublet of integrity.

parole.significato: plural of entrail
parole.testo: From Middle English entraille, entrailles, from Old French entrailles, from Vulgar Latin intrālia, from Latin interānea, from interāneus, from inter. Compare Spanish entraña.

parole.significato: The act of entering.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English entre, from Old French entree (feminine past participle of the verb entrer, Modern French entrée). From Latin intrō. Doublet of entrada and entrée.

parole.significato: To surround, enclose or enfold.
parole.testo: From Middle English envolupen, from Old French anveloper, envoluper (modern French envelopper), from en- + voloper, vloper (“to wrap, wrap up”) (compare Italian -viluppare; Old Italian alternative form goluppare (“to wrap”)) from Vulgar Latin *vuloppare (“to wrap”), from Proto-Germanic *wlappaną, *w

parole.significato: Resentful desire of something possessed by another or others (but not limited to material possessions).
parole.testo: From Middle English envie, from Old French envie, from Latin invidia (“envy”), from invidere (“to look at with malice”), from in- (“on, upon”) + videre (“to look, see”). Doublet of envie. Cognate to Proto-Slavic *zavistь (“envy”). Displaced native Old English æfest and Old English nīþ.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Epicurus or Epicureanism, his philosophy.
parole.testo: From Old French Epicurien, from Latin Epicureus, from Ancient Greek Ἐπικούρειος (Epikoúreios, “Epicurean”), from Ἐπίκουρος (Epíkouros, “Epicurus”) + -ειος (-eios, “-ey: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: An inscription on a gravestone in memory of the deceased.
parole.testo: From Old French epitafe, from Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “relating to a funeral”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis epi- + -taph.

parole.significato: The act or process of equating two or more things, or the state of those things being equal (that is, identical).
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin aequātiō (“an equalizing”). Morphologically equate + -ion

parole.significato: Of or relating to the spring or autumnal equinox.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English equinoctial, equinoccial, equinoxial, from Old French equinoxial, from Latin (circulus) aequinoctiālis, from aequinoctium + -alis.

parole.significato: Fairness, impartiality, or justice as determined in light of "natural law" or "natural right".
parole.testo: From Middle English equitee, equytee, from Old French equité, from Latin aequitās (“uniformity; impartiality; fairness”).

parole.significato: A logical fallacy resulting from the use of multiple meanings of a single expression.
parole.testo: c. 1380, from Middle English equivocacion, from Old French equivocation, from Medieval Latin aequivocātiō, from aequivocō, from Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”), from Latin aequus (“equal”) + vocō (“call”); a calque of Ancient Greek ὁμωνυμία (homōnumía).

parole.significato: To make a mistake.
parole.testo: From Middle English erren, from Old French errer (“to wander, err, mistake”), from Latin errō (“wander, stray, err, mistake”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ers- (“to be angry, lose one's temper”). Cognate with Old English eorre, ierre (“anger, wrath, ire”), Old English iersian (“to be angry wit

parole.significato: A writing.
parole.testo: From Old French escrit, from Latin scrīptum, from scribō (“to write”).

parole.significato: Exceptional in importance or significance; special.
parole.testo: From Middle English especial, via Old French especial, from Latin specialis, from species (“appearance, form, beauty”), from specere (“to look”). Doublet of special. Related to species.

parole.significato: A betrothal.
parole.testo: From Middle English espousal, espousaille, from Old French espousailles, from Latin sponsalia (“a betrothal”), neuter plural of sponsalis, from spōnsus (“one betrothed, a spouse”); see spouse. By surface analysis, espouse + -al.

parole.significato: To marry.
parole.testo: From Middle English espousen, borrowed from Old French espouser, from Latin spōnsāre (frequentative of spondeō), from Proto-Indo-European *spend-.

parole.significato: To find out or observe (someone or something, especially if not easy to see) by spying or looking; to catch sight of; t…
parole.testo: From Middle English aspien, espien (“to make covert observations of (a person or place) with hostile intent, to spy on; to seek to discover by spying; to act as a spy; to catch sight of, see; to look over, observe; to wait in ambush, to ambush; to plot against; to look for, seek to find; to inquire

parole.significato: A lawyer.
parole.testo: From Middle English esquier, from Old French escuyer, escuier, properly, a shield-bearer (compare modern French écuyer (“shield-bearer, armor-bearer, squire of a knight, esquire, equerry, rider, horseman”)), from Late Latin scūtārius (“shieldmaker, shield-bearer”), from Latin scūtum (“shield”); prob

parole.significato: To excuse for failure to appear in court.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English essoyne, from Old French essoignier, from Medieval Latin exoniō, essoniō (“excuse oneself; accept an excuse”), from ex- + sonium + -ō, sonium being from Proto-West Germanic *sunnju (“care, need”).

parole.significato: To make stable or firm; to confirm.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English establissen, from Old French establiss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of establir (modern French établir), from Latin stabiliō, stabilīre, from stabilis (“firm, steady, stable”).

parole.significato: Worthy of esteem; admirable.
parole.testo: From Middle English estimable, estymable, from Old French estimable, from Latin aestimābilis. Equivalent to esteem + -able and estimate + -able.

parole.significato: The process of making an estimate.
parole.testo: From Middle English estimacioun, estimacion, from Old French estimacion, from Latin aestimatio. Morphologically estimate + -ion.

parole.significato: Of or relating to summer.
parole.testo: From Middle English estival, from Old French estival, from Latin aestivalis.

parole.significato: A six-pointed star whose rays are wavy, as opposed to the straight lines of a mullet.
parole.testo: Old French, from Latin stēlla. Doublet of étoile, stella, and stelo; related to aster and star.

parole.significato: A legal principle in the law of equity that prevents a party from asserting otherwise valid legal rights against anothe…
parole.testo: From Middle English *estoppel (found only as stoppel, stoppell, stopple, etc.), probably from Old French estoupail, estopail, estopaille, a bung made of oakum (étoupe), from Latin stuppa ("flax, tow"), from Ancient Greek στύππη (stuppē).

parole.significato: To cause to feel less close or friendly; alienate. To cease contact with (particularly of a family member or spouse, es…
parole.testo: From Old French estranger (“to treat as a stranger”), from Latin extraneus (“foreigner, stranger”) (from which also strange, stranger). Also see Spanish extraño.

parole.significato: Lasting forever; unending.
parole.testo: From Middle English eternal, from Old French eternal, from Late Latin aeternālis, from Latin aeternus (“eternal”), from aevum (“age”). Displaced native Old English ēċe.

parole.significato: Eternal.
parole.testo: From Middle English eterne, from Old French eterne, from Latin aeternus.

parole.significato: Existence without end, infinite time.
parole.testo: From Middle English eternyte, from Old French eternité, from Latin aeternitās. Displaced native Old English ēcnes.

parole.significato: A set of principles of right and wrong behaviour guiding, or representative of, a specific culture, society, group, or…
parole.testo: From Middle English etik, ethik, from Old French ethique, from Late Latin ēthica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

parole.significato: The scientific study of the origin and evolution of a word's semantic meaning across time, including its constituent mo…
parole.testo: From Middle English ethymologie, from Old French ethimologie, from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) and -λογία (-logía, “study or logic of”), from λόγος (lógos, “word; explanation”). By surface analysis, etymo- + -logy.

parole.significato: A Christian sacrament commemorating the Last Supper of Christ, with the physical forms of bread and usually wine which…
parole.testo: From Middle English eukarist, from Old French, from Ecclesiastical Latin eucharistia, from Ancient Greek εὐχαριστία (eukharistía, “gratitude, giving of thanks”). Displaced native Old English hūsl.

parole.significato: The act of evacuating; leaving a place in an orderly fashion, especially for safety.
parole.testo: From Middle English evacuacioun, from Old French evacuation, from Late Latin ēvacuātiō. Equivalent to evacuate + -ion.

parole.significato: The Christian gospel.
parole.testo: From Middle English evaungel, evangile, from Old French evangile, from Late Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”), from εὐάγγελος (euángelos, “bringing good news”), from εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + ἀγγέλλειν (angéllein, “to announce”) (English angel). The word gospel is f

parole.significato: Pertaining to the doctrines or teachings of the Christian gospel or Christianity in general.
parole.testo: From evangelic + -al, from Old French evangelique, from Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”).

parole.significato: An itinerant or special preacher, especially a revivalist, who conducts services in different cities or locations, now…
parole.testo: From Old French evangeliste, equivalent to evangel + -ist, from ecclesiastical Latin evangelista, from ecclesiastical Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs, “bringer of good news”), from εὐαγγελίζεσθαι (euangelízesthai, “to evangelize”), from εὐάγγελος (euángelos, “bringing good news”), from εὖ (

parole.significato: To tell people about (a particular branch of) Christianity, especially in order to convert them; to preach the gospel t…
parole.testo: From Old French évangéliser, equivalent to evangel + -ize, from Late Latin evangelizare, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō). Displaced native Old English godspellian (literally “to gospel”).

parole.significato: To vanish.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French esvanir, compare Latin evanescere. See evanesce, vanish.

parole.significato: Facts or observations presented in support of an assertion.
parole.testo: From Middle English evidence, from Old French [Term?], from Latin evidentia (“clearness, in Late Latin a proof”), from evidens (“clear, evident”); see evident.

parole.significato: Obviously true by simple observation.
parole.testo: From Middle English evident, from Old French evident, from Latin ēvidēns (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”) (compare Late Latin ēvideor (“to appear plainly”)), from ē (“out”) + videō (“see”), present participle vidēns, deponent videor (“to appear, seem”). Displaced native Old English sweotol.

parole.significato: To honor; to hold in high esteem; to praise or worship.
parole.testo: From Middle English exalten, from Old French exalter, from Latin exaltō.

parole.significato: The act of exalting or raising high; also, the state of being exalted; elevation.
parole.testo: From Middle English exaltacioun, exaltatioun, from Old French exaltacion and Latin exaltātiō (“exaltation, elevation”), from exaltō (“raise, elevate, exalt”), from ex (“from, out of”) + altus (“high”). By surface analysis, exalt + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of examining.
parole.testo: From Middle English examinacioun, from Old French examinacion, from Latin exāminātiō. Morphologically examine + -ation.

parole.significato: To observe carefully or critically to learn about someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle English examinen, examenen, from Old French examiner, from Latin exāmināre.

parole.significato: Something that is representative of all such things in a group.
parole.testo: From Middle English example, exaumple, from Old French example, essaumple, from Latin exemplum (“sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.”, literally “what is taken out”); see exempt. Doublet of exemplum and sample. Displaced native Middle English forebisne, from Old English forebȳsn; and

parole.significato: To be larger, greater than (something).
parole.testo: From Middle English exceden, from Old French exceder, from Latin excēdō (“to go beyond”), from ex- (“out, forth”) with cēdō (“to go”); see cede and compare accede etc. Partly displaced native Old English ofersteppan, whence Modern English overstep.

parole.significato: To surpass someone or something; to be better or do better than someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle English excellen, from Old French exceller, from Latin excellere, excelsum; ex (“out”) + *cellō, an unattested verb root found in culmen (“height, top”); Compare French exceller. See also culminate, column.

parole.significato: The quality of being excellent; brilliance
parole.testo: From Middle English excellence, from Old French excellence, from Latin excellentia.

parole.significato: Having excelled, having surpassed.
parole.testo: From Middle English excellent, from Old French excellent, from Latin excellēns (“elevated, exalted”), present participle of excellō (“elevate, exult”), equivalent to excel + -ent.

parole.significato: The state of surpassing or going beyond a limit; the state of being beyond sufficiency, necessity, or duty; more than w…
parole.testo: From Middle English exces (“excess, ecstasy”), from Old French exces, from Latin excessus (“a going out, loss of self-possession”), from excedere, excessum (“to go out, go beyond”). See exceed.

parole.significato: Exceeding the usual bounds of something; too much (of amount); extravagant; immoderate.
parole.testo: From Middle English excessive, excessif, from Old French excessif, from Medieval Latin excessivus, equivalent to excess + -ive.

parole.significato: The act of exciting or putting in motion; the act of rousing up or awakening.
parole.testo: From Middle English excitacion, excitacioun, from Old French excitation, from Latin excitātiō. Morphologically excite + -ation.

parole.significato: To stir the emotions of; to cause to feel excitement.
parole.testo: From Middle English exciten, from Old French exciter, from Latin excitō (“to call out, call forth, arouse, wake up, stimulate”), frequentative of excieō (“to call out, arouse, excite”), from ex (“out”) + cieō (“to call, summon”). See cite and compare to accite, concite, incite.

parole.significato: The act of excluding or shutting out; removal from consideration or taking part.
parole.testo: From Middle English exclusion, exclusioun, from Old French [Term?] and Latin exclusiō, from exclūdō. By surface analysis, exclude + -sion.

parole.significato: Possible to excuse; worthy of being excused.
parole.testo: From Old French escusable, from Latin excusabilis.

parole.significato: Of the poorest quality.
parole.testo: From Old French execrable, from Latin execrabilis.

parole.significato: To kill, especially as punishment for a capital crime.
parole.testo: From Old French executer (French exécuter), from Latin exsecutus, past participle of exsequor (“to follow (up/through)”, particularly in the sense “to go through with a deed or punishment”), from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”).

parole.significato: The act, manner or style of executing (actions, maneuvers, performances).
parole.testo: From Old French execution (c.1360), from Latin exsecutiō, an agent noun from exsequor (“to follow out”), from ex (“out”) + sequor (“follow”). Equivalent to execute + -ion.

parole.significato: An act of exempting.
parole.testo: From Old French exemption, from Latin exemptiō, from eximō, equivalent to exempt + -ion.

parole.significato: Funeral rites.
parole.testo: A back-formation from exequies, from Middle English exequies, from Old French exequies, from Latin exsequiās, accusative of exsequiae (“a funeral, seeing-off procession”).

parole.significato: Any activity designed to develop or hone a skill or ability.
parole.testo: From Middle English exercise, from Old French exercise, from Latin exercitium. Displaced native Old English plega (“an exercise”) whence Modern English play.

parole.significato: To urge; to advise earnestly.
parole.testo: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + hortārī (“to incite, spur”).

parole.significato: The act or practice of exhorting.
parole.testo: From Middle English exhortacioun, from Old French exhortacion, from Latin exhortātiōnem, accusative singular of exhortātiō (“encouraging; exhortation”), from exhortor (“to encourage, exhort”), from ex (“out of, from”) + hortor (“encourage”). By surface analysis, exhort + -ation.

parole.significato: The state of being banished from one's home or country.
parole.testo: From Middle English exil, borrowed from Old French essil, exil, from Latin exsilium, exilium (“state of exile”), derived from exsul, exul (“exiled person”).

parole.significato: The state of being, existing, or occurring; beinghood.
parole.testo: From Middle English existence, from Old French existence, from Late Latin existentia (“existence”), from existēns, from existō, exsistō (“I am, I exist”), from ex (“out”) + sistere (“to set, place”) (related to stare (“to stand, to be stood”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from t

parole.significato: Exceeding proper limits; excessive or unduly high; extravagant.
parole.testo: From Middle English exorbitant, through Old French from Late Latin exorbitāns, present active participle of exorbitō (“to go out of the track”), from ex (“out”) + orbita (“wheel-track”); see orbit. Compare French exorbitant.

parole.significato: The ritual act of driving out evil spirits from persons, places or things that are possessed by them.
parole.testo: From Old French exorciser, from Late Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to ward off, to charge under oath, adjure”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos).

parole.significato: Marked by expectation.
parole.testo: From Old French expectant, from Latin expectans.

parole.significato: The quality of being fit or suitable to cause some desired end or the purpose intended; propriety or advisability under…
parole.testo: From Middle English expedience, from Old French expedience, from Late Latin expedientia, from Latin expediens.

parole.significato: Suitable to effect some desired end or the purpose intended.
parole.testo: From Middle English expedient, from Old French expedient, from Latin expediens (stem expedient-), present participle of expedire (“to bring forward, to dispatch, to expedite; impers. to be profitable, serviceable, advantageous, expedient”), from ex (“out”) + pēs (“foot, hoof”).

parole.significato: The effect upon the judgment or feelings produced by any event, whether witnessed or participated in; personal and dire…
parole.testo: From Middle English experience, from Old French, from Latin experientia (“a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience”), from experiens, present participle of experiri (“to try, put to the test, undertake, undergo”), from ex (“out”) + peritus (“experienced, expert”), past particip

parole.significato: A test under controlled conditions made to either demonstrate a known truth, examine the validity of a hypothesis, or d…
parole.testo: From Middle English experiment, from Old French esperiment (French expérience), from Latin experimentum (“experience, attempt, experiment”), from experior (“to experience, to attempt”), itself from ex + *perior, in turn from Proto-Indo-European *per-.

parole.significato: Extraordinary capable or knowledgeable.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English expert, derived from Old French expert (“experienced”), espert, from Latin expertus (contracted from *experitus), perfect active participle of experior (“to try”), from ex- + *-perior.

parole.significato: To make plain, manifest, or intelligible; to clear of obscurity; to illustrate the meaning of.
parole.testo: From Middle English explanen, from Old French explaner, from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”), from ex- (“out”) + planō (“to flatten, make level”), from planus (“level, plain”); see plain and plane. Compare esplanade, splanade. Displaced Old English reċċan.

parole.significato: To reveal; to uncover; to make visible; to bring to light.
parole.testo: From Middle English exposen, from Old French exposer (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin expōnō (“set forth”), with contamination from poser (“to lay, place”). Doublet of expone and expound (via Old French espondre (“to set forth, explain”)), from the same Latin term.

parole.significato: The action of exposing something to something, such as skin to the sunlight.
parole.testo: From Middle English exposicioun, from Old French esposicion, from Latin expositiō, from expōnere (“to put forth”). The sense meaning "exhibition" is a later semantic loan from French exposition.

parole.significato: To set out the meaning of; to explain or discuss at length.
parole.testo: From Middle English expounden, from Old French espondre, from Latin exponere. Doublet of expone and expose.

parole.significato: To convey or communicate; to make known or explicit.
parole.testo: From Old French espresser, expresser, from frequentative form of Latin exprimere.

parole.significato: To take by storm; capture.
parole.testo: From Middle English expugnen, from Old French expugner, from Latin expugnō (“to take by storm”), from ex- + pugnō (“fight”), from pugnus (“fist”).

parole.significato: The act of expelling or the state of being expelled.
parole.testo: From Middle English expulsioun, from Old French expulsion, from Latin expulsio, expulsionem.

parole.significato: The act of extracting or the condition of being extracted.
parole.testo: From Old French estraction, from Medieval Latin extractio.

parole.significato: Of a place, the most remote, farthest or outermost.
parole.testo: Borrowed into late Middle English from Old French extreme, from Latin extrēmus, the superlative of exter.

parole.significato: The most extreme or furthest point of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English extremite, from Old French extremité, from Latin extrēmitātem (“extremity; border, perimeter; ending”), from extrēmīs (“furthest, extreme”) + -itās (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being); see extreme. Extrēmīs is derived f

parole.significato: The act of exulting; great joy at success or victory, or at any advantage gained; rapturous delight
parole.testo: From Middle English exultacion, from Old French exultacion, from Latin exsultātiō, exsultātiōnem.

parole.significato: A journey taken by certain Medieval English itinerant judges (justices in eyre)
parole.testo: From Middle English eire, from Old French erre (“journey, march, way”), from Latin iter, itineris (“a going, way”), from the root of ire (“to go”). Compare errant, itinerant, issue.

parole.significato: The nest of a bird of prey.
parole.testo: From Middle English eire, aire, from Old French aire or Medieval Latin aeria. Old French aire, in the sense of an eagle's nest, may have derived from Latin ager, or may less likely be related to the other senses, ultimately from Latin ārea.

parole.significato: A fictitious narrative intended to enforce some useful truth or precept, usually with animals, etc. as characters; an a…
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French fable, from Latin fābula, from fārī (“to speak, say”) + -bula (“instrumental suffix”). See ban, and compare fabulous, fame. Doublet of fabula.

parole.significato: The front part of the head of a human or other animal, featuring the eyes, nose, and mouth, and the surrounding area.
parole.testo: From Middle English face, from Old French face, from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“form, appearance”). Doublet of facies. parole.significato: Something actual as opposed to invented.
parole.testo: From Old French fact, from Latin factum (“an act, deed, feat, etc.”); also Medieval Latin for “state, condition, circumstance”; neuter of factus (“done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). parole.testo: From Middle English faculte (“power, property”), from Old French faculte, from Latin facultas (“capability, ability, skill, abundance, plenty, stock, goods, property; in Medieval Latin also a body of teachers”), another form of facilitas (“easiness, facility, etc.”), from facul, another form of faci

parole.significato: A gender-neutral third-person singular subject pronoun, equivalent to singular they, and coordinate with gendered prono…
parole.testo: From Old French fae, from Medieval Latin fāda. The use of the pronoun appears c. 2013.

parole.significato: A bundle of sticks or brushwood intended to be used for fuel tied together for carrying. (Some sources specify that a f…
parole.testo: From Middle English fagot, from Old French fagot (“bundle of sticks”), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: To make a fagot of (objects); to bind (objects) together in a fagot or bundle.
parole.testo: Most likely from Italian fagotto, from Latin fascis.

parole.significato: To be unsuccessful.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English failen, borrowed from Old French falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallire, alteration of Latin fallere (“to deceive, disappoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰāl- (“to lie, deceive”) or Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el- (“to stumble”). Compare Alemannic German fääle (“to lack”)

parole.significato: Lacking strength; weak; languid; inclined to lose consciousness
parole.testo: From Middle English faynt, feynt (“weak; feeble”), from Old French faint, feint (“feigned; negligent; sluggish”), past participle of feindre, faindre (“to feign; sham; work negligently”), from Latin fingere (“to touch, handle, form, shape, frame, form in thought, imagine, conceive, contrive, devise,

parole.significato: A community gathering to celebrate and exhibit local achievements.
parole.testo: From Middle English feyre, from Old French foire, from Latin fēriae.

parole.significato: A mythical being of human form with magical powers, known in many sizes and descriptions, although typically depicted a…
parole.testo: From Middle English faierie, fairie, from Old French faerie, from fae (from Latin fāta (“goddess of fate”)) + -erie. Equivalent to fay + -ry. parole.significato: A trust or confidence in the intentions or abilities of a person, object, or ideal from prior empirical evidence.
parole.testo: From Middle English faith (also fay), borrowed from Old French fei, feid, from Latin fidem. Doublet of foy. Displaced native Old English ġelēafa, which was also a word for belief. * Old French had [θ] as a final devoiced allophone of /ð/ from lenited Latin /d/; this eventually fell silent in the 12t

parole.significato: A somewhat curved, single-edged medieval sword of European origin, with the cutting edge on its convex side, whose desi…
parole.testo: From Middle English fauchoun, from Old French fauchon (cognate with Italian falcione), from Vulgar Latin *falciōnem, from Latin falx.

parole.significato: Any bird of the genus Falco, all of which are birds of prey.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English faucoun, falcon, faulcon, from Old French falcun, from Late Latin falcō (“falcon”), of Germanic origin, probably via Frankish *falkō (“falcon, hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *falkô (“falcon”), from Proto-Indo-European *pol̑- (“pale”), from *pel- (“fallow”). parole.significato: Characterized by fallacy; false or mistaken.
parole.testo: From Old French fallacieux (whence -acious), from Latin fallācia, from fallāx, from fallere.

parole.significato: Deceptive or false appearance; that which misleads the eye or the mind.
parole.testo: From Middle English fallaci, fallace, fallas, from Old French fallace (whence -acy), from Latin fallācia (“deception, deceit”), from fallāx (“deceptive, deceitful”), from fallere (“to deceive”).

parole.significato: Something said or reported; gossip, rumour.
parole.testo: From Middle English fame, from Old French fame (“celebrity, renown”), itself borrowed from Latin fāma (“talk, rumor, report, reputation”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéh₂-meh₂, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak, say, tell”).
