parole.significato: The imagination.
parole.testo: From Middle English fansy, fantsy, a contraction of fantasy, fantasye, fantasie, from Old French fantasie, from Medieval Latin fantasia, from Late Latin phantasia (“an idea, notion, fancy, phantasm”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to render visible”), from φαντός

parole.significato: A vestment reserved only for the Pope for use during a pontifical Mass.
parole.testo: From Middle English fanon, fanoun, from Old French fanon, from Medieval Latin fanō, from Frankish *fano, from Proto-Germanic *fanô. Doublet of fane and vane.

parole.significato: That which comes from one's imagination or the act of imagining things.
parole.testo: Noun inherited from Middle English fantasie, from Old French fantasie (“fantasy”), from Latin phantasia (“imagination”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía, “apparition”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to render visible”), from φαντός (phantós, “visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to make visible”); from

parole.significato: Someone or something that farms, as:
parole.testo: From Middle English fermour (“a steward, bailliff, collector of taxes”), from Old French fermier (“a farmer, a lessee, husbandman, bailliff”), from Medieval Latin firmarius (“one to whom land is rented, a collector of taxes, deputy”), from firma; equivalent to farm + -er. Compare Old English feormer

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; alternatively; or from; nodo incerto nell'albero
parole.significato: An exposed plumbing fitting; a tap or spigot; a regulator for controlling the flow of a liquid from a reservoir.
parole.testo: From Middle English faucet, fawcett, from Old French fausset, of uncertain origin: * Possibly from Late Latin falsāre (“to falsify”) or from a diminutive of Latin faux, faucēs (“throat”). * Alternatively, from Old Norse foss, fors (“waterfall”), thus, cognate with English force, foss.

parole.significato: flattery; cajolery; deceit
parole.testo: From Old French favele, from Latin fabella (“short fable”), diminutive of fabula. See fable.

parole.significato: A kind or helpful deed; an instance of voluntarily assisting (someone).
parole.testo: From Middle English favour, favor, faver, from Anglo-Norman favour, from mainland Old French favor, from Latin favor (“good will; kindness; partiality”), from faveō (“to be kind to”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂weh₁yeti (“to be favourable to”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂

parole.significato: Apt to win favour; pleasing.
parole.testo: From Middle English favourable, from Old French favorable, from Latin favōrābilis, from favor. By surface analysis, favour + -able.

parole.significato: A young deer.
parole.testo: From Middle English fawne, fowne, foun, from Old French faon, foon, feon, from Vulgar Latin *fētōnem, from Latin fētus (“offspring, young”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle, nurse”). Displaced native Old English hindċealf (literally “deer calf”). Doublet of fetus.

parole.significato: A fair, a market.
parole.testo: From Old French foire, from Latin fēriae.

parole.significato: A holiday, festival, especially a religious one
parole.testo: From Middle English feeste, feste, borrowed from Old French feste, from Late Latin festa, from the plural of Latin festum (“holiday, festival, feast”), from Proto-Italic *fēs-tos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“god, godhead, deity”); see also Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god, goddess”)

parole.significato: To partake in a feast, or large meal.
parole.testo: From Middle English feesten, festen, from Old French fester, from Medieval Latin festāre, from the noun. See above.

parole.significato: Neat, pretty.
parole.testo: From Middle English fetis, from Old French fetis, faitis, from Latin factīcius. Doublet of factitious. The spelling reflects an assumption that the word was derived from feat (“dexterous, neat”) + -ous.

parole.significato: An amount charged in return for permission to do something
parole.testo: From Middle English fee, fe, feh, feoh, from Old English feoh (“cattle, property, wealth, money, payment, tribute, fee”) with contamination from Old French fieu, fief (from Medieval Latin fevum, a variant of feudum (see feud), from Frankish *fehu (“cattle, livestock”); whence fief), both from Proto-

parole.significato: To make a false show or pretence of; to counterfeit or simulate.
parole.testo: From Middle English feynen, feinen, borrowed from Old French feindre (“to pretend”), from Latin fingere (“to form, shape, invent”). Compare French feignant (present participle of feindre, literally “feigning”). Also compare feint, figment and fiction.

parole.significato: The condition of being happy.
parole.testo: From Middle English felicite (“bliss, happiness, joy; delight, pleasure; a source of happiness; good fortune; prosperity; well-being; of a planet: in an influential position”) [and other forms], borrowed from Old French felicité (modern French félicité (“bliss, happiness; felicity”)), from Latin fēl

parole.significato: Of a person or animal, their actions, thoughts, etc.: brutal, cruel, harsh, heartless; also, evil, wicked.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle English feloun, felun (“base, wicked; hostile; of an animal: dangerous; of words: angry, harsh, slanderous; of things: dangerous, deadly; false, fraudulent; unlucky”) [and other forms], from Old French felon (“bad, evil, immoral”) (compare fel (“evil; despicable,

parole.significato: A small infected sore; an abscess, a boil.
parole.testo: From Middle English feloun, felone (“type of carbuncle or sore with pus; swelling on a hawk’s body”), possibly from Old French *felon, from Latin fel (“bile, gall; bitterness; poison; venom”): see etymology 1.

parole.significato: One of the female (feminine) sex or gender.
parole.testo: From Middle English female, an alteration of Middle English femele, from Old French femele, femelle (“female”), from Medieval Latin fēmella (“a female”), from Latin fēmella (“a girl, a young female, a young woman”), diminutive of fēmina (“a woman”). The English spelling and pronunciation were remode

parole.significato: The lantern, louvre, or covering placed in the ridge of a hall roof for the purpose of ventilation or letting out the s…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle English fumerelle, from Old French fumeraille; ultimately derived from Latin fumus (“smoke”). Likely a doublet of fumarole.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the female gender.
parole.testo: From Middle English feminine, femynyne, femynyn, from Old French feminin, feminine, from Latin fēminīnus, from fēmina (“woman”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-eh₂ (“(the one) nursing, breastfeeding”). Related to fetus, feminism, filial, fellatio.

parole.significato: A woman; a wife; (now chiefly Canada, US) a young woman or girl.
parole.testo: From Middle English femme, itself borrowed from Old French fame (whence French femme), from Latin femina (“woman”). Doublet of feme, femina, and hembra.

parole.significato: To take care of oneself; to take responsibility for one's own well-being.
parole.testo: From Middle English fenden (“defend, fight, prevent”), shortening of defenden (“defend”), from Old French deffendre (Modern French défendre), from Latin dēfendō (“to ward off”), from dē- + *fendō (“hit, thrust”), from Proto-Italic *fendō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- (“strike, kill”).

parole.significato: A slit or crack.
parole.testo: From Old French fente, from Latin findēre (“to cleave”).

parole.significato: Any of the species leguminous plant, Trigonella foenum-graecum, eaten as a vegetable and with seeds used as a spice.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English fenygreke, borrowed from Old French fenigrec, from Latin foenum-graecum (literally “Greek hay”), from foenum (“hay”, variant of faenum) + graecus (“Greek”).

parole.significato: The grant of a feud or fee.
parole.testo: From Old French feoffement, fieffement. Compare Latin feoffamentum.

parole.significato: A holiday.
parole.testo: From Middle English ferie, from Old French ferie, from Latin feriae (“holidays”). See fair.

parole.significato: An often domesticated mammal (Mustela putorius furo) rather like a weasel, descended from the European polecat and ofte…
parole.testo: From Middle English furet, ferret, from Old French furet, from Vulgar Latin *furittum (“weasel, ferret”), diminutive of Latin fūr (“thief”).

parole.significato: The medieval chess piece that developed into the modern queen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle English fers, from Old French fierce, from Medieval Latin ferzia, from Classical Persian فَرْزِین (farzīn).

parole.significato: Very hot; burning, scorching; also, glowing with heat.
parole.testo: From Middle English fervent, from Old French fervent (modern French fervent), from Latin ferventem, the accusative masculine or feminine singular form of fervēns (“burning, fiery; hot; zealous; etc.”), the present active participle of ferveō (“to burn; to be hot; (figurative) to be agitated, fired u

parole.significato: An intense, heated emotion; passion, ardor.
parole.testo: From Middle English fervour, from Old French, from Latin fervor (“a boiling or raging heat, heat, vehemence, passion”), from fervere (“to boil, be hot”); see fervent. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + -or (“abstract noun suffix”).

parole.significato: A straw, wire, stick, etc., used chiefly to point out letters to children when learning to read.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English festu, from Old French festu (modern fétu), from Late Latin *festūcum, from Latin festūca (“stalk, stem, straw”).

parole.significato: A horizontal band across the middle of the shield.
parole.testo: From Middle English fesse, from Old French fesse, an alteration of faisse, from Latin fascia. Cognate with fajita, fascia, and fascism.

parole.significato: A fistula.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English festre, festur, borrowed from Old French festre (cognate with Italian fistola, Occitan fistola, Spanish fístula), from Latin fistula. The verb is derived from the noun, while the “condition of something that festers” noun sense is derived from the verb. Doublet of fistu

parole.significato: Pertaining to a feast or feast day; festive. (Now only as the noun used attributively.)
parole.testo: From Middle English festival (adjective), from Old French festival (“festive”), from Late Latin fēstīvālis, from Latin fēstīvus (“festive”). By surface analysis, festive + -al. Displaced native Old English frēols. The noun is shortened from festival day, from Middle English festival dai, festiuall d

parole.significato: Of, or relating to feudalism.
parole.testo: From Old French feodal, from Medieval Latin feodalis, from feodum, feudum, fevum (“fief, fee”), from Frankish *fehu (“cattle, owndom, property, fee”), from Proto-Germanic *fehu (“cattle”). By surface analysis, feud (“estate”) + -al. More at fee.

parole.significato: A higher than normal body temperature of a person (or, generally, a mammal), usually caused by disease.
parole.testo: From Middle English fever, fevere, from Old English fefer, fefor (“fever”) and Old French fievre (“fever”), from Latin febris (“a fever”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”). Displaced native Old English hriþ (“fever”). Compare also Saterland Frisian Fiewer, German Fieber, Danish feber, S

parole.significato: A support or holder for a spear, attached to a saddle or breastplate.
parole.testo: From Middle English feuter, fewtre, from Old French feutre, from Medieval Latin filtrum, of Germanic origin. Doublet of filter.

parole.significato: Literary type using invented or imaginative writing, instead of real facts, usually written as prose.
parole.testo: From Middle English ficcioun, from Old French ficcion (“dissimulation, ruse, invention”), from Latin fictiō (“a making, fashioning, a feigning, a rhetorical or legal fiction”), from fingō (“to form, mold, shape, devise, feign”). Displaced native Old English lēasspell (literally “false story”); see f

parole.significato: Often followed by to or towards: faithfulness or loyalty towards a person, a group, one's civic or moral duties, etc.;…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English fidelite (“allegiance, fealty; faithfulness, trust; agreement made in good faith”), from Old French fidélité (“faithfulness, fidelity”) (modern French fidélité), from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness, fidelity”), from fidēlis (“dependable, trustworthy; faithful, loyal”) + -tās

parole.significato: Sometimes followed by on or upon: used to express distaste, disgust, or outrage.
parole.testo: From Middle English fy, from Old French fi, from Latin fī. (with a possible additional influence from Old Norse). Compare Swedish fy.

parole.significato: Exceedingly violent, severe, ferocious, cruel or savage.
parole.testo: From Middle English fers, fiers, borrowed from Old French fers (“wild", "ferocious”), nominative of fer, from Latin ferus (“wild", "untamed”).

parole.significato: Representing by means of a figure; emblematic.
parole.testo: From Old French figural, from late Latin figūrālis, from figūra (“figure”).

parole.significato: A drawing or diagram conveying information.
parole.testo: From Middle English figure, borrowed from Old French figure, from Latin figūra (“form, shape, form of a word, a figure of speech, Late Latin a sketch, drawing”), from fingō (“to form, shape, mold, fashion”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold, shape, form, knead”). Cognate with Ancient Gree

parole.significato: To commit (official papers) to some office.
parole.testo: From Old French fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”). Doublet of filum.

parole.significato: A headband; a ribbon or other band used to tie the hair up, or keep a headdress in place, or for decoration.
parole.testo: From Middle English filet, vylette, felet, filette, flette, from Old French filet, diminutive of fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

parole.significato: A final examination; a test or examination given at the end of a term or class; the test that concludes a class.
parole.testo: From Middle English final, fynal, fynall, from Old French final, from Latin fīnālis (“of or relating to the end or to boundaries”), from fīnis (“end”); see fine. Replaced native English endly (“final”).

parole.significato: Senses referring to subjective quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English fin, fyn, from Old French fin (“fine, minute, exact”), of obscure origin, but probably derived from Latin fīnīre (“to finish”) or fīnis (“boundary, limit, end”), with an abstract sense of fine or thin also arising in many Romance languages (compare Italian, Portuguese, and Spanis

parole.significato: A fee levied as punishment for breaking the law.
parole.testo: From Middle English fyn, fyne, from Old French fin, from Medieval Latin fīnis (“a payment in settlement or tax”). Doublet of fin and finis.

parole.significato: Especially in Gothic architecture: an ornament, often in the form of a bunch or knot of foliage, on the peak of the gab…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English finial (“(adjective) final; (noun) ornament at the upper extremity of a pinnacle, spire, etc.”) [and other forms], a variant of final (“pertaining to the close or end of something, last, final”), from Old French final (“last, final; definitive”) (modern French final), from L

parole.significato: An end; the end of anything.
parole.testo: From Middle English finishen, finisshen, finischen, from Old French finiss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of finir, from Latin fīnīre, from fīnis (“end, limit, border, boundary”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, set up”) or from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”)

parole.significato: Steadfast, secure, solid (in position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ferme, borrowed from Old French ferme, from Medieval Latin ferma. From Middle English ferme, from Old French ferme, from Latin firmus (“strong, steady”). Doublet of dharma.

parole.significato: To make firm or strong; fix securely.
parole.testo: From Middle English fermen (“to make firm”), partly from (either through Old French fermer or directly) Latin firmō, from firmus (“firm”, adjective), and partly a new formation on the adjective.

parole.significato: A long, narrow crack or opening made by breaking or splitting, especially in rock or earth.
parole.testo: From Middle English fissure, from Old French fissure, from Latin fissūra (“a cleft, chink”), from findō (“to cleave, split, divide”) + -tūra (nominal suffix).

parole.significato: To pierce; now generally replaced by transfix.
parole.testo: From Middle English fixen, borrowed from Old French *fixer (attested only as ficher, fichier; > English fitch), from fix (“fastened; fixed”), from Latin fīxus (“immovable; steady; stable; fixed”), from fīgō (“to drive in; stick; fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to jab; stick; set”). Rel

parole.significato: Guilty of terrible crimes; wicked, criminal.
parole.testo: From Old French flagitieux or Latin flāgitiōsus, both ultimately from flāgitium (“shameful crime”), related to flagrum (“whip”).

parole.significato: A natural or innate talent or aptitude.
parole.testo: From Middle English flayre, from Old French flair (“scent, odour”), from flairier (“to reek, smell”), from Latin flāgrō, dissimilated variation of frāgrō (“emit a sweet smell”, verb). More at fragrant.

parole.significato: A long, shallow basket with two handles.
parole.testo: From Middle English flasket, from Old French flaschet, diminutive of Old French flasche, from Late Latin flasca. Related to Welsh fflasged (“a vessel of straw or wickerwork”), fflasg (“flask, basket”), and English flask.

parole.significato: The quality produced by the sensation of taste or, especially, of taste and smell in combined effect.
parole.testo: From Middle English flavour meaning “smell, odour”, usually pleasing, borrowed from Old French flaour (“smell, odour”) (cfr. Sicilian ciàguru, its etymology and semantic), from Vulgar Latin *flātor (“odour, that which blows”), from Latin flātor (“blower”), from flō, flāre (“to blow, puff”), ultimate

parole.significato: A flan (custard-based dessert)
parole.testo: From Middle English flaun, flaon, flawn, from Old French flaon, from Late Latin fladonem, accusative of flado, from Frankish *flaþō. Doublet of flan, flathe, and flathon.

parole.significato: Coarse tufts of wool or cotton used in bedding.
parole.testo: From Middle English flok (“tuft of wool”), from Old French floc (“tuft of wool”), from Late Latin floccus (“tuft of wool”), probably from Frankish *flokko (“down, wool, flock”), from Proto-Germanic *flukkōn-, *flukkan-, *fluksōn- (“down, flock”), from Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“hair, fibres, tuft

parole.significato: To thrive or grow well.
parole.testo: From Middle English floryschen, from Old French florir (via the arrhizotonic stem floriss-), from Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre, from Latin flōrem (“flower”, noun). Corresponds to flower + -ish.

parole.significato: A ravine or gorge, usually one with water running through.
parole.testo: From Middle English flum, from Old French flum, flun, from Latin flumen, from fluere (“to flow”).

parole.significato: The act of flowing; a continuous moving on or passing by, as of a flowing stream.
parole.testo: From Old French flux, from Latin fluxus (“flow”).

parole.significato: To prevent (something) from being accomplished.
parole.testo: From Middle English foilen (“spoil a scent trail by crossing it”), from Old French fouler (“tread on, trample”), ultimately from Latin fullō (“to trample, full”).

parole.significato: A thrust.
parole.testo: From Old French foene (“harpoon, fizgig”), from Latin fuscina (“trident”).

parole.significato: An abundance, a rich supply of.
parole.testo: From Middle English foisoun, from Old French foison, from Latin fūsiōnem. Doublet of fusion.

parole.significato: A type of light and fast-sailing ship.
parole.testo: From Old French fuste (“stick, boat”), from Latin fustis (“cudgel”).

parole.significato: A cask for wine.
parole.testo: From Old French fust (whence also French fût), from Latin fustis.

parole.significato: To incite or cause troublesome acts; to encourage; to instigate.
parole.testo: From Middle English fomenten, a borrowing from Old French fomenter, from Late Latin fōmentāre, from Latin fōmentum (“lotion”), from fovēre (“heat, cherish”).

parole.significato: A person with poor judgment or little intelligence.
parole.testo: From Middle English fol (“fool”), from Old French fol (cf. modern French fou (“mad”)) from Latin follis. Doublet of fals and follis. Displaced native Old English dwæs.

parole.significato: Marked by unthinking recklessness with disregard for danger; boldly rash; hotheaded.
parole.testo: From Middle English folehardy, foolhardi, folherdi, from Old French fol hardi (“foolishly bold”), from Old French fol (“foolish, silly; insane, mad”) (from Latin follis (“bellows; purse, sack; inflated ball; belly, paunch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”)) + Old French har

parole.significato: Ability to influence; strength or energy of body or mind; active power; vigour; might; capacity of exercising an influe…
parole.testo: From Middle English force, fors, forse, from Old French force, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise, high, hill”).

parole.significato: To make someone or something do something, often regardless of their will.
parole.testo: From Middle English forcen, from Old French forcier, from Late Latin *fortiāre, from Latin fortia.

parole.significato: Located outside a country or place, especially one's own.
parole.testo: From Middle English foreyn, forein, from Old French forain, from Vulgar Latin *forānus (“outsider, outlander”), from Latin forās (“outside, outdoors”) or forīs (“outside, outdoors”). Displaced native Old English elþēodiġ (“foreign”) and now-dialectal English fremd, from Old English fremde (“strange,

parole.significato: A penalty for or consequence of a misdemeanor.
parole.testo: From Middle English forfait from ca. 1300, from Old French forfait (“crime”), originally the past participle of forfaire (“to transgress”), and Medieval Latin foris factum. During the 15th century, the sense shifted from the crime to the penalty for the crime.

parole.significato: A furnace or hearth where metals are heated prior to hammering them into shape.
parole.testo: From Middle English forge, from Old French forge, early Old French faverge, from Latin fabrica (“workshop”), from faber (“workman in hard materials, smith”) (genitive fabri). Cognate with Franco-Provençal favèrge. Doublet of fabric and fabrica. Partially displaced English smithy. * Computing sense p

parole.significato: In accordance with established forms.
parole.testo: From Middle English formel, borrowed from Old French formel, from Latin fōrmālis, from fōrma (“form”); equivalent to form + -al.

parole.significato: The act of assembling a group or structure.
parole.testo: From Middle English formacioun, formation, borrowed from Old French formacion, from Latin fōrmātiō, from fōrmō (“form”, verb); see form as verb. Morphologically form + -ation.

parole.significato: Capable of forming something.
parole.testo: From Middle English formatyve, formatif (“having the ability to form”), from Old French formatif, formative (modern French formatif), from Medieval Latin formātīvus, from Latin fōrmātus + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘doing’ or ‘related to doing’). Fōrmātus is the perfect passive

parole.significato: A writ of right for a tenant in tail in case of a discontinuance of the estate tail.
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?], from Latin [Term?], so called because the plaintiff claimed “by the form of the gift”: per formam doni.

parole.significato: Causing fear, dread, awe, or discouragement as a result of size, strength, or some other impressive feature; commanding…
parole.testo: From Middle English formidable, from Old French formidable, formible, from Latin formīdābilis (“formidable, terrible”) (whence -able), from formīdō (“fear, dread”).

parole.significato: Beauty.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English formosite, formosyte, from Old French formosité, from Latin fōrmōsitās (“beauty”). Cognate to French formosité, Scots formosite.

parole.significato: Sexual intercourse by people who are not married to each other, or which is considered illicit in another way.
parole.testo: From Middle English fornicacioun, from Old French fornicacion, from Latin fornicātiō, from fornix (“brothel”).

parole.significato: To give power, strength, or vigour to (oneself or someone, or to something); to strengthen.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English fortifien, fortfien (“to strengthen (a castle, etc.) from attack; to strengthen (an army, etc.); to strengthen (a person), aid, support; to reinforce, support; to improve; to increase the efficacy of”), from Old French fortifier (modern French fortifier), from Late Latin for

parole.significato: Mental or emotional strength that enables courage in the face of adversity.
parole.testo: From Middle English fortitude, from Old French, from Latin fortitūdō (“bravery, strength”), from fortis (“brave, strong”).

parole.significato: A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; for example a fort, a castle; a str…
parole.testo: Early 14 c., from Old French forteresce, forteresse, forterece (“strong place, fortification”), variant of fortelesse, from Medieval Latin fortalitia, from Latin fortis (“strong”) (see fort) + -itia, added to adjectives to form nouns of quality or condition. French -ess, from Latin -itia is also in

parole.significato: Destiny, especially favorable.
parole.testo: From Middle English fortune, from Old French fortune, from Latin fortuna (“fate, luck”). The plural form fortunae meant “possessions”, which also gave fortune the meaning of “riches”.

parole.significato: To flash like lightning; to lighten; to gleam; to thunder.
parole.testo: From Middle English fouldre (“lightning”), from Old French foudre also fouldre (modern French foudre), from Latin fulgur. See fulgor.

parole.significato: To start (an institution or organization).
parole.testo: From Middle English founden, from Old French founder (Modern French: fonder), from Latin fundāre. Compare fund.

parole.significato: To melt, especially of metal or glass in an industrial setting.
parole.testo: From Middle English founden, from Old French fondre, from Latin fundere. Cognate with Spanish fundir and hundir, and French fondre.

parole.significato: The act of founding, fixing, establishing, or beginning to erect.
parole.testo: From Middle English foundacioun, fundacioun, from Old French fondacion, from Latin fundātiō (“founding, foundation”).

parole.significato: One who founds or establishes (a company, project, organisation, state, etc.).
parole.testo: From Old French fondeur, from Latin fundātor, equivalent to found + -er.

parole.significato: A natural source of water; a spring.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?]; from Old French fontaine (whence modern fontaine); from Late Latin fontana, from Latin fontanus, fontaneus, adjectives from fons (“source, spring”).

parole.significato: An instance of breaking, a place where something has broken.
parole.testo: From Middle English fracture, from Old French fracture, from Latin frāctūra (“a breach, fracture, cleft”), from frangere (“to break”), past participle frāctus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-, whence also English break. See fraction. Doublet of fraktur.

parole.significato: Easily broken physically; not firm or durable; liable to fail and perish.

parole.significato: The Holy Grail.

parole.significato: A book of offices in the Roman Catholic Church; a gradual.
parole.testo: From Middle English grayel, from Old French grael, ultimately from Latin graduale. Doublet of gradual.

parole.significato: The harvested seeds of various grass food crops, especially wheat, maize, rye, barley, and rice.

parole.significato: A granary.
parole.testo: From Middle English graunge, borrowed from Old French grange (“granary; barn; small farm”), from Vulgar Latin *grānica, from Latin grānum (“grain”).

parole.significato: Small fragments of rock, used for laying on the beds of roads and railways, and as ballast.
parole.testo: From Middle English gravel, grauel, from Old French gravele, diminutive of grave (“gravel, seashore”), from Medieval Latin grava, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *grāwā (“gravel, pebbles”) (compare Breton groa, Cornish grow, Welsh gro), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰroh₁weh₂, from *gʰreh₁w- (“to grind”).

parole.significato: One of a flight of steps.
parole.testo: From Middle English gre, from Old French gré, from Latin gradum (“step”). Compare degree. Doublet of grade.

parole.significato: Pleasure, goodwill, satisfaction.

parole.significato: Suffering, hardship.

parole.significato: To cause sorrow or distress to.

parole.significato: A mythical creature with the body of a lion and head and wings of an eagle.
parole.testo: From Middle English griffoun, from Old French griffon, from Late Latin grȳphus, from Classical Latin grȳps, from Ancient Greek γρῡ́ψ (grū́ps).

parole.significato: To grunt; to growl; to snarl; to murmur.
parole.testo: From Middle English groynen, from a mixture of Old French groignier, grougnier (from Latin grunniō) and Old English grunnian (from Proto-Germanic *grunnōną).

parole.significato: A vulture, Gyps fulvus; the griffin.
parole.testo: From Middle English gripe, from Old French gripe, from Latin gryps, grȳphus, from Ancient Greek γρῡ́ψ (grū́ps).

parole.significato: A person who, or thing that, protects or watches over something.
parole.testo: From Middle English garde, from early Middle French or late Old French guarde (“a guardian, warden, keeper”) (whence modern French garde), from the verb guarder. Doublet of garda, which is from Irish.

parole.significato: The throat or esophagus.
parole.testo: From Middle English golet, borrowed from Old French goulet, from Latin gula.

parole.testo: From Middle English habitacioun, from Old French habitacion, abitacion (“act of dwelling”), from Latin habitātiōnem, accusative of Latin habitātiō.

parole.significato: Herbs collectively.

parole.significato: Someone whose beliefs are contrary to the fundamental tenets of a religion they claim to belong to.

parole.significato: Somebody who possesses great bravery and carries out extraordinary or noble deeds.

parole.significato: The quality of being horrible.

parole.significato: The consecrated bread of the Eucharist.

parole.significato: Dampness, especially that of the air.
parole.testo: From Middle English humidite, borrowed from Old French humidité, from Medieval Latin hūmiditās, from Latin ūmidus (“damp, moist, wet”). By surface analysis, humid + -ity.

parole.significato: The characteristic of being humble; humbleness in character and behavior.

parole.significato: Dropsical; pertaining to or suffering from dropsy (edema).
parole.testo: From Middle English ydropik, ydropyk, from Old French ydropique, from Latin hydropicus, from Ancient Greek ὑδρωπικός (hudrōpikós), from ὕδρωψ (húdrōps).

parole.significato: Any of the medium-sized to large feliform carnivores of the family Hyaenidae, native to Africa and Asia and noted for t…
parole.testo: From Middle English hiena, variant of hyene, from Old French hiene, from Medieval Latin hyēna, from Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα (húaina). Displaced native Old English nihtgenġe (literally “night walker”).

parole.significato: A song of praise or worship, especially a religious one.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymne, from Old English ymen (reinforced by Old French ymne), from Latin hymnus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos).

parole.significato: The writing, composing, or singing of hymns or psalms.
parole.testo: From Old French hymnodie, from Latin hymnodia, from Ancient Greek ὑμνῳδία (humnōidía), from ὑμνῳδέω (humnōidéō, “to sing a hymn”), from ὕμνος (húmnos, “song of praise”) + ἀείδω (aeídō, “to sing”).

parole.significato: The contrivance of a false appearance of virtue or goodness, while concealing real character or inclinations, especiall…
parole.testo: From hypo- + Ancient Greek κρί(σις) (krí(sis)) + -isy. From Middle English ipocrisie, from Old French ypocrisie, from Late Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “answer, stage acting, pretense”), from ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrínomai, “I answer (a fellow actor on stage), play a part,

parole.significato: Someone who practices hypocrisy, who pretends to hold beliefs, or whose actions are not consistent with their claimed b…
parole.testo: From Old French ypocrite (Modern French hypocrite), from Latin hypocrita, from Ancient Greek ὑποκριτής (hupokritḗs, “actor, hypocrite”), from ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrínomai, “to answer, act, feign”). Displaced native Old English līċettere.

parole.significato: The ninth letter of the English alphabet, called i and written in the Latin script.
parole.testo: Old French i, from Latin ī, from Etruscan I (i).

parole.significato: A person of low general intelligence.
parole.testo: From Middle English idiote, ydiote, from Old French idiote (later idiot), from Latin idiota, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “a private citizen, one who has no professional knowledge, layman”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one's own, pertaining to oneself, private”). Doublet of idiota. By surface analys

parole.significato: A graven image or representation of anything that is revered, or believed to convey spiritual power.
parole.testo: From Middle English ydole, from Old French idole, from Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos (“seeing, image”), from *weyd- (“to see”). Doublet of aidoru, eidolon, and idolum and related to idea.

parole.significato: The worship of idols.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ydolatrie, from Old French idolatrie, from Ecclesiastical Latin īdōlatrīa, from Late Latin īdōlolatrīa, from Ancient Greek εἰδωλολατρίᾱ (eidōlolatríā, “worship of idols”), back-formation from εἰδωλολάτρης (eidōlolátrēs), from εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “idol”) & λάτρις (látris,

parole.significato: Fiery; of or pertaining to fire.
parole.testo: From Old French ignel, from Late Latin *ignealis, from Latin igneus (“fiery”), from ignis (“fire”).

parole.significato: The condition of being uninformed or uneducated; lack of knowledge or information.
parole.testo: From Middle English ignoraunce, ignorance, from From Old French ignorance, from Latin ignōrantia. By surface analysis, ignor(e) + -ance.

parole.significato: Unknowledgeable or uneducated; characterized by ignorance.
parole.testo: From Old French ignorant, from Latin ignōrāns (“unaware, unknowing”). By surface analysis, ignore + -ant.

parole.significato: Synonym of illuminate.
parole.testo: From Middle English illuminen (“to light, light up; to shine; (figuratively) to enlighten spiritually; to make illustrious”) [and other forms], from Old French illuminer (“to light up, illuminate; (figuratively) to enlighten”) (modern French illuminer), from Latin illūmināre, the present active infi

parole.significato: A distortion of sensory perception where real stimuli lead to a false or misleading impression of reality.
parole.testo: From Old French illusion, from Latin illūsiō, from illūdere, from in- (“at, upon”) + lūdere (“to play, mock, trick”). Displaced native Old English dwimmer.

parole.significato: A visual or other representation of the external form of something in art.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymage, borrowed from Old French image, from Latin imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym-; the same PIE root is the source of imitari (“to copy, imitate”); see imitate. Doublet of imago.

parole.significato: The image-making power of the mind; the act of mentally creating or reproducing an object not previously perceived; the…
parole.testo: From Middle English ymaginacioun, from Old French imaginacion, ymaginacion, from Latin imāginātiō. Equivalent to imagine + -ation.

parole.significato: To stain [with in or with ‘blood, slaughter, etc.’].
parole.testo: From Middle English embrewen, from Old French *embrever (whence Middle French embreuver), metathetic variant of embevrer (“to imbibe, steep, penetrate, soak”) (with same stem variation found in French abreuver and beuverie), from Vulgar Latin imbiberāre.

parole.significato: Happening right away, instantly, with no delay.
parole.testo: From Old French immediat (French immédiat), borrowed from Late Latin immediātus (“without in-between, moderation”), from Latin in + mediātus, perfect passive participle of mediō (“to halve, to be in the middle”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, im-

parole.significato: Huge, gigantic, very large.
parole.testo: From Middle English immens, inmens, from Old French immense, from Latin immensus, from in- (“not”) + mensus (“measured”). Compare incommensurable.

parole.significato: unmeasurable, immeasurable; not able to be measured, therefore connoting extremely large
parole.testo: From Middle English immensurable, from Old French, from Latin immēnsūrābilis, from im- (“not”) (variant form of in-) + mēnsūra (“measure”) + -bilis (“able”).

parole.significato: Fixed, not movable.
parole.testo: From Old French immobile, from Latin immōbilis, equivalent to im- + mobile.

parole.significato: The condition of being immortal.
parole.testo: From Middle English immortalitee, immortalite, from Old French immortalité, from Latin immortālitās. Morphologically immortal + -ity.

parole.significato: The state of being insusceptible to something; notably:
parole.testo: From Middle English immunite, from Old French immunité, from Latin immūnitās, in the legal sense; for the medical use see immunization. Equivalent to immune + -ity. Displaced native Old English frēols (“privilege, immunity”).

parole.significato: To weaken; to affect negatively; to have a diminishing effect on.
parole.testo: From Middle English impairen, empeiren, from Old French empeirier, from Early Medieval Latin impeiōrāre, from in- + Late Latin peiōrāre (“worsen”), from peiōrem (“worse”), comparative of malus (“bad”).

parole.significato: The quality of being impatient; lacking patience; restlessness and intolerance of delays; anxiety and eagerness, especi…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English impacience, from Old French impacience (modern French impatience), from Latin impatientia. By surface analysis, im- + patience.

parole.significato: Restless, short of temper, and intolerant of delays.
parole.testo: From Old French impacient (modern French impatient), from Latin impatiēns. By surface analysis, im- + patient.

parole.significato: Not perfect.
parole.testo: From Middle English imperfit, from Old French imparfit (modern French imparfait), from Latin imperfectus. Spelling modified 15c. to conform Latin etymology. See im- + perfect.

parole.significato: Those qualities or features that are imperfect; the characteristic, state, or quality of being imperfect.
parole.testo: From Old French imperfeccion, from Latin imperfectiōnem, accusative of imperfectiō, from in- + perfectiō. By surface analysis, im- + perfection.

parole.significato: Related to an empire, emperor, or empress.
parole.testo: From Middle English imperial, from Old French imperial, from Latin imperiālis (“of the empire or emperor, imperial”), from imperium (“empire, imperial government”) + -ālis, from imperō (“command, order”), from im- (“form of in”) + parō (“prepare, arrange; intend”). Displaced Old English cāserlīċ.

parole.significato: Making arbitrary decisions, especially in an impulsive and forceful manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).

parole.significato: The state of being impious.
parole.testo: From Old French impieté, from Latin impietas, from in- (“not”) + pietas (“piety”), from pius (“pious, devout”) + -tās (“-ty, -dom”). By surface analysis, impious + -ety.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being implacable.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin implacabilitas (“unappeasable”).

parole.significato: Not able to be placated or appeased.
parole.testo: From Middle English implācāble (“immitigable, unappeasable”) from Old French implacable (“harsh, unrelenting; implacable”) (modern French implacable), from Latin implācābilis (“unappeasable, implacable; irreconcilable”), from im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’)) + plācābilis (“placable; appea

parole.significato: To have as a necessary consequence; to lead to (something) as a consequence.
parole.testo: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”). Doublet of employ and implicate.

parole.significato: Something brought in from an exterior source, especially for sale or trade.
parole.testo: From Middle English importen, from Old French emporter, importer, from Latin importō (“bring in from abroad, import”, verb), from in (“in, at, on; into”) + portō (“to carry, bear; convey”).

parole.significato: The act of imposing, laying on, affixing, enjoining, inflicting, obtruding, and the like.
parole.testo: From Middle English imposicioun, from Old French imposicion, from Latin impositio.

parole.significato: An abscess.
parole.testo: From Old French empostume, alteration of apostume (“apostume, large abscess”), from Latin apostema, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστεμα (apóstema, “separation of pus into an abscess”).

parole.significato: Lacking physical strength or vigor; weak
parole.testo: From Old French impotent, from Latin impotēns, from in- (expresses negation) + potēns (“powerful”).

parole.significato: To impregnate; to make fruitful.
parole.testo: First attested in the early 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; from Middle English impregnen (“to make a woman pregnant, impregnate”), from Old French enpreignier, enpreigner (French imprégner), ultimately from Medieval Latin impraegnō. Doublet of impregnate.

parole.significato: Of a fortress or other fortified place: able to withstand all attacks; impenetrable, inconquerable, unvanquishable.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English imprenable, impregnable (“impossible to capture, impregnable”), from Old French imprenable (modern French imprenable (“impregnable”)), from im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + prenable (“(military) of a building, position, etc.: takable”) (from prendre (“to take”)

parole.significato: The act of making pregnant; fertilization.
parole.testo: From Middle English impregnacioun, from Old French impregnacion, in turn from Late Latin impregnatio.

parole.significato: The indentation or depression made by the pressure of one object on or into another.
parole.testo: From Old French impression, from Latin impressio. Equivalent to impress + -ion.

parole.significato: An impression; the mark left behind by printing something or by pressing on something, or the figurative counterpart of…
parole.testo: From Old French empreinte, from the past participle of empreindre, from Latin imprimere.

parole.significato: To leave a print, impression, image, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English emprinten, enprinten, from Old French empreinter, from the past participle of empreindre, from Latin imprimere.

parole.significato: The act of impelling or driving onward, or the state of being impelled; the sudden or momentary agency of a body in mot…
parole.testo: From Middle English impulsioun, from Old French impulsion, from Latin impulsio, impulsionem.

parole.significato: The act of removing the contents of something; the state of being empty.
parole.testo: From Middle English inanicioun, borrowed from Old French inanition, itself borrowed from Late Latin inānītio, from inānīre (“to make empty”), from inānis (“empty, vain”); see inane.

parole.significato: The act or process of using formulas and/or usually rhyming words, sung or spoken, with occult ceremonies, for the purp…
parole.testo: From Middle English incantacioun, from Old French incantation, from Latin incantatio. More at enchant.

parole.significato: An incarnate being or form.
parole.testo: From Middle English incarnacion, borrowed from Old French incarnacion, from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin incarnatio, from Late Latin incarnari (“to be made flesh”).

parole.significato: Capable of, or used for, or actually causing fire.
parole.testo: From Middle English incendiarie, from Old French incendiaire, from Latin incendiārius (“setting alight”), from incendium (“destructive fire”), from incendō (“to set on fire, kindle”), from in- (“into, in, on, upon”) + candeō (“to be hot”).

parole.significato: Biotic material that releases fragrant smoke when burnt, often used in religious rites or for aesthetic reasons.
parole.testo: From Middle English encens, from Old French encens (“sweet-smelling substance”) from Late Latin incensum (“burnt incense”, literally “something burnt”), neuter past participle of incendō (“to set on fire”). Compare incendiary. Doublet of incienso. Displaced native Old English rēcels.

parole.significato: A physical tilt or bend.
parole.testo: From Middle English inclinacioun, inclinacyon, from Old French inclination and Latin inclīnātiō. Morphologically incline + -ation.

parole.significato: To bend or move (something) out of a given plane or direction, often the horizontal or vertical.
parole.testo: From Middle English enclinen, from Old French encliner (modern incliner), from Latin inclīnō (“incline, tilt”), from in- + clīnō (compare -cline), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean).

parole.significato: Lack of self-restraint, an inability to control oneself; unchastity.
parole.testo: From Middle English incontinence, from Old French incontinence or its etymon Latin incontinentia. Doublet of incontinency.

parole.significato: Unable to contain or retain.
parole.testo: From Middle English incontinent, from Old French incontinent, from Latin incontinens, from in + continens.

parole.significato: The quality of being inconvenient.
parole.testo: From Middle English inconvenience, from Old French inconvenience (“misfortune, calamity, impropriety”) (compare French inconvenance (“impropriety”) and inconvénient (“inconvenience”)), from Late Latin inconvenientia (“inconsistency, incongruity”).

parole.significato: The act of incorporating, or the state of being incorporated.
parole.testo: From Middle English incorporacioun, from Old French incorporacion, from Late Latin incorporatio. By surface analysis, incorporate + -ion.

parole.significato: Unwillingness or inability to believe; doubt about the truth or verisimilitude of something; disbelief.
parole.testo: Attested since 1430. From Middle English incredulite, from Old French incredulité, from Late Latin incredulitas, from Latin incredulus (“unbelieving”) + -itas (“-ity”), equivalent to incredulous + -ity.

parole.significato: Of an illness, condition, etc, that is unable to be cured; healless.
parole.testo: From Old French incurable, from Late Latin incurabilis.

parole.significato: A military action consisting of armed forces of one geopolitical entity entering territory controlled by another such e…
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French, from Latin incursiō.

parole.significato: A cut or notch in the margin of anything, or a recess like a notch.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle English indenten (“to dent in”), equivalent to in- + dent (see dent); partly from Middle English indenten, endenten, from Old French endenter (“to cut notches into”), from en- (“in-, en-”) + dent (“tooth”), from Latin dēns.

parole.significato: An act of pointing out or indicating.
parole.testo: From Old French indication, from Latin indicātiō (“a showing, indicating the value of something; valuation”), from indicō (“point out, indicate, show; value”); see indicate; compare French indication, Spanish indicación, Italian indicazione. By surface analysis, indicate + -ion.

parole.significato: index
parole.testo: From Old French indice, from Latin indicium, from index.

parole.significato: A fiscal period of fifteen years, instituted by Constantine in 313 C.E. (but counting from 1st September 312), used thr…
parole.testo: From Old French indiction or its source, Latin indictiōnem, accusative singular of indictiō, from indicere.

parole.significato: Ambivalent; unconcerned; uninterested, apathetic.
parole.testo: From Old French indifferent, from Latin indifferens. By surface analysis, in- + different.

parole.significato: Extreme poverty or destitution.
parole.testo: From Middle English indigence, late 14th century, from Old French indigence (13th century), from Latin indigentia, from indigentem, form of indigēre (“to need”), from indu (“in, within”) + egēre (“be in need, want”). Only relation to antonym affluence is common Latinate suffix + -ence.

parole.significato: Poor; destitute; in need.
parole.testo: From Middle English indigent, from Old French indigent, from Latin indigēns, present participle of indigeō (“to need”), from indu (“in, within”) + egeō (“to be in need, want”).

parole.significato: A condition of heartburn, nausea, or other stomach-related pain, sometimes caused by eating too quickly.
parole.testo: From Middle English indigestioun, from Old French indigestion, from Late Latin indigestio, by surface analysis, in- + digestion.

parole.significato: An anger aroused by something perceived as an indignity, notably an offense or injustice.
parole.testo: From Middle English indignacioun, borrowed from Old French indignation, from Latin indignātiō, from indignor (“to scorn, resent”), from indignus (“unworthy, not fitting”), from in- (“not”) + dignus (“worthy, appropriate”). Attested since ca. 1374. Doublet of indignatio.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being indiscreet; lack of discretion
parole.testo: From Old French, from Late Latin indiscrētiō.

parole.significato: To physically make (letters and words) on a writing surface; to inscribe.
parole.testo: Originally a variant of indict; from Middle English enditen, endyten, from Old French enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from in- + dictare (“to declare”). Doublet of indict.

parole.significato: An act of inducting.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English induction, from Old French induction, from Latin inductiō, from indūcō (“to lead”). By surface analysis, induct + -ion or induce + -tion.

parole.significato: Hardness.
parole.testo: From Middle English induracioun, from Old French induracion (“hardness, obstinacy”) or directly from Medieval Latin induratiō.

parole.significato: The tendency to work persistently.
parole.testo: From Middle English industry, industrie, from Old French industrie, from Latin industria (“diligence, activity, industry”), from industrius (“diligent, active, zealous”), from Old Latin indostruus (“diligent, active”); origin unknown. Perhaps from indu (“in”) + ūst-, ūstr-, stem of ūrō (“burn, burn

parole.significato: Absence of equality.
parole.testo: From Middle English inequalite, from Old French inequalité, from Medieval Latin inaequālitās, from Latin inaequālis (“unequal”), from in- (“not”) + aequālis (“equal”). Morphologically inequal + -ity and in- + equality.

parole.significato: The state of being infamous.
parole.testo: From late Middle English infamie, from Old French infamie, from Latin īnfāmia (“infamy”), from īnfāmis (“infamous”), from in- (“not”) + fāma (“fame, renown”). Displaced native Old English unhlīsa (literally “bad fame”).

parole.significato: The act or process of infecting.
parole.testo: From Old French infection, from Late Latin īnfectiō. Equivalent to infect + -ion.

parole.significato: To inhabit a place in unpleasantly large numbers; to plague, harass.
parole.testo: From Middle English infesten, from Old French infester (“to infest”), from Latin īnfestō (“assail, molest”, verb), from īnfestus (“hostile”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Indefinably large, countlessly great; immense.
parole.testo: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinit and its etymon Latin īnfīnītus, from in- (“not”) + fīnis (“end”) + the perfect passive participle ending -ītus. By surface analysis, in- + finite. Doublet of infinito. Displaced native Old English unġeendodlīċ.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being infinite or having no limit.
parole.testo: From Old French infinité, from Latin infinitas (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + finis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tas.

parole.significato: Endlessness, unlimitedness, absence of a beginning, end or limits to size.
parole.testo: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinité, from Latin īnfīnitās (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + fīnis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tās. By surface analysis, infinite + -ity.

parole.significato: To set (someone or something) on fire; to cause (someone or something) to burn, flame, or glow; to kindle.
parole.testo: From Middle English inflammen, enflamen, enflaumen (“to set (something) on fire; to be on fire; (figurative) to enrage (someone); to become enraged; to incite (someone) to do evil; to inspire (someone); (medicine) to cause inflammation of (a body part)”), from Old French enflamer, enflammer (“to set

parole.significato: An act, instance of, or state of expansion or increase in size, especially by injection of a gas or liquid.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French inflation (“swelling”), from Latin īnflātiō (“expansion", "blowing up”), from īnflātus, the perfect passive participle of īnflō (“blow into, expand”), from in (“into”) + flō (“blow”). By surface analysis, inflate + -ion.

parole.significato: The power to affect, control or manipulate something or someone; the ability to change the development of fluctuating t…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English influence, from Old French influence, borrowed from Medieval Latin īnfluentia, from Latin īnfluēns + -ia. Doublet of influenza.

parole.significato: To instruct, train (usually in matters of knowledge).
parole.testo: From Middle English informen, enformen, borrowed from Old French enformer, informer (“to train, instruct, inform”), from Latin īnfōrmō (“to shape, form, train, instruct, educate”), from in- (“into”) + fōrma (“form, shape”), equivalent to in- + form.

parole.significato: A product consisting of a liquid which has had other ingredients steeped in it to extract useful qualities.
parole.testo: From Middle English infusioun, from Old French infusion, from Latin infusio, infusionem (“a pouring into, a wetting, a dyeing, a flow”), from infundo.

parole.significato: A lack or absence of gratitude; thanklessness.
parole.testo: From in- + gratitude, from Old French ingratitude, from Late Latin ingrātitūdō. By surface analysis, in- + Latin grat(us) + -itude.

parole.significato: To live or reside in.
parole.testo: From Old French enhabiter, from Latin inhabitāre (in + habitāre).

parole.significato: Someone or thing who lives in a place.
parole.testo: From Middle English inhabitantes (n. plural) and inhabitaunt (adj.), from Old French inhabitant, from Latin inhabitāns, present participle of inhabitō (“to inhabit”), from in- (“in”) + habitō (“to dwell”) (frequentative of habeō (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *ghabh- (“to seize, take, hold, h

parole.significato: To receive (property, a title, etc.), by legal succession or bequest, usually after the previous owner's death.
parole.testo: From Middle English enheriten, from Old French enheriter, from Late Latin inhereditare (“make heir”). Displaced native Old English ierfan.

parole.significato: The act of inhibiting.
parole.testo: From Middle English inhibicioun, inhibicione from Old French inibicion, from Latin inhibitio. Morphologically inhibit + -ion.

parole.significato: Deviation from what is right; gross injustice, sin, wickedness.
parole.testo: From Middle English iniquite, jniquite (“evil, wickedness, iniquity; evil act; hostility, malevolence; hostile act; a calamity, misfortune”), from Old French iniquité (modern French iniquité (“iniquity”)), from Latin inīquitās (“iniquity; inequality, unfairness; inequity, injustice”), from inīquus (

parole.significato: The act of enjoining; the act of directing, commanding, or prohibiting.
parole.testo: From Middle English iniunccyon, iniunccion, from Old French injonctïon, from Latin iniūnctiō (“command, injunction”).

parole.significato: Absence of justice; unjustice.
parole.testo: From Middle English injustice, from Old French injustice, from Latin iniustitia. Equivalent to in- + justice. Displaced native Old English unrihtwīsnes.

parole.significato: A pigment (or dye)-based fluid used for writing, printing etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English ynke, from Old French enque, from Latin encaustum (“purple ink used by Roman emperors to sign documents”), from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον (énkauston, “burned-in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + καίω (kaíō, “burn”). In this sense, displaced native Old English blæc (“ink”, literally “black”).

parole.significato: Absence of responsibility for a crime, tort, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English innocence, from Old French innocence, inocence, from Latin innocentia. Doublet of innocency. Displaced native Old English unsċyld.

parole.significato: Free from guilt, sin, or immorality.
parole.testo: From Middle English innocent, from Old French innocent, inocent, borrowed from Latin innocēns (“harmless, inoffensive”), from in- (“not”) + nocēns, present participle of noceō (“to hurt”). By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + nocent (“harmful; guilty”). Displaced native Old English unsċyldiġ.

parole.significato: Not obedient; disobedient.
parole.testo: From Middle English inobedient, from Old French inobedient, from Latin inoboediens (“not obedient”), present participle of inoboedire (“to disobey”). Compare French inobedient. See obedient.

parole.significato: The act of inquiring; a seeking of information by asking questions; interrogation; a question or questioning.
parole.testo: From Middle English enquery, from the Old French verb enquerre, from Latin inquīrō, composed of in- (“in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”). parole.significato: An inquiry or investigation into the truth of some matter.

parole.testo: From Middle English launce, from Old French lance, from Latin lancea.

parole.significato: A body of words, and set of methods of combining them (called a grammar), understood by a community and used as a form…
parole.testo: From Middle English langage, language, from Old French language, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”), from Old Latin dingua (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue, speech, language”). Doublet of langaj. Displaced native Old English ġeþēod

parole.significato: A tongue-shaped implement, specifically:
parole.testo: From Old French languete (modern French languette), diminutive of langue (“tongue”), from Latin lingua.

parole.significato: Alternative form of languet.
parole.testo: From Old French languete (modern French languette), diminutive of langue (“tongue”), from Latin lingua. By surface analysis, Old French langue + -ette.

parole.significato: A case of translucent or transparent material made to protect a flame, or light, used to illuminate its surroundings.
parole.testo: From Middle English lanterne (13th century), via Old French lanterne from Latin lanterna (“lantern”), itself a corruption of Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr, “torch”) (see lamp, λάμπω (lámpō)) by influence of Latin lucerna (“lamp”). The spelling lanthorn was current during the 16th to 19th centuries

parole.significato: Fat from the abdomen of a pig, especially as prepared for use in cooking or pharmacy.
parole.testo: From Middle English lard, from Old French lard (“bacon”), from Latin lārdum, lāridum (“bacon fat”).

parole.significato: To stuff (meat) with bacon or pork before cooking.
parole.testo: From Middle English larden, from Old French larder and Medieval Latin lārdō.

parole.significato: Of considerable or relatively great size or extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English large, from Old French large, from Latin larga, feminine of largus (“abundant, plentiful, copious, large, much”), of uncertain ultimate origin; see there for more. Along with big, it mostly displaced Middle English stoor and muchel (the latter surviving in much under a different

parole.significato: Existing or present, but concealed or inactive.
parole.testo: From Middle English latent, latente, from Old French latent, from Latin latēns, present participle of lateō (“lie hidden”).

parole.significato: Synonym of interpreter.
parole.testo: From Old French latimier, latinier (“interpreter”), etc. and directly from Vulgar Latin latimarus, from Latin latinarius (“interpreter, speaker of Latin”), from lingua Latina + -arius (“-ary”). Equivalent to Latin + -er and compare Latiner.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Latin: the language spoken in ancient Rome and other cities of Latium.
parole.testo: From Middle English Latyn, Latyne, Latin, from Old French latin, latyn, from Latin latīnus, from Latium (“the region around Rome”) + -īnus (adjective suffix). Displaced or merged with Old English Lǣden. Doublet of Ladin and Ladino.

parole.significato: The angular distance north or south from a planet's equator, measured along the meridian of that particular point.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French latitude, from Latin lātitūdō (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”), from older stlātus. Possibly related with lateral, though this is uncertain.

parole.significato: Glorification or praise.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lauden, from Old French lauder, from Latin laudō, laudāre, from laus (“praise, glory, fame, renown”), from echoic Proto-Indo-European root *leh₁wdʰ- (“song, sound”). Cognate with Old English lēoþ (“song, poem”), German Lied (“song”). Doublet of leed.

parole.significato: Worthy of being lauded.
parole.testo: From Middle English laudable, from Old French laudable or directly from Latin laudabilis; equivalent to laud + -able.

parole.significato: A washerwoman or washerman.
parole.testo: Contracted from Middle English lavender, from Old French lavandiere, from Late Latin lavandera, from Latin lavō (“to wash”).

parole.significato: A laundering; a washing.
parole.testo: From Middle English lavendrie, from Old French lavanderie, from Latin lavandaria. See launder.

parole.significato: To bathe or wash (someone or something).
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English laven (“to bathe, wash; to bail or draw water, drain, exhaust; to dampen, wet; to pour; of water, etc.: to flow, stream”), and then partly: * from Old French laver (“to be washed; to wash”) (modern French laver (“to wash (oneself)”)), from Latin lavāre, the pr

parole.significato: Any of a group of European plants, genus, Lavandula, of the mint family.
parole.testo: From Middle English lavendre, from Anglo-Norman lavendre (French lavande), from Medieval Latin lavendula, possibly from Latin lividus (“bluish”), but influenced by lavō (“to wash”) due to the use of lavender in washing clothes.

parole.significato: Where one laves, a washroom, particularly a lavatorium, the washing area in a monastery.
parole.testo: From Middle English laver, lavour, from Old French laveoir, laveor, laveour, lavor, lavur, from Latin lavātōrium. Doublet of lavatorium and lavatory.

parole.significato: Not belonging to the clergy, but associated with them.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lay, from Old French lai, from Latin lāicus, from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós). Doublet of laic.

parole.significato: Synonym of leper: a person suffering from Hansen's disease; a person suffering any contagious disease requiring similar…
parole.testo: From Middle English lazare, from Old French lazare, from Medieval Latin lazarus (“leper”), an antonomasia from Lazarus, from Koine Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος (Lā́zāros), the given name of the Biblical figure found in Luke 16, from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר (“Eleazar”), a given name shared by various figures in the Hebre

parole.significato: Any agent used to make dough rise or to have a similar effect on baked goods.
parole.testo: From Middle English levayn, borrowed from Old French levain, from Vulgar Latin *levāmen, a noun based on Latin levō (“raise”).

parole.significato: A stand with a slanted top used to support a Bible from which passages are read during a church service.
parole.testo: 15th century partial re-Latinization of early 14th century Middle English lettorne, lettron, from Old French leitrun, from Medieval Latin lectrinum, from Late Latin lectrum, from lectus (from whence also lecture), form of Latin legō (“to read”).

parole.significato: The act of reading.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French lection, from Latin lēctiōnem, form of lēctiō, from legō (“to read; to gather”). Doublet of lesson.

parole.significato: The sediment that settles during fermentation of beverages, consisting of dead yeast and precipitated parts of the frui…
parole.testo: From Old French lies, from Medieval Latin lias (“lees, dregs”) (descent via winemaking common in monasteries), from Gaulish *ligyā, *legyā (“silt, sediment”) (compare Welsh llai, Old Breton leh (“deposit, silt”)), from Proto-Celtic *legyā (“layer”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie (down)”).

parole.significato: Money or property bequeathed to someone in a will.
parole.testo: From Middle English legacie, from Old French legacie and Medieval Latin lēgātia, from Latin lēgātum. Compare legatee. The boardgame sense was coined by game designer Rob Daviau in 2011 with the game Risk Legacy.

parole.significato: A deputy representing the pope, specifically a papal ambassador sent on special ecclesiastical missions.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old English legat(e), from Old French legat, from Latin lēgātus, substantivized from the perfect passive participle of lēgō (“to bequeath, send as envoy”).

parole.significato: The life story of a saint (such stories are often embellished, but any kind is called a legend).
parole.testo: From Middle English legende, from Old French legende, from Medieval Latin legenda (“a legend, story, especially the lives of the saints”), from Latin legenda (“things which ought to be read”), from lego (“to read”).

parole.significato: Numerous; vast; very great in number.
parole.testo: Attested (in Middle English, as legioun) around 1200, from Old French legion, from Latin legiō, legionem, from legō (“to gather, collect”); akin to legend, lecture. Doublet of León, which was borrowed from Spanish. Generalized sense of “a large number” is due to an allusive phrase in Mark 5:9, "My n

parole.significato: Any of several plants of the genus Lens, especially Lens culinaris, from southwest Asia, that have edible, lens-shaped…
parole.testo: From Middle English lentile, from Old French lentille from Latin lenticula, diminutive of lēns, from a pre-Indo-European substrate source shared by German Linse, Ancient Greek λάθυρος (láthuros) and Lithuanian lęšis. Doublet of lenticula.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of a lion; lionlike.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English leonin, leonine (“characteristic of a lion, lionlike”), from Old French leonin, and from its etymon Latin leōnīnus (“of or pertaining to a lion”), from leō (“lion”) (from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn, “lion”); further etymology uncertain) + -īnus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertainin

parole.significato: A large wild cat with a spotted coat native to Africa and Asia (Panthera pardus).
parole.testo: From Middle English leopard, leopart, lepard, leperd, from Old French leopard (“leopard”), from Late Latin leopardus (“leopon, lipard”) from late Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos, “leopon, lipard”), from λέων (léōn, “lion”) + πάρδος (párdos, “pard, male leopard”), from earlier πάρδαλις (párdalis,

parole.significato: A person who has leprosy, a person suffering from Hansen's disease.
parole.testo: From Middle English lepre, leprosy, from Old French [Term?], from Latin leprae, lepra, from Ancient Greek λέπρα (lépra).

parole.significato: A wound or injury.
parole.testo: From Middle English lesioun (“physical injuring of the body”), from Old French lesion (“hurt, offense, wrong, injury, wound”), from Latin laesiō (“hurt, harm, injury”) (whence -ion (“noun suffix denoting action, result, process, state, condition”)), from laesus (“hurt, injured, wounded, damaged”), p

parole.significato: To instruct to teach.
parole.testo: From Middle English lessoun, from Old French leçon, from Latin lēctiō, lēctiōnem (“a reading”), from legō (“to read; to gather”). Doublet of lection.

parole.significato: To print, inscribe, or paint letters on something.
parole.testo: From Middle English letter, lettre, from Old French letre, from Latin littera (“letter of the alphabet"; in plural, "epistle”). Displaced Old English bōcstæf (literally “book staff”) in sense 1 and ǣrendġewrit (literally “message writing”) in sense 2.

parole.significato: An edible plant, Lactuca sativa and its close relatives, having a head of green or purple leaves.
parole.testo: From Middle English letuse, of uncertain precise origin, probably from the plural form Old French laitues, derived from Latin lactūca (“lettuce”), from lac (“milk”), because of the milky fluid in its stalks. Replaced Old English lēahtric. (money): Likely from the green color of US banknotes.

parole.significato: The same height at all places; parallel to a flat ground.
parole.testo: From Middle English level, from Old French livel, liveau m, later nivel, niveau, from Latin libella f (“a balance, a level”), diminutive of libra f (“a balance, a level”); see libra, librate. Doublet of libella and niveau. The verb is from Middle English levelen, from the noun.

parole.significato: A rigid piece which is capable of turning about one point, or axis (fulcrum), and in which are two or more other points…
parole.testo: From Middle English lever, levore, levour, from Old French leveor, leveur (“a lifter, lever (also Old French and French levier)”), from Latin levātor (“a lifter”), from levō (“to raise”). Doublet of levator.

parole.significato: A young hare less than one year old.
parole.testo: From Middle English leveret(te), from Old French leveret, diminutive of lievre (“hare”), from Latin leporem, of obscure origin.

parole.significato: Bound or obliged in law or equity; responsible; answerable.
parole.testo: From Old French lier (“to bind”), from Latin ligō, ligāre (“to bind, to tie”). Compare typologically Russian обя́занный (objázannyj), обяза́тельный (objazátelʹnyj) (akin to вяза́ть (vjazátʹ)).

parole.significato: A written or pictorial false statement which unjustly seeks to damage someone's reputation.
parole.testo: From Middle English libel, from Old French libelle, from Latin libellus (“petition”, literally “booklet”). Doublet of libelle.

parole.significato: Generous; permitting liberty; willing to give unsparingly.
parole.testo: The adjective is from Old French liberal, from Latin līberālis (“befitting a freeman”), from līber (“free”); it is attested since the 14th century. The noun is first attested in the 1800s.

parole.significato: The property of being liberal; generosity; charity.
parole.testo: From Middle English liberalite, from Old French liberalité, from Latin līberālitās (“a noble, kind, or friendly disposition; generosity”), equivalent to liberal + -ity.

parole.significato: The condition of being free.
parole.testo: From Middle English liberte, from Old French liberté, from Latin libertas (“freedom”), from liber (“free”); see liberal.

parole.significato: To authorize officially.
parole.testo: From Middle English licencen, licensen, lisensen, licent, from Old French licencer, licencier, licenciier, licenser, from Medieval Latin licentiō (cf. English licentiate).

parole.significato: A plant of species Glycyrrhiza glabra, or sometimes in North America, the related American licorice plant Glycyrrhiza l…
parole.testo: From Middle English lycorys, from Old French licoresse, from Late Latin liquiritia, alteration of Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza): γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”) (English glucose, English rhizome). Doublet of glycyrrhiza.

parole.significato: Being a fixed limit game.
parole.testo: From Middle English limit, from Old French limit, from oblique stem of Latin līmes, līmit- (“a cross-path or balk between fields, hence a boundary, boundary line or wall, any path or road, border, limit”). Displaced native Old English ġemǣre. Doublet of limes.

parole.significato: To restrict; to circumscribe; not to allow to go beyond a certain bound, to set boundaries.
parole.testo: From Middle English limiten, from Old French limiter, from Latin līmitō (“to bound, limit, fix, determine”), from līmes; see noun.

parole.significato: To draw or paint; to delineate.
parole.testo: From Middle English limnen, limyne, lymm, lymn, lymne (“to illuminate (a manuscript)”), a variant of luminen (“to illuminate (a manuscript)”), short form of enluminen (“to shed light on, illuminate; to enlighten; to make bright or clear; to give colour to; to illuminate (a manuscript); to depict, de

parole.significato: Descent in a line from a common progenitor; progeny; descending line of offspring or ascending line of parentage.
parole.testo: From Middle English linage, from Old French linage, from ligne, from Latin linea (“line”); equivalent to line + -age.

parole.significato: Pertaining to lines; consisting of lines.
parole.testo: From Old French lineal, from Latin līneālis, from līnea (“a line”) + -ālis (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, line + -al. Doublet of linear.

parole.significato: Clinging fuzzy fluff that clings to fabric or accumulates in one's pockets or navel etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English lynet, linet, from Old French linette (“grain of flax”), diminutive of lin (“flax”); or, from Medieval Latin linteum, from Latin līnum (“flax”).

parole.significato: A big cat, Panthera leo, native to Africa, India and formerly much of Europe.
parole.testo: From Middle English lyoun, lion, leon, borrowed from Old French lion, from Latin leō, (accusative: leōnem), from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn), of unclear origin. Doublet of Leo, leu, lev, and Lyon. Displaced Old English lēo, from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: A substance that is flowing, and keeping no shape, such as water; a substance of which the molecules, while not tending…
parole.testo: From Middle English liquide, from Old French liquide, from Latin liquidus (“fluid, liquid, moist”), from liqueō (“to be liquid, be fluid”). Doublet of liquidus. parole.significato: A pendent part of the old clerical tippet.
parole.testo: From Old French liripipion, liripion, Latin liripipium. Said to be corrupted from cleri ephippium (“the clergy's caparison”).

parole.significato: A strip of fabric, especially from the edge of a piece of cloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English lī̆st, lī̆ste (“band, stripe; hem, selvage; border, edge, rim; list, specification; barriers enclosing area for jousting, etc.”), from Old English līste (“hem, edge, strip”), or Old French liste, listre (“border; band; strip of paper; list”), or Medieval Latin lista, all from Pro

parole.significato: A ritual liturgical prayer in which a series of prayers recited by a leader are alternated with responses from the cong…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French letanie, from Latin litania, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”), from λιτή (litḗ, “prayer, entreaty”).

parole.significato: The body of all written works.
parole.testo: From Middle English literature, from Old French littérature, from Latin literatura or litteratura, from littera (“letter”), from Etruscan, from Ancient Greek διφθέρᾱ (diphthérā, “tablet”). Displaced native Old English bōccræft, literally "book + -craft", see Modern English bookcraft.

parole.significato: lead monoxide (PbO) a toxic solid formed from oxidation of lead in air, and used as a pigment.
parole.testo: From Middle English litarge, from Old French litarge, from Latin lithargyrus, from Ancient Greek λιθάργυρος (lithárguros), from λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + αργυρός (argurós, “silver”).

parole.significato: A bottom-feeding freshwater fish in the superfamily or suborder Cobitoidea.
parole.testo: From Middle English loche, from Old French loche, further origin uncertain, possibly from Vulgar Latin *laukka (“loach”), which could be from Gaulish *leuca (“loach, slug”), also attested as the feminine name Leuca, from leux (“bright, light”), a reference to slugs' bright appearance, the fish later

parole.significato: To be firmly fixed in a specified position.
parole.testo: From Middle English logge, from Old French loge (“an arbour, a covered walk-way”). See also Medieval Latin lobia, laubia; also Old High German louba (“a porch, a gallery”) (German Laube (“bower, arbor”)), Old High German loub (“leaf, foliage”), Old English lēaf (“leaf, foliage”). Doublet of loggia a

parole.significato: Logical.
parole.testo: From Middle English logike, from Old French and Latin logicus, from Ancient Greek λογῐκός (logĭkós). Displaced native Old English flitcræftlīċ.

parole.significato: A method of human thought that involves thinking in a linear, step-by-step manner about how a problem can be solved. Lo…
parole.testo: From Middle English logik, from Old French logike, from Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”), from feminine of λογικός (logikós, “of or pertaining to speech or reason or reasoning, rational, reasonable”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, reason”). Displaced native Old English flitcræ
