parole.significato: The part of the body (of humans and quadrupeds) at each side of the backbone, between the ribs and hips.
parole.testo: From Middle English loyne, from Old French loigne, from Vulgar Latin *lumbea, from Latin lumbus, of uncertain origin, possibly from Oscan-Umbrian *londwo- or Proto-Germanic *lundwuz, both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“kidney, waist”). Cognate with Modern English lend (“loin”), Dutch

parole.significato: A member of a Germanic people who invaded Italy in the 6th century.
parole.testo: From Middle English Lombard, Lumbard, borrowed from Old French Lombard, Lombart (“a Lombard”), from Late Latin langobardus, longobardus (“a Lombard”), from Germanic, derived from the Proto-Germanic *langabardaz from elements *langaz + *bardaz; equivalent to long + beard. Some sources derive the seco

parole.significato: Angular distance measured west or east of the prime meridian.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French longitude, from Latin longitūdō (“length, a measured length”), from longus (“long”).

parole.significato: Praise; fame; reputation.
parole.testo: From Middle English loos, lōs (“reputation, renown, fame, infamy, rumor, news”), from Old French los, from Latin laus (“praise, glory, fame, renown”). Doublet of laud.

parole.significato: A person who makes the bits and other metal parts of a horse's bridle, and other small metal pieces.
parole.testo: From Old French lormier, loremier, from Latin loranum (“bridle”), lorum (“thong, the rein of a bridle”).

parole.significato: A type of turret on the roof of certain medieval buildings designed to allow ventilation or the admission of light.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English lover, from Old French lovier, lover (“skylight”), from Medieval Latin *lōdārium (attested as lōvārium), extension of lōdium, of unclear origin, but probably of Germanic origin and related to Frankish *laubijā (“shelter”). Compare Old Norse ljóri.

parole.significato: The pike, Esox lucius, when fully grown.
parole.testo: From Old French lus, luis, from Latin lūcius.

parole.significato: A device for making braided cord.
parole.testo: From Middle English lucet (“heraldic representation of a pike fish”), from Old French lucet (“small pike”), from Old French lus + -et, from Latin lucius (“pike fish”).

parole.significato: Money, riches, or wealth, especially when seen as having a corrupting effect or causing greed, or obtained in an underh…
parole.testo: From Middle English lūcre, lucor, lucour, lucur (“gain in money, profit; money; wages; illicit gain; advantage, benefit”), from Old French lucre or Latin lucrum (“advantage, profit; love of gain, avarice”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“gain, profit”) + *-tlom (variant of *-trom (suffix forming

parole.significato: The drug LSD.
parole.testo: From Middle English Lucy, from Old French Lucie (notably after the Christian martyr Lucia of Syracuse), from Latin Lucia (feminine of Lucius, a Roman praenomen), from lux (“light”). parole.significato: One who is an inspiration to others; one who has achieved success in one's chosen field; a leading light.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English lūminārī, lūminārīe (“lamp; source of spiritual light, example of holiness; glory”), borrowed from Old French luminarie (“lamp, lights, lighting; candles; brightness, illumination”), variant of luminaire (“light fixture”) (modern French luminaire), from Medieval Latin lūminā

parole.significato: To illuminate.
parole.testo: From Middle English lūminen, clipping of enlūminen, from Old French enluminer, from Latin illūminō, from lūminō, from lūmen.

parole.significato: An insane person.
parole.testo: From Middle English lunatik, from Old French lunatique, from Late Latin lunaticus (“moonstruck”), derived from Latin luna (“moon”), the connection stemming from the belief that changes of the moon caused intermittent insanity.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Lupinus in the family Fabaceae.
parole.testo: From Middle English lupyne, lupine, from Old French lupin, from Latin lupīnus (“pertaining to the wolf”), because of the wolf-like “fang” within the blossom. It has also been linked to an assumed depletion of nutrients in the soil.

parole.significato: To swallow or eat greedily; to devour; hence, to swallow up.
parole.testo: From Middle English *lurchen (recorded only in Middle English lurcare, lurcard (“glutton”)), from Old French *lurcher, from Latin lurcō (“eat greedily, guzzle”), of uncertain origin. Compare Middle High German slurken (“to slurp”) (whence German schlurken).

parole.significato: Chiefly preceded by the.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from fever-lurgy, possibly influenced by or related to lurk (“to hang out or wait”). parole.significato: Thick sticky clay or cement used to close up a hole or gap, especially to make something air-tight.
parole.testo: From Old French lut, ultimately from Latin lutum (“mud”).

parole.significato: Very fine in quality and comfortable.
parole.testo: From Middle English luxurious, from Old French luxurios (modern French luxurieux), from Latin lū̆xuriōsus (“rank, luxuriant, profuse, excessive, immoderate”), from lū̆xuria (“rankness, luxury”), from lū̆xus (“extravagance, luxury”). By surface analysis, luxury + -ous.

parole.significato: Very wealthy and comfortable surroundings; the state of being that they create.
parole.testo: From Middle English luxurie, from Old French luxurie, from Latin luxuria (“rankness, luxury”), from luxus (“extravagance, luxury”).

parole.significato: An ancient stringed musical instrument (a yoke lute chordophone) of Greek origin, consisting of two arms extending from…
parole.testo: From Middle English lire (13th c.), from Old French lire, from Latin lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρᾱ (lúrā, “lyre, a stringed instrument with a sounding-board formed of the shell of a tortoise”). Doublet of lira, lyra, and Lyra.

parole.significato: A heavy fighting club.
parole.testo: From Middle English mace, borrowed from Old French mace, mache, from Vulgar Latin *mattia, *mattea, matia, (compare Italian mazza, Spanish maza), probably from Proto-West Germanic *mattjō (“cutting tool, hoe”).

parole.significato: A polite form of address for a woman or lady.
parole.testo: From Middle English madame, from Old French madame, from ma (“my”) + dame (“lady”), from post-classical Latin mea domina. Doublet of Madonna.

parole.significato: The application of rituals or actions, especially those based on occult knowledge, to subdue or manipulate natural or s…
parole.testo: From Middle English magik, magyk, from Old French magique (noun and adjective), from Latin magicus (adjective), magica (noun use of feminine form of magicus), from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós, “magical”), from μάγος (mágos, “magus”). Ultimately from Old Iranian, probably derived from Proto-Indo-E

parole.significato: grandeur, brilliance, lavishness or splendor
parole.testo: From Middle English magnificence, from Old French magnificence, from Latin magnificentia.

parole.significato: One of several kinds of bird in the family Corvidae, especially Pica pica.
parole.testo: From Mag, a nickname for Margaret that was used to denote a chatterer, + archaic pie (“magpie”), from Middle English pie, pye, from Old French pie, from Latin pīca, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peyk- (“woodpecker, magpie”). Displaced native Old English agu (“magpie”) and Middle English aguster (“mag

parole.significato: Armour consisting of metal rings linked together.
parole.testo: From Middle English mayle (“mail armor”), borrowed from Old French maille (“loop, stitch”), from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“blemish, mesh”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *smh₁-tleh₂, from *smeh₁- (“smear, rub”). Compare maillot.

parole.significato: To keep up; to preserve; to uphold (a state, condition etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English mayntenen, from Old French maintenir, from Late Latin manūteneō, manūtenēre (“I support”), from Latin manū (“with/in/by the hand”, ablative of manus) + tenēre (“to hold”).

parole.significato: a term of address for royalty and imperiality
parole.testo: From an alternative capitalization of English majesty, from Middle English maieste, mageste, from Old French majesté, from Latin māiestās, derived from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂s (“great”).

parole.significato: The quality of being impressive, great, dignified, powerful, sovereign, or any combination thereof.
parole.testo: From Middle English majeste, mageste, from Old French majesté, from Latin maiestātem, (literally, "the quality of being greater”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂s (“great”) See mega-.

parole.significato: bad, badly
parole.testo: From Old French mal- from Latin male (“badly”), from malus (“bad”).

parole.significato: Any ailment or disease of the body; especially, a lingering or deep-seated disorder.
parole.testo: From Middle English maladie, from Old French maladie (“sickness, illness, disease”), from malade (“ill, sick”), from Latin male habitus (“ill-kept, not in good condition”), 1st century AD. See also malice and habit.

parole.significato: One of the male (masculine) sex or gender.
parole.testo: From Middle English male, borrowed from Old French malle, masle (Modern French mâle), from Latin masculus (“masculine, a male”), diminutive of mās (“male, masculine”). Doublet of macho. Displaced native Old English wǣpned (“male”, literally “weaponed”).

parole.significato: Having or displaying ill will; wishing harm on others.
parole.testo: From Middle English *malevolent (suggested by Middle English malevolence), from Old French malivolent and Latin malevolentem, from male (“badly, wrongly”) + volens (“willing, wishing”), from velle (“to wish”).

parole.significato: Wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From Old French malfaisance, derived from malfaire, maufaire (“to do evil”), from Latin malefaciō (“to do evil”), from male (“evilly”) + faciō (“to do, make”).

parole.significato: Intention to harm or deprive in an illegal or immoral way. Desire to take pleasure in another's misfortune.
parole.testo: From Middle English malice, borrowed from Old French malice, from Latin malitia (“badness, bad quality, ill-will, spite”), from malus (“bad”).

parole.significato: Intending to do harm; characterized by spite and malice.
parole.testo: From Middle English malicious, from Old French malicios, from Latin malitiōsus, from malitia (“malice”), from malus (“bad”). Displaced native Middle English ivelwilled and ivelwilly (“malicious”), related to Old English yfelwillende (literally “evil-willing”). By surface analysis, malice + -ious.

parole.significato: Evil or malignant in disposition, nature, intent or influence.
parole.testo: From Middle English maligne, from Old French maligne, from Latin malignus, from malus (“bad”) + genus (“sort, kind”). Compare benign.

parole.significato: A curse, a malediction.
parole.testo: From Middle English malisoun, from Old French maleison, from Latin maledictiō, from the past participle stem of maledīcō (“to speak ill of”), from male (“wickedly, badly”) + dīcō (“say, speak”). Doublet of malediction.

parole.significato: manacle
parole.testo: From Middle English manicle, from Old French manicle, from Latin manicula, diminutive form of manus (“hand”).

parole.significato: A person in charge of purchasing and storing food and other provisions in a monastery, college, or court of law.
parole.testo: From Middle English maunciple, from Old French manciple, from Medieval Latin mancipiolum (“lowly servant”), diminutive of Latin mancipium (“slave”).

parole.significato: A skin disease of nonhuman mammals caused by parasitic mites (Sarcoptes spp., Demodecidae spp.).
parole.testo: From Middle English manjewe, manjeue, from Old French manjue, derived from mangier (“to eat”) (modern French manger (“to eat”)), from Latin manducare.

parole.significato: A military engine formerly used for throwing stones and burning objects.
parole.testo: From Old French mangonel, from Latin manganellus, manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγανον (mánganon).

parole.significato: A landed estate.
parole.testo: From Middle English maner, manour; from Old French manoir, from earlier maneir, from Latin manēre. Doublet of maenor.

parole.significato: Synonym of handbook.
parole.testo: From Middle English manuel, from Old French manuel, from Late Latin manuāle (“handbook, manual”).

parole.significato: A visual representation of an area, whether real or imaginary, showing the relative positions of places and other featu…
parole.testo: Shortening or back-formation of Middle English mappemounde, mapemounde (“world map”), from Old French mapamonde, from Medieval Latin mappa mundī, compound of Latin mappa (“napkin, cloth”) and mundus (“world”). See mop for more on the first component. Doublet of mop, nape, and nappe.

parole.significato: A herb of the mint family, Origanum majorana, having aromatic leaves.
parole.testo: From Old French majorane, from Medieval Latin maiōrana.

parole.significato: A mixed earthy substance, consisting of carbonate of lime, clay, and possibly sand, in very variable proportions, and a…
parole.testo: From Middle English marle, from Old French marle, from Late Latin margila, diminutive of marga (“marl”). Doublet of marla.

parole.significato: A nobleman in England, France, and Germany, of a rank next below that of duke, but above a count. Originally, the marqu…
parole.testo: From Middle English markis, from Old French markis, marchis, from Late Latin marchensis, from Old High German marcha and Frankish *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary”). Meaning is “lord of the march”, in sense of march (“border country”).

parole.significato: The state of being married.
parole.testo: From Middle English mariage, from Old French mariage, from marier (“to marry”), from Latin marītō (“marry”, verb, literally “give in marriage”), from marītus (“lover”, “nuptial”), from mas (“male, masculine, of the male sex”). Equivalent to marry + -age. Doublet of maritage. Displaced native Old Eng

parole.significato: A kind of fabric made from two series of threads interlacing each other, thus forming a double cloth, quilted in the lo…
parole.testo: From Old French Marseilles (nominative of Marseille), from Latin Massilia, Marsilia, from Ancient Greek Μασσαλία (Massalía), probably from a pre-Latin language of Italy, perhaps Ancient Ligurian mas (“spring”).

parole.significato: A hammer, especially a war hammer.
parole.testo: From Middle English martel, from Old French martel m (modern French marteau m), from Late Latin martellus m, from Latin martulus m, a variant of marculus m (“small hammer”).

parole.significato: That which causes wonder; a prodigy; a portent.
parole.testo: First attested from 1300, from Middle English merveile, from Old French merveille (“a wonder”), from Vulgar Latin *miribilia, from Latin mīrābilia (“wonderful things”), from neuter plural of mīrābilis (“strange, wonderful”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”). Doublet of mirabilia

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the male gender.
parole.testo: From Middle English masculyne, masculyn, from Old French masculin, from Latin masculīnus, diminutive of masculus (“male, manly”), itself a diminutive of mās (“male”). Displaced native Old English werlīċ (literally “manly”).

parole.significato: The principal liturgical service of the Church, encompassing both a scripture service (Liturgy of the Word) and a eucha…
parole.testo: From Middle English messe, from Old English mæsse and Old French messe, both from Late Latin missa, from Latin mittō (“to send, dismiss”), compare French messe. In the ancient churches, the public services at which the catechumens were permitted to be present were called missa catechumenorum, ending

parole.significato: The Eucharist, now especially in Roman Catholicism.
parole.testo: From Middle English messe, masse, from Old English mæsse (“the mass, church festival”) and Old French messe, from Vulgar Latin *messa (“Eucharist, dismissal”), from Late Latin missa, noun use of feminine past participle of classical Latin mittere (“to send”), from ite, missa est (“go, (the assembly)

parole.significato: Executed in the manner of a master; showing competence and skill; masterful.
parole.testo: PIE word  *méǵh₂s From Middle English maisterli, from maister (“leader, ruler; high official; official in charge of a place; person in control; employer; owner; schoolmaster, teacher; scholar, sage; holder of a master's degree; religious teacher; master craftsman; expert; magician; social superior;

parole.significato: An evergreen shrub or small tree, Pistacia lentiscus (mastic tree), native to the Mediterranean.
parole.testo: From Middle English mastik, from Old French mastic, from Latin mastiche, from Ancient Greek μαστίχη (mastíkhē), from μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to chew”) (note the chewing gum sense). Related to masticate. The broad sense for cements came via extension from predecessor cements made with the tree's resin.

parole.significato: One of an old breed of powerful, deep-chested, and smooth-coated dogs, used chiefly as watchdogs and guard dogs.
parole.testo: From Middle English mastif, mastyf, an aberrant derivation (with influence from Old French mestif) from Old French mastin (modern French mâtin), from Vulgar Latin *mansuetinus (“tamed (animal)”), from Latin mansuetus (“tamed”).

parole.significato: A small wooden stick specially treated with chemicals to produce flame upon contact with another chemical, from the fri…
parole.testo: From Middle English macche, mecche (“wick (of a candle)”), from Old French mesche, meische, from Vulgar Latin micca (compare Catalan metxa, Spanish mecha, Italian miccia), which in turn is probably from Latin myxa (“nozzle, curved part of a lamp”), from Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “lamp wick”).

parole.significato: To confuse; to confound.
parole.testo: From Middle English maten (“to overpower”), from Old French mater (“to kill”), from Vulgar Latin *mattō, of unclear origin.

parole.significato: Mathematical.
parole.testo: From Middle English mathematik, from Old French mathematique or directly from Latin mathēmaticus, from Ancient Greek μᾰθημᾰτῐκός (măthēmătĭkós), from μάθημα (máthēma, “learning; mathematics”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”, adjective suffix).

parole.significato: An abstract representational system studying numbers, shapes, structures, quantitative change and relationships between…
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1545. From mathematic (noun) + -ics, from Middle English mathematique, methametik, matematik, matamatik, from Old French mathematique, from Latin mathēmatica (“mathematics”), from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “on the matter of that which is learned”), from μάθημα (má

parole.significato: A female leader of a family, a tribe or an ethnic or religious group.
parole.testo: Of Latin origin, via or reinforced by Old French matriarche, from Latin māter (“mother”) + -archa, -arches, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχός (arkhós, “chief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ergʰ- (“to begin, rule, command”). By surface analysis, matri- + -arch.

parole.significato: Marriage; the state of being married.
parole.testo: From Old French matremoine, from Latin mātrimōnium (“marriage, wedlock”), from mātri(s) (“mother”) + -mōnium (“obligation”). By surface analysis, matri- + -mony. Compare patrimony.

parole.significato: A mature or elderly woman, especially one of a higher social rank.
parole.testo: From Middle English matrone, from Old French matrone, from Latin mātrōna (“married woman”), from māter (“mother”). Doublet of matrona.

parole.significato: The state of being mature, ready or ripe; the prime state of productibility and self expression.
parole.testo: From Middle English maturitee, maturyte, from Old French maturité, from Latin mātūritātem. By surface analysis, mature + -ity.

parole.significato: The Magdalene; Mary Magdalene.
parole.testo: From Middle English Maudelen, a dialectal form of Mary Magdalene (typically depicted weeping), from Old French Madelaine (whence Madeleine), from Late Latin Magdalena (see Magdalena, Magdalene, and Maudlin).

parole.significato: A long stylised sleeve.
parole.testo: From Middle English maunche, from Old French maunche, one of the variants of manche, from Latin manica. Doublet of manche.

parole.significato: A commandment.
parole.testo: From Middle English maundee, maunde, from Old French mandée (“mandated”), from Latin mandatum (“commandment”). Doublet of mandate. The word came to refer to the foot-washing ceremony performed on Thursday before Easter because of the phrase used by Jesus to explain his act of foot-washing, which in

parole.significato: Having the mean as its value; average.
parole.testo: From Middle English meene, borrowed from Old French meien (French moyen), Late Latin mediānus (“that is in the middle, middle”), from Latin medius (“middle”). Cognate with mid. For the musical sense, compare the cognate Italian mezzano. Doublet of median and mizzen.

parole.significato: A red spot of the kind that appears on the skin of someone suffering from measles.
parole.testo: From Middle English mesel, from Old French mesel (“leprous”), from Latin misellus (“wretched", "unfortunate”), diminutive of miser (“wretched, sick”), of unknown ultimate origin.

parole.significato: A prescribed quantity or extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English mesure, from Old French mesure, from Latin mēnsūra (“a measure”), mētior (“to measure”, supine stem in mēns-) + -tūra. Largely displaced native Old English metan ("to measure" whence modern mete) and ġemet (“a measure”). See also -ure.

parole.significato: mechanical; relating to mechanics or the laws of motion in physics
parole.testo: From Middle English mekanyk (“mechanical”), from Old French mecanique, from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines or mechanics, inventive”), from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines or contrivance, mechanic, ingenious, inventive”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine,

parole.significato: A devotional exercise of, or leading to, contemplation.
parole.testo: From Old French meditacion, from Latin meditatio, from meditatus, the past participle of meditārī (“to meditate, to think over, consider”), itself from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure, limit, consider, advise”).

parole.significato: Mespilus germanica, common medlar (now often Crataegus germanica).
parole.testo: From Middle English medler, medeler, from Old French medler, meslier, from medle, mesdle (“medlar fruit”), from Latin mespilum, from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon). Related to the rare mesple, via Proto-West Germanic *mespilā. Displaced Old English openærs (“open-arse”) (and similar names, from a

parole.significato: A sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase.
parole.testo: From Middle English melodie, melodye, from Old French melodie, from Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā, “singing, chanting”), from μέλος (mélos, “musical phrase”) + ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”), contracted form ᾠδή (ōidḗ).

parole.significato: Some of the plants of the family Cucurbitaceae grown for food, generally not including the cucumber.
parole.testo: From Middle English meloun, melon, from Old French melon, from Late Latin melonem, from Latin melopeponem, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn), from μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”) + πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”).

parole.significato: One who belongs to a group.
parole.testo: From Middle English membre, from Old French membre, from Latin membrum (“limb, body part”), from Proto-Italic *memzrom, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms, *mēms-rom (“flesh”). Akin to Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌼𐌶 (mimz, “meat, flesh”), Crimean Gothic menus. Coexists with native limb, from Old English lim (“limb, joint,

parole.significato: A perceived threat or danger.
parole.testo: From Middle English manace, from Old French manace, menace, &c., from Late Latin minācia (“threat, menace”), from Latin mināx (“threatening”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: the state of being a beggar; mendicancy or beggary
parole.testo: From Old French mendicité, from Latin mendicitas.

parole.significato: A speaking or noticing of anything, usually in a brief or cursory manner.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English mencioun, mention, from Old French mention, from Latin mentiōnem, accusative of mentiō (“a mention, calling to mind”).

parole.significato: A Eurasian blackbird, Turdus merula.
parole.testo: From Middle English merle, from Old French merle (French merle), from Latin merula (“blackbird”) (whence the directly borrowed Middle English merule, and compare the taxonomic name Turdus merula), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂mes- (“black, blackbird”). Compare Breton moualch (“ouzel”), Welsh mwyalch

parole.significato: A communication, or what is communicated; any concept or information conveyed.
parole.testo: From Middle English message, from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange”). Partially displaced Old English ærende (whence errand).

parole.significato: Chemical elements or alloys, their ores, and the mines where their ores come from.
parole.testo: From Middle English metal, a borrowing from Old French metal, from Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”).

parole.significato: The field of study of metaphysics.
parole.testo: From Middle English methaphesik, methaphisik, methaphisique, metaphesyk, methafisik, metaphesyk, methephysyk, from Old French metafisique, methaphisique and Medieval Latin metaphysica, methephisica; equivalent to meta- + physic.

parole.significato: The branch of philosophy which studies fundamental principles intended to describe or explain all that is, and which ar…
parole.testo: 1560s; plural of metaphysic, from Middle English methaphesik, methaphisik, methaphisique, metaphesyk, methafisik, metaphesyk, methephysyk, from Old French metafisique, methaphisique and Medieval Latin metaphysica, methephisica, from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσικά (metaphusiká), from the title of the col

parole.significato: A boundary or other limit; a boundary-marker; mere.
parole.testo: From Middle English mete, from Old French mete (“boundary, boundary marker”), from Latin mēta (“post, goal, marker”). Cognate with the second element in Old English wullmod (“distaff”).

parole.significato: A severe, disabling headache, usually affecting only one side of the head, and often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, p…
parole.testo: First appears c. 1425. A respelling (following French) of the late 14th century Middle English megrim, from the 13th century Old French migraigne, from Vulgar Latin pronunciation of Latin hemicrania (“a pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρανία (hēmikranía), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hem

parole.significato: Common yarrow, Achillea millefolium.
parole.testo: From Old French milfoil (modern French mille-feuille), from Latin millefolium, from mīlle + folium. Doublet of mille-feuille.

parole.significato: Characteristic of members of the armed forces.
parole.testo: From Middle English militari, from Old French militaire, from Latin mīlitāris, from mīles (“soldier”) + -āris (whence -ary). Doublet of militaire.

parole.significato: An excavation from which ore or solid minerals are taken, especially one consisting of underground tunnels.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French mine, from Late Latin mina, from Gaulish (compare to Welsh mwyn, Irish mianach (“ore”)), from Proto-Celtic *meinis (“ore, metal”).

parole.significato: Any naturally occurring solid material that has a (more or less) definite chemical composition and characteristic physi…
parole.testo: From Middle English mineral, borrowed from Old French mineral, (French minéral), from Medieval Latin minerale, from minera (“ore”), probably ultimately derived from Latin mina (“ore, mine”).

parole.significato: A person who is trained to preach, to perform religious ceremonies, and to afford pastoral care at a Protestant church.
parole.testo: From Middle English ministre, from Old French ministre, from Latin minister (“an attendant, servant, assistant, a priest's assistant or other under official”), from minor (“less”) + -ter; see minor. Doublet of Minorite.

parole.significato: The act of ministering; an instance of providing aid, care, or assistance.
parole.testo: From Middle English ministracioun, from Old French ministracïon, from Latin ministrātio; equivalent to minister + -ation.

parole.significato: A government department at the administrative level, normally headed by a minister (or equivalent rank, e.g. secretary…
parole.testo: From Middle English mynisterie, borrowed from Old French menistere, in turn borrowed itself from Latin ministerium; equivalent to minister + -y.

parole.significato: A unit of time which is one sixtieth of an hour (sixty seconds).
parole.testo: From Middle English mynute, minute, mynet, from Old French minute, from Medieval Latin minūta (“60th of an hour; note”). Doublet of menu and menudo.

parole.significato: An event that appears inexplicable by the laws of nature and so is held to be supernatural in origin.
parole.testo: From Middle English miracle, from Old French miracle, from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meyh₂- (“to smile, to be astonished”). Doublet of milagro and miraculum. Partially displaced native wonder, from Old En

parole.significato: A smooth surface, usually made of glass with reflective material painted on the underside, that reflects light so as to…
parole.testo: From Middle English mirour, from Old French mireor (“mirror”, literally “looker, watcher”), from mirer (“look at”), from Latin mīror (“wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- (“to laugh, to be glad”). Displaced native Middle English schewere, schawere, from Old English

parole.significato: Conduct that playfully causes petty annoyance.
parole.testo: From Middle English myschef, meschef, meschief, mischef, from Old French meschief, from meschever (“to bring to grief”), from mes- (“badly”) + chever (“happen; come to a head”), from Vulgar Latin *capare, from Latin caput (“head”).

parole.significato: Relaxation of monastic rules.
parole.testo: From 1200–1250, from Middle English misericorde (“an act of clemency”) from Old French, from Latin misericordia (“pity”). Doublet of misericordia.

parole.significato: Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress; woe.
parole.testo: From Middle English miserie, from Old French miserie (modern: misère), from Latin miseria, from miser, equivalent to miser + -y. Doublet of misère and mizeria.

parole.significato: The act of mixing.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French misture, from Latin mixtūra (“a mixing”), from mixtus, perfect passive participle of misceō (“mix”); compare mix.

parole.significato: A deep, wide defensive ditch, normally filled with water, surrounding a fortified habitation.
parole.testo: From Middle English mote, from Old French mote (“mound, embankment”); compared also to Old French motte (“hillock, lump, clod, turf”), from Medieval Latin mota (“a mound, hill”), of Germanic origin, perhaps via Frankish *mot, *motta (“mud, peat, bog, turf”), from Proto-Germanic *mutô, *mudraz, *muþr

parole.significato: Capable of being moved, especially on wheels.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin mōbilis (“easy to be moved, moveable”), from moveō (“move”). parole.significato: A particular means of accomplishing something.
parole.testo: From Old French mode (masculine), from Latin modus (“measure, due measure, rhythm, melody”). Doublet of modus.

parole.significato: To toil, to work hard.
parole.testo: From Middle English mollen (“to soften by wetting”), borrowed from Old French moillier with the same meaning, from Vulgar Latin *molliō, *molliare, from mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: A hollow form or matrix for shaping a fluid or plastic substance.
parole.testo: From Middle English molde (“mold, cast”), from Old French modle, mole, from Latin modulus, from Latin modus. Doublet of module, modulus, and model.

parole.significato: To sexually assault or sexually harass.
parole.testo: From Middle English molesten, from Old French molester, from Latin molestō (“to trouble, annoy, molest”), from molestus (“troublesome”), from moles (“a burden, difficulty, labor, trouble”); see mole.

parole.significato: The act of molesting.
parole.testo: From Old French molestacion, from Latin molestatio. By surface analysis, molest + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of mollifying.
parole.testo: From Old French mollificacion, from Latin mollificātiō, form of molliō. By surface analysis, mollify + -ification.

parole.significato: A government in which sovereignty is embodied within a single, today usually hereditary head of state (whether as a fig…
parole.testo: From Old French monarchie, from Late Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía), from μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “power, authority”). By surface analysis, mon- (“one, single”) + -archy (“rule, command”).

parole.significato: A residence for monks or others who have taken religious vows.
parole.testo: From Middle English monasterie, from Old French monastere, from Medieval Latin monastērium (“monastery”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermitage, monastery”), from μοναστήριος (monastḗrios, “alone, made alone”) + -ιον (-ion, “-ium”, suffix forming place names), from μονάζω (monázō,

parole.significato: A unicorn.
parole.testo: From Old French monoceros, from Latin monocerōs.

parole.significato: A terrifying and dangerous creature, especially one of an imaginary or fictional kind.
parole.testo: From Middle English monstre, from Old French monstre, mostre, moustre, from Latin mōnstrum. Displaced native Old English fīfel and Old English þyrs.

parole.significato: An ornamental, often precious receptacle, either open or with a transparent cover, in which the sacramental bread (cons…
parole.testo: From Middle English mustraunce, from Old French mostrance, monstrance, from post-classical Latin mōnstrantia, from classical Latin mōnstrāns, present participle of mōnstrāre (“to show”).

parole.significato: Hideous or frightful.
parole.testo: From Middle English monstrous, from Old French monstrueuse, monstrüos, from Latin mōnstrōsus. Compare monstruous. By surface analysis, monster + -ous.

parole.significato: Monstrous.
parole.testo: From Middle English monstruous, from Old French monstrueuse, monstrüos, from Latin mōnstruōsus.

parole.significato: To mark or memorialize with a monument.
parole.testo: From Middle English monument, from Old French monument, from Latin monumentum (“memorial, monument, tomb”), from monēre (“to remind”). Partially displaced Old English bēacn.

parole.significato: A member of an ancient Amazigh people from Mauretania.
parole.testo: From Middle English More, Moore, from Old French More (modern French Maure), from Latin Maurus (“a Moor, meaning a Mauretanian, an inhabitant of Mauretania”), from Ancient Greek Μαυρούσιος (Mauroúsios, “Mauretanian”). Doublet of Moro.

parole.significato: Of or relating to principles of right and wrong in behaviour, especially conforming to principles of rectitude.
parole.testo: From Middle English moral, from Old French moral, from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”) (first used by Cicero, to translate Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “moral”)), from mos (“manner, custom”).

parole.significato: A small fragment or share of something, commonly applied to food.
parole.testo: From Middle English morsel, from Old French morsel, from Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, perfect passive participle of mordeo (“to bite”). Compare French morceau, whence the English doublet morceau.

parole.significato: Susceptible to death by aging, sickness, injury, or wound; not immortal.
parole.testo: From Middle English mortal, mortel, from Old French mortal, and their source Latin mortālis, from mors (“death”). In this sense, displaced native deadly, from Old English dēadlīċ.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being mortal.
parole.testo: From Old French mortalite, from Latin mortālitās, from mortālis (“relating to death”), from mors (“death”); equivalent to mortal + -ity.

parole.significato: A mixture of lime or cement, sand and water used for bonding building blocks.
parole.testo: From Middle English morter, from Old French mortier, from Latin mortārium. Doublet of mortarium.

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of mold.
parole.testo: Via Middle English molde, moulde (“mould, cast”) and Old French modle, from Latin modulus.

parole.significato: A person who moulds dough into loaves for baking into bread.
parole.testo: Partly from the following: * From Middle English molder, moldere (“maker of bread, baker”), from molden (“to knead or shape (bread); to make bread, bake; to mix (something) by kneading; to shape, mould; to pulverize (?)”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns, especially names of people engaged in profe

parole.significato: Intercession; intervention.
parole.testo: From Middle English moyen, moene, a variation of mene, meene, borrowed from Old French meien (French moyen), Late Latin mediānus (“that is in the middle, middle”), from Latin medius (“middle”). Doublet of mid and mean.

parole.significato: A machine that mixes clay and sand under a roller for use in preparing a mould for metal casting.
parole.testo: From mull (“to mix (clay and sand) under a roller to prepare a mould”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns). Mull is possibly derived from mull (“(chiefly Northern England) to grind to powder, crumble, powder, pulverize”), from Middle English mollen, mullen (“to moisten (something); to soften (somethi

parole.significato: A fish of the family Mullidae (order Syngnathiformes).
parole.testo: From Middle English molet, mulett, from Old French mulet (now ‘grey mullet’), from Latin mullus (“red mullet”), from Ancient Greek μύλλος (múllos).

parole.significato: To increase the amount, degree or number of (something).
parole.testo: From Old French multiplier, from Latin multiplicō, from multi (“many”) + plicō (“to fold”). The noun presumably derives from the verb.

parole.significato: A great amount or number, often of people; abundance, myriad, profusion.
parole.testo: From Middle English multitude, multitud, multytude (“(great) amount or number of people or things; multitudinous”), borrowed from Old French multitude (“crowd of people; diversity, wide range”), or directly from its etymon Latin multitūdō (“great amount or number of people or things”), from multus (

parole.significato: A grinding of grain, or the grain that is ground.
parole.testo: From Middle English multūr, from Old French molture (modern French mouture), from Medieval Latin molitura, from the past participle stem of molere ‘grind’. Compare mill.

parole.significato: Worldly, earthly, profane, vulgar as opposed to heavenly.
parole.testo: From Middle English mondeyne, from Old French mondain, from Late Latin mundānus, from Latin mundus (“world”). Compare Danish mondæn. (ordinary): Compare typologically Russian несусве́тный (nesusvétnyj) (<~ не- (ne-) + (rare) сусве́тный (susvétnyj) < свет (svet)).

parole.significato: An officer in charge of the town walls, or their repairs.
parole.testo: From Middle English murager, from Old French muragier (“an officer in charge of town walls, receiving toll for repairs”), from murage (“tax levied for the building or repairing of town walls”), from Latin murus (“a wall”) + -aticum.

parole.significato: Any low, indistinct sound, like that of running water.
parole.testo: From Middle English murmur, murmor, murmour, from Old French murmure (modern French murmure), from Latin murmur (“murmur, humming, muttering, roaring, growling, rushing etc.”).

parole.significato: Of, belonging or relating to music, or to its performance or notation.
parole.testo: From Middle English musical, from Old French [Term?], from Medieval Latin mūsicālis, from Latin mūsica (“music”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives); equivalent to music + -al.

parole.significato: A greasy secretion with a powerful odour, produced in a glandular sac of the male musk deer and used in the manufacture…
parole.testo: From Middle English muske, borrowed from Old French musc, from Late Latin muscus, from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian [script needed] (mwšk' /⁠muʃk⁠/) whence Persian مشک (mošk). Ultimately from Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣka, “testicle”), the shape of the gland of animals secreting the s

parole.significato: The property of being stale or musty.
parole.testo: From Middle English must, from Old English must and Old French must, most, both from Latin mustum.

parole.significato: Of a dark yellow colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English mustard, from Old French moustarde (French moutarde), from moust (“must”), from Latin mustum. Compare Saterland Frisian Muster (“mustard”), Dutch mosterd (“mustard”), German Low German Musterd (“mustard”), Icelandic mustarður (“mustard”). Displaced Middle English senep, from Old

parole.significato: The quality or state of being mutable.
parole.testo: From Middle English mutabilite, from Old French mutabilite, from Latin mutabilitas; equivalent to mutable + -ity.

parole.significato: Changeable, dynamic, evolutive; inclined to change, evolve, mutate.
parole.testo: From Middle English mutable, from Old French mutable, from Latin mutabilis (“liable to change”). By surface analysis, muta- + -able.

parole.significato: The meat of sheep used as food; especially, that of adults.
parole.testo: From Middle English motoun, moton, from Old French mouton (“sheep”), from Vulgar Latin moltō, from Gaulish *multon-, from Proto-Celtic *moltos (“ram, wether”). Doublet of mouton.

parole.significato: The protruding part of an animal's head which includes the nose, mouth and jaws.
parole.testo: From earlier muzle, musle, mousle, mussel, mozell, from Middle English mosel, from Old French musel, museau, muzeau (modern French museau), from Late Latin mūsus (“snout”), probably expressive of the shape of protruded lips and/or influenced by Latin mūgīre (“to moo, bellow”). Doublet of museau. Dis

parole.significato: An evergreen shrub or small tree of the genus Myrtus, native to southern Europe and north Africa.
parole.testo: From Middle English mirtille, from Old French mirtille, mirtile, from myrte, from Latin myrtillus, from myrtus + -illus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to mystics, mysticism or occult mysteries; mystical.
parole.testo: From Old French mistique, from Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”), from μύστης (mústēs, “one who has been initiated”). Doublet of mystique.

parole.significato: The beliefs, ideas, or thoughts of mystics.
parole.testo: From mystic + -ism, from Old French mistique (“mysterious, full of mystery”), from Latin mysticus (“mystical, mystic, of secret rites”), from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”), from μύστης (mústēs, “one who has been initiated, initiate”) from μῡ́ω (mū́ō, “to close one's lips or eye

parole.significato: A tablecloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English nape, from Old French nape, nappe (“a cloth”), from Medieval Latin nappa, napa (“cloth, table-cloth, sheet”), alteration of Latin mappa (“a cloth, napkin, towel”). More at map, apron. Doublet of map, mop, and nappe.

parole.significato: A flowering plant of species Nardostachys jatamansi, in the valerian family, that grows in the Himalayas and is used as…
parole.testo: From Middle English narde, from Old French narde, Latin nardus, from Ancient Greek νάρδος (nárdos), from Phoenician [Term?], Sanskrit नलद (nálada, “Indian narde”). Doublet of nardus.

parole.significato: The rump of beef, especially the lower and back part of the rump.
parole.testo: From Old French nache, Late Latin natica, from Latin natis (“the rump, buttocks”). Compare aitchbone.

parole.significato: A historically constituted, stable community of people, formed based on a common language, territory, economic life, et…
parole.testo: From Middle English nacioun, nacion, from Old French nacion, from Latin nātiōnem, accusative of nātiō (“nation”). Displaced Old English þēod.

parole.significato: A person who is native to a place; a person who was born in a place.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English natif, from Old French natif, from Latin nātīvus, from nātus (“birth”). Doublet of naive and neif. Displaced native Middle English thedisch, equivalent to (puristic) theed + -ish. By surface analysis, Latin nat- + -ive. Compare also inborn.

parole.significato: Existing in nature.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English natural, borrowed from Old French natural, naturel, from Latin nātūrālis, from nātus, the perfect participle of nāscor (“be born”, verb). Displaced native Old English ġecynde. By surface analysis, natur(e) + -al.

parole.significato: The condition of being natural; nature, naturalness
parole.testo: From Middle English naturalitee, from Old French naturalité, from Latin nātūrālitās.

parole.significato: The way things are, the totality of all things in the physical universe and their order, especially the physical world…
parole.testo: From Middle English nature, natur, from Old French nature, from Latin nātūra (“birth, origin, natural constitution or quality”), future participle from perfect passive participle (g)natus (“born”), from deponent verb (g)nasci (“to be born, originate”) + future participle suffix -urus. Displaced nati

parole.significato: Required, essential, whether logically inescapable or needed in order to achieve a desired result or avoid some penalty.
parole.testo: From Middle English necessarye, from Old French necessaire, from Latin necessārius (“unavoidable, inevitable, required”), variant of necesse (“unavoidable, inevitable”), probably from ne or non cessum, from the perfect passive participle of cēdō (“yield; avoid, withdraw”); see cede. Older use as a n

parole.significato: The quality or state of being necessary, unavoidable, or absolutely requisite.
parole.testo: From Middle English necessite, from Old French necessite, from Latin necessitās (“unavoidableness, compulsion, exigency, necessity”), from necesse (“unavoidable, inevitable”); see necessary. Doublet of Necessitas.

parole.significato: Divination involving the dead or death.
parole.testo: Circa 1300, from Middle English nigromancye, from Old French nigromancie, from Medieval Latin nigromantia, from Latin necromantia, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía), νεκρός (nekrós, “dead”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”). Medieval Latin spelling, incorporating niger (“black”), influe

parole.significato: The act of negating something.
parole.testo: From Middle English negacioun, from Old French negacion, from Latin negātiō (“a denial; negative word”). Morphologically negate + -ion.

parole.significato: Not positive or neutral; bad; undesirable; unfavourable.
parole.testo: From Middle English negative, negatif, from Old French negatif, from Latin negātīvus (“that denies, negative”), from negāre (“to deny”); see negate.

parole.significato: The state of being negligent.
parole.testo: From Middle English necligence, negligence, from Old French negligence, from Latin neglegentia.

parole.significato: Careless or inattentive.
parole.testo: From Middle English necligent, negligent, from Old French negligent, from Latin negligēns.

parole.significato: A son of one's sibling, brother-in-law, or sister-in-law; either a son of one's brother (fraternal nephew) or a son of…
parole.testo: From Middle English nevew, neveu (“nephew, grandson”), from Old French neveu, from Latin nepos, nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts (“nephew, grandson”), whence also French neveu, Italian nipote. Displaced or absorbed the inherited English neve (“nephew, grandson, male cousin”), from Middle English n

parole.significato: Free from extraneous substances; pure; unadulterated; neat.
parole.testo: From Middle English net, nette, from Old French net, from Latin nitidus. Doublet of neat and nitid.

parole.significato: Pleasant, satisfactory, complimentary.
parole.testo: From Middle English nyce, nice, nys, from Old French nice, niche, nisce (“simple, foolish, ignorant”), from Latin nescius (“ignorant, not knowing”); compare nesciō (“to know not, be ignorant of”), from ne (“not”) + sciō (“to know”).

parole.significato: A daughter of one’s sibling, brother-in-law, or sister-in-law; either the daughter of one's brother ("fraternal niece")…
parole.testo: From Middle English nece (“niece, granddaughter”), from Old French nece (“niece, granddaughter”) (Modern French nièce (“niece”)) from Late Latin neptia, representing Latin neptis (“granddaughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *néptih₂ (“granddaughter, niece”). Doublet of nift.

parole.significato: A serf or bondsman born into servitude.
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?], from Latin nativus (“natural”). Doublet of naif and native.

parole.significato: Necromancy; magic involving death.
parole.testo: From Middle English nigromauncy, from Old French nigromancie, nigremance, from Late Latin nigromantia, a blend of niger (“black”) and necromantīa (“necromancy”). Compare black art.

parole.significato: A mineral form of potassium nitrate (saltpetre) used in making gunpowder.
parole.testo: From Middle English niter, nitere, nitre, nytre, from Old French nitre, from Latin nitrum (“native soda, natron”), from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron). Ultimately from Egyptian nṯrj (“natron”). Doublet of natron and trona. Compare also natrium, nitrogen. Compare reconstructed Proto-Germanic *lauþrą (

parole.significato: A noble or privileged social class, historically accompanied by a hereditary title; aristocracy.
parole.testo: From Old French nobilité, from Latin nobilitas. Equivalent to noble + -ity.

parole.significato: An aristocrat; one of aristocratic blood.
parole.testo: From Middle English noble, from Old French noble, borrowed from Latin nōbilis (“knowable, known, well-known, famous, celebrated, high-born, of noble birth, excellent”), from nōscere, gnōscere (“to know”). False cognate of Arabic نبيل (nabīl). Displaced native Middle English athel, from Old English æ

parole.significato: Giving a name; naming; designating.
parole.testo: From Middle English nominatyf, either via Old French nominatif or directly from Latin nōminātīvus (“pertaining to naming, nominative”).

parole.significato: A lawyer of noncontentious private civil law who drafts, takes, and records legal instruments for private parties, and…
parole.testo: From Middle English notarie, from Old French notarie (French notaire), from Latin notārius.

parole.significato: A nurse.
parole.testo: From Middle English norischen, from Old French nouriss-, stem of one of the conjugated forms of norrir, from Latin nutriō (“to suckle, feed, foster, nourish, cherish, preserve, support”).

parole.significato: Newly made, formed or evolved; having no precedent; of recent origin; new.
parole.testo: From Middle English novel, from Old French novel (“new, fresh, recent, recently made or done, strange, rare”) (modern nouvel, nouveau), from Latin novellus (“new, fresh, young, modern”), diminutive of novus (“new”). Doublet of nouveau.

parole.significato: A novelty; something new.
parole.testo: From Middle English novel, from Old French novelle, from Latin novella, feminine of novellus.

parole.significato: The state of being new or novel; newness.
parole.testo: From Middle English novelte, from Old French novelté (Modern French nouveauté), from the adjective novel, ultimately from Latin novellus. By surface analysis, novel + -ty.

parole.significato: A person involved in providing direct care for the sick:
parole.testo: From Middle English norice, from Old French norrice, from Late Latin nūtrīcia, noun based on Latin nūtrīcius (“that which nourishes”), from nūtrīx (“wet nurse”), from nūtriō (“to suckle”).

parole.significato: The act of nourishing or nursing; tender care
parole.testo: From Middle English norture, noriture, from Old French norriture, norreture, from Late Latin nutritura (“nourishment”), from Latin nutrire (“to nourish”).

parole.significato: Any female nature spirit associated with water, forests, grottos, wind, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English nimphe, from Old English nymphē and Old French nimphe, both from Latin nympha (“nymph, bride”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, young maiden”). Doublet of nympha.

parole.significato: The vocative particle, used for direct address.
parole.testo: From Middle English O, o, from Old English o, from Latin o and Ancient Greek ὦ (ô, interjection). Featured prominently in William Tyndale's 1525 translation of the New Testament.

parole.significato: Willing to comply with the commands, orders, or instructions of those in authority; biddable.
parole.testo: From Middle English obedient, from Old French obedient, from Latin oboediēns, present active participle of oboediō (“obey”).

parole.significato: Demonstration of an obedient attitude, especially by bowing deeply; a deep bow which demonstrates such an attitude.
parole.testo: From Middle English obeisaunce (“obedience, obeisance”), from Old French obeïssance, derived from obeïssant (“obedient”), participle of obeïr (“to obey”), from Latin oboediō, obēdiō; ob- (“to, for”) + audiō (“to hear”). Cognate with obedience.

parole.significato: A thing that has physical existence but is not alive.
parole.testo: From Old French object, from Medieval Latin obiectum (“object”, literally “thrown against”), from obiectus, perfect passive participle of obiciō (“to throw against”), from ob- (“against”) + iaciō (“to throw”), as a calque of Ancient Greek ἀντικείμενον (antikeímenon). Doublet of objectum and objet.

parole.significato: The offering of worship, thanks etc. to a deity.
parole.testo: From Middle English oblacioun, from Old French oblacion, from Latin oblātiō (“offering”), from offerō (“to offer, present”). By surface analysis, oblate + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of binding oneself by a social, legal, or moral tie to someone.
parole.testo: From Middle English obligacioun, from Old French obligacion, from Latin obligatio, obligationem, from obligatum (past participle of obligare), from ob- (“to”) + ligare (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).

parole.significato: To constrain someone by force or by social, moral or legal means.
parole.testo: From Middle English obligen, from Old French obligier, obliger, from Latin obligō, obligāre, from ob- + ligō. Doublet of obligate, taken straight from Latin.

parole.significato: Dark, faint or indistinct.
parole.testo: From Middle English obscure, from Old French obscur, from Latin obscūrus (“dark, dusky, indistinct”), from ob- + *scūrus, from Proto-Italic *skoiros, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃-. Doublet of oscuro.

parole.significato: The last office for the dead.
parole.testo: From Middle English obseque, from Old French obseque, osseque, from Latin obsequiī (“complaisant, yielding”), alteration of obsequia (“compliance”) (by confusion, in association with exsequia (“funeral rites”), from exsequī (“follow or accompany to the grave”)).

parole.significato: The practice of complying with a law, custom, command or rule.
parole.testo: From Old French observance, from Latin observantia. Equivalent of observe + -ance.

parole.significato: Something that impedes, stands in the way of, or holds up progress, either physically or figuratively
parole.testo: From Middle English obstacle, from Old French obstacle, from Latin obstāculum.

parole.significato: The part of the horizon where the sun last appears in the evening; that part of the earth towards the sunset; the west.
parole.testo: From Middle English occident, from Old French occident, from Latin occidentem (“western sky, part of the sky in which the sun sets”), from occido (“go down, set”).

parole.significato: To take or use.
parole.testo: From Middle English occupien, occupyen, borrowed from Old French occuper, from Latin occupāre (“to take possession of, seize, occupy, take up, employ”), from ob (“to, on”) + capiō (“to take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Doublet of occupate, now obsolete.

parole.significato: One of the large bodies of water separating the continents.
parole.testo: From Middle English *ocean, occean, occian, occyan, from Old French occean (later reborrowed or reinforced by Middle French ocean), from Latin Ōceanus, originally from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós, “Oceanus”, a water deity). Displaced native Old English gārseċġ. Also commonly referred to as the oc

parole.significato: A clay earth pigment containing silica, aluminum and ferric oxide.
parole.testo: From Old French ocre and its source Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra, “pale yellow”), from ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “pale, ocher”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).

parole.significato: A type of ale traditionally brewed in October.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French octobre, from Latin Octōber (“eighth month”), from Latin octō (“eight”), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw (“twice four”); + Latin -ber, from -bris, an adjectival suffix; October was the eighth month in the Roman calendar.

parole.significato: Arousing or meriting strong dislike, aversion, or intense displeasure.
parole.testo: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).

parole.significato: The act of offending.
parole.testo: From Middle English offence, from Old French offense, from Latin offensa (“a striking against; displeasure; injury”).

parole.significato: Assault; attack, offensive; offense.
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?], from Latin offensio (“an offense”).

parole.significato: To propose or express one's willingness (to do something).
parole.testo: From Middle English offren, offrien. In the religious senses inherited from Old English offrian (“to offer, sacrifice, bring an oblation”); otherwise from Old French ofrir. parole.significato: To provide (someone) with an office.
parole.testo: From Middle English office, from Old French office, from Latin officium (“personal, official, or moral duty; official position; function; ceremony, esp. last rites”), contracted from opificium (“construction: the act of building or the thing built”), from opifex (“doer of work, craftsman”) + -ium (“

parole.significato: Of or about an office or public trust.
parole.testo: From Middle English official, from Old French official, from Latin officiālis, from Latin officium (“duty, service”), by surface analysis, office + -ial.

parole.significato: A double curve in the shape of an elongated S; an object of that shape.
parole.testo: From Middle English *ogeve, egeve, egeove, from Old French œgive, ogive, augive, from Late Latin augiva, of uncertain origin; compare Late Latin ogis (“a support, prop”), Latin augeō (“to increase, strengthen”), Italian and Spanish auge (“highest point of power or fortune, apogee”). Doublet of ogive

parole.significato: Expression of surprise.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English o.

parole.significato: Liquid fat.
parole.testo: From Middle English oyle, oile (“olive oil”), borrowed from Old French oile, from Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”), from ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”). Compare Proto-Slavic *lojь. More at olive. Doublet of oleum. Supplanted Middle English ele (“oil”), from Old

parole.significato: A viscous preparation of oils and/or fats, usually containing medication, used as a treatment or as an emollient.
parole.testo: A later form (as if oint + -ment) of Middle English oinement, borrowed from Old French oignement (“an anointing”), from oigner, oindre, ongier (“to anoint”), from Latin ung(u)ō (“I anoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to smear, anoint”). Partly displaced native Old English sealf, whence mod

parole.significato: An ancient hunting horn, made of ivory.
parole.testo: From Middle English olifaunt, from Old French oliphaunt, from Latin elephantus. See elephant.

parole.significato: elephant
parole.testo: From Middle English oliphaunt, olifaunt, from Old French olifant, from Latin elephantus; see elephant for more information.

parole.significato: Drunk, pissed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Oliver, from Old French Olivier, by folk etymology derived from the Latin name Olīvārius, but probably representing an Old High German form of Old Norse Óleifr (“ancestral + relic”) (modern Danish Olaf and Swedish Olof), or Proto-Germanic *ala- (“all”) + *wēraz (“true”)

parole.significato: The act of omitting.
parole.testo: From Middle English omissioun, from Old French omission, from Late Latin omissio, omissionem, from Latin omitto.

parole.significato: Unlimited power; commonly attributed to a deity or deities.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English omnipotens, from Old French omnipotence, from Latin omnipotentia.

parole.significato: Having unlimited power, force or authority.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English omnipotent(e), from Old French omnipotent, from Latin omnipotēns, omnipotentem.

parole.significato: A banded variety of chalcedony, a cryptocrystalline form of quartz.
parole.testo: From Middle English onix (c. 1300), earlier oniche (c. 1250), from Old French oniche or onix, from Latin onyx, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux, “onyx”). Doublet of unguis.

parole.significato: The method by which a device performs its function.
parole.testo: From Middle English operacioun, from Old French operacion, from Latin operātiō, from the verb operor (“to work”), from opus, operis (“work”). Equivalent to operate + -ion.

parole.significato: Suitable for some particular purpose.
parole.testo: From Old French opportun, from Latin opportunus.

parole.significato: To attempt to stop the progression of; to resist or antagonize by physical means, or by arguments, etc.; to contend aga…
parole.testo: From Middle English opposen, from Old French opposer, from Latin ob (“before, against”) + Medieval Latin pono (“to put”), taking the place of Latin opponere (“to oppose”).

parole.significato: Located directly across from something else, or from each other.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English opposit, borrowed from Old French oposite, from Latin oppositus, perfect passive participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”). Compare oppose.

parole.significato: The action of opposing or of being in conflict.
parole.testo: From Middle English opposicioun, from Old French oposicion (whence French opposition), from Late Latin oppositiō, translating Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from the past participle stem of classical Latin oppōnō (“to set against”). Equivalent to oppose + -ition.

parole.significato: To keep down by unjust force.
parole.testo: From Middle English oppressen, from Old French oppresser, from Medieval Latin oppressare (“to press against, oppress”), frequentative of Latin opprimere, past participle oppressus (“to press against, press together, oppress”), from ob (“against”) + premere, past participle pressus (“to press”); see

parole.significato: The exercise of authority or power in a burdensome, cruel, or unjust manner.
parole.testo: From Middle English oppression, from Old French oppression, from Latin oppressiō (“a pressing down, violence, oppression”), from opprimō; see oppress.

parole.significato: Someone who oppresses another or others.
parole.testo: From Middle English oppressour, from Old French opressor and Latin oppressor; equivalent to oppress + -or.

parole.significato: A shrine dedicated to some prophetic deity.
parole.testo: From Middle English oracle, from Old French oracle m, from Latin ōrāculum n.

parole.significato: A spherical body; a sphere, especially one of the celestial spheres; a sun, planet, or star
parole.testo: From Middle English orbe, from Old French orbe, from Latin orbis (“circle, orb”). Compare orbit.

parole.significato: A blank window or panel.
parole.testo: From Old French orb (“blind”), from Latin orbus (“destitute”).

parole.significato: To prearrange unalterably.
parole.testo: From Middle English ordeynen, from Old French ordiner, from Latin ordinare (“to order”), from ordo (“order”). Doublet of ordinate.

parole.significato: Arrangement, disposition, or sequence.
parole.testo: From Middle English ordre, from Old French ordre, ordne, ordene (“order, rank”), from Latin ōrdinem, accusative of ōrdō (“row, rank, regular arrangement”, literally “row of threads in a loom”), from Proto-Italic *ordō (“to arrange”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂or-d-, from *h₂er-

parole.significato: To supply with an organ or organs; to fit with organs.
parole.testo: From Middle English organe, from Old French organe and Old English organ, both from Latin organum, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “an instrument, implement, tool, also an organ of sense or apprehension, an organ of the body, also a musical instrument, an organ”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ

parole.significato: Pertaining to or derived from living organisms.
parole.testo: From Middle English organic, organik, from Old French organique, from Latin organicus.

parole.significato: Pride.
parole.testo: In older uses, from Middle English orguile, from Old French orgueil, from Vulgar Latin *orgollium, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀgōllju, from Proto-Germanic *uzgōljō. parole.significato: A large polygonal recess in a building, such as a bay window, forming a protrusion on the outer wall.
parole.testo: From Middle English oriel, from Old French oriol (“gallery, corridor”), Late Latin oriolum (“portico, hall”), probably from Latin aureolus (“gilded”), applied to an apartment decorated with gilding. See oriole. Or a diminutive of Latin os (“mouth”).

parole.significato: The red silk banner of St Denis, which the abbot of St Denis gave to French kings as they rode to war in the Middle Age…
parole.testo: From Old French oriflambe, oriflamme, from Medieval Latin auriflamma (“golden flame”), from Latin aurum (“gold”) + flamma (“flame”).

parole.significato: The beginning of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English origine, origyne, from Old French origine, orine, ourine, from Latin orīgō (“beginning, source, birth, origin”), from orior (“to rise”); see orient. Doublet of origo.

parole.significato: Relating to the origin or beginning; preceding all others.
parole.testo: From Middle English original, from Old French original, from Late Latin orīginālis (“primitive, original”), from Latin orīgō (“beginning, source, origin”), equivalent to origin + -al; see origin.

parole.significato: To ornament; to adorn.
parole.testo: From Old French orner, from Latin ornō.

parole.significato: An element of decoration; that which embellishes or adorns.
parole.testo: From Middle English ornament, from Old French ornement, from Latin ornamentum (“equipment, apparatus, furniture, trappings, adornment, embellishment”), from ornāre (“to equip, adorn”). The verb is derived from the noun.

parole.significato: Arsenic trisulphide, occurring naturally in crystals or massive deposits, formerly used as a dye or pigment.
parole.testo: From Middle English orpyment, from Old French orpiment, from Latin auripigmentum (“orpiment”), from aurum (“gold”) + pigmentum (“pigment”).

parole.significato: Any of several temperate succulent plants of the family Crassulaceae, that have clusters of purple flowers, especially…
parole.testo: From Old French orpin, Old French orpiment, from Latin auripigmentum (“orpiment”), from aurum (“gold”) + pigmentum (“pigment”).

parole.significato: An excessively violent or vicious attack; an atrocity.
parole.testo: From Middle English outrage, from Old French outrage, oultrage (“excess”), from Vulgar Latin *ultrāticum ("a going beyond"), derived from Latin ultrā (“beyond”). Later reanalysed as out- + rage, whence the contemporary pronunciation, though neither of these are etymologically related. The verb is fr

parole.significato: The furthest degree or extremity, going beyond bounds or propriety.
parole.testo: From Old French oltrance (modern outrance (“excess”)), from outrer (“pass beyond”), from oltre, outre, utre, from Late Latin ultra-. Compare outrage.

parole.significato: Presumption, arrogance, self-conceit.
parole.testo: From Old French outrecuidance (whence modern French outrecuidance), from outre + cuidier (“think”), from Latin cogitare.

parole.significato: Presumptuous, arrogant, conceited.
parole.testo: From Old French outrecuidant (whence modern French outrecuidant), from outre + cuidier (“think”), from Latin cogitare.

parole.significato: equal
parole.testo: From Old French oel, owel, iwel, ivel, French égal, from Latin aequalis. Doublet of equal.

parole.significato: Hear ye. Attend. (Called by public criers or in court usually three times to secure silence or attentiveness).
parole.testo: From Middle English oyes, from Old French oyez, the imperative plural of oir (“to hear; to listen”), from Latin audīre. Commonly folk-etymologized as (and pronounced homophonously to) O + yes in the early modern period.

parole.significato: The art of painting.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English peynture, from Old French peinture, from Late Latin *pinctūra; by surface analysis, paint + -ure. See paint and compare picture.

parole.significato: Two alike or identical things taken together; often followed by of.
parole.testo: From Middle English paire, from Old French paire, from Latin paria (“equals”), neuter plural of par (“pair”). Related to pār (“equal”, adjective). Compare Saterland Frisian Poor (“pair”), West Frisian pear (“pair”), Dutch paar (“pair”), German Paar (“pair”), Italian paio (“pair”)

parole.significato: To impair, to make worse.
parole.testo: From Middle English pairen, peiren, shortened form of apeiren, empeiren, from Old French empeirier, empoirier, from Late Latin peiōrō.

parole.significato: The roof of the mouth, separating the cavities of the mouth and nose in vertebrates.
parole.testo: From Middle English palate, from Latin palātum (“roof of the mouth, palate”), perhaps of Etruscan origin.

parole.significato: (of an official or feudal lord) Having local authority and possessing royal privileges that elsewhere belongs only to a…
parole.testo: From late Middle English palatyne, from Old French palatin, from Medieval Latin palātīnus (“relating to the palace”), from palātium (“palace”) + -īnus (“-ine”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of paladin.

parole.significato: Light in color.
parole.testo: From Middle English pale, from Old French pale, from Latin pallidus (“pale, pallid”), from palleō (“to be pale; to grow pale; to fade”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelito-, from *pelH- (“gray”). Doublet of pallid. Displaced native Old English blāc.

parole.significato: A wooden stake; a picket.
parole.testo: From Middle English pale, pal, borrowed from Old French pal, from Latin pālus (“stake, prop”). English inherited the word pole (or, rather Old English pāl) from a much older Proto-Germanic borrowing of the same Latin word. Doublet of peel and pole.

parole.significato: Senses relating to cloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English pal, palle, from Old English pæl, pæll, from Old French paile and Latin pallium (“cloak; covering”) (and thus a doublet of pallium), probably from palla (“piece of cloth worn as apparel”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; hide, skin; cloth”)) + -ium (suff

parole.significato: Unnatural paleness, especially as a sign of sickness or distress.
parole.testo: From Middle English pallour, from Old French palor (“paleness, pallor”), from Latin pallor, from palleō (“to look pale, blanch”).

parole.significato: The inner and somewhat concave part of the human hand or other primate hand that extends from the wrist to the bases of…
parole.testo: From Middle English palme, paume, from Old French palme, paulme, paume (“palm of the hand, ball, tennis”), from Latin palma (“palm of the hand, hand-breadth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂(e)meh₂ (“palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Doublet of palmo, palma, and pam. Co

parole.significato: An individual sheet of glass or other transparent material in a window, door, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English pane, pan, from Old French pan, from Latin pannus, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂n- (“fabric”). Doublet of pagne and pannus.

parole.significato: Acorns and beech mast used as forage for pigs.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French pasnage (modern French panage), from Late Latin pasnadium, pastinaticum, from pastionare (“to feed on mast, as swine”), from Latin pastio (“a pasturing, grazing”). See pastor.

parole.significato: A large basket or bag fastened, usually in pairs, to the back of a bicycle or pack animal, or carried in pairs over the…
parole.testo: From Middle English panere, panȝere, panyere, from Old French panier, paniere, from Latin pānārium (“a bread basket”), from pānis (“bread”). Doublet of panary.

parole.significato: A quick breathing; a catching of the breath; a gasp: the panting of animals such as a dog with their tong hung out- as…
parole.testo: From Middle English panten, whence also English dialectal pank. Possibly from Old French pantoyer, a byform or of Old French pantoisier (“to be breathless”) (compare modern French panteler (“to gasp for breath”)), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pantasiō (“struggling for breath when

parole.significato: Any of various big cats with black fur; most especially, the black-coated leopard of Africa and Asia.
parole.testo: From Middle English pantere, panter, from Old French pantere, from Latin panthēra, from Ancient Greek πάνθηρ (pánthēr, “panther”).

parole.significato: A small room, closet, or cabinet usually located in or near the kitchen, dedicated to shelf-stable food storage or stor…
parole.testo: From Middle English panetrie, from Old French paneterie, related to Latin panis (“bread”).

parole.significato: Having to do with the pope or the papacy.
parole.testo: From Middle English papal, from Old French papal and Medieval Latin pāpālis (“papal”).

parole.significato: A type of document or edict from the Pope.
parole.testo: From Middle English bulle, from Old French bulle, from Medieval Latin bulla (“a round seal”), from Latin bulla (“bubble”).

parole.significato: A short narrative illustrating a lesson (usually religious/moral) by comparison or analogy.
parole.testo: From Middle English parable, from Old French parable, parabole, from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison”). Doublet of parabola, parole, and palaver.

parole.significato: The place where sanctified souls are believed to live after death.
parole.testo: From Middle English paradis, paradise, paradys, from Late Old English paradīs, borrowed from Old French paradis, from Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah. Doublet of parvis. Displaced Old English neorxnawang.

parole.significato: At the bottom; lowest (said of feudal tenants).
parole.testo: From Old French par aval (“below”), from par (“through”) (Latin per) + aval (“down”), from a- (Latin ad) + val (“a valley”) (Latin vallis). Compare paramount.

parole.significato: To boil food briefly so that it is partly cooked.
parole.testo: From Middle English parboyle, from Old French parbouillir (“to boil thoroughly”), from Medieval Latin perbulliō, from Latin per (“thoroughly”) + bulliō (“to boil”). parole.significato: A package wrapped, as for shipment or transport.
parole.testo: From Middle English parcel, from Old French parcelle (“a small piece or part, a parcel, a particle”), from Late Latin particella, diminutive of Latin particula (“particle”), diminutive of partem (“part, piece”). Doublet of particle.

parole.significato: To divide among parceners
parole.testo: Probably a back-formation from parcener, from Old French parçonier, from parçon (“part, portion, share, division”), from Latin partītiō, partītiōnem (“division”), from partīre, from pars.

parole.significato: A coheir, a coparcener
parole.testo: From Middle English parcener, from Old French parçonier, from parçon (“part, portion, share, division”), from Latin partītiō, partītiōnem (“division”), from partīre, from pars. See partition and compare partner. By surface analysis, parcen + -er.

parole.significato: Material, made from the polished skin of a calf, sheep, goat or other animal, used like paper for writing.
parole.testo: From Middle English parchemyn, parchement, from Old French parchemin, via Latin pergamīna, from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós, “of Pergamon”), which is named for the ancient city of Pergamon (modern Bergama) in Asia Minor, where it was invented as an expensive alternative for papyrus. parole.significato: A leopard; a panther.
parole.testo: From Middle English parde, from Old French, from Latin pardus, from Ancient Greek πάρδος (párdos), possibly of Iranian origin and related to other Sanskrit and Ancient Greek terms (see leopard).

parole.significato: Forgiveness for an offence.
parole.testo: From Middle English pardonen, from Old French pardoner (modern French pardonner), from Late Latin perdōnāre, from per- + dōnāre, possibly a calque (if not vice-versa) of a Germanic word represented by Frankish *firgeban (“to forgive, give up completely”), from *fir- + *geban. parole.significato: A coat of cement mortar on the face of rough masonry, the earth side of foundation and basement walls.
parole.testo: Probably from parget (verb) (perhaps influenced by sparge (verb)), from Old French porjeter, progeter, pourgeter (“to cast; to plaster a wall”) (compare Old French parjeter (“to cast (especially light) widely”); Middle French pourgetter (Lille and Tournai), Norman porjeter (“to plaster”); French por

parole.significato: To coat with gypsum; to plaster, for example walls, or the interior of flues.
parole.testo: From Middle English pargetten, from Old French pargeter, parjeter (“to throw about”), from par- (intensive prefix) (from Latin per-) + jeter (“to throw”) (from Latin iactō, frequentative of iaciō). The noun is derived from the verb.

parole.significato: An administrative part of a diocese that has its own church.
parole.testo: From Middle English parisshe, from Old French paroisse (compare the obsolete variant paroch, from Anglo-Norman paroche, parosse), from Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”).

parole.significato: An area of land set aside for environment preservation or recreation.
parole.testo: From Middle English park, from Old French parc (“livestock pen”), from Medieval Latin parcus, parricus, from Frankish *parrik (“enclosure, pen, fence”).
