parole.significato: A conference, especially one between enemies.
parole.testo: From Middle English parlai (“speech, parley”), from Old French parler (“to talk; to speak”), from Late Latin parabolō, from Latin parabola (“comparison”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παρά (pará, “beside”) with βολή (bolḗ, “throwing”). Doublet of palaver.

parole.significato: Used in or appropriate for a parlor.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English parlour, from Old French parleor, parloir, parleoir, from the verb parler (“to speak”); compare Medieval Latin parlātōrium. Doublet of parloir. Displaced native Old English sprǣchūs.

parole.significato: Attended with peril; dangerous, risky.
parole.testo: From Middle English parles, parlous, perlous, [and other forms], a contraction of perilous (“dangerous; dreadful, terrible; morally corrupt, sinful, wicked; inauspicious, unlucky”) (and thus a doublet of perilous), from Old French perilleus, perillos, perillous, perilluse, perilleuse, perilleux (“ve

parole.significato: To avoid, deflect, or ward off (an attack, a blow, an argument, etc.).
parole.testo: From earlier parree, from Middle English *parree, *paree, from Old French paree (“preparation, ceremony, parade”), from Medieval Latin parāta (“preparation, parade”), from parāre (“to ward off, guard, defend, prepare, get ready”). More at pare. The English verb is taken from the noun. Doublet of par

parole.significato: To resolve (a sentence, etc.) into its elements, pointing out the several parts of speech, and their relation to each o…
parole.testo: Possibly from Middle English pars (“parts, shares; parts of speech, grammar”), from Old French pars (plural of part (“part, portion, share”)), from Latin pars (“part, piece, share”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to carry forth; to sell”).

parole.significato: A bright green, biennial herb, Petroselinum crispum, having many cultivars.
parole.testo: From Middle English persely, from Old French peresil, from Latin petroselīnum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon, “parsley”), from πέτρος (pétros, “rock, stone”) + σέλῑνον (sélīnon, “celery”). Displaced Old English petersiliġe, which goes back to the same root.

parole.significato: A biennial plant, Pastinaca sativa, related to the carrot.
parole.testo: From 16th-century parsnepe, from Middle English passenep, a modification of Old French pasnaie by influence of Middle English nepe (“turnip”), from Latin pastināca (“parsnip, carrot”), from pastinum (“two-pronged fork”) as in pastināre (“to dig up the ground”).. parole.significato: A portion; a component.
parole.testo: From Middle English part, from Old English part (“part”) and Old French part (“part”); both from Latin partem, accusative of pars (“piece, portion, share, side, party, faction, role, character, lot, fate, task, lesson, part, member”), from Proto-Indo-European *par-, *per- (“to sell, exchange”). parole.significato: To leave the company of (each other, or someone/something [with with or from]).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English parten, borrowed from Old French partir.

parole.significato: Existing as a part or portion; incomplete.
parole.testo: From Middle English partiall, parcial, from Old French parcial (“biased or particular”), from Late Latin partiālis (“of or pertaining to a part”), from Latin pars (“part”).

parole.significato: A form of a verb that may function as an adjective, noun or adverb. English has two types of participles: the present p…
parole.testo: From Middle English participle, from Old French participle (1388), variant of participe, from Latin participium.

parole.significato: An action which divides a thing into parts, or separates one thing from another.
parole.testo: Recorded c.1430, "division into shares, distinction," from Middle English particioun, from Old French particion (modern partition), from Latin partitio, partitionem (“division, portion”), from partitus, the past participle of partire (“to split (up), part(ition)”).

parole.significato: Either of a pair of people or things that belong together.
parole.testo: From Middle English partener, partiner, alteration (due to Middle English part) of Middle English parcener, from Old French parçonier, parçonneour (“joint heir”) from parçon (“partition”), from Latin partītiōnem, singular accusative of partītiō (“portion”). parole.significato: Any bird of a number of genera in the family Phasianidae, notably in the genera Perdix and Alectoris.
parole.testo: From Middle English partrich, partriche, pertriche, perdriz, from Old French perdriz, partriz, from Latin perdīx (“partridge”), from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix, “partridge”), probably from πέρδομαι (pérdomai, “to fart”).

parole.significato: Divided; in part.
parole.testo: From Middle English party, from Old French parti (“parted”), from Latin partītus (“parted”), past participle of partiō (“to divide”). More at part.

parole.significato: An enclosed courtyard in front of a building, especially a cathedral.
parole.testo: From Middle English parvys, parvis, borrowed from Old French parvis, parevis, from Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah. parole.significato: Passover.
parole.testo: From Middle English Pask, Paske, Paskes, from Old French pasches (modern French Pâques), from Ecclesiastical Latin pascha, from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha), from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā), from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésaḥ). Doublet of Pascha, paska, paskha, and Pesach.

parole.significato: To change place.
parole.testo: From Middle English passen, from Old French passer (“to step, walk, pass”), from Vulgar Latin *passāre (“step, walk, pass”), derived from Latin passus (“a step”), from Proto-Italic *pat-s-tus, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread, stretch out”). parole.significato: Able to suffer, or feel pain.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French passible, from Late Latin passibilis.

parole.significato: A soft moist mixture, in particular:
parole.testo: From Middle English paste, from Old French paste (modern pâte), from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá). Doublet of pasta. The verb is from the noun. parole.significato: The part of a horse's leg between the fetlock joint and the hoof.
parole.testo: From Middle English pastron, pastroun, pasturne, from Old French pasturon, diminutive of pasture (“shackle for a horse in pasture”), alteration of Late Latin pastōria after the suffix -ure.

parole.significato: A flavoured candy or sweet, often round and somewhat flat in shape.

parole.significato: Someone who tends to a flock of animals: synonym of shepherd.
parole.testo: From Middle English pastour, from Old French pastor (Modern French pasteur), from Latin pāstor.

parole.significato: A baked food item made from flour and fat pastes such as pie crust; also tarts, bear claws, napoleons, puff pastries, e…
parole.testo: From Middle English pastre, pastri, from pastree (variant of pasterie, from Old French pastaierie and Medieval Latin pasteria, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá)) or paste + -ri (modern paste + -ry).

parole.significato: The plate used to hold the host during the Eucharist.
parole.testo: From Middle English patene, from Old French patene, from Latin patina, from Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē). Doublet of patina, patine, and patena.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to one's father, his genes, his relatives, or his side of a family.
parole.testo: From Old French paternal (“of a father”) (12th c.), from Vulgar Latin paternālis (“paternal”), from Latin paternus (“of or pertaining to a father, paternal”), from pater (“father”).

parole.significato: The quality of being patient.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pacience, from Old French pacience (modern French patience), from Latin patientia (“suffering; endurance, patience”), from patiens, present active participle of patior (“suffer, experience, wait”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hurt”). parole.significato: One who protects or supports; a defender or advocate.
parole.testo: From Middle English patroun, patrone, from Old French patron, from Latin patrōnus, derived from pater (“father”). Doublet of padrone, Patronus, patroon, and pattern.

parole.significato: Any of various types of footwear with thick soles, often used to elevate the foot, especially wooden clogs.
parole.testo: From Middle English patyn, patin, pateyn, from Old French patin, from patte (“paw, hoof”), from Latin patta, of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Model, example.
parole.testo: From earlier patten, paterne, from Middle English patron (“patron; example”), from Old French patron, from Medieval Latin patrōnus (“patron”). Doublet of padrone, patron, Patronus, and patroon.

parole.significato: To cover something with paving slabs.
parole.testo: From Old French paver (“to pave, to cover”), from Vulgar Latin *pavāre (“to beat down, to smash”), from Latin pavīre (“to beat, strike, ram, tread down”).

parole.significato: To give money or other compensation to in exchange for goods or services.
parole.testo: From Middle English payen, from Old French paiier (“pay”), from Medieval Latin pācāre (“to settle, satisfy”) from Latin pācāre (“to pacify”). In this sense, displaced native Old English ġield (“pay”) and ġieldan (“to pay”), whence Modern English yield.

parole.significato: To cover (the bottom of a vessel, a seam, a spar, etc.) with tar or pitch, or a waterproof composition of tallow, resin…
parole.testo: From Old French peier, from Latin picāre (“to cover with pitch”).

parole.significato: Any tree of species Prunus persica, native to China and now widely cultivated throughout temperate regions, having pink…
parole.testo: From Middle English peche, borrowed from Old French pesche (French pêche), Vulgar Latin *pessica (cf. Medieval Latin pesca) from Late Latin persica, from Classical Latin mālum persicum, from Ancient Greek μᾶλον περσικόν (mâlon persikón, “Persian apple”). Displaced Middle English persogȝe, from Old E

parole.significato: To set or adorn with pearls, or with mother-of-pearl.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English perle, from Old French perle of uncertain etymology. Probably via unattested Medieval Latin *pernula, from Latin perna (“haunch; a marine bivalve shaped like a leg of lamb”) but also derived from Medieval Latin perla, from Latin perula (“little bag”). Its typographic us

parole.significato: To remove the skin or outer covering of.
parole.testo: From Middle English pelen, from Old English pilian and Old French peler, pellier; both from Latin pilō, pilāre (“to remove hair from, depilate”), from pilus (“hair”). Doublet of pill.

parole.significato: A shovel or similar instrument, now especially a pole with a flat disc at the end used for removing pizza or loaves of…
parole.testo: From Middle English pele, from Old French pele (modern French pelle), from Latin pāla, from the base of plangō (“fix, plant”). Doublet of pala.

parole.significato: Constantly complaining, especially in a childish way due to insignificant matters; fretful, whiny.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English pievish, peuysche, pevish, pevysh (“capricious, wilful; perverse, wayward”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from one of the following: * From an unattested Old French word, from Latin perversus (“corrupted, perverted, subverted; overthrown”),

parole.significato: Pain or punishment.
parole.testo: From Old French peine, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Doublet of pain.

parole.significato: A pilgrim.
parole.testo: From Middle English pelerin, from Old French pelerin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner, traveler”). Doublet of pilgrim.

parole.significato: A small, compressed, hard chunk of matter.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pelote, pelet, from Old French pelote (“small ball”), from Vulgar Latin *pilotta, diminutive of Latin pila (“ball”). Doublet of pelota.

parole.significato: Of or relating to punishment.
parole.testo: From Old French peinal, from Medieval Latin penalis, from Latin poenalis, from poena (“punishment”), from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “punishment”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂.

parole.significato: Capable of being penetrated, entered, or pierced.
parole.testo: From Middle English penetrable, penytrable, from Old French penetrable, from Medieval Latin penetrābilis.

parole.significato: The act of penetrating something.
parole.testo: From Middle English penetracioun, from Old French penetracïon, and its source, Latin penetrātiō, from the participle stem of penetrō (“pierce”, verb). Morphologically penetrate + -ion.

parole.significato: The condition of being penitent; a feeling of regret or remorse for doing wrong or sinning.
parole.testo: First attested circa 13th century, from Middle English penitence, from Old French penitence, from Latin paenitentia (“repentance, penitence”), from paenitēns (“penitent”), present active participle of paeniteō (“regret, repent”). Equivalent to penitent + -ence. Doublet of penance.

parole.significato: Feeling pain or sorrow on account of one's sins or offenses; feeling sincere guilt.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin paenitēns, poenitēns (“penitent”), present participle of paeniteō, poeniteō (“to cause to repent; to regret, repent”). Doublet of penitente.

parole.significato: A flag normally used by naval vessels to represent a special condition.
parole.testo: From Middle English penon, penoun, pynoun, Old French penon, French pennon, from Latin penna (“feather”). See pen (“a feather”), and compare pennon, pinion.

parole.significato: Engaged in, involving, or reflecting deep or serious thought.
parole.testo: From Middle English pensif, pensyfe, pencyve, from Old French pensif (“thoughtful”), from penser (“to think”) (from Latin pēnsō) + -if (English -ive).

parole.significato: Denoting the sense "by" or "per", as in perchance or perhaps.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English per-.

parole.significato: To become aware of, through the physical senses, to see; to understand.
parole.testo: From Middle English perceyven, borrowed from Old French percevoir, perceveir, from Latin percipiō, past participle perceptus (“take hold of, obtain, receive, observe”), from per (“by, through”) + capiō (“to take”); see capable. Compare conceive, deceive, receive.

parole.significato: Any of the three species of spiny-finned freshwater fish in the genus Perca.
parole.testo: From Middle English perche, from Old French perche, from Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē, “perch”), cognate with περκνός (perknós, “dark-spotted”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ-, whence also Old English forn (“trout”), German Forelle (“trout”).

parole.significato: A rod, staff, tree branch, ledge, etc., used as a roost by a bird.
parole.testo: From Middle English perche, from Old French perche, from Latin pertica (“staff, long pole, measuring rod”).

parole.significato: Eternal damnation.
parole.testo: From Middle English perdicioun, from Old French perdiciun, from Late Latin perditio, from Latin perdo (“to destroy, to lose”).

parole.significato: Very durable; long-lasting.
parole.testo: From Middle English perdurable, from Old French pardurable, from Medieval Latin perdūrābilis, from Latin perdurāre (“to endure”), from per- (“throughout”) + durare (“to last”).

parole.significato: Wandering, travelling, migratory.
parole.testo: From Middle English peregrin, borrowed from Old French peregrin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreign”). Doublet of pilgrim.

parole.significato: Fitting its definition precisely.
parole.testo: From Middle English perfit, from Old French parfit (modern: parfait), from Latin perfectus, perfect passive participle of perficere (“to finish”), from per- (“through, thorough”) + facere (“to do, to make”). The spelling was modified in the 15th century to conform to its Latin etymon. Doublet of par

parole.significato: The quality or state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing substandard remains; the highest attainable state or…
parole.testo: From Middle English perfeccioun, from Old French perfection, from Latin perfectiō. By surface analysis, perfect + -ion. Displaced native Old English fulfremednes.

parole.significato: A situation of serious and immediate danger.
parole.testo: From Middle English peril, from Old French peril, from Latin perīculum. Doublet of periculum.

parole.significato: To decay and disappear; to waste away to nothing.
parole.testo: From Middle English perishen, borrowed from Old French perir (via the stem periss- used in various conjugations), from Latin perīre (“pass away, perish”), from per (“through”) + īre (“pass, go”).

parole.significato: permitted.
parole.testo: From Middle English permyssyble, from Old French permissible, from Medieval Latin permissibilis.

parole.significato: One of the ways something exists, or the ways a set of objects can be ordered.
parole.testo: From Middle English permutacioun, permutacyoun, from Old French permutacïon, promutatïon and Medieval Latin permūtātiōnem, accusative of permūtātiō. Morphologically permute + -ation.

parole.significato: To change the order of.
parole.testo: From Middle English permuten, from Old French permuter, from Latin permūtāre.

parole.significato: Causing much harm in a subtle way.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).

parole.significato: Lasting forever, or for an indefinitely long time.
parole.testo: From Middle English perpetuel, from Old French perpetuel, from Latin perpetuālis (“universal”), from perpetuus, from petō.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being perpetual; endless duration; uninterrupted existence.
parole.testo: From Middle English perpetuitee, perpetuite, perpetuyte, from Old French perpetüité, ultimately from Latin perpetuitās.

parole.significato: To cause to feel baffled; to puzzle.
parole.testo: From Old French, from Latin perplexus (“entangled, confused”), from per (“through”) + plexus, perfect passive participle of plectō (“plait, weave, braid”).

parole.significato: A fermented alcoholic beverage made from pears, similar to hard apple cider.
parole.testo: From Middle English perre; from Old French peré; from Vulgar Latin *piratum; from Latin pirum.

parole.significato: A very dark (almost black) purple or blue-gray colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English pers, from Old French, from Medieval Latin persus, back-formed from Persicus (“Persian”), from Ancient Greek Περσικός (Persikós). Compare peach.

parole.significato: The act of persecuting, especially a specific group of people; an instance of persecution.
parole.testo: Equivalent to persecute + -ion. From Middle English persecucioun, from Old French persecucion, from Ecclesiastical Latin persecūtio (“persecution; chase, pursuit”), from Latin persequor (“follow up, pursue”), from per- (“through”) + sequor (“follow”). Displaced native Old English ēhtnes.

parole.significato: A person or thing that persecutes or harasses.
parole.testo: From Middle English persecutour, from Old French persecutor and Latin persecūtor. Displaced native Old English ēhtere.

parole.significato: Continuing in a course of action without regard to discouragement, opposition or previous failure.
parole.testo: From Middle English perseveraunce, from Old French perseverance, from Latin persevērantia.

parole.significato: To persist steadfastly in pursuit of an undertaking, task, journey, or goal, even if hindered by distraction, difficult…
parole.testo: From Middle English perseveren, from Old French perseverer, from Latin persevērāre (“to continue steadfastly, persist, persevere”), from perseverus (“very strict or earnest”), from per (“through, by the means of”) + severus (“strict, earnest”). Doublet of perseverate.

parole.significato: A view, vista or outlook.
parole.testo: From Middle English perspective, perspectif, attested since 1381, from Old French or Middle French, from the first word of the Medieval Latin perspectiva ars (“science of optics”), the feminine of Latin perspectivus (“of sight, optical”), from perspectus, the past participle of perspicere (“to inspe

parole.significato: To belong to or be connected as a part, adjunct, attribute, or accessory.
parole.testo: From Middle English pertenen, from Old French partenir, pertenir (modern French appartenir), in turn from Latin pertineō, pertinēre.

parole.significato: Holding tenaciously to an opinion or purpose.
parole.testo: From pertinace + -ious, from Old French pertinace, from Latin pertinax, from per- (“very”) + tenax (“tenacious”).

parole.significato: A right that attaches to land, in Scots law.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pertinent, borrowed from Old French pertinent and Latin pertinēns, pertinentem.

parole.significato: Turned aside while against something, splitting off from a thing.
parole.testo: From Middle English perverse, pervers, from Old French pervers, from Latin perversum (“thoroughly turned”), past participle of pervertere, from per- (“thoroughly”) + vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: One who has been perverted; one who has turned to error, or adopted a twisted sense of values or morals.
parole.testo: From Old French pervertir, itself from the Latin pervertō.

parole.significato: A medical device similar to the outer ring of a contraceptive diaphragm, most commonly used to support a displaced uter…
parole.testo: From Middle English pessarie, from Old French pessaire, from Latin pessarium.

parole.significato: Any epidemic disease that is highly contagious, infectious, virulent and devastating.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin pestilentia (“plague”), from pestilens (“infected, unwholesome, noxious”); equivalent to pestilent + -ence.

parole.significato: A club-shaped, round-headed stick used in a mortar to pound, crush, rub or grind things.
parole.testo: From Middle English pestel, pestell, from Old French pestel, from Latin pistillum, from pīnsō (“pound, beat”). Doublet of pistil and pistillum.

parole.significato: Petite: small, little.
parole.testo: From Middle English petit, from Old French petit, from Late Latin *pitittus, diminutive of Latin *pit-, possibly from Proto-Celtic *pett- (“part, bit, piece”) (see Latin pettia), or of imitative origin. Compare also Latin pitinnus (“small”), pitulus, Italian pezza. Doublet of petty.

parole.significato: A formal written request made by an individual or a group of people to a sovereign or political authority, often contai…
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French peticiun, from stem of Latin petitio, petitionem (“a request, solicitation”), from petere (“to require, seek, go forward”).

parole.significato: One of the long benches in a church, seating several persons, usually fixed to the floor and facing the chancel.
parole.testo: From Middle English pewe, from Old French puiee, puïe (“balustrade, balcony”), from Latin podia, plural of podium (“parapet, podium”), from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “little foot”), from πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of podia.

parole.significato: An alloy of approximately 93–98% tin and 1–2% copper, and the balance of antimony.
parole.testo: From Middle English peutre, from Old French peautre, from Vulgar Latin *peltrum (“pewter”), which is of uncertain origin. Possibly related to spelter.

parole.significato: Something seen but having no physical reality; a phantom or apparition.
parole.testo: A learned variant of phantom; from Middle English fantosme, from Old French fantosme, fantasme, from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma). Doublet of phantom.

parole.significato: Illusive.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English fantome, fanteme, from Old French fantosme, fantasme, from Latin phantasma (“an apparition, specter; (in Late Latin also) appearance, image”), from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “phantasm, an appearance, image, apparition, specter”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to mak

parole.significato: A bird of family Phasianidae, often hunted for food.
parole.testo: From Middle English fesaunt, fesant, from Old French fesan, from Latin phāsiānus, from Ancient Greek φᾱσιανός (phāsianós), meaning “[bird] of the river Φᾶσις (Phâsis)”, from where, it was supposed, the bird spread to the west. Replaced native Old English wōrhana, a variant of mōrhana. More at moorhe

parole.significato: Synonym of philosophical.
parole.testo: From Middle English philosophik, phylosophyk, from Old French filosofique and Latin philosophicus; equivalent to philosophy + -ic.

parole.significato: An academic discipline that seeks truth through reasoning rather than empiricism, often attempting to provide explanati…
parole.testo: From Middle English philosophie, Old French philosophie, and their source, Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía), from φίλος (phílos, “loving”) + σοφία (sophía, “wisdom”). By surface analysis, philo- + -sophy. Displaced Old English ūþwitegung.

parole.significato: The opening of a vein, either to withdraw blood or for letting blood; venesection.
parole.testo: From Old French flebothomie (French phlébotomie), from Late Latin phlebotomia, from Ancient Greek φλεβοτόμος (phlebotómos, “that opens a vein”), from φλέψ (phléps, “vein”). By surface analysis, phlebo- + -tomy.

parole.significato: One of the four humors making up the body in ancient and mediaeval medicine; said to be cold and moist, and often ident…
parole.testo: From Middle English flewme, fleume, fleme, from Old French fleume, Middle French flemme (French flegme), and their source, Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame; inflammation; clammy humor in the body”), from φλέγειν (phlégein, “to burn”). Possible burning sensation when coughing

parole.significato: Not easily excited to action or passion; calm; sluggish.
parole.testo: From Middle English fleumatik, flewmatik, flematik, fleumatyke, flewmatyk, from Old French fleumatique, from Latin phlegmaticus, from Ancient Greek φλεγματικός (phlegmatikós), from φλέγμα (phlégma), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with mildness

parole.significato: A mythological bird, said to be the only one of its kind, which lives for 500 years and then dies by burning to ashes o…
parole.testo: From Old English and Old French fenix, from Medieval Latin phenix, from Latin phoenīx, from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix), from Egyptian b-n:nw*w-G31 (bnw, “grey heron”). Doublet of Bennu. The grey heron was venerated at Heliopolis and associated in Egypt with the cyclical renewal of life because t

parole.significato: A medicine or drug, especially a cathartic or purgative.
parole.testo: From Middle English fysike (noun) and phisiken, fisike (verb; from the noun), from Old French fisike (“natural science, art of healing”), from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φῠσῐκός (phŭsĭkós, “natural; physical”), see above.

parole.significato: A practitioner of physic, i.e. a specialist in internal medicine, especially as opposed to a surgeon; a practitioner wh…
parole.testo: From Middle English fisicien, from Old French fisicïen (“physician”) (modern French physicien (“physicist”)), from fisique (“art of healing”), from Latin physica (“natural science”), from Ancient Greek φυσική ἐπιστήμη (phusikḗ epistḗmē, “knowledge of nature”), from φυσικός (phusikós, “pertaining to

parole.significato: The branch of science concerned with the study of the properties and interactions of space, time, matter and energy.
parole.testo: 1580s; from physic (see also -ics), from Middle English phisik, from Old French fisike (“natural science, art of healing”), from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φυσικός (phusikós, “natural; physical”), from Ancient Greek φύσις (phúsis, “or

parole.significato: A type of pastry that consists of an outer crust and a filling. (Savory pies are more popular in the UK and sweet pies…
parole.testo: From Middle English pye, pie, pey (“baked dish, filled pastry”), possibly attested earlier (c. 1199) in the surname Piehus (“pie-house?”). Further origin uncertain. Relation to Middle English pie, pye (“magpie”) has been suggested due to correspondences between other similar foods and the names of b

parole.significato: Magpie.
parole.testo: From Middle English pye, from Old French pie, from Latin pīca, feminine of pīcus (“woodpecker”). Doublet of pica and speight.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A part of a larger whole, usually in such a form that it is able to be separated from other parts.
parole.testo: From Middle English pece, peece, peice, from Old French piece, from Late Latin pecia, petia (“broken piece, fragment; parcel of land”), of uncertain origin. Possibly ultimately from Gaulish *pettyā, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis (“piece, portion, quota”). Compare Welsh peth (“thing, stuff, junk”), Bret

parole.significato: Having two or more colors, especially black and white.
parole.testo: From archaic pie (“magpie”), from Old French pie, from Latin pica. Compare typologically Polish srokaty < sroka.

parole.significato: To puncture; to break through.
parole.testo: From Middle English perce, from conjugated forms of Old French percier such as (jeo) pierce (“I pierce”), probably from Vulgar Latin *pertūsiō, from Latin pertūsus, past participle of pertundō (“thrust or bore through”), from per- (“through”) + tundō (“beat, pound”). Displaced native Old English þȳr

parole.significato: One of several birds of the family Columbidae within the order Columbiformes.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pygeoun, borrowed from Old French pyjon, inherited from Late Latin pīpiōnem (“chirping bird”), derived from Latin pīpiāre (“to chirp”), of imitative origin. Partly displaced native English dove.

parole.significato: A mass of things heaped together; a heap.
parole.testo: From Middle English pyle, from Old French pile, from Latin pīla (“pillar, pier”).

parole.significato: One who travels to visit a site of religious significance.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pilegrim, from Old English pilegrī̆m, from Old French pelegrin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner”). Doublet of peregrine. The change of /r…r/ to /l…r/ is an effect of dissimilation in early Romance; compare Italian pellegrino.

parole.significato: To loot or plunder by force, especially in time of war.
parole.testo: From Old French pillage, from piller (“plunder”), from an unattested meaning of Late Latin piliō, probably a figurative use of Latin pilō (“to remove (hair)”), from pilus (“hair”).

parole.significato: A large post, often used as supporting architecture.
parole.testo: From Middle English piler, from Old French pilier, from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin *pilāre (“a pillar”), from Latin pila (“a pillar, pier, mole”).

parole.significato: A wing.
parole.testo: From Middle English pynyon, from Old French pignon, from Latin penna (“feather”).

parole.significato: The highest point.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French pinacle, pinnacle, from Late Latin pinnāculum (“a peak, pinnacle”), from Latin pinna (“a pinnacle”); see pin. Doublet of panache.

parole.significato: A unit of volume, equivalent to:
parole.testo: From Middle English pinte, from Old French pinte, assumed from Vulgar Latin *pincta (“a mark used to indicate a level of quantity against a larger measure”), from Latin picta (“painted”), from Latin pingō (“paint”, verb). Doublet of pinto and Pinto.

parole.significato: A criminal who plunders at sea; commonly attacking merchant vessels, though often pillaging port towns.
parole.testo: From Middle English pirate, pirat, pyrat, from Old French pirate, from Latin pīrāta (“pirate”), from Ancient Greek πειρατής (peiratḗs), from πεῖρα (peîra, “trial, attempt, plot”). Displaced native Old English wīċing, which was the word for both "pirate" and "viking".

parole.significato: A collar or gorget of mail (or, rarely, plate), protecting the neck and upper chest; a standard.
parole.testo: From Middle English pisan, from an Old French word variously spelled pizaine, pizane, pesine, etc, found also in phrases like colarete(s) pizaine, gorgerete(s) pizaine. Probably from Old French piz (“chest”), from Latin pectus, extended like in poitrine, although it has also been suggested that it c

parole.significato: Urine.
parole.testo: From Middle English pisse (noun) and pissen (verb), from Old French pissier, possibly from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, probably of imitative origin. Compare Old Norse pissa (“to urinate, piss”). Displaced Old English miċġe (“urine”) and mīgan (“to urinate”).

parole.significato: A small allowance of food and drink; a scanty meal.
parole.testo: From Middle English pitaunce, from Old French pitance, pitence, from Medieval Latin *pietāntia, from Latin pietās (“piety”).

parole.significato: An area; somewhere within an area.
parole.testo: From Middle English place, conflation of Old English plæċe (“place, an open space, street”) and Old French place (“place, an open space”), both from Latin platēa (“plaza, wide street”), from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”), from Proto-Indo-Eur

parole.significato: The bubonic plague, the pestilent disease caused by the virulent bacterium Yersinia pestis.
parole.testo: From Middle English plage, borrowed from Old French plage, from Latin plāga (“blow, wound”), from plangō (“to strike”). Cognate with Middle Dutch plāghe (> Dutch plaag), plāghen (> Dutch plagen); Middle Low German plāge; Middle High German plāge, pflāge (> German Plage); plāgen (> German plagen); Sw

parole.significato: Several similar marine flatfish of the righteye flounder family Pleuronectidae:
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English playce, plays, from Old French plaiz, from Late Latin platessa, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad”). See platy-, plat and flat.

parole.significato: To level; to raze; to make plain or even on the surface.
parole.testo: From Old French plain, from Latin plānum (“level ground, a plain”), neuter substantive from plānus (“level, even, flat”). Doublet of llano, piano, and plane.

parole.significato: Full, complete in number or extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleyn, borrowed from Old French plein, from Latin plēnus (“full, filled, complete”). Ultimately from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Doublet of plene, plenary, and full.

parole.significato: A deciduous tree of the genus Platanus.
parole.testo: From Middle English plane, borrowed from Old French plane, from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos), from πλατύς (platús, “wide, broad”).

parole.significato: Each of the seven major bodies which move relative to the fixed stars in the night sky—the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Su…
parole.testo: From Middle English planete, from Old French planete, from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”) (itself an ellipsis of ἀστέρες πλανῆται (astéres planêtai, “wandering stars”)), from Ancient Greek πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, stray”), of unknown origin. Cognate

parole.significato: A long, broad and thick piece of timber, as opposed to a board which is less thick.
parole.testo: From Middle English plank, planke, borrowed from Old French planke, Old Northern French planque (compare French planche, from Old French planche), from Vulgar Latin planca, from palanca, from Latin phalanga. The Latin term derives from the Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx), so it is thus a doublet of p

parole.significato: A member of the dynasty which held the English throne from 1154 to 1485.
parole.testo: Originally a sobriquet of Geoffrey of Anjou (1113-1151), founder of the line, who was said to have worn a yellow broom blossom in his hat, Old French plante genest (French plante genêt), from Latin planta genista (“sprig of broom”), whence Medieval Latin Plantagenistae; subsequently adopted as a sur

parole.significato: A slightly curved but almost flat dish from which food is served or eaten.
parole.testo: From Middle English plate, from Old French plate, from Medieval Latin plata, from Vulgar Latin *plat(t)us, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat, wide”). Compare Spanish plato. (foot): Cockney rhyming slang, from "plates of meat" for "feet".

parole.significato: To cover the surface material of an object with a thin coat of another material, usually a metal.
parole.testo: From Middle English platen, from Old English platian and Old French plater, both ultimately from Latin plata (see above).

parole.significato: An appeal, petition, urgent prayer or entreaty.
parole.testo: From Middle English ple, from Old French plait, plaid, from Medieval Latin placitum (“a decree, sentence, suit, plea, etc., Latin an opinion, determination, prescription, order; literally, that which is pleasing, pleasure”), neuter of placitus, past participle of placere (“to please”). Cognate with

parole.significato: To present (an argument or a plea), especially in a legal case.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleden, plaiden, from Old French plaider (“to plead, offer a plea”), from plait, from Medieval Latin placitum (“a decree, sentence, suit, plea, etc.", in Classical Latin, "an opinion, determination, prescription, order; literally, that which is pleasing, pleasure”), neuter of pla

parole.significato: To make happy or satisfy; to give pleasure to.
parole.testo: From Middle English plesen, plaisen, borrowed from Old French plaise, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleHk- (“pleasingness, permission”). In this sense, displaced native Old English līcian, whence Modern English like

parole.significato: A state of being pleased or contented; gratification.
parole.testo: From Early Modern English pleasur, plesur, alteration (with ending accommodated to -ure) of Middle English plaisir (“pleasure”), from Old French plesir, plaisir (“to please”), infinitive used as a noun, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Pro

parole.significato: In plenty; abundant.
parole.testo: From Middle English plentewos, plentevous, et al., circa 1300, from Old French plentiveus (“fertile, rich”) (early 13th century), from plentif (“abundant”), from plenté (“abundance”) (Modern French pleinté, English plenty), from Latin plenitatem, accusative of plenitas (“fullness”), from plenus (“co

parole.significato: Inflammation of lung pleura.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleuresi, pleresye, that borrowed from Old French pleuresie (French pleurésie), from Late Latin pleurisis, alteration of Latin pleuritis. By surface analysis, pleur- + -isy.

parole.significato: A little mass of lead, or the like, attached to a line, and used by builders, etc., to indicate a vertical direction.
parole.testo: From Middle English plumbe, plumme, from Old French *plombe, from Latin plumba, plural of plumbum.

parole.significato: One who works in or with lead.
parole.testo: From Middle English plumber, from Old French plummier (French plombier); from Latin plumbārius, from plumbum (“lead or lead shot”). The verb sense “to botch” is perhaps from the negative stereotype of the occupation.

parole.significato: A piece of lead attached to a line, used in sounding the depth of water; a plumb bob or a plumb line.
parole.testo: From Middle English plommet (“ball of lead, plumb of a bob-line”), recorded since 1382, from Old French plommet or plomet, the diminutive of plom, plum (“lead, sounding lead”), from Latin plumbum (“lead”). The verb is first recorded in 1626, originally meaning “to fathom, take soundings", from the n

parole.significato: Consisting of or containing more than one of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English plurelle, from Old French plurel (“plural”), Borrowed from Latin plūrālis (“of or belonging to more than one, belonging to many”, adjective), from plūs, plūris (“more”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: The state of being plural.
parole.testo: From plural + -ity, from Middle English pluralite, from Old French pluralité (“multitude, state of being plural”), from Latin plūrālitās.

parole.significato: To work at (something) diligently.
parole.testo: From apply; compare Middle English plīen, pli, plie, pleie (“to place (something) around, on, or over, to cover; to apply, use; to strive”), short for aplīen, applīen (“to combine, join; to attach; to assemble; to use, be of use; to allot; to apply; to inflict; to go; to ply, steer; to comply, submi

parole.significato: A person who writes poems.
parole.testo: From Middle English poete, from Old French poete, from Latin poēta (“poet, author”), from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, maker, author, poet”), from ποιέω (poiéō, “to make, compose”). Displaced native Old English sċop and lēoþwyrhta (literally, "leedwright" or "poem-writer"). Doublet of p

parole.significato: Literature composed in verse or language exhibiting conscious attention to patterns and rhythm.
parole.testo: From Middle English poetrye, poetrie, a borrowing from Old French pöeterie, pöetrie, from Medieval Latin poētria, from poēta (“poet”), from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “poet; author; maker”). Displaced native Old English lēoþcræft.

parole.significato: Point taken; understood; got it.
parole.testo: From Middle English poynt, from Old French point m (“dot; minute amount”), from Latin pūnctum (“a hole punched in; a point, puncture”), substantive use of pūnctus m, perfect passive participle of pungō (“to prick, punch”); alternatively, from Old French pointe f (“sharp tip”), from Latin pūncta f (p

parole.significato: To extend the index finger in the direction of something in order to show where it is or to draw attention to it.
parole.testo: From Middle English pointen, poynten, from Old French pointier, pointer, poynter, from point from Latin pūnctum.

parole.significato: A sharp instrument; any sharp-pointed thing.
parole.testo: From Old French [Term?], from Latin punctillum (“a little point”). Cognate with Spanish puntilla (“tiptoe; small dagger used in bullfighting”). Doublet of pontil.

parole.significato: A substance that is harmful or lethal to a living organism when ingested.
parole.testo: From Middle English poysoun, poyson, pusoun, from Old French poison, poisun, from Latin pōtiōnem (“drink, a draught, a poisonous draught, a potion”), from pōtō (“to drink”). See also potion and potable (from the same root). Mostly displaced native Old English ātor and lybb. See more at atter.

parole.significato: A principle of behaviour, conduct which an entity (government, organization, etc.) applies or seeks to follow, especial…
parole.testo: From Middle English policie, from Old French policie, pollicie and police, from Late Latin politia (“citizenship; government”), classical Latin polītīa (in Cicero), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “citizenship; polis, (city) state; government”), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”). Doublet of p

parole.significato: A substance used to polish.
parole.testo: From Middle English polishen, from Old French poliss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of polir, from Latin polīre (“to polish, make smooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to drive, strike, thrust”), from the notion of fulling cloth.

parole.significato: A mixture of aromatic substances, made into a ball and carried by a person to impart a sweet smell or as a protection a…
parole.testo: From Old French pome d'embre (literally “apple of ambergris”), from Medieval Latin pōmum dē ambra: pōmum (“fruit”) (possibly from *po-emo (“picked off”)); ambra (“amber; ambergris”) (probably from ambrosia (“food or unguent of the gods”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́μβροτος (ắmbrotos, “divine, immortal; b

parole.significato: To grow to a head, or form a head in growing.
parole.testo: From Middle English pome (“fruit, meatball”), from Old French pome (“apple”), from Latin pōmum. For the verb, compare French pommer. Doublet of pomme.

parole.significato: The upper front brow of a saddle.
parole.testo: From Middle English pomel, from Old French pomel and Medieval Latin pomellum, pumellum, presumedly via Vulgar Latin *pomellum (“ball, knob”), the diminutive of Late Latin pōmum (“apple”). Compare French pommeau, Spanish pomo, and Swedish pumla.

parole.significato: Show of magnificence; parade; display; power.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English pomp, pompe, from Old French pompe, from Latin pompa (“pomp”), from Ancient Greek πομπή (pompḗ, “a sending, a solemn procession, pomp”), from πέμπω (pémpō, “to send”). The verb is derived from Middle English pompen, from pomp, pompe (see above).

parole.significato: Affectedly grand, solemn or self-important.
parole.testo: From Middle English pompous, from Old French pompeux, pompos, from Late Latin pomposus, from Latin pompa (“pomp”), from Ancient Greek πομπή (pompḗ, “a sending, a solemn procession, pomp”), from πέμπω (pémpō, “to send”), equivalent to pomp + -ous. Doublet of pomposo.

parole.significato: To wonder, think of deeply.
parole.testo: From Middle English ponderen, from Old French ponderer (“to weigh, balance, ponder”) from Latin ponderāre (“to weigh, ponder”), from pondus (“weight”), from pendere (“to weigh”); see pendent and pound.

parole.significato: With no or few possessions or money, particularly in relation to contemporaries who do have them.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English povre, povere, from Old French and Anglo-Norman povre, poure, from Latin pauper, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”). Doublet of pauper. Displanced native wantsome, Middle English unlede (“poor”, from Old English unlǣde), Middle English unweli, un

parole.significato: A covered entrance to a building, whether taken from the interior, and forming a sort of vestibule within the main wall…
parole.testo: From Middle English porche, from Old French, from Latin porticus (“portico”). Doublet of portego, portico, and porticus.

parole.significato: Any of several rodents of either of the taxonomic families Hystricidae (Old World porcupines) or Erethizontidae (New Wo…
parole.testo: From Middle English porke despyne, from Old French porc-espin, from Latin porcus (“pig”) + spinus (“spine”), hence also spine pig. Cognate with Spanish puercoespín, Italian porcospino, Portuguese porco-espinho.

parole.significato: A tiny opening in the skin.
parole.testo: From Middle English pore, from Old French pore, from Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “passage”). Displaced native English sweat hole from Middle English swet hole, which might have been a reformation of Old English swātþȳrel (literally “sweat hole”), which competed with līcþēote (liter

parole.significato: The meat of a pig.
parole.testo: From Middle English pork, porc, via Anglo-Norman, from Old French porc (“swine, hog, pig; pork”), from Latin porcus (“domestic hog, pig”). Cognate with Old English fearh (“piglet”). Doublet of farrow. Compare also other West Germanic words for pigs: Ferkel, Ferke, and varken. Used in English since t

parole.significato: Full of tiny pores that allow fluids or gasses to pass through.
parole.testo: From Old French poros, from Latin porus (“an opening”). By surface analysis, pore + -ous.

parole.significato: A medieval pudding or stew of leeks and other vegetables (and sometimes meat) simmered in fresh almond milk and/or meat…
parole.testo: From Middle English porrey, from Old French poree (“leek soup”), diminutive of por (“leek”), from Latin porrum (“leek(s)”). Doublet of porret.

parole.significato: A scallion; a leek or small onion.
parole.testo: From Middle English poret, from Old French por(r)et, porete, from Medieval Latin porretum. See porraceous.

parole.significato: To carry, bear, bring, or transport. See porter.
parole.testo: From Old French porter, from Latin portāre (“carry”). Akin to transport, portable.

parole.significato: An entrance, entry point, or means of entry.
parole.testo: From Middle English portal, porttol, from Old French portal and Medieval Latin portāle, from porta.

parole.significato: A gate in the form of a grating which is lowered into place at the gateway of a castle, a fort, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English portcolyse, from Old French porte colëice, from porte (“door”) + feminine of colëiz (“sliding”), ultimately from Latin colāre.

parole.significato: An allocated amount.
To place in an attitude or fixed position, for the sake of effect.
parole.testo: From Middle English posen, from Old French poser (“to put, place, stell, settle, lodge”), from Vulgar Latin pausāre (“to blin, cease, pause”), from Latin pausa (“pause”), from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis); influenced by Latin pōnere. Doublet of pause.

parole.significato: A place or location.
parole.testo: From Middle English posicioun, from Old French posicion, from Latin positiō (“a putting, position”), from positus (“placed, situated”), past participle of pōnō (“to place”); see ponent. Compare apposition, composition, deposition; see pose.

parole.significato: Included, present, characterized by affirmation.
parole.testo: From Old French positif, from Latin positivus, from the past participle stem of ponere (“to place”). Compare posit.

parole.significato: Able but not certain to happen; neither inevitable nor impossible.
parole.testo: From Middle English possible, from Old French possible, from Latin possibilis (“possible”), from posse, possum (“to be able”); see power. Displaced Middle English acumendlic (“possible”), from Old English ācumendlīċ (“possible”). Compare also Old English mihtelīċ (“strong, capable, powerful, possibl

parole.significato: A long dowel or plank protruding from the ground; a fencepost; a lightpost.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English post, from Old English post (“pillar, door-post”) and Old French post (“post, upright beam”), both from Latin postis (“door, post, doorpost”).

parole.significato: The act of drinking.
parole.testo: From Middle English potacion, from Old French potacion, from Latin pōtātiō.

parole.significato: A powerful leader; a monarch; a ruler.
parole.testo: From Middle English potentat, from Old French, from Late Latin potentātus (“rule, political power”), from Latin potēns (“powerful, strong”), the active present participle of possum (“to be able”).

parole.significato: A chief ruler; a potentate.
parole.testo: From Middle English potestat, from Old French potestat, from Latin potestās, potestātem.

parole.significato: A small portion or dose of a liquid which is medicinal, poisonous, or magical.
parole.testo: From Middle English pocioun, borrowed from Old French pocion, from Latin pōtiō (“a drinking”), pōtiōnis, from pōtāre (“to drink”). Displaced native Old English drenċ whence Modern English drench. Doublet of poison.

parole.significato: A young bird, a chick; now especially, a young game bird (turkey, partridge, grouse etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English pult, a variant of pulet, polet, from Old French poulet (“young fowl”), diminutive of poule (“hen”), from Latin pulla. For the development of the stressed vowel, see poultry. Doublet of pullet.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being poor; lack of money
parole.testo: From Middle English poverte, from Old French poverté (Modern French pauvreté), from Latin paupertās, from pauper (“poor”) + -tas (“noun of state suffix”). Cognates include pauper, poor.

parole.significato: To reduce to fine particles; to pound, grind, or rub into a powder.
parole.testo: From Middle English poudre, pouder, pouldre, borrowed from Old French poudre, poldre, puldre, from Latin pulverem, accusative singular of Latin pulvis (“dust, powder”). Doublet of pulver. Compare pollen (“fine flour”), polverine, pulverize.

parole.significato: A support structure.
parole.testo: From Old French poi (“small hill”), from Latin podium.

parole.significato: A person concerned with action or practice, as opposed to one concerned with theory.
parole.testo: From Middle English practic, practik, partly from Old French practique and partly from its etymon, Late Latin prācticus (“active”), from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, “of or pertaining to action, concerned with action or business, active, practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “to do”). Doublet of

parole.significato: To give praise to; to commend, glorify, or worship.
parole.testo: From Middle English praisen, preisen, from Old French proisier, preisier (“to value, prize”), from Late Latin pretiō (“to value, prize”) from pretium (“price, worth, reward”). Displaced native Middle English herien from Old English herian (“to praise”).

parole.significato: A practice of communicating with one's God, or with some spiritual entity.
parole.testo: From Middle English preiere, from Old French preiere, from Early Medieval Latin precāria, derived from Latin precem. Displaced native Old English ġebed (whence modern English bead).

parole.significato: To give a sermon.
parole.testo: From Middle English prechen, from Old French prëechier, precchier (Modern French prêcher), from Latin praedicō (“to proclaim, announce”, literally “to fore-assign, pre-dedicate”). Doublet of predicate. The Latin word is also the source of Old English predician (“to preach”), Saterland Frisian preetj

parole.significato: Someone who preaches a worldview, philosophy, or religion, especially someone who preaches the gospel and especially a…
parole.testo: From Middle English precher, prechere; partly equivalent to preach + -er, and partly continuing Middle English prechour, prechiour, from Old French preecheor (French prêcheur), from Latin praedicator (“public praiser, proclaimer”). See preach. Displaced native Old English bydel.

parole.significato: A short preliminary statement or remark, especially an explanatory introduction to a formal document or statute.
parole.testo: From Middle English preamble, from Old French preambule (French préambule), from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from praeambulō (“to walk before”).

parole.significato: Of high value or worth.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English precious, borrowed from Old French precios (“valuable, costly, precious, beloved, also affected, finical”), from Latin pretiōsus (“of great value, costly, dear, precious”), from pretium (“value, price”); see price.

parole.significato: One who precedes; one who has preceded another in any state, position, office, etc.; one whom another follows or comes…
parole.testo: From Middle English predecessour, from Old French predecesseor (“forebear”), from Late Latin praedēcessor, from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + Latin dēcessor (“retiring officer”), from Latin dēcēdō (“to retire, to die”) (English decease).

parole.significato: The doctrine that everything has been foreordained by God or by fate.
parole.testo: From Middle English predestinacion, from Old French predestination, from Late Latin praedēstinātiō. By surface analysis, predestine + -ation. Displaced native Old English foreteohhung.

parole.significato: To determine the future or the fate of something in advance; to preordain.
parole.testo: From Old French prédestiner, from Medieval Latin praedestinare. By surface analysis, pre- + destine. Displaced native Old English foreteohhian.

parole.significato: A definite class, state or condition.
parole.testo: From Middle English predicament, from Old French predicament, from Late Latin praedicāmentum (“that which is predicated, a predicament, category”).

parole.significato: The part of the sentence (or clause) which states a property that a subject has or is characterized by.
parole.testo: From Middle English predicat(e), from Old French predicat (French prédicat), from Medieval Latin praedicātum (“thing said of a subject, predicate”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of praedicātus, the perfect passive participle praedicō (“to proclaim”), see -ate (noun-forming suff

parole.significato: A beginning or introductory portion that comes before the main text of a document or book, typically serving to context…
parole.testo: Late 14th century, from Middle English preface, prefas, from Old French preface (from which derives the modern French préface), from Medieval Latin prefātia, for classical Latin praefātiō (“a saying beforehand”), from praefor (“to speak beforehand”), from prae- (“beforehand”) + for (“to speak”).

parole.significato: An official of Ancient Rome who controlled or superintended a particular command, charge, department, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English prefect and prefecte, from Old French prefect (Mod. French préfet), from Latin praefectus (“one placed in charge, overseer, director, prefect”), from praeficere (“to place in charge”).

parole.significato: Carrying developing offspring within the body.
parole.testo: From Middle English preignant, from Old French preignant, pregnant, also prenant (compare archaic Modern French prégnant), and their source, Latin praegnāns (“pregnant”), probably from prae- (“pre-”) + *gnāscī, an archaic form of nāscī (“to be born”). Displaced Old English bearnēacen (literally "chi

parole.significato: Pregnancy.
parole.testo: From Middle English pregnacioun, from Old French pregnacion and Latin praegnātiō.

parole.significato: An adverse judgment or opinion formed beforehand or without knowledge of the facts.
parole.testo: From Middle English prejudice, from Old French prejudice, derived from Latin praeiūdicium (“previous judgment or damage”), from prae- (“before”) + iūdicium (“judgment”).

parole.significato: Exhibiting prejudice or bias.
parole.testo: From Middle English prejudiceele, prejudicial, prejudiciall, prejudiciel, prejudiciell, prejudycyall, from Old French prejudicial, prejudiciel and Medieval Latin prēiūdiciālis.

parole.significato: A clergyman of high rank and authority, having jurisdiction over an area or a group of people; normally a bishop.
parole.testo: From Old French prelat (French prélat), from Medieval Latin praelātus, perfect passive participle of praeferō (“to carry before, prefer, exceed”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix). Doublet of prefer. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as collate and confer among others.

parole.significato: A proposition antecedently supposed or proved; something previously stated or assumed as the basis of further argument;…
parole.testo: From Middle English premise, premisse, from Old French premisse, from Medieval Latin premissa (“set before”) (premissa propositio (“the proposition set before”)), feminine past participle of Latin praemittere (“to send or put before”), from prae- (“before”) + mittere (“to send”). Sense 4, a piece of

parole.significato: Any of a class of non-inflecting words and multiword terms typically employed to connect a following noun or a pronoun,…
parole.testo: From Middle English preposicioun, from Old French preposicion, from Latin praepositio, praepositionem, from praepono (“to place before”), equivalent to pre- + position. Compare French préposition. So called because it is placed before the word with which it is phrased, as in a bridge of iron, he com

parole.significato: The foreskin, or retractable fold of tissue covering the glans penis.
parole.testo: From Middle English prepuce, prepuse, from Old French prepuce (“foreskin”), from Latin praepūtium (“prepuce, foreskin”), a combination of prae- (“fore-”) + Old Latin pūtos (“penis”).

parole.significato: Knowledge of events before they take place.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English prescience, from Old French prescience, from Latin praescientia.

parole.significato: To make or become present.
parole.testo: Through Old French presence, from Latin praesentia (“a being present”), from praesentem. Displaced native Old English andweardnes.

parole.significato: Relating to now, for the time being; current.
parole.testo: From Middle English present, from Old French present, from Latin praesent-, praesens, present participle of praeesse (“to be present”), from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + esse (“to be”). Displaced Old English andweard (“present, current”).

parole.significato: A gift, especially one given for birthdays, Christmas, anniversaries, graduations, weddings, or any other special occas…
parole.testo: From Middle English presenten, from Old French presenter, from Latin praesentāre (“to show”), from praesent-, praesens, present participle of praeesse (“be in front of”).

parole.significato: The act of presenting, or something presented.
parole.testo: From Old French presentation (French présentation), from Latin praesentātiōnem, accusative singular of praesentātiō (“representation, exhibition”). Morphologically present + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of preserving; care to preserve; act of keeping from destruction, decay or any ill.
parole.testo: From Old French preservacion, from Medieval Latin preservatio. Morphologically preserve + -ation.

parole.significato: Any agent, natural or artificial, that acts to preserve, especially when added to food.
parole.testo: From Old French preservatif, from Medieval Latin praeservativus.

parole.significato: A sweet spread made of any of a variety of fruits.
parole.testo: From Middle English preserven, from Old French preserver, from Medieval Latin prēservāre (“keep, preserve”), from Late Latin praeservāre (“guard beforehand”), from prae (“before”, adverb) + servāre (“maintain, keep”). Displaced native Old English nerian.

parole.significato: To act as president or chairperson.
parole.testo: From Old French presider, from Latin praesidēre (“preside”), from pre- (“before”) + sedere (“to sit”). Displaced Old English foresittan, which might have been a calque of the Latin.

parole.significato: The head of state of a republic, sometimes also the head of government as well, particularly (US politics) the head of…
parole.testo: From Old French president, from Latin praesidēns (“presiding over; president, leader”) (accusative: praesidentem). The Latin word is the substantivized present active participle of the verb praesideō (“preside over”). The verb is composed from prae (“before”) and sedeō (“sit”). The original meaning

parole.significato: To exert weight or force against, to act upon with force or weight; to exert pressure upon.
parole.testo: From Middle English pressen (“to crowd, thring, press”), from Old French presser (“to press”) (Modern French presser) from Latin pressāre, from pressus, past participle of premere "to press". Displaced native Middle English thringen (“to press, crowd, throng”) (from Old English þringan (“to press, c

parole.significato: To give as a loan; to lend.
parole.testo: From Middle English prest, borrowed from Old French prester, from Latin praesto, praestare.

parole.significato: Making unwarranted presumptions or assumptions, often out of arrogance or excessive self-confidence, and thus exceeding…
parole.testo: From Middle English presumptuous, borrowed from Old French presumpcieus, presumptieus, presumptuos and its etymon Medieval Latin praesūmptuōsus.

parole.significato: Showing an action at a determined moment in the past.
parole.testo: From Middle English preterit, from Old French preterit (13th century), from Latin praeteritum (as in tempus praeteritum (“time past”)), the past participle of praetereō (“to go by, go past”), itself from praeter (“beyond, before, above, more than”) (comparative of prae (“before”)) + itum (the past p

parole.significato: To be superior in strength, dominance, influence, or frequency; to have or gain the advantage over others; to have the…
parole.testo: From Middle English prevailen, from Old French prevaler, from Latin praevaleō (“be very able or more able, be superior, prevail”), from prae (“before”) + valeō (“be able or powerful”). Displaced native Old English rīcsian.

parole.significato: Advance knowledge; foresight.
parole.testo: From Middle English previsioun, from Old French prevision, from Late Latin praevisio, praevisionem, from Latin praevideo.

parole.significato: To act as a predator.
parole.testo: From Middle English praien, prayen, preyen, partly from the noun and partly from Old French praer, preer, earlier preder, from Late Latin praedō, collateral form of Latin praedor, from praeda (“plunder, booty, loot”) + -ō (verbal suffix). Doublet of prede.

parole.significato: The cost required to gain possession of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English price (“price, prize, value, excellence”), borrowed from Old French pris, preis, from Latin pretium (“worth, price, money spent, wages, reward”); compare praise, precious, appraise, appreciate, depreciate, etc.

parole.significato: The state or condition of being prime or first, as in time, place, rank, preference etc.
parole.testo: From Old French primacie, from Medieval Latin primatia (“office of a church primate”), from Latin primas plus a suffix corresponding to -acy. By surface analysis, prime + -acy.

parole.significato: In the Catholic Church, a rare title conferred to or claimed by the sees of certain archbishops, or the highest-ranking…
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1275. From Middle English primat(e), from Old French primat (French primat), from Late Latin prīmās, prīmātis (“chief bishop”), substantivisation of prīmās (same as Etymology 1), from prīmus (“prime, first in rank (also as a substantive)”). Compare English primus, of similar der

parole.significato: First in importance, degree, or rank.
parole.testo: From Middle English prime, from Old French prime and its etymon, Latin prīmus (“first”), from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“beyond, before”). Doublet of primo and primus. The noun sense "apostrophe-like symbol" originates from the

parole.significato: An original or primary word; a word not derived from another, as opposed to derivative.
parole.testo: From Middle English primitif, from Old French primitif, from Latin prīmitīvus (“first or earliest of its kind”), from prīmus (“first”); see prime. Doublet of primitivo.

parole.significato: A flowering plant of the genus Primula.
parole.testo: From Middle English primerose, from Old French primerose, from Medieval Latin prima (“first”) + rosa (“rose”). The designation may derive from the fact that certain species of primroses are among the earliest flowers to bloom in the spring season.

parole.significato: Primary; most important; first level in importance.
parole.testo: From Middle English principal, from Old French principal, from Latin prīncipālis.

parole.significato: To equip with principles; to establish, or fix, in certain principles; to impress with any tenet or rule of conduct.
parole.testo: From Middle English principle, from Old French principe, from Latin prīncipium (“beginning, foundation”), from prīnceps (“first”). By surface analysis, prīmus (“first”) + -ceps (“catcher”); the former ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”); see also prince.

parole.significato: An item's relative importance.
parole.testo: From Old French priorite, from Latin priōritās. Surface analysis: prior + -ity.

parole.significato: A place or institution where people are held against their will, in the US especially for long-term confinement, as of…
parole.testo: From Middle English prisoun, prison, from Old English prisūn, a borrowing from Old French prison, from Latin prehensiōnem, accusative singular of prehensiō, from the verb prehendō. Doublet of prehension.

parole.significato: Private, exclusive; not public; one's own.
parole.testo: From Middle English pryvy, prive, from Old French privé (“private”), from Latin prīvātus (“deprived”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive; to free, release”). Doublet of private.

parole.significato: That which is taken from another; something captured; a thing seized by force, stratagem, or superior power.
parole.testo: From Middle English prise, from Old French prise (“a taking, capture, a seizure, a thing seized, a prize, booty, also hold, purchase”), past participle of prendre (“to take, to capture”), from Latin prēndere (“to take, seize”); see prehend. Compare prison, apprise, comprise, enterprise, purprise, re

parole.significato: To consider highly valuable; to esteem.
parole.testo: From Middle English prysen, borrowed from Old French preisier (“to set a price or value on, esteem, value”), from pris (“price”), from Latin pretium (“price, value”), whence price; see also praise, a doublet. Compare appraise, apprize.

parole.significato: Likely or most likely to be true.
parole.testo: From Middle English probable, from Old French probable, from Latin probābilis (“that may be proved, credible”), from probāre (“to test, examine”); see probe, probity, prove. Compare recent doublet provable.

parole.significato: Tending to prove a particular proposition or to persuade someone of the truth of an allegation.
parole.testo: From Middle English probatiffe, from Old French probatif, from Latin probātīvus (“belonging to proof”), from Latin probare (“show, prove, demonstrate”) (See prove). Originally in terme probatiffe (“a period of time assigned for the proving of an allegation”). First attested in the mid-15th century.

parole.significato: To move, pass, or go forward or onward; to advance; to carry on.
parole.testo: From Middle English proceden, from Old French proceder, from Latin prōcēdō (“to go forth, go forward, advance”), from prō (“forth”) + cēdō (“to go”); see cede.

parole.significato: A series of events leading to a result or product.
parole.testo: From Middle English proces, from Old French procés (“journey”), from Latin prōcessus (“course, progression”), nominalization of prōcēdō (“proceed, advance”).

parole.significato: The act of progressing or proceeding.
parole.testo: From Middle English processioun, borrowed from Old French pourciession, from Latin prōcessiō (“a marching forward, an advance, in Late Latin a religious procession”), from prōcēdere, past participle prōcessus (“to move forward, advance, proceed”); see proceed.

parole.significato: To announce or declare.
parole.testo: From Middle English proclamen, proclaime, from Old French proclamer, from Latin prōclāmō, prōclāmāre, from prō- (“forth”) + clāmō (“to shout, cry out”). Spelling altered by influence of claim, from the same Latin source (clāmō).

parole.significato: The process by which an organism produces others of its biological kind
parole.testo: From Old French procreacion, from Latin prōcreātiō (“generation”), the noun of action from prōcreāre (“to bring forth”), itself from prō- (“forth”) + creāre (“to create”). First attested in c. 1386.

parole.significato: To acquire or obtain.
parole.testo: From Middle English procuren, from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, administer”), from prō (“on behalf of”) + cūrō (“to care for”).

parole.significato: Wasteful extravagance.
parole.testo: From prodigal + -ity, from Old French prodigalite, from Late Latin prodigalitas.

parole.significato: The act of producing, making or creating something.
parole.testo: From Middle English produccioun, from Old French production, from Latin prōductiō, prōductiōnem (“a lengthening, prolonging”). Equivalent to produce + -tion. See produce.

parole.significato: An introduction, preface or preamble.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English proheme, from Old French proheme, from Latin prooemium, from Ancient Greek προοίμιον (prooímion).

parole.significato: To utter; to pronounce.
parole.testo: From Middle English proferen, from Old French proferer, from Latin proferre (“to bring forth, produce, utter”).

parole.significato: To administer the vows of a religious order to (someone); to admit to a religious order.
parole.testo: From Old French professer, and its source, the participle stem of Latin profitērī, from pro- + fatērī (“to confess, acknowledge”).

parole.significato: To benefit (somebody), be of use to (somebody).
parole.testo: From Middle English profit, from Old French profit (Modern French profit), from Latin prōfectus (“advance, progress, growth, increase, profit”), from proficiō (“to go forward, advance, make progress, be profitable or useful”). Doublet of profect.

parole.significato: Offspring or descendants considered as a group.
parole.testo: From Middle English progenie, from Old French progenie, from Latin prōgeniēs, from prōgignō (“beget”).

parole.significato: A statement about or prior knowledge of the future.
parole.testo: From Old French pronosticacion, from Medieval Latin prognosticatio.

parole.significato: Movement or advancement through a series of events, or points in time; development through time.
parole.testo: From Middle English progresse, from Old French progres (“a going forward”), from Latin prōgressus (“an advance”), from the participle stem of prōgredī (“to go forward, advance, develop”), from pro- (“forth, before”) + gradi (“to walk, go”). Displaced native Old English forþgang.

parole.significato: The act of moving from one thing to another.
parole.testo: From Middle English progressioun, from Old French progression and its etymon Latin prōgressiō. By surface analysis, progress + -ion.

parole.significato: Tediously lengthy; dwelling on trivial details.
parole.testo: From Old French prolixe, from Latin prōlixus (“stretched out; courteous, favorable”). The verb is derived from the adjective.

parole.significato: Long-windedness, tiresome length, an excess of words.
parole.testo: From Old French prolixite, from Latin prolixitas. By surface analysis, prolix + -ity.

parole.significato: A speech or section used as an introduction, especially to a play or novel.
parole.testo: From Middle English prologue, prologe, from Old French prologue, from Latin prologus, from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos). Equivalent to pro- + -logue.

parole.significato: The act of prolonging.
parole.testo: From Middle English prolongacioun, from Old French prolongation, from Late Latin prōlongātiō, from prōlongātus, perfect passive participle of Latin prōlongō, from prō + longus. By surface analysis, prolong + -ation.

parole.significato: An oath or affirmation; a vow.
parole.testo: From Middle English promis, promisse, borrowed from Old French promesse, from Medieval Latin prōmissa, Latin prōmissum (“a promise”), feminine and neuter past participles of prōmittō (“to send forth, to say beforehand, to promise”), from pro (“forth”) + mittere (“to send”); see mission. Compare admi

parole.significato: An advancement in rank or position.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Old French promocion, from Late Latin prōmotiō, from Latin prōmoveō (“to move forward”). Equivalent to promote + -ion.

parole.significato: To declare formally, officially or ceremoniously.
parole.testo: Recorded since c.1330 as Middle English pronouncen (“to utter, declare officially”), from Old French prononcier, from Latin prōnūntiō, itself from prō- (“forth, out, in public”) + nūntiō (“to announce”) from nūntius (“messenger”).

parole.significato: An effort, process, or operation designed to establish or discover a fact or truth; an act of testing; a test; a trial.
parole.testo: From Middle English proof, from Old French prove, from Late Latin proba (“a proof”), from Latin probō (“to prove”); see prove; compare also the doublet probe.

parole.significato: A prediction, especially one made by a prophet or under divine inspiration.
parole.testo: From Middle English prophecie, from Old French prophetie, from Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía, “prophecy”), from προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “speaker of a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”). Displaced native Old English wītgung. Doublet of prophesy.

parole.significato: A female prophet.
parole.testo: From Middle English prophetesse, from Old French prophetesse, from Late Latin prophetissa. By surface analysis, prophet + -ess.

parole.significato: To act as a prophet; to prophesy; to make prophecies.
parole.testo: From Middle English prophetise, from Old French prophetisier, from Latin prophētizō, from Ancient Greek προφητίζω (prophētízō, “to prophesy”). By surface analysis, prophet + -ize.

parole.significato: nearby; close at hand
parole.testo: From propinqu(ity) + -ent, from Old French propinquite and Latin propinquitatem, from propinquitas, from propinquus, from prope.

parole.significato: A quantity of something that is part of the whole amount or number.
parole.testo: From Middle English proporcion, from Old French proportion, from Latin prōportiō (“comparative relation, proportion, symmetry, analogy”), from pro (“for, before”) + portio (“share, part”); see portion. By surface analysis, pro- + portion.

parole.significato: To make an offer or suggestion to (someone).
parole.testo: From Middle English proposicioun, from Old French proposicion, from Latin prōpositiō, from the verb prōponō.

parole.significato: To suspend (a parliamentary session) or to discontinue the meetings of (an assembly, parliament etc.) without formally…
parole.testo: From Old French proroger, proroguer, from Latin prōrogō (“prolong, defer”).

parole.significato: Language, particularly written language, not intended as poetry.
parole.testo: From Middle English prose, from Old French prose, from Latin prōsa (“straightforward”) from the term prōsa ōrātiō (“a straightforward speech – i.e. without the ornaments of verse”). further etymology and related terms The term prōsa (“straightforward”), a colloquial form of prorsa (“straight forward

parole.significato: One who has converted to a religion or doctrine, especially a gentile converted to Judaism.
parole.testo: From Old French proselite, from Late Latin proselytus (“proselyte, alien resident”), from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos, “newcomer, convert”) (from πρός (prós, “to, towards”) and the stem -ηλυ- of ἐλήλυθα (elḗlutha), perfect of ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “come”)), translation of Hebrew גר (ger) in th

parole.significato: To be successful; to succeed; to be fortunate or prosperous; to thrive; to make gain.
parole.testo: From Old French prosperer, from Latin prosperō (“to render happy”), from prosperus (“prosperous”), from Proto-Italic *prosparos, from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- (“to succeed”), whence also Latin spēs (“hope, expectation”).

parole.significato: The condition of being prosperous: having good fortune and a fortune.
parole.testo: From Middle English prosperite, from Old French prosperitet, from Latin prosperitās, equivalent to prosper + -ity.

parole.significato: The process of keeping (something or someone) safe.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French, from stem of Late Latin prōtectiō (“a covering over”), from Latin prōtēctus, perfect passive participle of prōtegere (“to protect, cover in front”). Displaced native Old English ġesċildnes. Equivalent to protect + -ion.

parole.significato: To make a strong objection.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From the Middle English verb protesten, from Old French protester, from Latin prōtestārī, from prō + testor, from testis (“witness”).

parole.significato: A formal solemn objection or other declaration.
parole.testo: From Old French protestacion, from Latin prōtestātiō.

parole.significato: Feeling honoured (by something); feeling happy or satisfied about an event or fact; gratified.
