parole.significato: A church official who looks after a church building and its graveyard and may act as a gravedigger and bell ringer.
parole.testo: From Old French segrestien, from Medieval Latin sacristanus, based on Latin sacer (“sacred”). Doublet of sacristan.

parole.significato: A sacristy; vestry; a room for holy objects.
parole.testo: From Middle English sextriȝe, cextrye, sextrye, sextry, probably a reduced form of Old French secresterie or Anglo-Latin secrestāria, a variant of Medieval Latin sacristāria.

parole.significato: A mediaeval double-reed wind instrument with a conical wooden body.
parole.testo: From Middle English shalmuse, from Old French chalemel (modern French chalumeau), from Late Latin calamellus, from Latin calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Doublet of caramel, chalumeau, and qalam, as well as related to calame, calamus, culm, and haulm.

parole.significato: Military action.
parole.testo: From Middle English sege, from Old French sege, siege, seige (modern French siège), from Vulgar Latin *sēdicum, from Latin sēdicŭlum, sēdēcula (“small seat”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”). The military sense of the term is derived from the notion of an army "sitting down" in front of its target.

parole.significato: A visible fact that shows that something exists or may happen.
parole.testo: From Middle English signe, sygne, syng, seine, sine, syne, from Old English seġn (“sign; mark; token”) and Old French signe, seing (“sign; mark; signature”); both from Latin signum (“a mark; sign; token”); root uncertain. Doublet of signum and signal. Partially displaced native token.

parole.significato: A sequence of states representing an encoded message in a communication channel.
parole.testo: From Old French segnal, seignal or Medieval Latin signāle; noun use of the neuter of Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum; verb use from 1805, as a shortened from signalize (1650s). Doublet of signum and sign.

parole.significato: An object (especially a ring) formerly used to impress a picture into the sealing wax of a document as a proof of its o…
parole.testo: From Old French signet (“small seal”), from Medieval Latin signētum, diminutive of Latin signum (“sign”).

parole.significato: signification, meaning
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English signifiaunce, from Old French senefiance, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin significantia. Doublet of significance.

parole.significato: The act of signifying, or something that is signified; significance.
parole.testo: From Old French significacion, from Latin significātiō.

parole.significato: To create a sign out of something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English signifien, from Old French signifier, from Latin significare.

parole.significato: The absence of any sound.
parole.testo: From Middle English silence, from Old French silence, from Latin silentium (“silence”), from silēns (“quiet, silent”, present participle of silēre) + -ium. Displaced native Old English swīġe and sālnes.

parole.significato: Similarity or resemblance to something else.
parole.testo: From Old French similitude, from Latin similitūdō. By surface analysis, similar + -itude.

parole.significato: A rich fruit cake, with a decorated marzipan covering, traditionally eaten on Simnel Sunday or Easter.
parole.testo: From Middle English simenel (also simle), from Old French simenel (“fine wheat flour; flat bread cake, Lenten cake”), probably by dissimilation from Vulgar Latin *siminellus, a diminutive of Latin simila (“fine flour”) (see semolina). Compare also Middle Dutch semel, Middle Low German semele.

parole.significato: The buying or selling of spiritual or sacred things, such as ecclesiastical offices, pardons, or consecrated objects.
parole.testo: From Middle English simonie, symonye, from Old French simonie, from Late Latin simonia, named after Simon Magus (Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Šimʻôn, “Simon”)), with reference to Acts 8:18–20.

parole.significato: Uncomplicated; lacking complexity; taken by itself, with nothing added.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English symple, from Old French simple, from Latin simplex (“simple”, literally “onefold”) (as opposed to duplex (“double”, literally “twofold”)), from semel (“the same”) + plicō (“to fold”). See same and fold. Compare single, singular, simultaneous, etc. Partially displaced na

parole.significato: The state or quality of being simple
parole.testo: From Middle English simplicite, from Old French simplicite, from Latin simplicitās, from simplex (“simple”). See simple. By surface analysis, simple + -icity. Partially displaced native English onefoldness.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being sincere.
parole.testo: From Middle English sinceritie, from Old French sincerité and Medieval Latin sincēritās; both from Latin sincēritās, from sincērus + -tās. Equivalent to sincere + -ity.

parole.significato: Not accompanied by anything else; one in number.
parole.testo: From Middle English single, sengle, from Old French sengle, saingle, sangle, from Latin singulus, a diminutive derived from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one”). Akin to Latin simplex (“simple”). See simple, and compare singular.

parole.significato: Being only one of a larger population; single, individual.
parole.testo: From Middle English singuler, from Old French, from Latin singulāris (“alone of its kind”), from Latin singulus (“single”).

parole.significato: Inauspicious, ominous, unlucky, illegitimate.
parole.testo: From Middle English sinistre (“unlucky”), from Old French senestre, sinistre (“left”), from Latin sinister (“left hand”).

parole.significato: A shade of red; sinoper.
parole.testo: From Old French sinople, from Latin Sinōpis, from Ancient Greek Σινωπίς (Sinōpís, “of Sinope”), a town that exported a red ocher. The unexpected change to meaning "green" in heraldry occurred in French texts around 1350 for unclear reasons.

parole.significato: A man of a higher rank or position.
parole.testo: From Middle English sir, unstressed form of sire, borrowed from Old French sire (“master, sir, lord”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”), from senex (“old”). Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, senior, señor, senyor, signore, and sire.

parole.significato: A lord, master, or other person in authority, most commonly used vocatively: formerly in speaking to elders and superio…
parole.testo: From Middle English sire, from Old French sire, the nominative singular of seignor; from Latin senior, from senex. Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, senior, señor, senyor, signore, and sir. Cognate with French monsieur.

parole.significato: One of a group of nymphs who lured mariners to their death on the rocks.
parole.testo: From Middle English siren, from Old French sereine and Latin Sīrēn, Sīrēna, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). parole.significato: To adjust the size of; to make a certain size.
parole.testo: Attested since the 14th century, originally meant a “law or regulation that determines the amount to be paid”, from Middle English syse, sise (“regulation, control, limit”), from Old French cise, sise, aphetism of assise (“assize”), from the verb asseoir (“to sit down”), from Latin assidēre, compose

parole.significato: A false or unsupported, malicious statement (spoken, not written), especially one which is injurious to a person's repu…
parole.testo: From Middle English slaundre, sclaundre, from Old French esclandre, from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum (“stumbling block, temptation”), from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon, “scandal”). Doublet of scandal.

parole.significato: A person who is held in servitude as the property of another person, and whose labor (and often also whose body and lif…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sclave, from Old French esclave, from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”), traditionally assumed to be because Slavs were often forced into slavery in the Middle Ages. The Latin word is from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos); see that entr

parole.significato: To fly high with little effort, like a bird.
parole.testo: From Middle English soren, from Old French essorer (“to fly up, soar”), from Vulgar Latin *exaurare (“to rise into the air”), from Latin ex (“out”) + aura (“the air, a breeze”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breath”). Compare aura, and exhale.

parole.significato: Not drunk; not intoxicated.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sober, from Old French sobre, from Latin sōbrius, from se- (“without”) + ebrius (“intoxicated”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“drink”). In the sense "not drunk," displaced native undrunken, from Old English undruncen.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being sober.
parole.testo: From Old French sobriete, from Latin sobrietas.

parole.significato: One who practices sodomy; a sodomist.
parole.testo: From Middle English sodomyte, sodomite, from Old French Sodomite and Latin sodomīta, from Ancient Greek σοδομίτης (sodomítēs). Equivalent to Sodom + -ite.

parole.significato: A short stay somewhere.
parole.testo: From Middle English sojourne (noun) and sojournen (verb), from Old French sojor, sojorner (modern séjour, séjourner), from (assumed) Vulgar Latin *subdiurnāre, from Latin sub- (“under, a little over”) + Late Latin diurnus (“lasting for a day”), from Latin dies (“day”).

parole.significato: An old coin from France and some other countries worth 12 deniers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Old French sol (“French coin”) (modern French sou), from Latin solidum, the accusative singular of solidus (“Roman gold coin; (adjective) solid”). Doublet of sold, soldo, solid, solidus, sou, and xu.

parole.significato: Comfort or consolation in a time of loneliness or distress.
parole.testo: From Old French solas, from Latin sōlācium (“consolation”), root from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”).

parole.significato: Any of various easily melted alloys, commonly of tin and lead, that are used to mend, coat, or join metal objects, usua…
parole.testo: From Middle English souder, soudere, soudur (noun), from Old French soldure, soudeure (noun), from Old French souder, solder (“to solder”, verb) (> Middle English souden (“to solder”)), from Latin solidāre (“make solid”).

parole.significato: A member of a ground-based army, of any rank, but especially an enlisted member.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English soudeour, from Old French soudier or soudeour (“mercenary”), from Medieval Latin soldarius (“soldier (one having pay)”), from Late Latin solidus, a type of coin. Displaced Old English cempa (whence obsolete kemp). (red herring): An allusion to soldiers' red uniforms; re

parole.significato: Only.
parole.testo: From Middle English sole, soule, from Old French sol, soul (“alone”), from Latin sōlus (“alone, single, solitary, lonely”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé (reflexive pronoun). Perhaps related to Old Latin sollus (“whole, complete”), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“safe, healthy”). More

parole.significato: The quality of being deeply serious and sober or solemn.
parole.testo: From solemn + -ity, from Middle English solemnity (“observance of formality and ceremony”), frequently in the phrases in solemnity, with solemnity, which from Old French solemnite, from Latin sollemnitās, from sollemnis. (Compare solemn.)

parole.significato: To make solemn, or official, through ceremony or legal act.
parole.testo: From Middle English solempnisen, from Old French solemnisier, from Medieval Latin solemnizare, from Latin solemnis.

parole.significato: To persistently endeavor to obtain an object, or bring about an event.
parole.testo: From Middle English soliciten, solliciten, from Old French soliciter, solliciter, borrowed from Latin sollicitō (“stir, disturb; look after”), from sollicitus (“agitated, anxious, punctilious”, literally “thoroughly moved”), from sollus (“whole, entire”) + perfect passive participle of cieō (“shake,

parole.significato: The state of being solicitous; uneasiness of mind occasioned by fear of evil or desire for good; anxiety.
parole.testo: From Middle English solicitude, from Old French sollicitude, from Latin sollicitūdō (“anxiety”), from sollicitus, solicitus (“anxious, solicitous”). See solicitous.

parole.significato: That can be picked up or held, having a texture, and usually firm. Unlike a liquid, gas or plasma.
parole.testo: From Middle English solide, borrowed from Old French solide, from Latin solidus (“solid”), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂-i-dʰ-o-s (“entire”), suffixed form of root *solh₂- (“integrate, whole”). Doublet of sol, sold, soldo, solidus, sou, and xu.

parole.significato: Aloneness; the state of being alone, solitary, or by oneself.
parole.testo: From Middle English solitude, from Old French solitude, from Latin sōlitūdō. By surface analysis, sole + -itude.

parole.significato: A solar, or garret room.
parole.testo: From Old French soler, solier, from Latin solarium (“a terrace or flat roof”), from sol (“sun”).

parole.significato: One of the two points in the ecliptic at which the sun is furthest from the celestial equator. This corresponds to one…
parole.testo: From Middle English solstice, from Old French solstice, from Latin sōlstitium.

parole.significato: Able to be dissolved.
parole.testo: From Middle English soluble, from Old French soluble, from Late Latin solūbilis, from Latin solvere (“to loosen”) + -bilis. Piecewise doublet of solvable.

parole.significato: A homogeneous mixture, which may be liquid, gas or solid, formed by dissolving one or more substances.
parole.testo: From Middle English solucioun, from Old French solucion (French solution), from Latin solūtiōnem, accusative singular of solūtiō, from the verb solvō. Compare solve, -tion.

parole.significato: The school of the sophists in antiquity; their beliefs and method of teaching philosophy and rhetoric.
parole.testo: From Middle English sophim, from Old French soffime, sofime, sofisme, sophisme, from Latin sophisma (“fallacy, sophism”), from Ancient Greek σόφῐσμᾰ (sóphĭsmă), from σοφίζω (sophízō) + -μα (-ma).

parole.significato: Enlightenment or education.
parole.testo: From Middle English sophisticacion, sophisticacioun, sophisticacoun, from Old French sofisticacion, sophisticacion, from Medieval Latin sophisticātiōnis. By surface analysis, sophisticate + -ion.

parole.significato: The actions or arguments of a sophist.
parole.testo: From Middle English safistre, soffistre, sofystry, sophestrie, sophestry, sophestrye, sophistre, sophistri, sophistrie, sophistry, sophistrye, sophystrye, from Old French sofisterie, sophistrie and Medieval Latin sophistria, Anglo-Latin sophestria, from Latin sophista, from Ancient Greek σοφιστής (s

parole.significato: A flock of mallards.
parole.testo: From Middle English sowrde, from Old French sourdre (“to rise”), that is, "to rise in flight, as a flock of birds", from Latin surgō. Related to surge.

parole.significato: A general type.
parole.testo: From Middle English sort, soort, sorte (cognate Dutch soort, German Sorte, Danish sort, Swedish sort), borrowed from Old French sorte (“class, kind”), from Latin sortem, accusative form of sors (“lot, fate, share, rank, category”).

parole.significato: To separate items into different categories according to certain criteria that determine their sorts.
parole.testo: From Middle English sorten, from Old French sortir (“to allot, sort”), from Latin sortīre (“draw lots, divide, choose”), from sors.

parole.significato: Witchcraft, magic, especially as a means of making decisions or predictions.
parole.testo: From Old French sortilège, from Medieval Latin sortilegium (“witchcraft”), from Latin sortilegus (“sorcerer, diviner”), from sors (“fate”) + legere (“choose”).

parole.significato: Any of various dishes commonly made by combining liquids, such as water or stock, with other ingredients, such as meat…
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English soupe, sowpe, from Old French soupe, souppe, sope, from Late Latin suppa (“sopped bread”), from Proto-Germanic *supô (compare Middle Dutch sope (“broth”)). Doublet of sop and zuppa. See also sup and supper. The verb is from the noun.

parole.significato: The person, place, or thing from which something (information, goods, etc.) comes or is acquired.
parole.testo: From Middle English sours, from Old French sorse (“rise, beginning, spring, source”), from sors, past participle of sordre, sourdre, from Latin surgō (“to rise”), which is composed of sub- (“up from below”) + regō (“lead, rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃réǵeti (“to straighten; right”)

parole.significato: To arise, issue or emerge; to give rise.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sourden, from Old French sourdre, from Latin surgō, contraction of earlier subrigō. Compare source. Doublet of surge.

parole.significato: Exercising power of rule.
parole.testo: From Middle English sovereyn, from Old French soverain (whence also modern French souverain), from Vulgar Latin *superānus (compare Italian sovrano, Spanish soberano) from Latin super (“above”). Spelling influenced by folk-etymology association with reign. Doublet of soprano, from the same Latin roo

parole.significato: Having plenty of space; roomy; capacious.
parole.testo: From Middle English spacious, from Old French spacios, from Latin spatiōsus. By surface analysis, space + -ious.

parole.significato: A sudden, involuntary contraction of a muscle, a group of muscles, or a hollow organ.
parole.testo: From Middle English spasme, from Old French spasme, from Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm, convulsion”), from σπάω (spáō, “to draw out, pull out”).

parole.significato: A spatula.
parole.testo: From Middle English spatyll, spatyl, spatule, from Old French spatule, espatule, from Late Latin spatula.

parole.significato: The shoulder.
parole.testo: From Middle English spawde, spaude, spalde, from Old French espalde (French épaule), from Latin spatula. Doublet of spatula.

parole.significato: Distinguished by a unique, particular, or unusual quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English *special, especial, especiall, from Old French especial (whence also French spécial), from Latin speciālis (from speciēs). In this sense displaced native Old English synderlīċ. Doublet of especial.

parole.significato: That in which one specializes; a chosen expertise or talent; bailiwick.
parole.testo: From Middle English specialte, Old French specialte, especialte, from Latin specialitas.

parole.significato: Explicit or definite.
parole.testo: From Old French specifique, from Late Latin specificus (“specific, particular”), from Latin speciēs (“kind”) + -ific.

parole.significato: To state explicitly, or in detail, or as a condition.
parole.testo: From Middle English specifien, from Old French specifier, especefier, or directly from Medieval Latin specificō, from specificus (“specific”).

parole.significato: The process or act of thinking or meditating on a subject.
parole.testo: From Middle English speculacioun, speculation, from Old French speculation (compare French spéculation), from Late Latin speculātiō, speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor. Morphologically speculate + -ion.

parole.significato: Characterized by speculation; based on guessing, unfounded opinions, or extrapolation.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English speculatyf, borrowed from Old French speculatif or directly from Late Latin speculativus, from Latin speculor.

parole.significato: A cave, cavern or grotto.
parole.testo: From Middle English spelunke, from Old French spelonque and/or Latin spelunca, from Ancient Greek σπῆλυγξ (spêlunx, “cave”), related to σπέος (spéos). Cognates include Middle Dutch spelunke, spelonke, German Spelunke.

parole.significato: A surface in three dimensions consisting of all points equidistant from a center. .
parole.testo: From Middle English spere, from Old French sphere, from Late Latin sphēra, earlier Latin sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), of unknown origin. Not related to superficially similar Persian سپهر (sepehr, “sky”) . Displaced Old English cliewen

parole.significato: One who seasons with spice.
parole.testo: From Middle English spicer, spycer, spycere, from Old French espicier (> French épicier), from Latin speciarius (“dealer in spices”), equivalent to spice + -er.

parole.significato: To breathe.
parole.testo: From Old French spirer, and its source, Latin spīrō (“to breathe”).

parole.significato: The soul of a person or other creature.
parole.testo: From Middle English spirit, from Old French espirit (“spirit”), from Latin spīritus (“breath; spirit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys- (“to blow, breathe”). Compare inspire, respire, transpire, all ultimately from Latin spīrō (“to breathe, blow, respire”). In this sense, displaced native Middle

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the spirit or the soul.
parole.testo: From Middle English spiritual, spirituel, from Old French spirituel, from Late Latin spīrituālis, from Latin spīritus. By surface analysis, spirit + -ual.

parole.significato: Density, thickness; the state or quality of being inspissated or thickened.
parole.testo: From Middle English spissitude, from Old French spissitude and Latin spissitūdō, from spissus (“thick”).

parole.significato: Ill will or hatred toward another, accompanied with the desire to unjustifiably irritate, annoy, or thwart; a want to d…
parole.testo: From Middle English spit, a shortening of despit (whence despite), from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from Latin dēspiciō (“to look down, despise”). parole.significato: Shining; glossy; lustrous.
parole.testo: From Middle English splendaunt, from Old French splendiant, present participle of esplendiier, and esplendent, and Latin splendēns, splendentis, present participle of splendēre (“to shine”).

parole.significato: To strip (someone who has been killed or defeated) of arms or armour.
parole.testo: From Middle English spoilen, spuylen, borrowed from Old French espoillier, espollier, espuler, from Latin spoliō, spoliāre (“pillage, ruin, spoil”).

parole.significato: To draw a (specifically) pixel art sprite.
parole.testo: From Middle English sprite, spryt, spreyte, from Old French esprit (“spirit”), from Latin spīritus. Doublet of spirit, spiritus, spirytus, spright, and esprit. parole.significato: Foam or froth of liquid, particularly that of seawater.
parole.testo: From Middle English spume, from Old French espume, from Latin spūma.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Euphorbia, a diverse genus of over 2,000 species.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English spurge, from Old French espurge, from espurgier (“to purge”), from Latin expurgo (“to purge”); the bitter milky sap of these plants was formerly used as a purgative.

parole.significato: Any of several European annual herbs of the genus Spergula.
parole.testo: Dutch or Old French spurrie; compare German Spergel, New Latin spergula.

parole.significato: Shaped like a square (the polygon).
parole.testo: From Middle English square, sqware, squyre; from Old French esquarre, esquerre, (modern French équerre), from Vulgar Latin *exquadra, from Latin ex- + quadro, from quadrus (compare English quad and quadra). Doublet of squad and squadra. Displaced Old English fēowerecge (fēower nominative + ecg accus

parole.significato: A sport played in a walled court with a soft rubber ball and bats like tennis racquets.
parole.testo: From Middle English squachen, squatchen, from Old French esquacher, escachier, from Vulgar Latin *excoāctiāre, from Latin ex + coāctāre. parole.significato: A shield-bearer or armor-bearer who attended a knight.
parole.testo: From Middle English esquire, from Old French escuier, from Latin scūtārius (“shield-bearer”), from scūtum (“shield”).

parole.significato: The condition of being stable or in equilibrium, and thus resistant to change.
parole.testo: From Middle English stabletee, stabilite, from Old French stabilité, from Latin root of stabilitas (“firmness, steadfastness”), from stabilis (“steadfast, firm”). Displaced native Old English staþolfæstnes.

parole.significato: A kind of coarse woollen cloth from England.
parole.testo: From Old French estamine (modern French étamine), from Medieval Latin stāminea (“kind of woollen cloth”), from Latin stāmineus (“trimmed with thread”), from stāmen (“warp (of a loom)”).

parole.significato: A vertical pole, post, or support.
parole.testo: From Old French estanson, estanchon, (Modern French étançon), from estance (“a stay, a prop”), from Latin stāns (“standing”), present participle of stō.

parole.significato: Water retained by an embankment; a pool of water.
parole.testo: From Old French estanc, (French étang), from Latin stagnum (“a pool”). Compare stagnant, stagnate.

parole.significato: A condition; a set of circumstances applying at any given time.
parole.testo: From Middle English stat (as a noun); adopted c. 1200 from both Old French estat and Latin stātus (“manner of standing, attitude, position, carriage, manner, dress, apparel; and other senses”), from stāre (“to stand”). Doublet of estate and status. The sense of "polity" develops in the 14th century.

parole.significato: A three-dimensional work of art, usually representing a person or animal, usually created by sculpting, carving, moldin…
parole.testo: From Old French statue, from Latin statua, derived from statuō (“set up or erect”). Doublet of statua.

parole.significato: A person or animal's natural height when standing upright.
parole.testo: From Middle English stature, from Old French stature, from Latin statūra.

parole.significato: A written law or ordinance passed by a legislative body.
parole.testo: From Middle English statut, from Old French statut, from Late Latin statutum (“a statute”), neuter singular of Latin statutus, past participle of statuō (“to set up, establish”).

parole.significato: To make (an animal or person) unconscious or cause (an animal or person) to die by preventing breathing; to smother, to…
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English stuflen (“to have difficulty breathing due to heat, stifle; to suffocate by drowning, drown”) [and other forms]; further etymology uncertain. Also found in Middle English forstyflyd (“stifled, choked”, past participle). Perhaps derived from Middle English

parole.significato: An organ in animals that stores food in the process of digestion.
parole.testo: From Middle English stomak, from Old French estomac, from Latin stomachus, from Ancient Greek στόμαχος (stómakhos), from στόμα (stóma, “mouth”). Partially displaced native Old English maga, whence Modern English maw.

parole.significato: To tell as a story; to relate or narrate about.
parole.testo: From Middle English storie, storye, from Anglo-Norman estorie by aphesis, from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ῐ̔στορῐ́ᾱ (hĭstorĭ́ā, “learning through research”). Doublet of history and storey.

parole.significato: To hold tightly, to clasp.
parole.testo: From Middle English straynen, streinen, streynen, from Old French estreindre (whence French étreindre (“to grip”)), from Latin stringō (“to draw tight together, to tie”).

parole.significato: A narrow channel of water connecting two larger bodies of water.
parole.testo: From Middle English streit, from Old French estreit (modern form étroit), from Latin strictus, perfect passive participle of stringō (“compress, tighten”). Doublet of stretto and strict.

parole.significato: To kill someone by squeezing the throat so as to cut off the oxygen supply.
parole.testo: From Middle English stranglen, from Old French estrangler, from Latin strangulō, strangulāre, from Ancient Greek στραγγαλόομαι (strangalóomai, “to be strangled”), from στραγγάλη (strangálē, “a halter”); compare στραγγός (strangós, “twisted”) and string. parole.significato: A long, narrow, pliable strip of leather, cloth, or the like.

parole.significato: A tactic or artifice designed to gain the upper hand, especially one involving underhanded dealings or deception.
parole.testo: From Middle English stratageme, from Old French stratageme, from Latin strategema, from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (stratḗgēma, “the act of a general, a piece of generalship”), from στρατηγέω (stratēgéō, “to be a general, command an army”), from στρατηγός (stratēgós, “a general, the leader or commande

parole.significato: To wander, as from a direct course; to deviate, or go out of the way.
parole.testo: From Middle English strayen, partly from Old French estraier, from Vulgar Latin via strata, and partly from Middle English strien, streyen, streyȝen (“to spread, scatter”), from Old English strēġan (“to strew”).

parole.significato: To apply force to (a body or structure) causing strain.
parole.testo: From a shortening of Middle English destresse, borrowed from Old French destrecier, from Latin distringō (“to stretch out”). parole.significato: Straw.
parole.testo: From Old French *estramaille (“straw for bedding”), from Latin stramen (“straw for bedding”), from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to spread”).

parole.significato: A person who studies or learns about a particular subject.
parole.testo: From Middle English student, studient, from Old French estudiant, estudiente, from Latin studēns, present participle of studeō (“dedicate oneself to, study”). Equivalent to stud(y) + -ent.

parole.significato: Mental effort to acquire knowledge or learning.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English studie, from Old French estudie (Modern French étude), borrowed from Latin studium (“zeal, dedication, study”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewd- (“to push, to hit”). Doublet of etude and studio.

parole.significato: Rape.
parole.testo: From Old French stupration or its source, Latin stuprationem.

parole.significato: Of firm build; stiff; stout; strong.
parole.testo: From Middle English sturdy, stourdy, stordy (“bold, valiant, strong, stern, fierce, rebellious”) (perhaps influenced by Middle English sture, stoure, stor (“strong, robust, harsh, stern, violent, fierce, sturdy”); see English stour), from Old French estourdi (“dazed”), form of estourdir, originally

parole.significato: To overcome, quieten, or bring under control.
parole.testo: From Middle English subdewen, subduen, sodewen, from Old French souduire, from Latin subdūcō (“to draw away”), perhaps influenced by subdō (“to subdue, subject”).

parole.significato: Likely to be affected by or to experience something; liable.
parole.testo: From Middle English subget, from Old French suget, from Latin subiectus (“lying under or near, adjacent, also subject, exposed”), as a noun, subiectus (“a subject, an inferior”), subiectum (“the subject of a proposition”), past participle of subiciō (“throw, lay, place”), from sub (“under, at the fo

parole.significato: The act of submitting or yielding; surrender.
parole.testo: From Middle English submissioun, from Old French soubmission, from Latin submissio, from submitto.

parole.significato: Physical matter; material.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English substance, from Old French substance, from Latin substantia (“substance, essence”), from substāns, present active participle of substō (“exist”, literally “stand under”), from sub + stō (“stand”). Displaced native Old English andweorc.

parole.significato: Having a substance; actually existing.
parole.testo: From Middle English substancial, substantiall, from Old French substanciel, substantiel and its etymon Latin substantiālis.

parole.significato: The quality of being subtle.
parole.testo: From Middle English sotilte, from Old French sutilté, inherited from Latin subtīlitās, from subtīlis (“subtle”). Equivalent to subtle + -ty. Doublet of subtility.

parole.significato: A residential area located on the outskirts of a city or large town that usually includes businesses that cater to its…
parole.testo: From Old French suburbe, subburbe, from Latin suburbium (from sub- (“under-”) + urbs (“city”)). Displaced native Old English underburg (literally “underborough”).

parole.significato: To overturn from the foundation; to overthrow; to ruin utterly.
parole.testo: From Middle English subverten, from Old French subvertir, from Latin subvertō (“to overthrow”, literally “to underturn, turn from beneath”).

parole.significato: To follow something in sequence or time.
parole.testo: From Old French succeder, from Latin succedere (“to go under, go from under, come under, approach, follow, take the place of, receive by succession, prosper, be successful”). parole.significato: An act, process, or instance of succeeding:
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English [Term?], from Old French succession, from Latin successiō (noun).

parole.significato: Encircled by, or as if by, a girdle; drawn up or wrapped tightly.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English succinte, succynt (“having one’s waist encircled with something, girdled; brief, concise, succinct”), borrowed from Old French succinct (modern French succinct), or directly from its etymon Latin succīnctus (“belted, girdled; enclosed or tightly wrap

parole.significato: To yield to an overpowering force or overwhelming desire.
parole.testo: From Old French succomber, from Latin succumbō.

parole.significato: To undergo hardship.
parole.testo: From Middle English suffren, from Anglo-Norman suffrir, from Latin sufferre (“to offer, hold up, bear, suffer”), from sub- (“up, under”) + ferō (“to carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”). Displaced native Old English þrōwian.

parole.significato: The condition or quality of being sufficient; sufficiency.
parole.testo: From Old French sufficience, from Late Latin sufficientia.

parole.significato: An adequate quantity of; enough.
parole.testo: From Old French sufisanz, soficient, from Latin sufficiēns, present participle of sufficiō.

parole.significato: A quantity obtained by addition or aggregation.
parole.testo: From Middle English summe, from Old French summe, from Latin summa (“highest point; sum”), from summus (“highest”).

parole.significato: A call to do something, especially to come.
parole.testo: From Middle English somouns (“order or command to do something”), borrowed from Old French sumunce (modern French semonce), from Vulgar Latin *summonsa, a noun use of the feminine past participle of summoneō, summonēre (“to summon”).

parole.significato: The driver of a packhorse.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old French sommetier (“pack-horse driver”), from Late Latin *sagmatarius, from Latin sagma, from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma, “pack-saddle”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being superfluous; overflowingness.
parole.testo: From superflu(ous) + -ity, Old French superfluite, from Medieval Latin superfluitas, from Latin superfluus.

parole.significato: Higher in rank, status, or quality.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French superiour, from Latin superior (“higher, upper”).

parole.significato: The state of being superior.
parole.testo: From Middle English superiorite, from Old French superiorite, from Medieval Latin superioritas, from Latin superior. Morphologically superior + -ity.

parole.significato: Having the power to carry something or someone above, over or beyond others.
parole.testo: From Middle English superlatyf, from Old French superlatif, from Late Latin superlātīvus, from Latin superlātus (“carried above, over; extravagant, of hyperbole”), past participle of superfero (“carry over”), from super (“above”) + fero (“bear, carry”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to heaven or to the sky; celestial.
parole.testo: From Old French supernel or Medieval Latin supernālis, from Latin supernus, from superum (“celestial regions, heavenly bodies”).

parole.significato: Susceptible to superstitions.
parole.testo: From Old French superstitieux, from Latin superstitiōsus, from superstitio + -ōsus. Cognate with Dutch superstitieus.

parole.significato: To take the place of; to replace, to supersede.
parole.testo: From Middle English supplanten, supplaunten, from Old French supplanter, from Latin supplantō (“trip up”), from sub (“from below, under”) + planta (“sole”).

parole.significato: An act of supplicating; a humble request.
parole.testo: From Middle English supplicacioun, supplication, from Old French supplication, from Latin supplicatio, supplicationem, from supplicare (“to supplicate”). By surface analysis, supplicate + -ion.

parole.significato: To provide (something), to make (something) available for use.
parole.testo: From Middle English supplien, borrowed from Old French soupleer, souploier, from Latin suppleo (“to fill up, make full, complete, supply”). The Middle English spelling was modified to conform to Latin etymology.

parole.significato: To help keep from falling.
parole.testo: From Middle English supporten, from Old French supporter, from Latin supportō.

parole.significato: To take for granted; to conclude, with less than absolute supporting data; to believe.
parole.testo: From Middle English supposen, borrowed from Old French supposer, equivalent to prefix sub- (“under”) + poser (“to place”); corresponding in meaning to Latin supponere (“to put under, to substitute, falsify, counterfeit”), suppositum. See pose.

parole.significato: A syncopic variant of super-.
parole.testo: From Middle English sur-, from Old French sur-, sour-, sor-, soure-, a syncopic form of the Latin super. Doublet of super-, over-, and hyper-.

parole.significato: The portion of a person's name that is generally hereditary or treated as an indicator of a person's family, which may…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English surname, a partial calque of Old French surnum, surnoun (“surname; nickname”) (whence Middle English surnoun), from Late Latin supernōmen, suprānōmen (“surname”), from super- (“over, above, beyond”) and nōmen (“name”), equivalent to sur- + name.

parole.significato: A liturgical vestment of the Christian Church in the form of a tunic of white linen or cotton material, with wide or mo…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English surplys, from Old French surpeliz, from Medieval Latin superpelliceum, from Latin super (“over”) and pellis (“fur”).

parole.significato: The act of surveying; a general view.
parole.testo: From Middle English surveyen, from Old French sourveoir, surveer (“to oversee”), from sour-, sur- (“over”) + veoir, veeir (“to see”), from Latin videre. See sur- and vision. Related to supervision.

parole.significato: To imagine or suppose (something) to be true, or to exist, without proof.
parole.testo: From Old French suspect, from Latin suspectus, perfect passive participle of suspiciō (“mistrust, suspect”), from sub (“under”), + speciō (“watch, look at”).

parole.significato: To halt something temporarily.
parole.testo: From Old French sospendre, from Latin suspendere.

parole.significato: Arousing suspicion.
parole.testo: From Old French sospecious, from Latin suspiciosus, suspitiosus.

parole.significato: To maintain, or keep in existence.

parole.significato: Something that provides support or nourishment.
parole.testo: From Middle English sustenaunce, from Old French sustenance, from sustenir with the suffix -ance, from Vulgar Latin *sustenire, from Latin sustinere. Compare also Late Latin sustinentia. Equivalent to sustain + -ance.

parole.significato: The act or the result of sustaining; sustainment; sustention.
parole.testo: First attested in 1382: from the Old French sustentacion, from the Latin sustentātio, from sustentō; compare the Italian sostentazione, the Occitan sustentacion, the Portuguese sustentação, and the Spanish sustentación. Doublet of sustentatio.

parole.significato: An argument whose conclusion is supported by two premises, of which one contains the term that is the predicate of the…
parole.testo: From Old French silogisme (“syllogism”), from Latin syllogismus, from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós, “inference, conclusion”). Doublet of syllogismus.

parole.significato: An extended piece of music of sophisticated structure, usually for orchestra.
parole.testo: From Middle English symphonye, from Old French simphonie, from Latin symphonia, from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). By surface analysis, sym- + -phony. Doublet of sinfonia, symphonia, tsampouna, and zampogna.

parole.significato: A place of worship for Jews.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English synagoge, from Old French synagoge, from Latin synagōga, from Ancient Greek σῠνᾰγωγή (sŭnăgōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”), from συνάγω (sunágō, “to gather together”), from σῠ́ν (sŭ́n, “with, together”) & ᾰ̓́γω (ắgō, “to lead”). By surface analysis, syn- + -agogue.

parole.significato: Any thick liquid that has a high sugar content and which is added to or poured over food as a flavoring.

parole.significato: Any temporary dwelling; a hut, tent, or booth.

parole.significato: A crisp, smooth woven fabric made from silk or synthetic fibers.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English, from Old French taffetas, from Medieval Latin taffata, from Classical Persian تافته (tāfta), from تافتن (tāftan).

parole.significato: A sharp, hooked claw of a bird of prey or other predatory animal.
parole.testo: From Middle English talon, taloun, from Old French talon (“heel, spur”), from Medieval Latin tālōnem, from Proto-Romance *tālōnis, from Latin tālus (“ankle”).

parole.significato: A tropical tree, Tamarindus indica.

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English tansy, tansey, syncopic forms of earlier tanesie, tanesei, from Old French tanesie, tanoisie, tanasie, tanaisie, from Medieval Latin tanacetum, atanacetum, attested since the 8th century, of obscure origin, speculated from Ancient Greek ἀθανασία (athanasía, “immortality

parole.significato: Slowness; tardiness.
parole.testo: From Middle English tardite, tarditee, from Old French tardeté and/or Latin tarditās, equivalent to tard(y) + -ity.

parole.significato: A type of small open pie, or piece of pastry, now typically containing jelly (US) / jam (UK) or conserve, or sometimes…
parole.testo: From Middle English tart, tarte, from Old French tarte, tartre (“flat pastry”) (compare Medieval Latin tarta), of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of Old French torte, tourte, from Latin turta, perhaps from tŏrta f (“twisted”), in which case it would be cognate to torta.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the people or culture of Tartars.
parole.testo: From Old French Tartaire, from Medieval Latin Tartarus (“Tartar, Mongol”), from Old Turkic 𐱃𐱃𐰺 (t¹t¹r¹), spelling influenced by Latin Tartarus (“Hell (in Greek mythology)”), from Ancient Greek Τάρταρος (Tártaros). Doublet of Tatar and tartare.

parole.significato: tartar
parole.testo: From Old French tartre, from Medieval Latin tartarum, from Byzantine Greek τάρταρον (tártaron).

parole.testo: From Middle English tassel, from Old French tassel, from Latin tāxillus (“small cube”), from tālus (“ankle”).

parole.significato: One of the sensations produced by the tongue in response to certain chemicals; the quality of giving this sensation.

parole.significato: Very high or tall.
parole.testo: Compare Old French tant (“so great”), French tant (“so much”), Latin tantus (“of such size, so great, so much”). See ataunt.

parole.significato: A restaurant or bar.
parole.testo: From Middle English taverne, from Old French taverne (“wine shop”), from Latin taberna (“inn”). Doublet of taberna and taverna.

parole.significato: Boring, monotonous, time-consuming, wearisome, livelong.
parole.testo: English tedi(um) + -ous, from Old French tedieus, from Late Latin taediōsus, from Latin taedium (“weariness, tedium”).

parole.significato: The lime tree, or linden.

parole.significato: Reckless boldness; foolish bravery.

parole.significato: A storm, especially one with severe winds.
parole.testo: From Old French tempeste (French tempête), from Latin tempestas (“storm”), from tempus (“time, weather”). Displaced native Old English hrīþ.

parole.significato: A Knight Templar, one of the Knights Templar.
parole.testo: From Middle English templer, from Old French templier; cf. the Medieval Latin templarius, from Latin templum (“temple”).

parole.significato: A barrister having chambers in the Inner Temple or Middle Temple.
parole.testo: From Middle English templer, from Old French templier; cf. the Medieval Latin templārius, from Latin templum (“temple”).

parole.significato: The slightly flatter region, on either side of the head of a vertebrate, including a human, behind the eye and forehead…
parole.testo: From Middle English temple, from Old French temple, from Vulgar Latin *temp(u)la, from Latin tempora (“the temples”), plural of tempus (“temple, head, face”). See temporal bone.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the material world, as opposed to sacred or clerical.
parole.testo: From Middle English temporal, temporel (“transitory, worldly, material, of secular society”), from Old French temporel or Latin temporālis (“of time (in grammar), temporary, relating to time as opposed to eternity”), from tempus (“time, period, opportunity”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: To provoke someone to do wrong, especially by promising a reward; to entice.
parole.testo: From Middle English tempten, from Old French tempter (French: tenter), from Latin temptare, from tentare (“to handle, touch, try, test, tempt”), frequentative of tendere (“to stretch”). Displaced native English costning (“temptation”).

parole.significato: The act of tempting.
parole.testo: From Old French temptacion, from Latin temptatio. Morphologically tempt + -ation.

parole.significato: A species of freshwater game fish, Tinca tinca.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenche, from Old French tenche, from Late Latin tinca.

parole.significato: Dark, tenebrous.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenebrose, from Old French tenebros, from Latin tenebrōsus (“dark, gloomy”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being tenebrose or tenebrous.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenebrosite, from Old French tenebrosité, ultimately from Latin tenebrae (“darkness”). Compare Medieval Latin tenebrōsitas, French ténébrosité. By surface analysis, tenebrose + -ity.

parole.significato: The property of indicating the point in time at which an action or state of being occurs or exists.
parole.testo: From Middle English tens, from Old French tens (modern French temps), from Latin tempus. Doublet of tempo and tempus.

parole.significato: To attend to; to heed.

parole.significato: A framework upon which cloth is stretched and dried.
parole.testo: Via Old French, perhaps from Latin tentorium.

parole.significato: The third hour of daylight (about 9 am).
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Old French terce, from Latin tertia (“third; the third hour”).

parole.significato: A Mediterranean tree (Pistacia terebinthus and, possibly, Pistacia palaestina)
parole.testo: From Middle English therebynte, from Old French terebinthe, from Latin terebinthus, from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos), from Pre-Greek. Related to turpentine and terpene.

parole.significato: That which limits the extent of anything; limit, extremity, bound, boundary, terminus.
parole.testo: From Middle English terme, borrowed from Old French terme, from Latin terminus (“a bound, boundary, limit, end; in Medieval Latin, also a time, period, word, covenant, etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *térmn̥ (“stump, end, boundary”). Doublet of terminus and termon. Old English had termen

parole.significato: Dreadful; causing terror, alarm and fear; awesome
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English terrible, from Old French terrible, from Latin terribilis (“frightful”), from terreō (“to frighten, terrify, alarm; to deter by terror, scare (away)”). parole.significato: A challenge, trial.
parole.testo: From Middle English test, teste, from Old French test, teste (“an earthen vessel, especially a pot in which metals were tried”), from Latin testum (“the lid of an earthen vessel, an earthen vessel, an earthen pot”), from *terstus, past participle of the root *tersa (“dry land”). parole.significato: A witness.
parole.testo: From Middle English teste, from Old French teste, test and Latin testis (“one who attests, a witness”).

parole.testo: From Middle English testament, from Old French testament, from Latin testāmentum (“the publication of a will, a will, testament, in Late Latin one of the divisions of the Bible”), from testor (“to be a witness, testify, attest, make a will”), from testis (“one who attests, a witness”). parole.significato: A canopy over a bed.

parole.testo: From trammel (“fishing net; shackle”), from Old French tramail (“net for catching fishes”), from Late Latin tremaculum.

parole.significato: A device or fixture used for urination, particularly
parole.testo: From Middle English urinal, urynal, orynal, from Old French urinal, orinal (“vessel for urination”), from Latin ūrīnālis (“urinary”). Use for plumbing fixtures attested from 1851.

parole.significato: A vase with a footed base.
parole.testo: From Middle English urne, from Old French urne, from Latin urna (“vessel”). Doublet of urna.

parole.significato: The act of using.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English use, from Old French us, from Latin ūsus (“use, custom, skill, habit”), from past participle stem of ūtor (“use”). Displaced native Middle English note (“use”) (see note) from Old English notu; Middle English nutte (“use”) from Old English nytt; as well as Old English f

parole.significato: To utilize or employ.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English usen, from Old French user (“use, employ, practice”), from Medieval Latin usare (“use”), frequentative form of past participle stem of Latin uti (“to use”). Displaced native Middle English noten, nutten (“to use”) (from Old English notian, nēotan, nyttian) and Middle En

parole.significato: Most commonly occurring; typical.
parole.testo: From Middle English usual, from Old French usuel, from Latin ūsuālis (“for use, fit for use, also of common use, customary, common, ordinary, usual”), from ūsus (“use, habit, custom”), from the past participle stem of ūtī (“to use”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃eyt- (“to take alo

parole.significato: To seize and hold or use (powers, an office, a coat of arms, a right or copyright, etc) from another, without right (us…
parole.testo: From Middle English usurpen, from Old French usurper, from Latin ūsūrpō.

parole.significato: The wrongful seizure of something by force, especially of sovereignty or other authority.
parole.testo: From Middle English usurpacioun, from Old French usurpacion, from Latin ūsurpātiō; equivalent to usurp + -ation.

parole.significato: An instrument or device for domestic use, especially in the kitchen.
parole.testo: From Middle English utensyl, from Old French utensile, from Latin ūtēnsilis (“useful, usable”).

parole.significato: The state or condition of being useful; usefulness.
parole.testo: From Middle English utilite, from Old French utilite, utilitet (“usefulness”), from Latin ūtilitās, from uti (“to use”). By surface analysis, utile + -ity.

parole.significato: Not occupied; empty.
parole.testo: From Old French vacant, from Latin vacāns.

parole.significato: A person on a trip of indeterminate destination and/or length of time.
parole.testo: From Old French vagabond, from Late Latin vagābundus, from Latin vagari (“wander”). Compare moribund.

parole.significato: Profit; return; proceeds.
parole.testo: From Middle English vayle, from Old French vail, from valoir (“to be worth”), from Latin valeō (“to be worth”).

parole.significato: Overly proud of oneself, especially concerning appearance; having a high opinion of one's own accomplishments with slig…
parole.testo: From Middle English veyn, from Old French vain, from Latin vānus (“empty”).

parole.significato: Possessing excessive vanity or unwarranted pride.
parole.testo: From Middle English veinglorious, from Old French vain glorios, from Latin vānus (“empty”) + glōriōsus.

parole.significato: Excessive vanity.
parole.testo: From Middle English waynglori (“worthless glory”), from Old French vaine glorie, from Medieval Latin vāna glōria, from Latin vāna (“empty, groundless, boastful”) + glōria (“fame, ambition, boasting”), apparently modelled after similar terms in Germanic languages. Compare Old English īdel wuldor (“va

parole.significato: A type of fur from a squirrel with a grey back and white belly, much used on garments in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: From Middle English veir, veire, from Old French vair, veir, from the accusative singular masculine form of Latin varius (“variegated”). Not related to Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“squirrel”).

parole.significato: A valley.
parole.testo: From Middle English vale, from Old French val (“valley”), from Latin vallis, valles. Displaced native Old English dell.

parole.significato: A hardy perennial flowering plant, Valeriana officinalis, with heads of sweetly scented pink or white flowers.
parole.testo: From Old French valeriane or Medieval Latin valeriāna, a reinterpretation of what is found as German Baldrian after valēre (“to be powerful”) or also the gentilic name Valerius, which is seemingly borrowed in the Dark Age period from the late 6ᵗʰ to early 8ᵗʰ century from Turkic or Proto-Mongolic, w

parole.significato: The quality that renders something desirable or valuable; worth.
parole.testo: From Middle English valew, value, from Old French value, feminine past participle of valoir, from Latin valēre (“be strong, be worth”), from Proto-Italic *walēō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“to be strong”).

parole.significato: Value.
parole.testo: From Middle English valure, from Old French valeur, valur, from Latin valor, reshaped as if suffixed with -ure. Doublet of valour.

parole.significato: To become invisible or to move out of view unnoticed.
parole.testo: Aphetic for obsolete evanish, from Middle English evanisshen, esvanisshen, from Old French esvanir, esvaniss- (modern French évanouir), from Vulgar Latin *exvanire (“to vanish, disappear, to fade out”), from Latin ēvānēscō, ēvānēscere, from vānus (“empty”). By surface analysis, Latin vān- + -ish (“v

parole.significato: That which is vain, futile, or worthless; that which is of no value, use or profit.
parole.testo: From va(i)n + -ity, from Middle English vanite, from Old French vanité, from Latin vānitas, from vānus, whence English vain. Doublet of vanitas.

parole.significato: To defeat (someone); to overcome.
parole.testo: From Middle English venquysshen, vaynquisshen, borrowed from a conjugated form of Old French veincre, from Latin vincō.

parole.significato: Cloudy diffused matter such as mist, steam or fumes suspended in the air.
parole.testo: From Middle English vapour, from Anglo-Norman vapour, Old French vapor, from Latin vapor (“steam, heat”).

parole.significato: Able to vary or be varied.
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle English in the 14th century from Old French variable, from Latin variare (“to change”), from varius (“different, various”). Equates to English vary + -able.

parole.significato: The act of varying or the state of being variable.
parole.testo: From Middle English variance, variaunce, equivalent to vary + -ance, from Old French variance or directly from Anglo-Latin variaunce, veriaunce, wariaunce; all from Latin variantia.

parole.significato: Showing variety, diverse.
parole.testo: From Old French variant, from Latin variāns, the present active participle of variō (“to change”). First attested in c. 1380.

parole.significato: A clear or translucent liquid coating composed of resin dissolved in a solvent, which dries by evaporation to form a ha…
parole.testo: From Middle English vernisch, vernish, from Old French vernis, from Medieval Latin vernix, veronix, from Byzantine Greek Βερενίκη (Bereníkē, “Berenice”), a town in Cyrenaica, now called Benghazi.

parole.significato: A metal ring bearing the owner's name or coat of arms, attached to a hawk's jesses. Used for identifying birds.
parole.testo: From Old French vervelle (“falcon's leg fetter”), from Vulgar Latin derivation of Latin vertibulum (“joint”).

parole.significato: To change with time or a similar parameter.
parole.testo: From Middle English varien, from Old French varier, from Latin variō (“to change, alter, make different”), from varius (“different, various”); see various.

parole.significato: The grantee of a fief, a subordinate granted use of a superior's land and its income in exchange for vows of fidelity a…
parole.testo: From Middle English vassal, from Old French vassal, from Medieval Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from Latin vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and Welsh gwas).

parole.significato: An arched masonry structure supporting and forming a ceiling, whether freestanding or forming part of a larger building.
parole.testo: From Middle English vaute, vowte, from Old French volte (modern voûte), from Vulgar Latin *volta < *volvita or *volŭta, a regularization of Latin volūta (compare modern volute (“spire”)), the past participle of volvere (“roll, turn”). Cognate with Spanish vuelta (“turn”) and Portuguese volta ("turn"

parole.significato: a subvassal; someone holding their lands from a vassal of the crown rather than from the crown directly
parole.testo: From Middle English vavasour, from Old French vavasour, from Medieval Latin vavassor, perhaps from vassus vassōrum (“vassal of vassals”).

parole.significato: Any plant.
parole.testo: From Middle English vegetable, from Old French vegetable, from Latin vegetābilis (“able to live and grow”), derived from vegetāre (“to enliven”). Displaced Old English wyrt and ofett, whence modern wort and ovest. Related to vigil, vigour, vajra, and waker.

parole.significato: An intense concentration, force or power.
parole.testo: From Middle English vehemens, vemance, from Old French vëemence, vehemence, from Latin vehementia (“eagerness, strength”), from vehemens (“eager”).

parole.significato: A blood vessel that transports blood from the capillaries back to the heart.
parole.testo: From Middle English veine, borrowed from Anglo-Norman veine, from Latin vēna (“a blood-vessel; vein; artery”) of uncertain origin. See vēna for more. Doublet of vena. Displaced native edre, from ǣdre (whence edder).

parole.significato: A type of parchment paper made from the skin of a lamb, baby goat, or calf.
parole.testo: From Old French velin (French vélin), from Latin vitulinus (“of a calf”), as if derived from Old French veel (“veal”).

parole.significato: To avenge; to punish; to revenge.
parole.testo: From Middle English vengen, from Old French venger, from Latin vindicare (“to avenge, vindicate”).

parole.significato: Able to be forgiven; worthy of forgiveness.
parole.testo: From Old French venial, borrowed from Late Latin veniālem (“pardonable”), from Latin venia (“forgiveness”).

parole.significato: An animal toxin intended for defensive or offensive use; a biological poison delivered by bite, sting, etc., to protect…
parole.testo: From Middle English venym, from Old French venim, from Vulgar Latin *venīmen, from Early Medieval Latin venīnum, from Classical Latin venēnum (“drug; poison; a charm”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”). Doublet of venin and venene.

parole.significato: Of or relating to words.
parole.testo: From Old French verbal, from Late Latin verbālis (“belonging to a word”). Equivalent to verb + -al.

parole.significato: To substantiate or prove the truth of something.
parole.testo: From Old French verifier (French: vérifier), from Medieval Latin vērificāre (“make true”), from Latin vērus (“true”) + faciō (“do, make”); see -fy.

parole.significato: Bright scarlet, vermilion.
parole.testo: From Middle English vermayle, from Old French vermeil (“vermilion”), from Latin vermiculus (“little worm”), from vermis (“worm”), ultimately in reference to Kermes vermilio, a type of scale insect used to make a crimson dye. Doublet of vermicule.

parole.significato: A vivid red synthetic pigment made of mercury sulfide, cinnabar.
parole.testo: From Middle English vermelioun, vermyloun, vermylon, vermilun, from Old French vermeillon (“vermilion”), from vermeil, from Latin vermiculus (“little worm”), from vermis (“worm”), ultimately in reference to Kermes vermilio, a type of scale insect used to make a crimson dye. Displaced native Old Engl

parole.significato: Any of various common types of small insects or other animals which cause harm and annoyance.
parole.testo: From Middle English vermyn, vermyne, from Old French vermine, from Vulgar Latin *verminum (“vermin”), collective noun formed from Latin vermis (“worm”). Compare vermiculate and vermivorous. See also worm.

parole.significato: A poetic form with regular meter and a fixed rhyme scheme.
parole.testo: From Middle English vers, from a mixture of Old English fers and Old French vers; both from Latin versus (“a line in writing, and in poetry a verse; (originally) row, furrow”), from vertō (“to turn around”).

parole.significato: One of a series of lines that are shorter than a standard line of verse, particularly in a hymn.
parole.testo: From Middle English versicle, from Old French versicule, from Latin versiculus.

parole.significato: to make or compose verses
parole.testo: From Middle English versifien, from Old French versifier, learned borrowing from Latin versificāre (“versify”), from versus (see verse) + faciō (“make”).

parole.significato: A green colour, now only in heraldry; represented in engraving by diagonal parallel lines 45 degrees counter-clockwise.
parole.testo: From Middle English vert, borrowed from Old French vert, from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Doublet of virid, which was borrowed directly from Latin.

parole.significato: Able to turn or to be turned; changeable.
parole.testo: From the Old French vertible, from Latin vertibilis from the stem of vertō (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Any herbaceous plant in the genus Verbena especially if used for medicinal purposes, primarily Verbena officinalis, com…
parole.testo: From Middle English verveyne, from Old French verveine, from Latin verbēna. Doublet of verbena.

parole.significato: To a great extent or degree.
parole.testo: From Middle English verray, from Old French verai (“true”), from Early Medieval Latin vērāgus, from Classical Latin vērāx, derived from vērus, from Proto-Italic *wēros, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros. Distantly cognate with Old English wǣr (“true”). Over time displaced the use of a number of Germ

parole.significato: The bell that summons worshippers to vespers; the vesper-bell.
parole.testo: From Old French vespre, from Latin vesper (“evening star”). The martini name was coined by English novelist Ian Fleming in 1953 in his novel Casino Royale, where fictional secret agent James Bond concocts the recipe and names it after the character Vesper Lynd.

parole.significato: The sixth of the seven canonical hours, an evening prayer service
parole.testo: From Middle English vespers, from Old French vespres (French vêpres), from Ecclesiastical Latin vesperae (“vespers”), substantivisation of relational Late Latin vesperus (“evening”), from vesper (“evening”) + -us. Euphemistic use first as Vèpres éphésiennes (“Ephesian Vespers”), coined in 1890 by hi

parole.significato: A craft for transportation on or in water, air, or space.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English vessel, vessell (“small container”); from Old French vaissel (compare modern French vaisseau and Catalan vaixell), from Late Latin vāscellum, diminutive of vāsculum, diminutive of vās (“vase, vessel”).

parole.significato: A dressing room or storeroom for clothes, especially in a church or other religious house.
parole.testo: From Old French vestiarie, from Latin vestiarium, from vestis (“clothing”). Doublet of vestry.

parole.significato: A robe, gown, or other article of clothing worn as an indication of office.
parole.testo: From Middle English vestement, vestment, from Old French vestement, from Latin vestīmentum. By surface analysis, vest + -ment. Compare French vêtement.

parole.significato: To annoy, irritate.
parole.testo: From Middle English vexen, from Old French vexer, from Latin vexāre (“disturb, agitate, annoy”). Displaced native Old English dreċċan and gremman.

parole.significato: A surrounding district; a neighbourhood.
parole.testo: From Old French visnage, respelled to more closer match its Latin source vīcīnus (“neighbor”). By surface analysis, vicine + -age.

parole.significato: To fight for superiority; to contend; to compete eagerly so as to gain something.
parole.testo: Apheretic form of envy, from Middle English envien, from Old French envier, from Latin invītō.

parole.significato: An instance of keeping awake during normal sleeping hours, especially to keep watch or pray.
parole.testo: From Middle English vigile (“a devotional watching”), from Old French vigile, from Latin vigilia (“wakefulness, watch”), from vigil (“awake”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be strong, lively, awake”). Doublet of Wigilia. See also wake and vigor, from the same root.

parole.significato: Active strength or force of body or mind; a capacity for exertion, physically, intellectually, or morally; energy.
parole.testo: From Middle English vigour, from Old French vigour, from vigor, from Latin vigor, from vigeō (“thrive, flourish”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be lively”). Related to vigil, vegetable, vajra, and waker.

parole.significato: To treat (something) as inconsequential or worthless; to despise, to look down on.
parole.testo: From Middle English vilipenden (“to treat (something) as contemptible”) [and other forms], from Old French vilipender (modern French vilipender (“to condemn, despise, revile, scorn, vilipend, vilify”)), or its etymon Latin vilipendō, from vīlis (“cheap, inexpensive; base, mean, vile, worthless”) (ul

parole.significato: A rural habitation of size between a hamlet and a town.
parole.testo: From Middle English village, from Old French village, from Latin vīllāticus, ultimately from Latin villa (English villa). Broadly overtook Old English wic, þorp, and ham. The Philippine sense is due to its frequent use in the names of gated communities.

parole.significato: To debase; to degrade .
parole.testo: Probably from Middle English vilein, from Old French vilein (modern French vilain), in turn from Late Latin vīllānus, meaning serf or peasant, someone who is bound to the soil of a Latin vīlla, which is to say, worked on the equivalent of a plantation in late Antiquity, in Italy or Gaul. Doublet of

parole.significato: A seller of wine.
parole.testo: From Middle English vyntener, variant of viniter, from Old French vineter, vinetier (“wine-merchant, grape-harvester”), from Medieval Latin vīnētārius (“wine dealer”), from vīnētum (“vineyard”), from vīnum (“wine”).

parole.significato: Extreme force.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English violence, borrowed from Old French violence, borrowed from Latin violentia, from violēns /violentus (“violent”) + -ia. See violent. Displaced native Old English stræc.

parole.significato: Involving extreme force or motion.
parole.testo: From Middle English violent, from Old French violent, from Latin violentus, from vīs (“strength”). Displaced native Old English stræc. For the verb, compare French violenter.

parole.significato: A person who has never had sexual intercourse, or (uncommonly) an animal that has never mated.
parole.testo: From Middle English virgine, from Old French virgine, from Latin virginem, accusative of virgō. Doublet of Virgo. Displaced native Old English fǣmne.

parole.significato: The state or characteristic of being a virgin.
parole.testo: From Middle English virginite, from Old French virginite, from Latin virginitas. Equivalent to virgin + -ity. Displaced native Old English mæġeþhād (compare modern English maidhood), originally meaning “girlhood.”

parole.significato: Able to be seen.
parole.testo: From Middle English visible, from Old French visible, from Late Latin visibilis (“that may be seen”), from Latin videre (“to see”), past participle visus; see vision. Displaced native Old English ġesewenlīċ.

parole.significato: To habitually go to (someone in distress, sickness etc.) to comfort them. (Now generally merged into later senses, belo…
parole.testo: From Middle English visiten, from Old French visiter, from Latin vīsitō, frequentative of vīsō (“behold, survey”), from videō (“see”). Cognate with Old Saxon wīsōn (“to visit, afflict”), archaic German weisen (“to visit, afflict”). Displaced native Old English sēċan (“to visit”) and sōcn (“a visit”)

parole.significato: neighborhood; vicinity; venue
parole.testo: From Old French visné, veisiné, visnet (“neighborhood”), from Vulgar Latin *vīcīnātus, from Latin vīcīnus (“neighboring, a neighbor”). See vicinity.

parole.significato: Relating to or characteristic of life.
parole.testo: From Middle English vital, from Old French vital, from Latin vītālis (“of life, life-giving”), from vīta (“life”), from vīvō (“to live”). Doublet of jiva and quick.

parole.significato: Any of various metal sulphates.
parole.testo: From Middle English vitriol, from Old French vitriol, from Medieval Latin vitriolum (“sulfuric acid”), from vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: To bring to life; to enliven.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French vivifier, from Late Latin vivificō.

parole.significato: A divine calling to establish one's lifestyle.
parole.testo: From Middle English vocacioun, from Old French vocation, from Latin vocātiō.

parole.significato: Containing nothing; empty; not occupied or filled.
parole.testo: From Middle English voide, voyde, from Old French vuit, voide, vuide (modern vide), in turn from Vulgar Latin *vocitum, ultimately from Latin vacuus.

parole.significato: Fickle, capricious, reckless.
parole.testo: From Old French volage, from Latin volāticus.

parole.significato: A three-dimensional measure of space that comprises a length, a width and a height. It is measured in units of cubic ce…
parole.testo: From Middle English volume, from Old French volume, from Latin volūmen (“book, roll”), from volvō (“roll, turn about”).

parole.significato: Done, given, or acting of one's own free will.
parole.testo: From Middle English voluntarie, from Old French volontaire, from Latin voluntārius (“willing, of free will”), from voluntās (“will, choice, desire”), from volēns, present participle of volo (“to will”). Displaced native Old English selfwille (literally “self-willed”).

parole.significato: A solemn promise to perform some act, or behave in a specified manner, especially a promise to live and act in accordan…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English vowe, voue, that from Old French vut, in turn from Latin vōtum (“a promise, dedication, vow”), from vovēre (“to promise, vow”). Not related to avow. Doublet of vote.

parole.significato: A sound produced by the vocal cords with relatively little restriction of the oral cavity, forming the prominent sound…
parole.testo: From Middle English vowel, from Old French vouel, a variant of voyeul (whence French voyelle), from Latin vōcālis (“voiced”), itself a semantic loan of Koine Greek φωνῆεν (phōnêen). Doublet of vocal and vocalis.

parole.significato: A kind of fine white bread or cake.
parole.testo: From Middle English wastel, from Old French wastel, gastel (> French gâteau), from Late Latin wastellum, from Frankish *wastil, perhaps from Proto-Germanic *wistiz (“sustenance, food”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to be”). Cognate with Middle High German wastel (“a kind of bread”). Compare Old

parole.significato: The fervour or tireless devotion for a person, cause, or ideal and determination in its furtherance; diligent enthusias…
parole.testo: From Middle English zele, from Old French zel, from Late Latin zēlus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- (“to search”). Related to jealous.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter Z/z.
parole.testo: From Middle English zed, zedde, zede, from Old French zede, from Late Latin zeta, from Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta), from Hebrew ז (zayin) with influence from βῆτα (bêta), ἦτα (êta) and θῆτα (thêta). The letter had a rare usage in Old English, such as in bezt, where it represented "ts" (compare the Ger

parole.significato: The belt-like region of the celestial sphere, approximately eight degrees north and south of the ecliptic, which includ…
parole.testo: From Middle English zodiak (late 14th century), from Old French zodiaque, from Latin zōdiacus, from Ancient Greek ζῳδιακός [κύκλος] (zōidiakós [kúklos], “[circle] of little animals”), from ζῴδιον (zōídion), the diminutive of ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).
